URL: https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/blogs/2022/11/nydfs-escalates-and-expands-cybersecurity-enforcement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Goodwin's Data, Privacy + Cybersecurity Insights blog (dated November 18, 2022) analyzes the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) escalation and expansion of cybersecurity enforcement under Part 500 of the New York Cybersecurity Regulation.

KEY EVENT: On October 18, 2022, NYDFS announced its sixth consent order for alleged Part 500 violations, imposing a $4.5 million fine on EyeMed Vision Care, LLC — one of the heftiest monetary penalties yet. This came just over two weeks before NYDFS released its official Proposed Amendments to Part 500, which would impose even more stringent requirements on covered entities.

HISTORY OF ENFORCEMENT: NYDFS did not enforce Part 500 (promulgated March 2017) vigorously initially. Its first action came July 22, 2020, against First American Title Insurance Company (alleging failure to remedy a vulnerability exposing millions of customers' data; the company challenged findings, case pending). In 2021, NYDFS entered three consent orders with fines ranging $1.5–$3 million. In 2022, three additional consent orders were entered against Carnival Corporation, Robinhood Crypto LLC, and EyeMed. Most recent actions imposed $4.5–$5 million penalties. Robinhood was an outlier: developed from a supervisory examination rather than a security incident, imposing a $30 million penalty for violations of Virtual Currency Regulation (Part 200), Money Transmitter Regulation (Part 417), and Transaction Monitoring Regulation (Part 504), in addition to Part 500.

CRITICAL ENFORCEMENT AREAS UNDER CURRENT REGULATION:
• MFA (Section 500.12(b)): top priority; all consent orders address failure to comply. Carnival's entity Princess Cruise Lines had not completed MFA rollout to Office 365 — showing companies may be held strictly liable for MFA violations affecting even a limited number of entities.
• Employee training (500.14): Carnival penalized; repetition of phishing incidents "within a period of less than four years, demonstrates that the Carnival Companies' training was inadequate."
• Risk assessments (500.02(b)): cited in Robinhood and EyeMed consent orders.
• New attention areas: EyeMed failed to limit user access privileges (nine employees shared credentials for one email account) violating 500.03 and 500.13; Robinhood depended on parent company's cybersecurity regime rather than ensuring its own tailored policies.

KEY PROPOSED CHANGES:
• "Class A Companies" — new subset of covered entities defined as those with $20M+ gross annual revenue in each of last two fiscal years with 2,000+ employees, or making $1B+ gross revenue annually. These face more onerous requirements: annual independent audit of cybersecurity programs, external experts for risk assessments every three years, and privileged access activity monitoring.
• Notification changes: two new scenarios triggering 72-hour notification (unauthorized access to a privileged account; ransomware deployed within a material part of the information system). New 24-hour notification when a ransomware payment is made, with explanation of necessity and alternatives considered.
• Annual certification: new alternative allowing written acknowledgment of non-compliance, requiring description of noncompliance areas and remedial plans with timelines — theoretically preventing multiple charges for the same infraction.
• Controls expansion: MFA required for remote/VPN access, applications where nonpublic information is accessible, and privileged accounts (currently only required for external network access by individuals).
• Clarification that failure to comply for any 24-hour period constitutes a violation — consistent with current enforcement practice but not yet codified.

The public comment period (60 days from State Register publication) ended January 9, 2023. The article concludes that the frequency of consent orders, increasing penalty sizes, and plans to strengthen the Regulation indicate rigorous accountability will continue into 2023.
</summary>

URL: https://www.dfs.ny.gov/system/files/documents/2020/07/ea20200721_first_american_notice_charges.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a formal Statement of Charges and Notice of Hearing issued by the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) against First American Title Insurance Company, dated July 21, 2020, with the hearing scheduled for October 26, 2020. The charges stem from a massive data security breach involving First American's EaglePro document-sharing application and its FAST document repository.

**Overview of the Breach:**
- From at least October 2014 through May 2019, First American exposed tens of millions of documents containing consumers' sensitive personal information—including bank account numbers and statements, mortgage and tax records, Social Security numbers, wire transaction receipts, and drivers' license images—through a known vulnerability on its public-facing website.
- The vulnerability was introduced during an application software update in May 2014 and went undetected for years. Due to the use of sequentially numbered ImageDocumentIDs in URLs with no expiration dates, anyone could manipulate a URL by one or more digits to access any of the 850+ million documents stored in FAST without any login or authentication.
- The vulnerability was discovered during a penetration test in December 2018, but First American failed to remediate it for six more months until cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs publicized the breach on May 24, 2019.

**Key Data Points:**
- FAST contained approximately 753 million documents in April 2018 (65 million tagged as containing NPI) and over 850 million documents by May 2019.
- A random sampling of 1,000 untagged documents showed 30% also contained NPI.
- More than 350,000 documents were accessed without authorization by automated "bots" or "scraper" programs during an 11-month period from June 2018 to May 2019.
- Brian Krebs revealed that 885 million documents dating back to 2003 were exposed, and he was easily able to view sensitive data including Social Security numbers, drivers' licenses, and tax and banking information.

**Failures Identified by DFS:**
1. The vulnerability was erroneously classified as "medium severity" based on the mistaken belief that EaglePro could not transmit NPI.
2. First American failed to follow its own cybersecurity policies—no security overview or risk assessment was performed for EaglePro.
3. The Cyber Defense Team reviewed only 10 of hundreds of millions of exposed documents, found no NPI in those 10, and failed to recognize the seriousness of the situation.
4. The director of the Cyber Defense Team accidentally re-classified the vulnerability from "medium" to "low" severity in January 2019, which incorrectly allowed 90 days for remediation.
5. Remediation was assigned to a new, unqualified employee who never received the penetration test report.
6. First American relied solely on a manual process where title agents added the "SEC" prefix to files containing NPI—a process acknowledged as "highly prone to error."
7. After the breach was publicized, information security personnel's recommendations to add authentication and technical controls were rejected by senior management.
8. First American failed to timely encrypt documents containing NPI as required by the Cybersecurity Regulation.

**Six Formal Charges (Violations of 23 NYCRR Part 500):**
- **Charge I (500.02):** Failure to maintain a cybersecurity program based on risk assessment; no risk assessments for FAST and EaglePro applications (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge II (500.03):** Failure to maintain and implement written cybersecurity policies, including inadequate data governance, classification, and access controls (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge III (500.07):** Failure to limit user access privileges to Information Systems providing access to NPI (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge IV (500.09):** Failure to conduct periodic, documented Risk Assessments sufficient to inform the cybersecurity program (violation period: March 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge V (500.14(b)):** Failure to provide adequate cybersecurity awareness training for employees and title agents (violation period: March 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge VI (500.15):** Failure to encrypt NPI at rest and in transit or implement approved compensating controls (violation period: September 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).

DFS is seeking civil monetary penalties under Financial Services Law Section 408, an order requiring remediation of the violations, and other just and appropriate relief. The charges were signed by Katherine A. Lemire (Executive Deputy Superintendent, Consumer Protection and Financial Enforcement) and Justin S. Herring (Executive Deputy Superintendent, Cybersecurity Division).
</summary>

URL: https://secureframe.com/blog/nydfs-nycrr-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Secureframe provides a comprehensive guide to the NYDFS NYCRR 500 Cybersecurity Regulation and a compliance checklist for 2024. The regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), first issued in March 2017, establishes cybersecurity requirements for all covered financial institutions in New York. Significant amendments were announced in November 2023 with an effective date of April 29, 2024.

**Who Must Comply:** NYDFS NYCRR 500 applies to all DFS-regulated entities including state-chartered banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, insurance companies, health insurers, money transmitters, and other financial services institutions. The regulation designates three company types:
- **Covered entities:** All DFS-regulated organizations
- **Class A companies:** Introduced in the 2023 amendments; entities with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue in each of the last two fiscal years AND either at least 2,000 employees (averaged over two years) or over $1 billion in gross annual revenue. These face additional obligations including independent audits and stronger monitoring.
- **Small businesses:** Qualify for limited exemption (Section 500.19) if combined affiliates have fewer than 20 employees, less than $7.5 million in annual gross revenue in each of the last three years, or less than $15 million in year-end total assets.

**Key Requirements:**
- Periodic risk assessments
- Cybersecurity program with policies including Information Security, Access Control, Business Continuity/Disaster Recovery, Incident Response (now requiring root cause analysis), Data Retention/Disposal, Third-Party Service Provider Security, Asset Inventory, and Vulnerability Management policies
- Appointment of qualified cybersecurity leadership (senior governing body and CISO)
- Technical controls: multi-factor authentication, encryption (compensating controls no longer allowed for encryption in transit over external networks), systems/network security, application security, physical/environmental controls, data privacy controls, and security awareness training
- Continuous monitoring with annual penetration testing (now required from both inside and outside systems) and bi-annual vulnerability assessments
- Audit trail systems with records kept minimum five years
- 72-hour notification to NYDFS of cybersecurity events reasonably likely to impact operations, plus new reporting of third-party incidents and extortion payments

**Certification:** Covered entities submit an annual Certificate of Compliance (typically April 15, pushed to April 29, 2024 this year). Class A companies must undergo annual independent compliance audits. Documentation must be kept for five years.

**Enforcement:** NYDFS monitors through self-certification, audits, and mandatory reporting. Historical penalties include Robinhood Crypto ($30 million), OneMain Financial Group ($4.25 million), Residential Mortgage Services ($1.5 million), SA Stone Wealth Management ($1.35 million), and First American Title Insurance Company ($1 million). The 2023 amendment reaffirmed that even a single act of non-compliance could constitute a violation.

The article also promotes Secureframe's compliance automation platform with features like AI-driven risk management, policy generation, continuous monitoring, vendor management, cross-mapping controls, regulatory change management, and security training.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Zscaler (Zpedia) explains the SEC's new cybersecurity disclosure rules announced on July 26, 2023, which apply to public companies. The rules mandate timely disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents and annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance.

**Key Requirements:**
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Material cybersecurity incidents must be reported within four business days of a materiality determination. A new, broader definition of "cybersecurity incident" now includes "a series of related unauthorized occurrences."

## SEC Issues New Requirements for Cybersecurity Disclosures

**Source:** Deloitte Heads Up, Volume 30, Issue 13  
**Date:** July 30, 2023 (Updated December 19, 2023)

### Background
On July 26, 2023, the SEC issued a final rule requiring registrants to provide enhanced and standardized disclosures regarding cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incidents. The rule addresses investor concerns over timely and consistent cybersecurity information amid rising digital threats.

### Key Requirements

**1. Material Cybersecurity Incidents (Form 8-K, Item 1.05)**
- Registrants must file a Form 8-K within four business days of determining a cybersecurity incident is material.
- A cybersecurity incident is defined as "an unauthorized occurrence, or a series of related unauthorized occurrences, on or conducted through a registrant's information systems that jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of a registrant's information systems or any information residing therein."
- Required disclosures include: material aspects of the nature, scope, timing of the incident, and the material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant (including financial condition and results of operations).
- Amended Form 8-K must be filed within four business days if information becomes available later or previously disclosed information is inaccurate.

**2. Materiality Assessment**
- Materiality determinations must be made "without unreasonable delay."
- Materiality is consistent with U.S. Supreme Court standards (TSC Industries, Basic, Matrixx).
- Factors include: probability of adverse outcome, potential significance of loss, nature and extent of harm to individuals, customers, vendor relationships, reputation, and competitiveness.
- Erik Gerding (SEC Division of Corporation Finance director) clarified that materiality may not be determined on the same date the incident occurred.

**3. Temporary Delay for National Security**
- The U.S. Attorney General may determine that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety.
- Initial delay: up to 30 days; secondary delay: additional 30 days; final extraordinary circumstances: up to 60 days; further delays via SEC exemptive order.
- The FBI provided guidance on requesting delays, noting early outreach is critical.

**4. Risk Management, Strategy, and Governance (Form 10-K, Item 1C)**
- Registrants must disclose processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats.
- Disclosures required on: integration into overall risk management, use of third-party assessors, and oversight of third-party service provider risks.
- **Board oversight:** Description of board's oversight of cybersecurity risks, identification of responsible committees, and processes for informing the board.
- **Management responsibilities:** Which positions/committees are responsible, their relevant expertise, processes for monitoring incidents, and reporting to the board.

### Transition Provisions
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Effective December 18, 2023 (all registrants except smaller reporting companies); June 15, 2024 (smaller reporting companies).
- **Regulation S-K Item 106 (Form 10-K):** Effective for annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.
- Inline XBRL tagging required one year after initial compliance dates.

### Changes from Proposed Rule
- Narrowed scope of cyber incident disclosures with added national security delay.
- Amended Form 8-K used instead of Forms 10-Q/10-K for updates.
- Aggregation of immaterial incidents removed (but series of related unauthorized occurrences may still require Form 8-K).
- Removed proposed requirement to disclose cybersecurity expertise of the board.
- Added transition provisions.

### All filers affected
Including domestic registrants, foreign private issuers (FPIs), smaller reporting companies, and emerging growth companies.

--- SOURCE 6: Court in SolarWinds Case Blows Down SEC's Cyber Enforcement ... ---
URL: https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/07/court-in-solarwinds-case-blows-down-secs-cyber-enforcement-authority

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 18, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York dismissed most of the SEC's landmark cyber enforcement litigation against SolarWinds Corp. and its Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) Timothy Brown. In a 107-page opinion in Securities and Exchange Commission v. SolarWinds Corp. & Timothy G. Brown (Judge Paul Engelmayer presiding), the court rejected the SEC's efforts to expand the Securities Exchange Act's "internal accounting controls" provision to encompass cybersecurity controls. The court also limited the SEC's use of the "disclosure controls and procedure" provision, finding that innocent errors are "an inadequate basis" on which to plead deficient disclosure controls. Only a subset of material misrepresentation claims related to the Security Statement published on the company's website survived, and the case proceeds toward discovery.

BACKGROUND: SolarWinds, a software company with the Orion Platform, posted a Security Statement on its website in late 2017. In January 2019, nation-state hackers exploited a vulnerability and inserted malicious code into Orion software builds - known as the SUNBURST attack. In 2020, SolarWinds was notified by the USTP and Palo Alto Networks of suspicious activity but couldn't determine the root cause. After Mandiant identified the malicious code, SolarWinds filed a Form 8-K on Dec. 14, 2020, detailing the attack. The SEC filed its complaint in 2023 and an amended complaint on Feb. 16, 2024, charging violations of antifraud provisions, disclosure controls, and internal controls.

KEY COURT RULINGS: 1) Internal Accounting Controls: The court found the SEC "clearly correct" to be challenged on the plain language of Section 13(b), holding that "cybersecurity controls are outside the scope of Section 13(b)(2)(B)" and dismissing the claim entirely. 2) Disclosure Controls: The court dismissed this claim, finding "[w]ithout more, the existence of two misclassified incidents is an inadequate basis on which to plead deficient disclosure controls," and that "second-guessing by hindsight" is disfavored. 3) Security Statement: The court found the SEC sufficiently alleged material misrepresentations concerning access controls and password protection policies on the company's public website. 4) Cyber Risk Disclosures: Dismissed, as fraud claims based on risk disclosures are actionable only where "the warned risk has already occurred." 5) Brown's public statements: Found to be "non-actionable corporate puffery." 6) Form 8-K disclosures: Dismissed as fraud by hindsight; the court found the Form 8-K "captured the big picture: the severity of the SUNBURST attack," noting the stock dropped 16% on filing day and 8% the next day.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The SEC failed to expand internal accounting controls to cover cybersecurity. The SEC must now allege systemic deficiencies (not innocent errors) for disclosure controls violations. Cyber risk disclosure fraud claims are limited to narrow circumstances where the warned risk has already occurred. Courts will consider practical time constraints (including the SEC Cybersecurity Rules' four-business-day disclosure requirement) when assessing Form 8-K filings. Companies should avoid warning about risks that have already occurred, and risk disclosures should convey severity without arming threat actors.

SUGGESTED ACTION ITEMS for issuers: 1) Develop well-designed disclosure controls and incident response plans. 2) Include risk disclosures that convey manner and severity without providing a road map to threat actors. 3) Have a practiced plan for responding to cyber incidents. 4) Engage experienced cybersecurity counsel. This Holland & Knight analysis was authored by Shardul Desai, Allison Kernisky, and Jessica B. Magee on July 24, 2024.
</summary>

**Key requirements under the final rule:**
- CIRCIA will impose mandatory cyber incident reporting on more than 300,000 entities across all 16 critical infrastructure sectors (including Chemical, Energy, Financial Services, Healthcare and Public Health, Transportation Systems, Water/Wastewater, etc.)
- The rule applies to entities exceeding the SBA small business size standard for their industry, exempting the smallest businesses
- **Covered cyber incident report**: 72 hours from when the entity "reasonably believes" a covered incident occurred (not from when investigation confirms it)
- **Ransomware payment report**: 24 hours from making a ransom payment
- **Supplemental reports**: Required when substantial new information becomes available
- Reports must include entity identification, incident description, affected systems, attacker TTPs (if known), categories of data affected, and contact information

**Protections for reported information**: Reports are not subject to FOIA, not admissible as evidence in civil litigation, and entities are immune from suit based solely on submitting a report.

**Reasons for delays**: Over 400 formal public comments, industry pressure to narrow scope and reduce burden, harmonization challenges with other federal reporting requirements (SEC 8-K, HIPAA, TSA, nuclear sector, financial sector), and federal appropriations lapses.

CIRCIA represents a structural shift from voluntary to mandatory federal cyber incident reporting for the private sector, giving CISA a structured pipeline of real-time incident data. SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," which supersedes an earlier advisory from October 1, 2020. The Updated Advisory is directed at not only organizations victimized by ransomware attacks but also financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and forensic and incident-response firms that assist victims.

Key points of the Updated Advisory include:

- **Continued Opposition to Ransomware Payments**: OFAC maintains that the U.S. government "strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands" and recommends focusing on defensive and resilience measures. Payments may violate U.S. sanctions prohibitions, and penalties may be imposed on a strict liability basis, meaning companies could face enforcement even if they didn't know a payment would violate sanctions.

- **New Mitigating Factors**: The Updated Advisory identifies two significant mitigating factors in any OFAC enforcement response:
  1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps taken to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices, such as those in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide (co-developed with MS-ISAC), will be considered a "significant mitigating factor."
  2. **Notification and Cooperation with U.S. Government**: Promptly reporting ransomware attacks to law enforcement, CISA, Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection (OCCIP), or other relevant agencies, along with ongoing cooperation (including providing technical details, ransom payment demands, and payment instructions), constitutes a "significant mitigating factor." Timely self-disclosure to these agencies may be considered a voluntary self-disclosure for mitigation purposes.

- **First-Ever Sanctions Designation of a Cryptocurrency Exchange**: Also on September 21, 2021, OFAC designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (also known as "Successful Exchange"), a Russian cryptocurrency exchange, for property-blocking sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13694 (as amended by EO 13757). OFAC alleged SUEX OTC facilitated numerous ransomware payments for malicious cyber actors. U.S. persons are now prohibited from engaging in virtually all transactions with SUEX OTC. The exchange was identified on the SDN List by name, address, and digital currency addresses in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether. OFAC had previously designated other parties by digital currency address in 2018 (two Iranian individuals in the SamSam ransomware scheme).

- **Anticipated Further Guidance**: Press reporting indicates further related guidance may be forthcoming, likely from FinCEN, including action on the proposed application of the travel rule to cryptocurrency transactions and additional anti-money laundering efforts. This aligns with FinCEN's October 1, 2020 advisory (issued in parallel with the 2020 OFAC Advisory) on "red flags" for suspicious ransomware transactions, which noted that consultants facilitating ransomware payments could be considered "money transmitters" under the Bank Secrecy Act.

The article was authored by Covington & Burling LLP attorneys Ashden Fein, Peter Flanagan, Jim Garland, Mike Nonaka, and Moriah Daugherty. The article notes that it remains unclear how OFAC will assess compliance with the new mitigating factors, including which agencies and standards will be used for evaluation, but emphasizes the importance of preparation—developing a strong cybersecurity posture before an attack and timely reporting to and cooperation with government agencies.
</summary>

## Overview of cyber-related sanctions programme

The United States has been at the forefront of establishing a cyber-focused economic sanctions regime,[[1]](#footnote-1) which is primarily administered by the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), although criminal prosecutions for certain wilful sanctions violations also are the responsibility of the US Department of Justice.

OFAC administers a variety of sanctions targeting malicious cyber-related activities, such as cyber espionage, cyber intrusions on critical infrastructure and computer networks, and disinformation campaigns conducted from abroad. The workhorse of OFAC’s cyber-related sanctions programme is Executive Order (EO) 13694 (also known as Cyber1),[[2]](#footnote-2) issued in 2015 in response to increasingly frequent and severe malicious cyber-enabled activities originating from foreign countries that were directed at both US government agencies and private sector US entities. EO 13694 was subsequently amended and strengthened in 2016 under EO 13757 (Cyber2)[[3]](#footnote-3) and again in 2025 under EO 14144 (Cyber3).[[4]](#footnote-4) EO 13694 (Cyber1) and EO 14144 (Cyber3) were further amended in June 2025 by EO 14306 (Cyber4).[[5]](#footnote-5) US Congress codified EOs 13694 (Cyber1) and 13757 (Cyber2) into statute under the Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA).[[6]](#footnote-6) OFAC implements these EOs through its Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations, Code of Federal Regulations, Title 31, Part 578, which include certain standard general licences that OFAC includes in other sanctions programmes.[[7]](#footnote-7)

OFAC also regularly uses authorities under other sanctions programmes to target malicious cyber-related activities, most notably EO 13722 of 15 March 2016 (Government of North Korea), EO 13848 of 12 September 2018 (election interference) and EO 14024 of 15 April 2021 (Russian harmful foreign activities),[[8]](#footnote-8) among others.

## Development of US cyber-related sanctions regimes

Before the establishment of OFAC’s cyber-related sanctions programme, US law enforcement agencies had legal authority to pursue charges against entities and individuals engaged in various types of cyber espionage or unauthorised intrusions into US government and private sector computers and networks.[[9]](#footnote-9) For example, on 19 May 2014, in its first major prosecution against a state actor for malicious cyber-enabled activities, the US Department of Justice indicted five Chinese nationals, allegedly affiliated with the Chinese military, for gaining unauthorised access to computer networks for the apparent purpose of engaging in economic espionage targeted at six US entities involved in the nuclear power, metals and solar products industries.[[10]](#footnote-10) In September 2014, President Obama said his administration viewed cyber-enabled theft of trade secrets as “an act of aggression that has to stop” and warned that the United States was prepared to impose countervailing actions “to get [China’s] attention”.[[11]](#footnote-11)

Nevertheless, facing an increasingly severe threat posed by foreign-based hackers targeting valuable US intellectual property and sensitive private data, among other things, US national security agencies viewed sanctions as a tool well-designed to address the extraterritorial nature of cyber-enabled attacks from foreign actors.

This culminated on 1 April 2015 when President Obama issued EO 13694, which declared a national emergency to deal with the “unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States” arising from “the increasing prevalence and severity of malicious cyber-enabled activities originating from, or directed by persons located, in whole or in substantial part, outside the United States”.[[12]](#footnote-12) As with most US economic sanctions authorities, this EO was issued pursuant to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA)[[13]](#footnote-13) and the National Emergencies Act.[[14]](#footnote-14)

On 28 December 2016, President Obama issued EO 13757 (Cyber2), which amended EO 13694 (Cyber1) to broaden the scope of cyber-related activities subject to sanctions. On 16 January 2025, President Biden issued EO 14144 (Cyber3), which further amended EO 13694 (Cyber1) to broaden the scope of cyber-related activities subject to sanctions, as well as lowering the threshold at which OFAC is authorised to bring actions, among other actions intended to strengthen US cybersecurity.

As amended, these EOs permit the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Attorney General and the Secretary of State, to impose blocking sanctions[[15]](#footnote-15) on persons determined:

> #### Section 1
>
> 1. … to be responsible for or complicit in, or to have engaged in, directly or indirectly, cyber-enabled activities originating from, or directed by persons located, in whole or in substantial part, outside the United States that are reasonably likely to result in, or have materially contributed to, a significant threat to the national security, foreign policy, or economic health or financial stability of the United States and that have the purpose or effect of:
>    1. harming, or otherwise significantly compromising the provision of services by, a computer or network of computers that support one or more entities in a critical infrastructure sector;
>    2. significantly compromising the provision of services by one or more entities in a critical infrastructure sector;
>    3. causing a significant disruption to the availability of a computer or network of computers;
>    4. causing a significant misappropriation of funds or economic resources, trade secrets, personal identifiers, or financial information for commercial or competitive advantage or private financial gain; or
>    5. tampering with, altering, or causing a misappropriation of information with the purpose or effect of interfering with or undermining election processes or institutions; and
> 2. any person determined by the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Attorney General and the Secretary of State:
>    1. to be responsible for or complicit in, or to have engaged in, the receipt or use for commercial or competitive advantage or private financial gain, or by a commercial entity, outside the United States of trade secrets misappropriated through cyber-enabled means, knowing they have been misappropriated, where the misappropriation of such trade secrets is reasonably likely to result in, or has materially contributed to, a significant threat to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States;
>    2. to have materially assisted, sponsored, or provided financial, material, or technological support for, or goods or services in support of, [certain activities described above] or any person whose property and interests in property are blocked pursuant to [EO 13694, as amended];
>    3. to be owned or controlled by, or to have acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, any person whose property and interests in property are blocked [pursuant to EO 13694, as amended]; or
>    4. to have attempted to engage in any of the activities described in [EO 13694, as amended].[[16]](#footnote-16)

## Cyber-related sanctions under Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act

On 2 August 2017, President Trump signed into law CAATSA, which, *inter alia*, codified certain EOs issued by President Obama, including EOs 13694 (Cyber1) and 13757 (Cyber2), such that the President cannot unilaterally remove these sanctions authorities. In addition, Section 224(a)(1) of CAATSA imposed mandatory sanctions, requiring that the President impose, on or after 60 days after the enactment of CAATSA, blocking sanctions on persons determined to have “(A) knowingly engage[d] in significant activities undermining cybersecurity against any person, including a democratic institution, or government on behalf of the Government of the Russian Federation; or (B) is owned or controlled by, or acts or purports to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly” that person.[[17]](#footnote-17) CAATSA also required the President to impose certain “less-than-blocking” sanctions on persons determined to have provided material support to the cyber-related activity described above.[[18]](#footnote-18) On 6 September 2022, OFAC implemented Section 224(a)(1) of CAATSA through reissued Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations.[[19]](#footnote-19) To date, OFAC does not appear to have imposed any “less-than-blocking” sanctions on persons under Section 224(a)(1) of CAATSA, likely concluding that blocking sanctions authorised under EO 13694, as amended are more likely to be effective and sufficient to achieve national security and foreign policy objectives.

## Cyber-related sanctions under the Executive Order targeting harmful foreign activities of Russia

On 15 April 2021, President Biden issued EO 14024, the aim of which is countering a wide array of malign Russian government-sponsored activities, including interference in the 2020 US presidential election and the SolarWinds cyberattack.[[20]](#footnote-20) EO 14024 significantly expands the categories of Russian persons who can be targeted for sanctions by the United States, and includes persons determined “to be responsible for or complicit in, or to have directly or indirectly engaged or attempted to engage in … malicious cyber-enabled activities”.[[21]](#footnote-21) Sanctions may also be imposed under EO 14024 on the spouses and adult children of persons subject to sanctions under this EO, as well as those determined by the Secretary of the Treasury, in consultation with the Secretary of State, to have materially assisted, sponsored or provided financial, material or technological support for, or goods or services to or in support of, among other things, malicious cyber-enabled activities.

EO 14024 was amended on 22 December 2023, with the issuance of EO 14114 “Taking Additional Steps with Respect to the Russian Federation’s Harmful Activities”, which authorises the imposition of “secondary sanctions” restricting the access of foreign financial institutions (FFIs), both inside and outside Russia, from access to the US financial system.[[22]](#footnote-22) Although intended to more broadly impose secondary sanctions to cut off Russia’s banking system from the world, EO 14114 also authorised OFAC to impose secondary sanctions on FFIs that have conducted or facilitated significant transactions for or on behalf of persons sanctioned in connection with Russian malign cyber activity, among other things. On 3 July 2024, OFAC confirmed that secondary sanctions risk under EO 14114 attaches to certain persons previously sanctioned in connection with cyber-related activity, including certain Russian companies operating in the technology sector of the Russian economy that support Russian intelligence services.[[23]](#footnote-23) Such persons are indicated on OFAC’s Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons list (SDN List) with a “secondary sanctions” tag.

## Office of Foreign Assets Control ransomware advisory

On 1 October 2020, OFAC issued its “Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments” (the 2020 Ransomware Advisory) to highlight the sanctions compliance risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments related to malicious cyber-enabled activities (eg, by providing cyber insurance, digital forensics and incident response, and financial services relating to processing ransom payments including by depository institutions and money services businesses).[[24]](#footnote-24) In the Advisory, OFAC warned that facilitating a ransomware payment may not only enable and embolden criminals, as well as adversaries with a nexus to a sanctioned party or country, but also, critically, may not guarantee that a victim regains access to stolen data, and noted that victims of a ransomware attack should (1) contact OFAC immediately if they believe a request for a ransomware payment may involve a sanctions nexus, and (2) contact the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection if an attack involves a US financial institution or may cause “significant disruption to a firm’s ability to perform critical financial services”.[[25]](#footnote-25)

OFAC expanded its guidance on 21 September 2021 in a publication entitled “Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments” (the 2021 Ransomware Advisory),[[26]](#footnote-26) which OFAC issued “to highlight the sanctions risks associated with ransomware payments” and “the proactive steps companies can take to mitigate such risks”, including those actions that OFAC would consider to be mitigating factors with respect to enforcement. The 2021 Ransomware Advisory adds to the 2020 Ransomware Advisory in several significant ways: it adds a strong discouragement of engaging in ransomware payments and a warning that entities making ransomware payments to a blocked person or a sanctioned jurisdiction are subject to strict liability and risk facing penalties, even without knowledge of a connection to a blocked person or sanctioned jurisdiction.[[27]](#footnote-27) Consequently, OFAC also recommends that companies expand controls to account for the risk of ransomware payments being made to prohibited persons.[[28]](#footnote-28) Further, OFAC strongly encourages, and even incentivises, companies to report ransomware demands to law enforcement and will consider cooperation with law enforcement as a mitigating factor when assessing penalties against entities that have been involved in making ransomware payments to blocked, or otherwise sanctioned, parties.[[29]](#footnote-29)

The 2021 Ransomware Advisory references several other agencies and encourages the adoption of practices laid out in the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s “Ransomware Guide”[[30]](#footnote-30) and consideration of applicable Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) regulatory obligations.[[31]](#footnote-31)

## Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry

On 15 October 2021, OFAC published guidance entitled “Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry” (the Virtual Currency Guidance), which provides an overview of compliance best practices.[[32]](#footnote-32) The Guidance clarifies that the sanctions compliance obligations imposed by OFAC apply equally to transactions involving virtual currencies and those involving traditional fiat currencies and that companies are responsible for ensuring that they do not engage in direct or indirect transactions that are prohibited by OFAC sanctions when dealing in virtual currency.[[33]](#footnote-33) The Virtual Currency Guidance acknowledges that OFAC sanctions have increasingly targeted persons who have used virtual currency in connection with various types of malign activity. Given the industry’s rising level of importance, the Guidance encourages companies to have in place a risk-based compliance programme, which includes internal controls to identify and stop virtual currency transactions that would violate OFAC sanctions. Ultimately, the Guidance makes clear that companies are under the same obligations with respect to virtual currency as they are for fiat currency when it comes to complying with OFAC sanctions.[[34]](#footnote-34)

## Financial Crimes Enforcement Network advisories

As noted above, OFAC’s 2021 Ransomware Advisory made note of guidance from other agencies, including FinCEN. On 1 October 2021, FinCEN issued an advisory entitled “Advisory on Ransomware and the Use of the Financial System to Facilitate Ransom Payments” (the FinCEN Advisory).[[35]](#footnote-35) The FinCEN Advisory lists several red flag indicators to assist in identifying, preventing and reporting ransomware attacks and reminds financial institutions of their regulatory obligations regarding reporting suspicious activity involving ransomware. Financial institutions should note that although OFAC strongly encourages reporting of ransomware attacks and payments, the FinCEN Advisory makes clear in some instances that financial institutions may be required to report incidents.

FinCEN has also issued periodic alerts providing guidance for financial institutions, regarding risks associated with cyber-related sanctions evasion. For instance, FinCEN issued an alert advising financial institutions of their responsibilities related to identifying and reporting terrorist financing activity in support of Hamas. The alert provides a series of red flags for financial institutions to use in identifying potential terrorist financing, and it reminds those institutions of the sanctioned status of Hamas and other terrorist organisations.[[36]](#footnote-36) More recently, FinCEN issued an alert on the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps’ use of digital asset infrastructure to evade sanctions.[[37]](#footnote-37)

## Office of Foreign Assets Control enforcement and recent illustrative cases

Since 2015, OFAC has designated numerous parties under cyber-related sanctions authorities, with designations of cyber-related persons, especially with ties to Russia increasing significantly from 2022 into the first few months of 2025.[[38]](#footnote-38) However, OFAC has, at least based on what has been made public, imposed relatively few civil penalties connected to cyber-related sanctions or other cyber-related sanctions compliance failures. Nevertheless, based on guidance issued in 2020 and OFAC’s willingness to impose civil penalties against certain internet-based businesses and entities involved in the use of digital currencies,[[39]](#footnote-39) it is clear that OFAC expects parties to implement fully fledged risk-based sanctions compliance programmes to address malign cyber activities and other cyber-related vulnerabilities. Criminal prosecutions for sanctions violations, which typically focus on the most egregious wilful misconduct, are within the purview of the US Department of Justice.

## Cyber-related sanctions designations

OFAC has designated numerous foreign persons under its cyber and related sanctions programmes during the past few years, with increased designations beginning in 2023 and continuing to the present day. Similar to other OFAC sanctions programmes focused on malign activity, such as counterterrorism and counter-narcotics, OFAC primarily implements US government cyber-related policy through designations, rather that regulations or licences. Persons designated under these authorities include:

* individual hackers;
* money launderers;
* non-state actors, such as:
  + organised “troll farms” (eg, Internet Research Agency);
  + international cybercriminal organisations (eg, Kimsuky, Genesis Market, Pyongyang University of Automation, Technical Reconnaissance Bureau, 110th Research Center, Evil Corp, Hydra Market, Garantex);[[40]](#footnote-40)
  + commercial spyware providers (Intellexa Consortium);[[41]](#footnote-41)
  + “exploit” brokers engaging in the theft or sale of US government cyber tools (Operation Zero);[[42]](#footnote-42)
  + purportedly legitimate cybersecurity companies that provided support to or employed individual hackers involved in malign activity (Integrity Technology Group, Incorporated, Sichuan Silence Information Technology Company, Limited);[[43]](#footnote-43)
  + front companies in China and Laos that provided the services of North Korean information technology workers (Chonsurim Trading Corporation);[[44]](#footnote-44)
  + virtual currency mixers (eg, Sinbad, Buy Cash);[[45]](#footnote-45) and
  + virtual currency exchanges (Cryptex);[[46]](#footnote-46) and
* foreign government agencies and associated front companies (eg, the Russian Federation Federal Security Service).

OFAC has mainly focused on actors residing in or associated with foreign nation states perceived as hostile to the United States – primarily Russia, China, Iran and North Korea – and engaging in certain malicious cyber-enabled activities, such as:

* development and distribution of malware, ransomware and phishing and spoofing scams;
* interference with electoral processes and institutions worldwide through false information or hacking;[[47]](#footnote-47)
* theft of economic resources, trade secrets, personal identifying information or financial information by cyber intrusions for private financial gain;
* publication of stolen sensitive documents obtained and sometimes manipulated through cyber intrusions;
* disruption of network access;
* compromise of US government entities and US critical infrastructure sectors; and
* the use of virtual currency or other digital assets to evade or otherwise violate US sanctions.

OFAC’s designations in recent years indicate its continued focus on the virtual currency industry’s role in sanctions evasion.

OFAC has been targeting state-backed groups engaging in cyber-enabled activities against the United States and its allies. In September 2022, for example, OFAC designated Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security and its Minister of Intelligence, which OFAC alleged “conducted malicious cyber operations targeting a range of government and private-sector organizations around the world and across various critical infrastructure sectors”, through networks of cyber threat actors such as the now-sanctioned groups MOIS and APT39, and engaged in malicious cyber activities that disrupted the Albanian government’s computer systems.[[48]](#footnote-48) OFAC also designated 10 individuals and two entities associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, which engaged in various forms of ransomware activity and cybercrime against small businesses, a children’s hospital, an accounting firm, a law firm, a New Jersey municipality, emergency service providers, healthcare practices, educational institutions and an electricity utility company serving a rural area. In January 2025, OFAC sanctioned a Shanghai-based cyber actor who was involved in a compromise of the Treasury’s own computer network.[[49]](#footnote-49)

As noted above, entities involved in providing cryptocurrency-related services are also becoming a more frequent target of OFAC sanctions designations, with several major cryptocurrency-related service providers being designated during the past few years, often for engaging in or facilitating money laundering, sanctions evasion and ransomware attacks. For example, on 19 May 2023, OFAC sanctioned Huriya Private FZE LLE, a private equity and corporate structuring entity, and its founder, John Hanafin, for assisting Russian nationals in protecting their assets from sanctions, primarily through moving their money into bank accounts in the United Arab Emirates and procuring fraudulent passports.[[50]](#footnote-50)

Other recent sanctions announcements indicate increased coordination between the United States and allied governments. For example, on 25 March 2024, the United States and United Kingdom jointly took actions against actors affiliated with a purported Chinese hacking group. OFAC sanctioned Wuhan Xiaoruizhi Science and Technology Company, which OFAC called a China-based Ministry of State Security’s front company, and two Chinese nationals affiliated with the company for “their roles in malicious cyber operations targeting US entities that operate within US critical infrastructure sectors”.[[51]](#footnote-51) On 9 February 2023, the United States and United Kingdom jointly announced that a group of seven individuals associated with a Russia-based cybercrime gang called Trickbot were being sanctioned for reportedly engaging in a string of illegal cyber activities, including ransomware attacks.[[52]](#footnote-52)

Cyber-related sanctions have continued under the second Trump administration. Notably, on 11 February 2025, OFAC sanctioned Zservers, a Russia-based bulletproof hosting services provider, for its role in supporting certain ransomware attacks.[[53]](#footnote-53) On 5 March 2025, OFAC sanctioned a Shanghai-based individual and his company for their role in acquiring, brokering and selling data from highly sensitive US critical infrastructure networks.[[54]](#footnote-54) Since then, OFAC has also sanctioned multiple Southeast Asia-based cyber scam networks.[[55]](#footnote-55)

## Tornado Cash and virtual currency “mixers”

OFAC has also sought to target virtual currency “mixers” (ie, software services that facilitate anonymous transactions by obfuscating the origins and destinations of digital asset transfers). While acknowledging the legitimate uses of such software services in the virtual currency ecosystem, OFAC has also noted their use for the “facilitation of heists, ransomware schemes, and other cybercrimes”.[[56]](#footnote-56) Some of these designations have been successful; others have been reversed by US courts.

In May 2022, OFAC designated the entity Blender.io under EO 13694, as amended, describing the entity as “a virtual currency mixer that operates on the Bitcoin blockchain and indiscriminately facilitates illicit transactions by obfuscating their origin, destination, and counterparties”.[[57]](#footnote-57) Similarly, in November 2023, OFAC designated Sinbad.io, a similar virtual currency mixer, for allegedly laundering millions of dollars in stolen virtual currency from the Lazarus Group, Horizon Bridge and Axie Infinity heists, under both EO 13694, as amended, and EO 13722, the authority used for its weapons of mass destruction sanctions programme.[[58]](#footnote-58) These designations remain in effect as of June 2026, generally prohibiting US persons from using such services, to the extent they are still in operation.

However, in the 2024 case *Van Loon v Treasury*,[[59]](#footnote-59) a US Court of Appeals overturned OFAC’s actions against Tornado Cash, a decentralised virtual currency mixer designated in August 2022[[60]](#footnote-60) (under EO 13694) and redesignated in November 2022[[61]](#footnote-61) (under EO 13722). The Court focused on the immutable nature (ie, self-executing without human control) of the “smart contracts” (ie, open-source software code) that Tornado Cash uses to effectuate the obfuscation of origins and destinations of digital asset transfers, holding that the software code was outside the definition of “property” or “services” that OFAC is authorised to block under IEEPA, the statutory workhorse of OFAC’s sanctions regimes. Following the US Court of Appeals decision, OFAC delisted the website and virtual currency addresses associated with Tornado Cash.[[62]](#footnote-62)

The impact of the Court’s holding remains to be seen. By its own reasoning, the *Van Loon*Court’s holding does not apply to mixers in which humans continue to maintain an ownership interest and may face a conflicting ruling in another Court of Appeals.[[63]](#footnote-63) The Court’s holding does not relieve the creators of immutable smart contracts from civil or criminal sanctions liability; two of the developers of the service were indicted for related criminal charges.[[64]](#footnote-64)On 6 August 2025, a jury in the Southern District of New York convicted one of the developers, Roman Storm, of conspiring to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business; the jury was unable to reach a unanimous verdict on conspiracy charges relating to money laundering and sanctions, and a retrial on those counts is anticipated.[[65]](#footnote-65) The case of the other developer, Roman Semenov, remains under a sealed indictment.[[66]](#footnote-66)

## Office of Foreign Assets Control civil penalties

In addition to designating and imposing blocking sanctions on bad actors, OFAC also brings enforcement actions against US and non-US persons for engaging with sanctioned bad actors, for example by providing services to or transferring the property of such persons. A recurring pattern in these enforcement actions is the failure of companies to effectively utilise pertinent and accessible information, including internet protocol (IP) addresses, know your customer (KYC) information, onboarding data and geolocation data, to identify, prevent or block prohibited users or transactions. In the following enforcement actions, US enforcement agencies, including OFAC and the Departments of Justice and Commerce, called particular attention to a company’s failure to integrate information provided by customers, particularly during the company’s customer onboarding process or through transactional information, into its screening controls:

* A settlement agreement that CoinList Markets LLC, a California-based virtual currency exchange, entered with OFAC on 13 December 2023, relating to 989 apparent violations of the Russia/Ukraine sanctions, where the company apparently failed to prevent customers apparently based in Russia, particularly those who provided addresses in Crimea, from engaging in virtual-currency transactions worth US$1,252,280.[[67]](#footnote-67)
* A settlement agreement that Binance Holdings, Ltd, a Cayman Islands virtual currency exchange, entered with OFAC on 21 November 2023 relating to 1,667,153 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programmes, where the company purportedly failed to prevent persons apparently located in sanctioned jurisdictions from using its platform to engage in virtual currency-related transactions worth US$706,068,127.[[68]](#footnote-68)
* A settlement agreement that Poloniex, LLC, a Boston-based online digital assets trading and settlement platform, entered with OFAC on 1 May 2023 relating to 65,942 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programmes, where the company purportedly failed to prevent customers apparently located in Crimea, Cuba, Iran, Sudan and Syria, based on KYC and IP address data, from engaging in online data asset-related transactions worth US$15,335,349.[[69]](#footnote-69)
* A settlement agreement that Uphold HQ Inc, a California-based money services business, entered with OFAC on 31 March 2023 relating to 152 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programmes, where the company purportedly failed to prevent persons apparently located in Iran and Cuba, or employees of the government of Venezuela, from using its platform to engage in virtual currency-related transactions worth US$180,575.80.[[70]](#footnote-70)
* A settlement agreement that US-based company, Bittrex, Inc, which provides an online virtual currency exchange and hosted wallet services, entered into with OFAC on 11 October 2022 relating to 116,421 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programmes, where the company purportedly failed to prevent persons apparently located in the Crimea region of Ukraine, Cuba, Iran, Sudan and Syria from using its platform to engage in virtual currency-related transactions worth more than US$263 million.[[71]](#footnote-71)

Through these settlements, OFAC emphasises that US persons and non-US persons with a nexus to the United States involved in the provision of digital currency services (including companies that facilitate or engage in online commerce or process transactions in digital currency) – like all other US persons – have sanctions compliance obligations. OFAC also cites to its Virtual Currency Guidance[[72]](#footnote-72) and “A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments”[[73]](#footnote-73) to underscore the importance of implementing a risk-based compliance programme, involving the use and integration of all pertinent and available location-related information and technical controls, such as IP address screening, IP blocking mechanisms, blockchain tracking and the use of KYC or other onboarding data, to mitigate sanctions risks in connection with digital currency services.

## Cyber-related sanctions compliance risks

### Ransom payments

As discussed in OFAC’s 2020 Ransomware Advisory, a compliance risk unique to cyber-related sanctions relates to ransomware attacks, specifically the payment of ransoms themselves.[[74]](#footnote-74) Unless OFAC grants a specific licence, a person who makes ransom payments to sanctioned parties or jurisdictions may face penalties for violating OFAC regulations. Particularly for ransom payments made in a digital currency, the difficulty of definitively determining whether the transaction involves a sanctioned party or sanctioned jurisdiction can create serious compliance challenges. Although no public civil penalty has been announced in connection with this type of violation, OFAC has emphasised the risks relating not only to direct payments of ransoms in contravention of sanctions regulations but also to facilitating these payments (eg, ransomware insurance businesses and payment processors). On 21 September 2021, OFAC released its “Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments”,[[75]](#footnote-75) which emphasises the US government’s strong discouragement of payment of cyber ransom or extortion demands and the importance of improving cybersecurity practices and reporting to, and cooperating with, the US government in the event of ransomware attacks.

## Digital currency sector

Via its enforcement actions and guidance,[[76]](#footnote-76) OFAC has also been clear that transactions and services involving digital currency present sanctions compliance risk. Therefore, businesses that allow digital currency payments or that are involved in the digital currency market or sector (eg, digital currency trading platforms, asset management and security) need to consider how to implement appropriate risk-based compliance measures that address the specific vulnerabilities of digital currency. Without appropriate compliance measures, a digital currency service provider could incur liability not only for violating sanctions (eg, by dealing with blocked persons or persons in sanctioned jurisdictions) but also for facilitating sanctions violations by other parties to a transaction (even if inadvertent).

For example, just as with fiat currency, businesses involved in digital currency transactions would be expected to deploy risk-based sanctions screening for involved parties and to ensure that the funds are not destined for a sanctioned jurisdiction.[[77]](#footnote-77) As described above, recent enforcement actions highlight OFAC’s expectation that internet-based businesses should use all relevant known information in the course of their business for sanctions compliance purposes as well. Specifically, OFAC has recently imposed civil penalties on multiple businesses that knew customers’ IP addresses (eg, by their use of internet services) but did not ensure that customers with IP addresses in sanctioned jurisdictions were screened or blocked from using their services or transacting on their platforms.

Cryptocurrency, a type of digital currency reliant on cryptography to secure and verify transactions, also presents risk because cybercriminals and other sanctioned parties (including the government of North Korea, Iranian entities and many Russian entities and individuals that have been designated by OFAC since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine) are allegedly known to resort to using cryptocurrency as a tool to evade sanctions, launder money and facilitate other illegal activities (eg, nuclear weapons proliferation[[78]](#footnote-78)).[[79]](#footnote-79) The proceeds of malicious cyber activities are regularly transferred to cryptocurrency exchanges and peer-to-peer marketplaces with negligible customer screening compliance programmes, or individual peer-to-peer or over-the-counter traders operating on exchanges that do not screen their customers.[[80]](#footnote-80) More broadly, digital currency infrastructure has been targeted by some cybercriminals who use illegitimate websites and malicious software to conduct phishing attacks on the digital currency sector.[[81]](#footnote-81) Due diligence and controls to determine whether digital currency has been tainted by sanctionable or criminal cyber activities may be needed in certain transactions or businesses. In relation to this, OFAC has emphasised how anti-money laundering and combating the financing of terrorism controls play a vital role in sanctions and law enforcement generally because these can force cybercriminals to take measures to circumvent the controls that leave trails of evidence and traceability.[[82]](#footnote-82) OFAC has been identifying certain digital currency addresses[[83]](#footnote-83) associated with Specially Designated Nationals (SDNs) and other blocked persons. This type of information, which OFAC expects to be part of standard screening protocols, typically entails a more arduous screening process owing to the difficulty of searching these addresses in the SDN List.[[84]](#footnote-84)

OFAC has also noted that as various sanctioned jurisdictions (eg, Iran, Russia and North Korea) resort to using or creating digital currencies, the risk entailed in the digital currency sector may increase.[[85]](#footnote-85) The mere use of certain digital currencies could be subject to blanket prohibition, which has already occurred with respect to the Petromoneda digital currency issued by the government of Venezuela.[[86]](#footnote-86) As more government-backed digital currencies are issued, this will be an evolving risk area.

## Inadvertent exports to sanctioned jurisdictions

Another potential area of compliance risk is the cybertheft of export-controlled information for use in a sanctioned jurisdiction. Any cyber-enabled theft may represent an unauthorised and illegal export of controlled US technology or software. While this type of event may raise more direct export control compliance concerns, especially depending on the nature of the stolen technology or software, OFAC could potentially consider a victim entity accountable for facilitating a sanctions violation for failing to implement appropriate risk-based measures to prevent the compromise and export of the controlled information (eg, inadequate data security). This scenario highlights that in addition to sanctions regulations, entities should also consider other areas of related compliance risk implicated by malicious cyber-enabled activities, including export controls.

## Practical considerations to mitigate cyber-related sanctions compliance risks

In response to the risks described above, and depending on the circumstances, companies may wish to consider some of the following compliance measures.

### Risk assessment and risk-based compliance programme

Depending on the nature of a company’s business activities, the risks and challenges in complying with cyber-related sanctions may differ substantially. Conducting an appropriate risk assessment and tailoring a risk-based compliance programme appropriately with sanctions compliance training for relevant personnel are essential steps in mitigating risk. Businesses of any size that utilise the internet, even if only for email, may face an increasing risk of ransomware attacks, which raises cyber-related sanctions compliance concerns. This is also a particular concern following Russia’s military invasion of Ukraine and the expansion of US sanctions and other restrictions that target numerous sectors of the Russian economy, including the financial, technology and energy sectors. Businesses involved in e-commerce could potentially face higher cyber-related sanctions compliance risks, including the risk of inadvertently providing goods or services to a sanctioned person or jurisdiction. Those involved in the digital currency sector, including companies that facilitate or engage in online commerce or process transactions using digital currencies, may be more likely to face malicious cyber-enabled attacks, incurring increased sanctions compliance risks and, given the expanded sanctions on Russia and other regions, may also have to contend with sanctioned parties seeking to use digital currencies to evade US sanctions. These risks could be even greater for companies involved in providing cyber insurance, digital forensics services, cyberattack incident response services and financial services that facilitate ransom payments.

### Risk-based screening, due diligence, intellectual property blocking and geolocation measures

Depending on a company’s risk profile, it is often best to ensure that all relevant parties are properly screened before engaging in a transaction, to ensure no payments or deliveries of goods or services are made to sanctioned parties or jurisdictions. Reliable screening depends on the collection and review of information reasonably accessible to the company, which means companies should proactively consider ways to verify users’ identities and locations. Merely relying on attestations from users concerning their locations without conducting any further due diligence may not suffice to meet compliance obligations in OFAC’s view.

As the world becomes more digitised, bad actors become more sophisticated and determined to conceal their identity or location, and certain sanctions programmes targeting particular jurisdictions (eg, Russia and the Crimea, Donetsk and Luhansk regions of Ukraine) are introduced, the screening function must adapt as well. Companies should consider including a party’s IP address information in the screening process when this information is available and utilising more advanced geolocation and IP spoofing detection tools to ensure that dealings with parties, including the provision of services and payments, do not involve parties in sanctioned jurisdictions. A company may need to implement IP blocking and geofencing measures to prevent sanctioned persons and persons in sanctioned jurisdictions from opening accounts on the company’s website or platform that would allow them to access the company’s services. This article, published 14 July 2026 in GIR's The Guide to Sanctions (Seventh Edition), examines practical issues in US cyber-related sanctions, particularly focusing on recent OFAC designations highlighting renewed attention on digital currency. Authored by Timothy O'Toole, Collmann Griffin, Melissa Burgess, and Arooshe Giroti of Miller & Chevalier, the article provides a comprehensive overview of the US cyber-related sanctions regime.

KEY LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
- The primary authority is Executive Order (EO) 13694 (Cyber1, issued 1 April 2015), amended and strengthened by EO 13757 (Cyber2, 2016), EO 14144 (Cyber3, 2025), and EO 14306 (Cyber4, 2025). Congress codified EOs 13694 and 13757 into statute under the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA, signed 2 August 2017).
- OFAC administers these through the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR Part 578). Other authorities used include EO 13722 (North Korea), EO 13848 (election interference), and EO 14024 (Russian harmful foreign activities, 15 April 2021, amended by EO 14114 in December 2023 to authorize secondary sanctions on foreign financial institutions).
- The sanctions target cyber-enabled activities including: harm to critical infrastructure computer networks, disruption of service availability, misappropriation of funds/trade secrets/personal identifiers, and election interference.

GUIDANCE AND ADVISORIES:
- 2020 Ransomware Advisory (1 October 2020) and 2021 Ransomware Advisory (21 September 2021) warn that ransomware payments to blocked persons carry strict liability penalties; cooperation with law enforcement is a mitigating factor.
- Virtual Currency Guidance (15 October 2021) clarifies that sanctions obligations apply equally to virtual and fiat currencies.
- FinCEN issued its own Ransomware Advisory (1 October 2021) with red flag indicators.

ENFORCEMENT AND DESIGNATIONS:
- OFAC has designated numerous parties including individual hackers, money launderers, troll farms (Internet Research Agency), cybercriminal organizations (Kimsuky, Genesis Market, Evil Corp, Hydra Market, Garantex), spyware providers (Intellexa Consortium), virtual currency mixers (Blender.io, Sinbad), and state-linked actors from Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea.
- Notable designations include Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (September 2022), Zservers (Russia-based bulletproof hosting, February 2025), and Southeast Asia-based cyber scam networks.
- OFAC civil penalty settlements have targeted virtual currency platforms for sanctions violations: CoinList Markets LLC ($1,252,280 in transactions), Binance Holdings ($706 million, 1,667,153 violations), Poloniex LLC ($15.3 million, 65,942 violations), Uphold HQ Inc ($180,575.80), and Bittrex Inc (over $263 million, 116,421 violations). A recurring theme was failure to use IP address, KYC, and geolocation data for screening.

NOTABLE LEGAL DEVELOPMENT:
- In Van Loon v Treasury (2024), a US Court of Appeals overturned OFAC's designations of Tornado Cash (a decentralized virtual currency mixer), holding that immutable "smart contracts" (self-executing software code) fall outside the definition of "property" or "services" OFAC can block under IEEPA. However, on 6 August 2025, a jury convicted Tornado Cash developer Roman Storm of conspiring to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business (deadlocked on money laundering and sanctions counts, with retrial anticipated). Co-developer Roman Semenov remains under sealed indictment.

COMPLIANCE RISKS:
- Ransom payments to sanctioned parties or jurisdictions risk penalties without a specific OFAC licence.
- Digital currency sector faces heightened scrutiny; businesses must implement risk-based screening, IP blocking, geofencing, and blockchain tracking.
- Cybertheft of export-controlled information may constitute unauthorized export and could expose victim entities to liability for failing to prevent compromise.
- OFAC expects companies to use all reasonably accessible information (IP addresses, KYC data, onboarding data, geolocation) in screening—merely relying on user location attestations is insufficient.

................................6 Strict Liability Regulations ...................................................6 OFAC Requirements and Procedures.......................................7 Reporting Requirements.....................................................7 Recordkeeping Requirements.............................................8 License Procedures.............................................................8 Consequences of Noncompliance...........................................9 Enforcement Procedures....................................................9 Enforcement Guidelines.................................................9 Enforcement Actions.
......................................................9 Voluntary Self-Disclosure.
...............................................9 Sanctions Compliance Best Practices for the Virtual Currency Industry.........................................................10 Management Commitment.................................................11 Risk Assessment..................................................................12  Case Study: Diagnosing Risky Relationships......................................12 Internal Controls.................................................................13  Case Study: Double-Duty Data..........................................................13 Sanctions Screening......................................................16 Remediating the Root Causes of Violations....................17 Risk Indicators...............................................................17 Testing and Auditing...........................................................18 Training..............................................................................19 OFAC Resources.
