This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
# Ransomware Attacks—Financial Crimes Compliance Requirements

# Ransomware Attacks—Financial Crimes Compliance Requirements

Client Alert

## Authors

* [### Jason C. Chipman](/en/people/jason-chipman)
* [### David M. Horn](/en/people/david-horn)

## Related Solutions

* [AML and Economic Sanctions Compliance and Enforcement](/en/solutions/aml-and-economic-sanctions-compliance-and-enforcement)
* [Cybersecurity and Privacy](/en/solutions/cybersecurity-and-privacy)
* [Business and Financial Integrity](/en/solutions/business-and-financial-integrity)
* [Blockchain and Cryptocurrency](/en/solutions/blockchain-and-cryptocurrency)

Backed by deep experience gained across the legal, government and corporate spheres, we guide clients through internal investigations, monitorships, and other crucial AML and economic sanctions matters.

We help companies protect data, comply with evolving regulations, and respond to investigations and litigation.

We help clients navigate the complex world of financial crimes compliance.

Advising clients where innovation and regulation collide.

## Share and Download

[![Download](/Images/Icon/icon-pdf.svg)Download](/api/sitecore/module/pdfgeneration?itemurl=%2fen%2finsights%2fclient-alerts%2f20201008-ransomware-attacks-financial-crimes-compliance-requirements&itemid=%7bbec0eada-ef58-473c-9973-94ef28a652fb%7d)

On October 1, 2020, the US Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) each issued advisories addressing the risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments: the [Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/126/ofac_ransomware_advisory_10012020_1.pdf) (OFAC Ransomware Advisory) and the [Advisory on Ransomware and the Use of the Financial System to Facilitate Ransom Payments](https://www.fincen.gov/sites/default/files/advisory/2020-10-01/Advisory Ransomware FINAL 508.pdf), FIN-2020-A006 (FinCEN Ransomware Advisory), respectively. These advisories represent the first time that OFAC and FinCEN have issued guidance that specifically addresses ransomware payments, which, as each has noted in the respective advisories, are increasing in demand during the COVID-19 pandemic and “are a growing concern for the financial sector because of the critical role financial institutions play in the collection of ransom payments.”\*  The advisories build on other US government guidance on ransomware attacks, such as an interagency [Ransomware Executive One-Pager and Technical Document](https://us-cert.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/publications/Ransomware_Executive_One-Pager_and_Technical_Document-FINAL.pdf), which acknowledges that “when businesses are faced with an inability to function, executives will evaluate all options to protect their shareholders, employees, and customers,” and [previous OFAC sanctions designations targeting cryptocurrency exchangers](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sm556) who facilitated the conversion of bitcoin earned in ransomware attacks into Iranian rials.

The advisories broadly identify two main areas of regulatory risk. The first is the risk of a violation of OFAC’s sanctions regulations. As OFAC reminds the public in its Ransomware Advisory, “OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations based on strict liability, meaning that a person subject to U.S. jurisdiction may be held civilly liable even if it did not know or have reason to know it was engaging in a transaction that is prohibited under sanctions laws and regulations administered by OFAC.” Indeed, this risk is often encountered by banks and other companies responding to ransomware attacks because the attacker can obscure its identity and because some prolific ransomware hackers are linked to sanctioned actors, such as the North Korean government and Russian cybercriminals who inhabit a gray zone between that country’s security services and its organized crime groups.

Furthermore, as FinCEN notes in the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory, “[m]any ransomware schemes involve convertible virtual currency (CVC), the preferred payment method of ransomware perpetrators,” which can further obfuscate the destination of the payout funds, thereby exacerbating the risk under the OFAC sanctions regulations that victims of ransomware attacks do not know the identity of their attackers. Victims and companies assisting them may use blockchain forensic tools and other open-source research methods to try to determine whether an address provided by an attacker has been associated with a sanctioned person. But where the identity of attackers is known to be the target of OFAC’s sanctions, OFAC has stated that it will review license applications “on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial.”

The second area of risk is the requirement that financial institutions file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) involving ransomware. Financial institutions are at particular risk when confronting ransomware attacks because they may be required to file a SAR whether they are the victim of the ransomware attack or are merely initiating or processing payments on behalf of their victimized clients. The FinCEN Ransomware Advisory reminds financial institutions that they “should determine if filing a SAR is required or appropriate when dealing with an incident of ransomware conducted by, at, or through the financial institution, including ransom payments made by financial institutions that are victims of ransomware.” It provides specific SAR filing instructions so that financial institutions reference the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory by associating the suspicious activity being reported with ransomware.

Although the OFAC Ransomware Advisory specifically calls on financial institutions to implement risk-based compliance programs to mitigate the risk of a sanctions violation arising from a ransomware attack, it also identifies cyber insurance, digital forensics and incident response firms as among those that should maintain compliance programs to “account for the risk that a ransomware payment may involve [a Specially Designated National or Blocked Person], or a comprehensively embargoed jurisdiction.” The FinCEN advisory also cautions that by facilitating ransomware payments, these firms may be engaging in money transmission, thereby requiring registration with FinCEN as money service businesses and triggering Bank Secrecy Act obligations, including filing of SARs. Such activity may also give rise to obligations under state money transmission laws, including licensing requirements.

Both advisories contemplate that those involved in responding to ransomware attacks will inform or otherwise support law enforcement as part of their response to attacks. OFAC helpfully affirms that it will consider a “self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement to be a significant mitigating factor in determining an appropriate enforcement outcome if the situation is later determined to have a sanctions nexus.” Such an interpretation of OFAC’s Enforcement Guidelines—under which OFAC will also consider the extent to which a company cooperated with law enforcement during and after a ransomware attack—tempers what would otherwise be a less flexible application of the strict liability sanctions regime. Where a SAR filing is not required, the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory contemplates voluntary filings “to aid law enforcement in protecting the financial sector.” The FinCEN Advisory also recognizes that financial institutions may share information with one another about computer fraud and extortion under Section 314(b) of the USA PATRIOT Act.

The FinCEN Advisory identifies five trends of ransomware attacks:

* increasing engagement by attackers on “larger enterprises to demand bigger payouts,” so-called big-game hunting;
* sharing of resources among cybercriminals, including ransomware exploit kits with “ready-made malicious codes and tools” and the formation of partnerships among cybercriminals;
* engaging in “double extortion schemes,” whereby attackers steal sensitive data, encrypt system files and demand ransom, followed by threatening to publish or sell the stolen data if ransom is not paid;
* using anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies, or AECs, and—in some cases—offering “discounted rates to victims who pay their ransoms in AECs”; and
* using “fileless” ransomware in which attackers can overcome a victim’s cyber defenses through the use of malicious code written into system memory.

Financial institutions should also review their financial crimes compliance controls in light of the new guidance. FinCEN also identified a number of red-flag indicators to help financial institutions, especially cryptocurrency exchanges, identify potentially reportable transactions. These include:

* transactions with digital forensics firms that are known to make ransomware payments;
* certain types of rapid back-to-back movements of cryptocurrencies (which resemble typologies of high-risk fiat currency payments);
* accounts established or transactions conducted that lack an obvious connection to the customer’s business or expected activity and may be a sign that the person is making a ransomware payment;
* signs that a customer is engaged in “chain-hopping,” a technique used to convert one type of cryptocurrency into another in order to further obfuscate the source or destination of funds; and
* customers engaging in transactions with cryptocurrency exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

Financial institutions should note at onboarding that a customer is a cyber insurance, digital forensics or incident response firm so that transaction monitoring can be appropriately tailored to detect the relevant red flags. As in the sanctions context, financial institutions may consider using a blockchain forensics tool to detect when a wallet address has been linked to ransomware or other malign activity.

While not creating new legal requirements, taken collectively the two advisories contemplate that financial institutions and other companies will design and implement risk-based compliance programs that mitigate the risk of regulatory violations derived from ransomware incidents and payments. They indicate that both OFAC and FinCEN expect a high level of coordination between victims of ransomware attacks and law enforcement. And indeed, the failure to report attacks to law enforcement and to cooperate with law enforcement during and after an attack may increase a company’s exposure to OFAC monetary penalties.

Given the serious potential regulatory consequences for paying a ransom and the potentially significant business consequences for not doing so, companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture to mitigate the impact of any potential attack and to blunt the impact of a vexing dilemma.

WilmerHale has experience advising clients on preparing for and responding to ransomware attacks, including to mitigate the risk of noncompliance with the laws and regulations administered by OFAC and FinCEN. We are available to work with clients on incorporating these latest advisories into their ransomware incident response plans.

---

\* An OFAC [advisory](https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/126/dprk_cyber_threat_advisory_20200415.pdf) earlier this year focused broadly on the North Korean cyber threat, of which ransomware is an important part.

This is a client alert from the law firm WilmerHale, authored by partners Jason C. Chipman and David M. Horn, analyzing two US government advisories issued on October 1, 2020, addressing the risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments: the OFAC Ransomware Advisory (regarding potential sanctions risks) and the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory (FIN-2020-A006, regarding ransomware and use of the financial system for ransom payments). These represented the first time OFAC and FinCEN issued guidance specifically addressing ransomware payments, which increased in demand during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The advisories identify two main areas of regulatory risk:
1. Violation of OFAC's sanctions regulations – OFAC may impose civil penalties based on strict liability (a person may be held civilly liable even without knowledge), particularly because ransomware attackers can obscure their identity and some are linked to sanctioned actors (e.g., North Korean government and Russian cybercriminals). Ransomware typically involves convertible virtual currency (CVC), which further obscures payouts. Where attackers are known targets of sanctions, OFAC reviews license applications "on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial."
2. Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing requirements for financial institutions – institutions may be required to file SARs whether they are victims of ransomware attacks or merely processing payments for victimized clients. The FinCEN advisory provides specific SAR filing instructions to reference the advisory.

The advisories also apply to cyber insurance, digital forensics, and incident response firms, which should maintain compliance programs and may face money transmission registration requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act and state money transmission laws. Both advisories encourage cooperation with law enforcement; OFAC considers a "self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement" as a significant mitigating factor in enforcement outcomes.

The FinCEN Advisory identifies five trends of ransomware attacks: (1) "big-game hunting" targeting larger enterprises for bigger payouts; (2) sharing of resources and partnerships among cybercriminals; (3) "double extortion schemes" involving data theft and threats to publish; (4) use of anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies (AECs) with discounted rates for AEC payments; and (5) "fileless" ransomware using malicious code in system memory. FinCEN also identified red-flag indicators for financial institutions, including transactions with digital forensics firms known to make ransom payments, rapid back-to-back cryptocurrency movements, accounts lacking obvious connection to customer business, "chain-hopping" techniques, and transactions with exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

While the advisories create no new legal requirements, they indicate that OFAC and FinCEN expect risk-based compliance programs and a high level of coordination with law enforcement. Failure to report attacks to law enforcement may increase exposure to OFAC monetary penalties. Companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture.

Research practical lessons and best practices for enterprises developing ransomware payment disclosure procedures in the U.S. as of mid-2026, synthesizing guidance from official sources and reputable expert commentary. Cover these areas with actionable specificity:

1. Under SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 (final rule effective December 18, 2023), how a company should determine materiality of a ransomware incident and the four-business-day timeline; the interplay between the materiality investigation period (which must still be reasonably prompt), the requirement to disclose ransomware payment details such as whether a ransom was paid, the amount, and whether a known sanctioned entity was involved; the two-part immaterial incident aggregation analysis the SEC staff described; and how legal, IT, and finance teams should operationalize a materiality determination workflow within 4 business days while the investigation is often still ongoing.

2. Coordination of the 8-K four-business-day deadline with other notification regimes: OFAC expectations, CISA's CIRCIA 72-hour and 24-hour ransom payment reporting (if final rule in effect by August 2026), bank regulator 36-hour notifications, NYDFS 72-hour notifications, HIPAA 60-day/HHS notification windows, TSA 12-hour pipeline reporting, state breach notification laws (30-45 days), and insurance/cyber insurer notification clauses — including practical tips for sequencing notifications, preserving privilege, and avoiding premature public disclosure that could complicate law enforcement or investor communications.

3. The pay vs. not-pay decision: OFAC compliance obligations before any payment (screening the recipient against the SDN list and sanctions programs, checking IP addresses and wallets against OFAC sanctions lists, considering whether the actor is a sanctioned entity or in a sanctioned jurisdiction, preventing payments to Specially Designated Nationals, using blockchain analytics, documenting due diligence, and evaluating license options); DOJ's "voluntary self-disclosure" and charging guidance (April 2022 DOJ memo — companies that report ransomware payments to law enforcement within 48 hours, in compliance with OFAC, and cooperate may be eligible for a presumption in favor of a declination or non-prosecution); CISA/FBI guidance discouraging payment and reporting all ransom payments to CISA or IC3; the "combating the financing of ransomware" money laundering reporting requirements (FinCEN's September 2021 advisory and May 2025 activities under Treasury's AML rules — report suspicious activity of ransomware-related payments); and state-level ransom payment prohibitions such as NYDFS 23 NYCRCR Part 500 rule (as of 2023, regulated financial entities may not pay ransoms absent explicit written approval from the NYDFS superintendent).

4. Internal governance and coordination: Roles of the CEO, board (including the Item 106 board cyber expertise disclosure), CISO, general counsel, CFO/treasury (who executes any wire), and communications teams; the importance of a pre-scripted ransomware response playbook; board notification obligations; coordination to ensure statements to investors, media, and regulators are consistent and not misleading (given SEC's SolarWinds enforcement theory about statements of material risk controls being misleading); pitfalls such as boilerplate risk-factor disclosures that are materially misleading post-incident; and the need for accurate statements about scope (e.g., Blackbaud's failure to disclose that sensitive bank and Social Security data had been accessed).

5. Common pitfalls that led to prior enforcement actions, with practical checklists: delayed disclosure pending internal investigation without justification; issuing an 8-K prematurely with incomplete scope that later required correction; disclosure that overstates or understates the incident; failure to aggregate immaterial incidents; failure to screen the ransom payee pre-payment; inconsistent statements to different stakeholders; and updating risk factors and cybersecurity disclosures in periodic reports (10-K/10-Q) to reflect actual incidents and governance.

Provide named sources where possible (e.g., the SEC's 2022-2025 enforcement orders, DOJ guidance, CISA StopRansomware advice, law firm client alerts with substantive analysis), with direct links to primary guidance documents where feasible, and organize the output as an actionable synthesis appropriate for an enterprise risk analyst drafting incident disclosure procedures. --- SOURCE 1: SEC Cybersecurity Rules: A Snapshot ---
URL: https://arch.bdo.com/sec-cybersecurity-rules-a-snapshot

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This BDO publication provides a snapshot of the SEC's cybersecurity rules, which require registrants to disclose material cybersecurity incidents in Form 8-K within four business days of determining materiality, and to make annual disclosures about cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance under Regulation S-K Item 106 and Form 20-F Item 16K.

**Key Requirements:**
- **Annual Disclosures (S-K Item 106):** Registrants must describe processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material cybersecurity risks, board oversight, and management's role. At the 2024 AICPA & CIMA Conference, SEC staff noted that mere statements that a process exists are insufficient; disclosure must clearly describe the process and individual expertise within management groups.
- **Incident Disclosures (Form 8-K Item 1.05):** Material cybersecurity incidents must be disclosed within four business days. Materiality follows the standard "reasonable investor" test, considering both quantitative and qualitative factors. Foreign private issuers file on Form 6-K.
- **Definitions:** A "cybersecurity incident" includes unauthorized occurrences on or through a registrant's information systems; "information systems" includes resources "used by" the registrant (including third-party systems).

**BDO Insights:**
- Incidents can include "a series of related unauthorized occurrences" (e.g., continuous small attacks by the same actor that are collectively material).
- Registrants must have processes and controls to evaluate incidents for disclosure.

**SEC Staff Guidance on Voluntary Disclosure (May 2024):**
- Material incidents must be disclosed under Item 1.05.
- Immaterial incidents or those with incomplete materiality assessments should be disclosed under Item 8.01, not Item 1.05, to avoid confusing investors.

**Ransomware Guidance (C&DIs):**
- Paying a ransom does not eliminate the obligation to assess materiality or disclose if material.
- Insurance reimbursement does not automatically make an incident immaterial.
- Small dollar ransom payments do not automatically make an incident immaterial; qualitative factors (e.g., reputational harm) must be considered.
- Multiple individually immaterial incidents that are related and collectively material require disclosure.

**Delay of Disclosure:**
- Disclosure may be delayed only if the U.S. Attorney General notifies the SEC in writing that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety. Initial delay up to 30 days, extendable up to 90 days total.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"If a registrant has a process for identifying, assessing, and managing significant cybersecurity risks, the disclosure should clearly describe this process to inform investors. Merely stating that a process exists is not enough.", "The SEC staff believes the distinction between disclosing a material cybersecurity incident under Item 1.05 and voluntarily disclosing under another item, such as Item 8.01, allows investors to make better investing and voting decisions related to material cybersecurity incidents.", "The registrant may not conclude the incident is immaterial based solely on the fact that all or a substantial portion of the ransomware payment was reimbursed under its insurance policy.", "The definition of a cybersecurity incident includes 'a series of related unauthorized occurrences' to reflect that cyberattacks can compound over time, rather than occurring at a point in time.", "The SEC staff reminded registrants that determining the materiality of a cybersecurity incident involves an assessment of both quantitative and qualitative factors and must be made without unreasonable delay."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article examines the first year of mandatory cybersecurity incident reporting under the SEC's new rules, which took effect on December 18, 2023. Key findings include:

**Background & Key Takeaways:**
- 26 companies reported cybersecurity incidents under Item 1.05 of Form 8-K in the first year.
- The SEC's May 21, 2024 Statement discouraged using Item 1.05 for voluntary disclosure of immaterial incidents, directing companies to use Item 8.01 instead.
- Following the Statement, only 9 companies disclosed under Item 1.05 (vs. 17 before), while 28 companies used Item 8.01 (vs. 6 before).
- The SEC conducted a "sweep" review issuing 14 comment letters focusing on proper use of Item 1.05 and expanding disclosure beyond financial impacts.

**SEC Guidance Clarity:**
- Item 1.05 should be reserved for incidents determined to have material impacts.
- Materiality assessments should consider qualitative factors (reputation, customer relationships, litigation risks) alongside quantitative factors.
- If materiality is determined but scope is unknown, companies should file under Item 1.05 and later amend.

**Enforcement Actions:**
- Flagstar Bancorp settled for $3.5 million for falsely stating no unauthorized access to customer data after a 2021 cyberattack.
- The SolarWinds case saw dismissal of SEC claims that cybersecurity deficiencies violated internal accounting controls, limiting the SEC's enforcement reach.

**Key Statistics:**
- Average time from detection to disclosure: 7.88 business days; median: 4.5 business days.
- 65% of registrants disclosed operational disruptions; 77% reported data access/exfiltration; 23% identified a threat actor; 50% filed an amendment.
- No companies disclosed paying a ransom.

**Conclusion:** Expectations have become clearer: companies should disclose only material incidents under Item 1.05, describe all reasonably likely material impacts, and maintain robust disclosure controls and procedures.
</summary>

<summary>
This Debevoise Data Blog post announces the Debevoise Tracker for Cybersecurity Incident Disclosure on Form 8-K, a resource tracking U.S. public company filings under the SEC's new cybersecurity rules. The SEC adopted rules for Cybersecurity Risk Management, Strategy, Governance, and Incident Disclosure, which went into effect on December 18, 2023. Under these rules, Item 1.05 of Form 8-K requires U.S. public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents.

Key requirements outlined include: the deadline to file a Form 8-K under Item 1.05 is within four business days after determining an incident is material, and this materiality determination must be made "without unreasonable delay." Companies may delay disclosure if the U.S. Attorney General determines disclosure could pose a substantial risk to national security or public safety, though this is expected to be invoked infrequently in practice.

Registrants filing an 8-K under Item 1.05 must disclose: (1) the material aspects of the nature, scope and timing of the incident (basic identifying details), and (2) the material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant, including financial condition and results of operations. Materiality follows the standard familiar from other securities law contexts, considering both quantitative and qualitative factors regarding whether a shareholder would consider the information important or if it would significantly alter the "total mix" of information.

The rules also impose a similar obligation on foreign private issuers (FPIs) listed in the U.S., but only requiring disclosure on Form 6-K after the incident is disclosed or required to be disclosed in a foreign jurisdiction. As a result, FPI disclosure will continue to be driven by home-country laws and regulations rather than SEC requirements.

The tracker was updated as of August 6, 2026, and includes links to all Form 8-K filings under the new requirements, along with relevant dates and amendments. The post was authored by Avi Gesser (Co-Chair of the Debevoise Data Strategy & Security Group), Benjamin R. Pedersen, John Jacob, Talia Lorch, and Alexander Bracco. URL: https://www.cherryhilladvisory.com/sec-cybersecurity-disclosure-rule-two-year-review

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cherry Hill Advisory research brief analyzes the first two years (December 18, 2023 to May 23, 2026) of the SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Rule, which requires public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents on Form 8-K within four business days. The analysis covers 78 total filings (47 mandatory Item 1.05 filings and 31 voluntary Item 8.01 filings) with verified day-after stock data on 73.

**Key Rule Mechanics:**
- Item 1.05 (mandatory): Clock starts on materiality determination, not incident discovery. Halliburton determined materiality in 2 days; UnitedHealth in 1 day; AT&T took 84 calendar days.
- Item 8.01 (voluntary): Used for defensive disclosure or vendor-driven incidents, notably the CDK Global cluster where six auto dealers filed on June 24, 2024.
- National-security delays invoked twice, both by AT&T in 2024.

**Landmark Event:** CB Financial Services (CBFV) filed the first-ever 8-K naming AI as the root cause of a cybersecurity incident on May 11, 2026. Unauthorized AI software exposed names, SSNs, and dates of birth. The market reaction was muted (-1.16% day-after), attributed to issuer size rather than subject matter.

**Market Reaction Findings:**
- 66% (48 of 73) of filings closed down the next trading day.
- Cybersecurity, tech, and crypto vendors averaged -6.6% single-day moves.
- Diversified mid- and large-caps averaged -0.1% (essentially flat).
- Micro-caps and nano-caps showed high variance due to thin trading volume.

**Five Strategic Insights:**
1. Market is pricing these disclosures with significant dispersion based on whether trust is part of the product.
2. Materiality clock is faster than discovery clock; pre-documenting the materiality framework is critical.
3. Vendor incidents drive Item 8.01 filings; third-party notification protocols need four-business-day awareness.
4. AI-incident disclosures have begun (only 1 of 78 so far, but Mayer Brown estimates AI-enabled phishing in ~16% of incidents).
5. Industry concentration is a leading indicator; healthcare, automotive retail, industrial/manufacturing, and tech cluster most filings.

**Six Notable Cases:**
- UnitedHealth/Change Healthcare: Largest US healthcare breach (192.7M individuals); $22M ransom; FY24 P&L hit of $3.09B.
- AT&T: First-ever DOJ national-security delay; 84-day pre-disclosure window; near-flat market reaction.
- Coinbase: Insider-enabled access; 69,461 customers exposed; $180-400M estimated remediation; recovered fully within a week.
- F5 Networks: China-nexus UNC5221/BRICKSTORM malware; triggered CISA Emergency Directive 26-01; largest T+5 decline (-13.21%).
- Johnson Controls: Flat day-after but Q1 2026 revenue missed consensus by 4.4%, explicitly attributed to cyber incident.
- Halliburton: Fastest materiality determination (2 days); -3.99% day-after; -8.94% T+5.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: OFAC Issues Updated Guidance on Ransomware Payments ---
URL: https://www.insideprivacy.com/cybersecurity-2/ofac-issues-updated-guidance-on-ransomware-payments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," which supersedes an earlier advisory from October 1, 2020. The Updated Advisory is directed at not only organizations victimized by ransomware attacks but also financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and forensic and incident-response firms that assist victims.

Key points of the Updated Advisory include:

- **Continued Opposition to Ransomware Payments**: OFAC maintains that the U.S. government "strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands" and recommends focusing on defensive and resilience measures. Payments may violate U.S. sanctions prohibitions, and penalties may be imposed on a strict liability basis, meaning companies could face enforcement even if they didn't know a payment would violate sanctions.

- **New Mitigating Factors**: The Updated Advisory identifies two significant mitigating factors in any OFAC enforcement response:
  1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps taken to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices, such as those in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide (co-developed with MS-ISAC), will be considered a "significant mitigating factor."
  2. **Notification and Cooperation with U.S. Government**: Promptly reporting ransomware attacks to law enforcement, CISA, Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection (OCCIP), or other relevant agencies, along with ongoing cooperation (including providing technical details, ransom payment demands, and payment instructions), constitutes a "significant mitigating factor." Timely self-disclosure to these agencies may be considered a voluntary self-disclosure for mitigation purposes.

- **First-Ever Sanctions Designation of a Cryptocurrency Exchange**: Also on September 21, 2021, OFAC designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (also known as "Successful Exchange"), a Russian cryptocurrency exchange, for property-blocking sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13694 (as amended by EO 13757). OFAC alleged SUEX OTC facilitated numerous ransomware payments for malicious cyber actors. U.S. persons are now prohibited from engaging in virtually all transactions with SUEX OTC. The exchange was identified on the SDN List by name, address, and digital currency addresses in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether. OFAC had previously designated other parties by digital currency address in 2018 (two Iranian individuals in the SamSam ransomware scheme).

- **Anticipated Further Guidance**: Press reporting indicates further related guidance may be forthcoming, likely from FinCEN, including action on the proposed application of the travel rule to cryptocurrency transactions and additional anti-money laundering efforts. This aligns with FinCEN's October 1, 2020 advisory (issued in parallel with the 2020 OFAC Advisory) on "red flags" for suspicious ransomware transactions, which noted that consultants facilitating ransomware payments could be considered "money transmitters" under the Bank Secrecy Act.

The article was authored by Covington & Burling LLP attorneys Ashden Fein, Peter Flanagan, Jim Garland, Mike Nonaka, and Moriah Daugherty. The article notes that it remains unclear how OFAC will assess compliance with the new mitigating factors, including which agencies and standards will be used for evaluation, but emphasizes the importance of preparation—developing a strong cybersecurity posture before an attack and timely reporting to and cooperation with government agencies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The U.S. government strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands and recommends focusing on strengthening defensive and resilience measures to prevent and protect against ransomware attacks."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The Guide to Sanctions - Seventh Edition - Practical issues in cyber-related sanctions as OFAC designations highlight renewed focus on digital currency - Global Investigations Review ---
URL: https://globalinvestigationsreview.com/guide/the-guide-sanctions/seventh-edition/article/practical-issues-in-cyber-related-sanctions-ofac-designations-highlight-renewed-focus-digital-currency

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published 14 July 2026 in GIR's The Guide to Sanctions (Seventh Edition), examines practical issues in US cyber-related sanctions, particularly focusing on recent OFAC designations highlighting renewed attention on digital currency. Authored by Timothy O'Toole, Collmann Griffin, Melissa Burgess, and Arooshe Giroti of Miller & Chevalier, the article provides a comprehensive overview of the US cyber-related sanctions regime.

KEY LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
- The primary authority is Executive Order (EO) 13694 (Cyber1, issued 1 April 2015), amended and strengthened by EO 13757 (Cyber2, 2016), EO 14144 (Cyber3, 2025), and EO 14306 (Cyber4, 2025). Congress codified EOs 13694 and 13757 into statute under the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA, signed 2 August 2017).
- OFAC administers these through the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR Part 578). Other authorities used include EO 13722 (North Korea), EO 13848 (election interference), and EO 14024 (Russian harmful foreign activities, 15 April 2021, amended by EO 14114 in December 2023 to authorize secondary sanctions on foreign financial institutions).
- The sanctions target cyber-enabled activities including: harm to critical infrastructure computer networks, disruption of service availability, misappropriation of funds/trade secrets/personal identifiers, and election interference.

GUIDANCE AND ADVISORIES:
- 2020 Ransomware Advisory (1 October 2020) and 2021 Ransomware Advisory (21 September 2021) warn that ransomware payments to blocked persons carry strict liability penalties; cooperation with law enforcement is a mitigating factor.
- Virtual Currency Guidance (15 October 2021) clarifies that sanctions obligations apply equally to virtual and fiat currencies.
- FinCEN issued its own Ransomware Advisory (1 October 2021) with red flag indicators.

ENFORCEMENT AND DESIGNATIONS:
- OFAC has designated numerous parties including individual hackers, money launderers, troll farms (Internet Research Agency), cybercriminal organizations (Kimsuky, Genesis Market, Evil Corp, Hydra Market, Garantex), spyware providers (Intellexa Consortium), virtual currency mixers (Blender.io, Sinbad), and state-linked actors from Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea.
- Notable designations include Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (September 2022), Zservers (Russia-based bulletproof hosting, February 2025), and Southeast Asia-based cyber scam networks.
- OFAC civil penalty settlements have targeted virtual currency platforms for sanctions violations: CoinList Markets LLC ($1,252,280 in transactions), Binance Holdings ($706 million, 1,667,153 violations), Poloniex LLC ($15.3 million, 65,942 violations), Uphold HQ Inc ($180,575.80), and Bittrex Inc (over $263 million, 116,421 violations). A recurring theme was failure to use IP address, KYC, and geolocation data for screening.

NOTABLE LEGAL DEVELOPMENT:
- In Van Loon v Treasury (2024), a US Court of Appeals overturned OFAC's designations of Tornado Cash (a decentralized virtual currency mixer), holding that immutable "smart contracts" (self-executing software code) fall outside the definition of "property" or "services" OFAC can block under IEEPA. However, on 6 August 2025, a jury convicted Tornado Cash developer Roman Storm of conspiring to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business (deadlocked on money laundering and sanctions counts, with retrial anticipated). Co-developer Roman Semenov remains under sealed indictment.

COMPLIANCE RISKS:
- Ransom payments to sanctioned parties or jurisdictions risk penalties without a specific OFAC licence.
- Digital currency sector faces heightened scrutiny; businesses must implement risk-based screening, IP blocking, geofencing, and blockchain tracking.
- Cybertheft of export-controlled information may constitute unauthorized export and could expose victim entities to liability for failing to prevent compromise.
- OFAC expects companies to use all reasonably accessible information (IP addresses, KYC data, onboarding data, geolocation) in screening—merely relying on user location attestations is insufficient.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OFAC administers a variety of sanctions targeting malicious cyber-related activities, such as cyber espionage, cyber intrusions on critical infrastructure and computer networks, and disinformation campaigns conducted from abroad."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) took two significant actions: (1) issued an updated advisory on sanctions risks for facilitating ransomware payments, and (2) designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. OFAC identified two "significant mitigating factors" in determining enforcement actions and penalty amounts for sanctions violations tied to ransomware payments (including self-reporting, which increases the likelihood of a non-public response such as a No Action Letter or Cautionary Letter).

The advisory recommends that companies, particularly in the virtual currency space, enhance due diligence procedures—paying attention to peer-to-peer exchangers, mixers, tumblers, and similar illicit-facilitating services—and warns U.S. persons with hosted wallets to consider risks of future asset restrictions if custodial entities are designated. Additional designations and enforcement actions are expected as more ransomware information becomes available.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: OFAC's Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual ... ---
URL: https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/913571/download?inline=

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the official "Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry" issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The guidance assists the virtual currency industry (technology companies, exchangers, administrators, miners, wallet providers, and users) in understanding and complying with OFAC sanctions requirements, which apply equally to transactions involving virtual currencies and traditional fiat currencies.

KEY CONTENT:
- OFAC administers over 35 sanctions programs that can be comprehensive (broad trade sanctions on countries like Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria, and Crimea) or targeted (government/regime sanctions, list-based sanctions, sectoral sanctions).
- The SDN (Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons) List contains over 9,000 names of designated individuals and entities. Under the "50 Percent Rule," entities owned 50% or more by blocked persons are also considered blocked.
- Enforcement examples: In March 2020, OFAC sanctioned two Chinese nationals involved in a North Korean money-laundering scheme (~$100 million in stolen virtual currency). In September 2021, OFAC designated a Russian virtual currency exchange facilitating transactions for ransomware actors (over 40% of transactions associated with illicit actors).
- Who must comply: All U.S. persons (citizens, lawful permanent residents, entities within the U.S., and entities organized under U.S. law, including foreign branches). Key point: OFAC enforces strict liability—civil penalties can be imposed even without knowledge of the violation.
- Blocked virtual currency must be reported to OFAC within 10 business days and annually thereafter; it need not be converted to fiat currency.

REQUIREMENTS:
- Reporting: Initial blocked property reports (10 business days), annual blocked property reports (by September 30), rejected transaction reports (10 business days), and on-demand reports via administrative subpoena.
- Recordkeeping: Five years of full and accurate records for each transaction and for blocked property (five years after unblocking).
- Licensing: General licenses (self-executing) and specific licenses (case-by-case applications).

CONSEQUENCES: Civil and criminal penalties can be substantial. Voluntary self-disclosure may reduce proposed civil penalties by 50%.

FIVE ESSENTIAL COMPONENTS OF A SANCTIONS COMPLIANCE PROGRAM (per A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments):
1. Management Commitment - senior management must endorse policies, provide resources, appoint a dedicated sanctions compliance officer.
2. Risk Assessment - routine, ongoing review of company's touchpoints to foreign jurisdictions/persons, tailored to products, services, customers, and geographic locations.
3. Internal Controls - screening, investigation, transaction monitoring; best practices include geolocation tools/IP address blocking, KYC procedures (collecting names, dates of birth, addresses, IP addresses, government IDs for individuals; entity names, ownership, location info for businesses), transaction monitoring and investigation software, and remedial measures.
4. Testing and Auditing - comprehensive, independent, and objective testing of program effectiveness, including sanctions list screening, keyword screening, IP blocking, and investigation/reporting procedures.
5. Training - sanctions-specific training for all appropriate employees at least annually, updating for new technologies.

Risk indicators/red flags to monitor: inaccurate/incomplete KYC information, access attempts from IP addresses/VPNs connected to sanctioned jurisdictions, refusal to provide updated information, and attempts to transact with virtual currency addresses associated with blocked persons.

OFAC began including virtual currency addresses in the SDN List in 2018, searchable via the "ID #" field in the Sanctions List Search tool. Companies should conduct historical lookbacks and use blockchain analytics tools.

OFAC contact resources include the Compliance Hotline (1-800-540-6322), and websites for the OFAC Reporting System, Licensing Portal, and Sanctions List Search tool.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OFAC sanctions compliance obligations apply equally to transactions involving virtual currencies and those involving traditional fiat currencies. Members of the virtual currency industry are responsible for ensuring that they do not engage, directly or indirectly, in transactions prohibited by OFAC sanctions, such as dealings with blocked persons or property, or engaging in prohibited trade- or investment-related transactions."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Bradley's BuildSmart blog (authored by Aron Beezley and Nathaniel Greeson) examines the intersection of two regulatory frameworks affecting government contractors: the U.S. Department of Justice's revised Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP) and the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) mandatory disclosure rule.

**Key Points:**

1. **DOJ's Revised CEP**: The DOJ recently expanded and clarified its CEP, creating a structured framework with predictable benefits. Under the revised policy, companies that (1) voluntarily self-disclose misconduct, (2) fully cooperate with investigators, (3) timely remediate, and (4) have no aggravating circumstances will purportedly receive a declination of prosecution. This represents a shift from prior versions that only offered a presumption of declination. Even with aggravating circumstances, self-disclosing companies may receive nonprosecution agreements, reduced penalties, or no corporate monitor. The key message: early disclosure is the most valuable form of cooperation.

2. **FAR Mandatory Disclosure Rule (FAR 52.203-13)**: Federal contractors must timely disclose credible evidence that a principal, employee, agent, or subcontractor committed violations of federal criminal law involving fraud, conflict of interest, bribery, gratuities, or the civil False Claims Act in connection with federal contracts, in writing to agency OIGs and contracting officers. Knowing failure to disclose may result in suspension or debarment.

3. **Tension Between Voluntary and Mandatory Disclosure**: The article addresses whether a disclosure required by regulation can still qualify as "voluntary" under DOJ's policy. While disclosures may be mandatory from a procurement perspective, they can still be considered voluntary in the criminal enforcement sense if made proactively before the government independently uncovers the misconduct. Contractors making FAR disclosures should simultaneously consider notifying DOJ directly to preserve CEP benefits.

4. **Practical Implications**: (a) Internal investigations become more critical since delays can undermine CEP benefits; (b) disclosure strategies must account for multiple enforcement regimes (criminal fraud statutes, False Claims Act, suspension/debarment, procurement integrity); (c) mandatory disclosures may trigger broader investigations involving DOJ civil and criminal attorneys; (d) robust compliance programs are increasingly important since both frameworks evaluate compliance effectiveness.

**Key Takeaway**: Companies that come forward early are often rewarded, but government contractors face a more complex calculus because the FAR already mandates disclosure. Contractors should seek legal counsel experienced in navigating both FAR and DOJ frameworks simultaneously.

--- SOURCE 7: DOJ Announces New Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy – Investigations and Enforcement Watch ---
URL: https://investigations.cooley.com/2026/03/18/doj-announces-new-corporate-enforcement-and-voluntary-self-disclosure-policy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The DOJ announced a new Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP) on March 10, 2026, creating a unified, department-wide framework to incentivize companies to come forward with potential misconduct. The policy applies to all DOJ corporate criminal matters except Sherman Antitrust Act violations.

Key requirements include: (1) prompt voluntary self-disclosure to the appropriate DOJ criminal component before the department independently learns of the conduct or an investigation is imminent/underway, and without being legally required to do so; (2) full cooperation with the DOJ (timely, truthfully, and accurately disclosing facts, proactive cooperation, making employees available for interviews); and (3) timely and appropriate remediation (compliance programs, disciplining employees, paying restitution).

The policy is structured around a three-tier treatment system:
- Tier 1 (Declination): DOJ declines to prosecute companies with fully compliant voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation, and remediation, provided there are no aggravating circumstances. Declinations require disgorgement and restitution payments and are made public.
- Tier 2 ("Near miss" cases): Companies that cooperate and remediate but fall short on technical self-disclosure requirements or have aggravating factors can receive favorable treatment, including non-prosecution agreements under three years, waiver of independent compliance monitors, and fine reductions of 50%-75% off the low end of the Sentencing Guidelines range.
- Tier 3 (All other cases): Companies failing Tiers 1 and 2 face fine reductions capped at 50% off the Sentencing Guidelines range, with a presumption that reductions are measured from the low end for companies that cooperate and remediate.

The policy was announced by Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche, who warned that the DOJ "will not hesitate to seek appropriate resolutions against companies and individuals alike that perpetrate white collar offenses that harm American interests" for companies that do not self-disclose. The article was authored by Cooley attorneys Andrew Goldstein, Russell Capone, Rebekah Donaleski, Tejal Shah, and Tyler Price.
</summary>

A company that fully cooperates with the DOJ and remediates its misconduct, but either falls short on the technical requirements for voluntary self-disclosure under Tier 1 or has aggravating factors that warrant a criminal resolution, is not eligible for declination. The updated CEP (policy 9-47.120) expands applicability to ALL corporate criminal matters handled by the DOJ Criminal Division, not just FCPA cases, and is effective prospectively only. The policy offers incentives for corporations to have effective compliance programs, voluntarily disclose misconduct, fully cooperate with investigations, and timely remediate misconduct.

Key provisions include:

The article also notes practical concerns: full cooperation may pressure companies to waive attorney-client and work-product privileges. In United States v. The article questions whether the policy will effectively encourage self-disclosure in practice.

This client alert from WilmerHale (authored by partners Jason C. Chipman and David M. Horn) analyzes two U.S. advisories issued on October 1, 2020, addressing ransomware payment risks: the OFAC "Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments" (OFAC Ransomware Advisory) and the FinCEN "Advisory on Ransomware and the Use of the Financial System to Facilitate Ransom Payments" (FIN-2020-A006, FinCEN Ransomware Advisory). These represent the first OFAC and FinCEN guidance specifically addressing ransomware payments, which increased during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The advisories identify two main regulatory risk areas:

1. **OFAC Sanctions Risk**: OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations based on strict liability—a person subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be held liable even without knowing a transaction was prohibited. This risk is heightened because attackers can obscure their identities and some ransomware hackers are linked to sanctioned actors (North Korean government, Russian cybercriminals). Many ransomware schemes use convertible virtual currency (CVC), further obscuring payment destinations. Where attackers are known targets of OFAC sanctions, license applications are reviewed "on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial."

2. **Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) Requirements**: Financial institutions may be required to file SARs whether they are ransomware victims themselves or merely process payments for victimized clients. FinCEN provided specific SAR filing instructions requiring reference to the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory.

Key compliance expectations: Cyber insurance, digital forensics, and incident response firms facilitating ransom payments may be deemed money transmitters, requiring FinCEN registration as money service businesses and triggering Bank Secrecy Act obligations and state money transmission licensing. OFAC will consider a "self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement" as a significant mitigating factor in enforcement outcomes. Voluntary SAR filings and information sharing under USA PATRIOT Act Section 314(b) are also contemplated.

**Five FinCEN-identified ransomware trends**: (1) "big-game hunting" of larger enterprises for bigger payouts; (2) resource sharing among cybercriminals (ransomware exploit kits and partnerships); (3) "double extortion schemes" (theft of data plus encrypted systems, with threats to publish/sell data); (4) use of anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies (AECs), sometimes with discounted rates for AEC payments; and (5) "fileless" ransomware using malicious code in system memory.

**Red-flag indicators** for financial institutions (especially cryptocurrency exchanges): transactions with digital forensics firms known to make ransom payments; rapid back-to-back cryptocurrency movements; accounts/trades lacking connection to customer's business; "chain-hopping" (converting between cryptocurrencies to obfuscate fund sources/destinations); and transactions with exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

While not creating new legal requirements, the advisories signal that OFAC and FinCEN expect risk-based compliance programs and high coordination with law enforcement. Failure to report and cooperate with law enforcement may increase exposure to OFAC monetary penalties. The alert concludes that companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture given the dilemma between regulatory consequences of paying ransoms and business consequences of not paying.
</summary>

On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) adopted a long-awaited amendment to its Cybersecurity Regulation at 23 NYCRR Part 500, which was originally enacted on March 1, 2017, for financial services companies licensed in New York. The amendment creates a new class of "Class A Companies" (large companies) with heightened requirements, expands exemptions, and imposes additional compliance obligations that take effect over a two-year period beginning November 1, 2023.

Key provisions include:
- CLASS A COMPANIES: Companies with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue from New York operations (plus affiliates) in each of the past two fiscal years, AND either an average of 2,000 employees (including affiliates) over the past two fiscal years OR more than $1 billion in global gross annual revenue. Class A companies must conduct independent cybersecurity audits, implement privileged access management solutions and automated password-blocking methods, and deploy endpoint detection and response solutions.
- EXEMPTIONS: The amendment fully exempts employees, agents, representatives, designees, and now wholly owned subsidiaries of covered entities. The small business exemption was expanded to cover entities with fewer than 20 employees/independent contractors, less than $7.5 million in gross annual revenue, or less than $15 million in year-end total assets, though certain requirements still apply to such businesses.
- INCIDENT REPORTING: Covered entities must notify NYDFS within 72 hours of a cybersecurity incident (including at affiliates or third-party service providers) and must report within 24 hours of making any ransomware extortion payment, with follow-up details within 30 days. These new reporting obligations took effect December 1, 2023.
- GOVERNANCE/TECHNICAL REQUIREMENTS: Incident response plans must now address recovery from backups and root cause analyses; Business Continuity and Disaster Recovery Plans (BCDRs) are newly required; annual testing of both plans is mandatory; CISOs have expanded board reporting obligations; risk assessments must be reviewed at least annually; multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required with limited CISO-approved alternatives; and annual compliance certification statements (signed by the highest-ranking executive and CISO) must be submitted by April 15, 2024, and annually thereafter.

The amendment's phased timeline: exemptions and enforcement provisions took effect November 1, 2023; cybersecurity incident notification requirements take effect December 1, 2023; and additional requirements take effect April 29, 2024. Violations include any single prohibited act or omission, failure to secure nonpublic information, or material noncompliance for any 24-hour period. --- SOURCE 20: What is 23 NYCRR Part 500? | Isora GRC ---
URL: https://www.saltycloud.com/blog/what-is-23-nycrr-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a comprehensive guide from SaltyCloud (Isora GRC) explaining 23 NYCRR Part 500, the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) cybersecurity regulation.

**Overview:** 23 NYCRR Part 500 is a New York regulation requiring financial institutions to implement cybersecurity programs, conduct risk assessments, and report incidents. It applies to all NYDFS-regulated entities such as banks, insurers, mortgage companies, and money transmitters.

**History:** Introduced March 2017 with a phased timeline (180 days to 2 years); fully enforced by March 1, 2019. First amendment (April 2020) moved annual certification deadline from February 15 to April 15. A second amendment (2023-2025) expanded scope, adding Class A Company requirements, 72-hour breach notification and 24-hour ransomware payment reporting, executive oversight, and new reporting processes. Deadlines continue through November 1, 2025.

**Who Must Comply:** Covered entities are any organization licensed/authorized by NYDFS. Class A Companies are those with at least $20M gross annual revenue in the last two years AND (more than 2,000 employees OR more than $1B gross annual revenue). They face enhanced obligations including annual independent audits, enhanced privileged access controls, and endpoint detection/response. Small business exemptions apply for entities with fewer than 20 employees, less than $7.5M annual revenue, and less than $15M in assets.

**Key Requirements by Section:**
- §500.2 Cybersecurity Program (comprehensive risk-based program)
- §500.3 Cybersecurity Policy (written, board-approved annually)
- §500.4 Governance (CISO designation, annual board reporting)
- §500.5 Vulnerability Management (annual penetration testing, automated scanning by May 1, 2025)
- §500.6 Audit Trail (5-year record retention)
- §500.7 Access Controls (annual access reviews by May 1, 2025)
- §500.8 Application Security
- §500.9 Risk Assessment (at least annually)
- §500.12 Multi-Factor Authentication (all access by November 1, 2025)
- §500.13 Asset Inventory (by November 1, 2025)
- §500.14 Monitoring and Training (includes social engineering training)
- §500.16 Incident Response Plan (tested yearly)
- §500.17 Notices/Certification (72-hour incident reporting, 24-hour ransomware payment reporting, annual certification by April 15 signed by CISO and senior executive, 5-year documentation retention)

**Reporting:** Cybersecurity incidents must be reported within 72 hours; ransomware payments within 24 hours (with explanation within 30 days). Annual Certification of Material Compliance or Acknowledgment of Noncompliance due April 15.

**Framework Guidance:** NYDFS does not mandate a specific framework; recommended frameworks include NIST CSF, CIS Controls (v8.1 has a direct mapping to Part 500), Cyber Risk Institute (CRI) Profile, ISO/IEC 27001/27002, and the Secure Controls Framework (SCF).

**Third-Party Responsibility:** Third parties are not directly regulated but covered entities bear responsibility for vendor oversight under §500.11, including vendor inventories, risk assessments, and contractual requirements (MFA, encryption, breach notification).

**Penalties:** Recent enforcement examples include Gemini Trust Co. fined $37M + $1.1B restitution (2024, vendor oversight failures), Block, Inc. fined $40M (2025, board-reviewed cyber policy and BCDR failures), and PayPal fined $2M (no MFA, undocumented access controls). Penalties can include per-violation fines, license revocation/suspension, and cease-and-desist orders under FSL §408. Top noncompliance risks: no written policies, missed risk assessments, missing MFA, inadequate incident response, poor vendor risk practices, and incomplete certifications.

**Compliance Management:** Six steps recommended: build structured cybersecurity program, operationalize asset/vendor inventory, conduct formal risk assessment, track risks in central register, apply documented risk-based safeguards, and certify/prepare for examination.

The page promotes Isora GRC as a compliance software solution for managing Part 500 requirements.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 22: Federal Banking Agencies Issue Long-Awaited Computer Security Incident Notice Rules ---
URL: https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/211122-computer-security-incident-notice-rules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 18, 2021, the U.S. federal banking agencies (FDIC, FRB, and OCC) issued long-awaited computer security incident rules ("the Rules") imposing new regulatory notice obligations for banks and certain service providers regarding significant computer security incidents. Covered entities must comply by May 1, 2022.

Key requirements:
- Banking organizations must notify their primary federal regulator as soon as possible but no later than 36 hours after determining a "notification incident" occurred (via email, phone, or similar method).
- A "notification incident" is a computer security incident that has materially disrupted/degraded, or is reasonably likely to disrupt/degrade: (1) a banking organization's ability to carry out banking operations or deliver products/services to a material portion of its customer base; (2) a product or service whose failure would result in material loss of revenue, profit, or franchise value; or (3) operations whose failure would threaten U.S. financial stability.
- A "computer security incident" is defined as an occurrence that results in "actual harm" to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or the information it processes.

Coverage:
- FDIC: insured state nonmember banks, insured state-licensed branches of foreign banks, state savings associations.
- FRB: U.S. bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, state member banks, U.S. operations of foreign banking organizations, Edge and agreement corporations.
- OCC: national banks, federal savings associations, federal branches and agencies of foreign banks.
- Rules also apply to "bank service providers" (under the Bank Service Company Act), who must notify affected bank customers as soon as possible after experiencing a computer security incident causing four or more hours of material service disruption. Notification must go to a bank-designated point of contact, or if none designated, to the CEO and CIO (or two comparable individuals). Scheduled maintenance/testing/updates previously communicated are exempt.
- The Rules do NOT apply to systemically important financial market utilities designated by the Financial Stability Oversight Council.

Key takeaways:
- The Rules are NOT breach notification rules—they focus on the impact of computer security events regardless of cause (including non-malicious events like fires, floods, failed upgrades, or earthquakes), emphasizing severe business disruption.
- The 36-hour notice requirement is faster than typical state breach laws, NYDFS (72 hours), and GDPR (72 hours).
- The Rules uniquely impose obligations directly on service providers, rather than flowing down through contracts.
- Events may overlap with GLBA incident response guidance and state data breach laws (e.g., a ransomware attack that also exfiltrates customer data).
- Banks and service providers should update incident response plans, designate points of contact in advance, and implement notification processes to avoid operational challenges during critical events.
</summary>

<summary>
This publication from Norton Rose Fulbright (January 2021) reports on a joint proposal by the US Department of the Treasury (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency), Federal Reserve, and FDIC, announced December 18, 2020, that would require banks to notify their regulators within 36 hours of a "computer-security incident" that rises to the level of a "notification incident." The 53-page proposed rule would also affect bank service providers (including data processing companies) under the Bank Service Company Act (12 U.S.C. §§ 1861–67).

Key definitions under the proposal:
- "Computer security incident": An occurrence resulting in actual or potential harm to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or the information it processes, stores, or transmits; or constituting a violation or imminent threat of violation of security policies, procedures, or acceptable use policies. Notably, this definition is NOT limited to personal information.
- "Notification incident": An incident a banking organization believes in good faith could materially disrupt, degrade, or impair its operations. The regulators provided non-exhaustive examples plus a catch-all expectation that banks consider other significant incidents as notification incidents.

Timeline: The 36-hour clock begins only once the bank has determined a notification incident has occurred, with agencies recognizing banks may not make this determination outside normal business hours.

Service provider requirements: Bank service providers must notify at least two individuals at affected banking organization customers IMMEDIATELY after experiencing a computer-security incident they believe in good faith could disrupt, degrade, or impair services for four or more hours. Providers are NOT expected to assess whether the incident rises to a notification incident level—that determination rests with the banking organization. Regulators would enforce the service provider notification requirement directly against service providers, not against banks.

Notice requirements: No specific information or prescribed forms are required; notices may be provided through any written or oral means (email, telephone) to a designated regulator contact. Notices and related information would be subject to agencies' confidentiality rules.

The comment period was to commence upon publication in the Federal Register and extend for 90 days. The regulators sought comments and answers to several specific questions.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Federal Register final rule published on November 23, 2021, by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Board), and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) regarding computer-security incident notification requirements for banking organizations and their bank service providers.

**Key Provisions:**
- Banking organizations must notify their primary Federal regulator of any "computer-security incident" that rises to the level of a "notification incident" as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after determining the incident occurred.
- Bank service providers must notify at least one bank-designated point of contact at each affected banking organization customer as soon as possible when they determine they've experienced a computer-security incident that has caused, or is reasonably likely to cause, a material service disruption or degradation for four or more hours.

**Dates:** Effective date April 1, 2022; Compliance date May 1, 2022.

**Document details:** Published as 86 FR 66424 (Document Number 2021-25510), covering pages 66424-66444 (21 pages), amending 12 CFR Parts 53, 225, and 304.

**Definitions:**
- "Banking organization" varies by agency: OCC covers national banks, Federal savings associations, and Federal branches/agencies of foreign banks; Board covers U.S. bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, state member banks, U.S. operations of foreign banking organizations, and Edge/agreement corporations; FDIC covers insured state nonmember banks, insured state-licensed branches of foreign banks, and insured state savings associations.
- "Computer-security incident" was narrowed from the proposed NIST-based definition to focus on actual (rather than potential) harm to an information system, removing the second prong regarding violations of internal policies/procedures.
- "Bank service provider" includes bank service companies or other persons performing "covered services" (services subject to the Bank Service Company Act, 12 U.S.C. 1861-1867).

- Excluded designated Financial Market Utilities (FMUs) from the definitions of "banking organization" and "bank service provider" to avoid regulatory overlap with existing SEC, CFTC, and Regulation HH requirements.
- Added "covered services" definition to clarify scope.
- Changed notification from two individuals to a bank-designated point of contact.

**Rationale:** Cyberattacks targeting financial services have increased in frequency and severity. Timely notification allows agencies to (1) have early awareness of emerging threats, (2) better assess threats and take action, (3) facilitate assistance through the Treasury OCCIP, (4) provide information and guidance, and (5) conduct horizontal analyses. The bank service provider requirement ensures banking organizations can assess whether incidents at third-party providers trigger their own notification obligations.

<webpage_content>
![Debevoise Data Blog](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2022/02/Data_Blog_banner_logo.png)

# A Summary of the Final Amendments to the NYDFS Cyber Rules

![](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/11/GettyImages-1009022860-1-1170x508.jpg "A Summary of the Final Amendments to the NYDFS Cyber Rules")

As will be discussed in our [November 28, 2023 webcast](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/2023/11/14/webcast-nydfs-cybersecurity-final-amendments/), on November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services (“NYDFS” or the “Department”) [announced](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/reports_and_publications/press_releases/pr202311011) the adoption of the second amendment to its Cybersecurity Regulation (the “Second Amendment” or “Final Amendment”) that reflects NYDFS’s revisions as a result of comments it received on the [proposed amendment](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/2023/07/10/nydfs-publishes-revised-amendments-to-its-cybersecurity-regulation/) released in June 2023 (the “June 2023 Proposal”). A redline of the Final Amendment against the version of Part 500 that is currently in effect can be found [here](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/11/Redline-NYDFS-Part-500-2017.doc-and-NYDFS-Part-500-Final-Second-Amendment-2023.pdf).

Throughout the amendment process, the Department was resolute in promulgating a set of standards for larger companies rather than deferring to those companies to make all risk-based decision-making. The Final Amendment reflects that the Department carefully considered public comments, and made revisions to its Cybersecurity Regulation that demonstrate an understanding of the complex nature of cybersecurity governance and oversight.

The Second Amendment’s compliance requirements will take effect in phases. For legal and compliance teams, the new requirements on certification, risk assessments, and governance will call for cross-functional participation throughout the coming year as companies assess their compliance with NYDFS’s Cybersecurity Regulation. To assist businesses impacted by the Second Amendment with tracking key compliance dates, NYDFS published Cybersecurity Implementation Timelines for [small businesses](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/implementation_timeline_small_businesses), [Class A businesses](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/implementation_timeline_class_a_businesses), and [covered entities](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/cybersecurity/implementation_timeline_covered_entities), and announced that it will host webinars to assist regulated entities with compliance.

Below we provide a high-level timeline for when the new and updated requirements contained within the Final Amendment will become effective:

**December 1, 2023:**

**April 15, 2024:**

**April 29, 2024:**

**November 1, 2024:**

**May 1, 2025:**

**November 1, 2025:**

A review of the [redline](https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2023/11/Redline-old-rev_rp_23a2_text_20230628-and-new-rf_fs_2amend23NYCRR500_text_20231101.pdf) of the June 2023 Proposal against the Final Amendment demonstrates that NYDFS incorporated several important changes in response to the comments it received. The Department also released a helpful 38-page [Assessment of Public Comments](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry_guidance/regulations/final_adoptions_fs/rf_fs_2amend23nycrr500_apc_20231101) (“APC”) that details why NYDFS accepted or rejected certain comments.

***The Six Key Updates to Part 500***

The changes in the Final Amendment can be roughly divided into six categories: New Obligations for Larger (“Class A”) Companies, Governance, Technical Requirements, Business Continuity, Breach Notification Obligations, and Enforcement.

**1.** **New Obligations for Class A Companies**

The Final Amendment creates a category of “Class A” companies that are covered entities with at least $20,000,000 in gross annual revenue in each of the last two years from all business operations of the entity and the business operations in New York State of its affiliates, and either (i) over 2,000 employees or (ii) $1 billion in gross annual revenue for each of the past two fiscal years for the global business operations of the covered entity and its affiliates. Importantly, when calculating the number of employees and the gross annual revenue, the term “affiliates” should include “only those that share information systems, cybersecurity resources, or all or any part of a cybersecurity program with the covered entity.”

Class A companies are subject to several additional cybersecurity obligations under the Final Amendment, including:

**2.** **New Governance Requirements for CISOs, Management, and the Board**

NYDFS views strong governance as a central aspect of good cybersecurity. The original Part 500 required cybersecurity reporting to the board, written policies approved by a senior officer, and the need for a CISO or equivalent. The Final Amendment provides several enhancements, including:

**3****.** **New Technical Requirements**

In addition to the technical requirements discussed above that apply only to Class A companies, the Final Amendment imposes the following new technical obligations on all covered entities:

*It may be acceptable, in some circumstances, depending on a covered entity’s specific cybersecurity risks, to use a device, such as an office workstation, mobile phone, or laptop, as one of the authentication factors required for MFA, especially if, for example, the device contains biometric capabilities or authenticator applications.*

The definition of MFA has also been changed to remove the reference to “text message on a mobile phone.” [500.1(j)]. The APC issued with the June 2023 Proposal indicated that NYDFS had eliminated this reference because “[t]ext message MFA, while still acceptable, is widely considered to be a weaker form of MFA, and the Department encourages the adoption of more secure forms of MFA, in particular phishing-resistant forms of MFA.” NYDFS indicated that mobile phone authenticator applications satisfy, and might be preferred for, the possession factor. NYDFS also recognized that it “will be too costly and burdensome at this time to require only phishing-resistant MFA for all covered entities[,]” but also noted that “physical security tokens, such as personal identity verification (‘PIV’) cards and security keys, offer phishing resistance[.]”

**4. Incident Response and Business Continuity Planning**

The Final Amendment introduces several new requirements for companies’ incident response and BCDR plans, including:

**5****.****Breach Notification Obligations**

The original Part 500 required covered entities to notify NYDFS within 72 hours of determining that a cybersecurity event occurred that (1) had a reasonable likelihood of materially harming normal operations of the entity, or (2) required notification to any other regulatory body. The Final Amendment expands these notification obligations, including by:
