California has signed into law Senate Bill No. 446, amending Section 1798.82 of its Civil Code (its data breach notification law) to require covered companies to notify affected California residents within 30 calendar days of discovery of a data breach. The amendment takes effect January 1, 2026.

Key points of the amendment:
- Replaces California's previous flexible "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" standard with a specific 30-day deadline.
- California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002, and as a leading privacy regulator, this move may prompt more states to adopt firm notice timelines.
- Several states already impose specific notice timeframes: New York (30 days), Texas (30 days), Colorado (30 days), Florida (30 days), and Delaware (60 days). Some states require notice to the attorney general simultaneously with or prior to notice to individuals—more stringent than California's requirement to notify the attorney general within 15 days of notice to individuals.
- In practice, many businesses make regulatory notices close in time to individual notices to address differing state obligations.

The authors (Annmarie Giblin and Susana Medeiros) offer a critical "take" on the change: shorter notice timelines do not necessarily improve notification outcomes. Even weeks after discovery, breach victims may not know the scope of impact, affected data types, or geographic residence of individuals—even with considerable investigative resources. While many state laws (including California's as amended) exempt disclosure where necessary to determine breach scope, this view is not universal. For example, the Connecticut Attorney General has clarified that Connecticut's 60-day notice requirement "runs from the date that a company becomes aware of suspicious activity, not the date it determines the full impact to personal information."

Companies in highly regulated sectors (critical infrastructure, insurance, banking) often face even shorter notice periods—as short as 72 hours—and regulators have fined companies for untimely reporting. The article advises companies to assess and update their incident response procedures, particularly for larger and more complex incidents, to meet shorter disclosure expectations.

If a breach affects **more than 500 California residents**, a sample copy of the consumer notification is required to the **California Attorney General “within 15 days** of notifying affected consumers of the security breach.”

* [Share](#) 

  + [Twitter](https://www.twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=Based%20on%20recent%20reports%20and%20enforcement%20actions%2C%20the%20risks%20and%20costs%20of%20substantial%20fines%20remain%20high%20for%20non-compliance%20with%20data%20breach%20notification%20statutes.https%3A%2F%2Fwww.pillsburylaw.com)

Based on recent reports and enforcement actions, the risks and costs of substantial fines remain high for non-compliance with data breach notification statutes.

10.31.25

On October 3, 2025, Governor Gavin Newsom signed into law [Senate Bill No. 446](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB446), which makes important changes to the California data breach notification statute. The new law, which takes effect on January 1, 2026, mandates deadlines for data breach notification to affected individuals and the state attorney general. SB 446 passed with no [votes in opposition](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB446).

In 2002, California was the [first state](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=200120020AB700) to [enact a data breach notification statute](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billStatusClient.xhtml?bill_id=200120020AB700). Since then, all [50 states](https://www.ncsl.org/technology-and-communication/security-breach-notification-laws) and four U.S. jurisdictions (District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Virgin Islands) enacted their own data breach notification requirements. On multiple occasions, we have assisted companies in managing and responding to data breaches for all 54 jurisdictions.

Since the original statute, California has mandated disclosure of a data breach “in the [most expedient time possible](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=200120020AB700) and without unreasonable delay, consistent with the legitimate needs of law enforcement, … or any measures necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore the reasonable integrity of the data system.” Thirty other states have a comparable standard.[[1]](#_ftn1)

The new law requires disclosure of a data breach “within **30 calendar days** of discovery or notification of the data breach,” unless one of two exceptions apply. (Cal. Civil Code Section § 1798.82(a)(2).) California joins five other states with a 30-day notification deadline (including Colorado, Florida, Maine, New York, Washington).[[2]](#_ftn2)

Under the new law, delayed notification is permitted under two exceptions: (1) “to accommodate the legitimate needs of law enforcement” or (2) as “necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore the reasonable integrity of the data system.” The statute recognizes that law enforcement may need to pursue an investigation without any disclosure about the data breach. Additionally, in warranted circumstances, the new law retains the same recognition and standard in place since 2003 that additional time may be needed to confirm “the scope of the breach and restore the reasonable integrity of the data system.” The new law builds on the existing statutory framework with mandatory deadlines.

**Change in California Attorney General Notification**Since 2012, California law has required notification to the California Attorney General of a data breach when notification was made “to more than 500 California residents as a result of a single breach of the security system.”[[3]](#_ftn3) The law did not provide a deadline for this notice.

Under the new law, disclosure of a data breach will be required to the California Attorney General “**within 15 days** of notifying affected consumers of the security breach” when more than 500 California residents have been notified. (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(f).)

State Senator Melissa Hurtado, the author of SB 446, [explained](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billAnalysisClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB446) that the absence of specific notification deadlines under current law means that:

affected individuals may not be informed for months—or even a year or more later—delaying their ability to take preventive measures …. By closing a critical loophole in California’s data protection laws, SB 446 upholds transparency and accountability while ensuring that residents are not left in the dark about threats to their data. Californians deserve the right to act swiftly when their personal information is compromised, and this bill provides the necessary framework to protect them.

The new statutory deadlines are intended to promote timely notification.

**Model Security Breach Notification Form**California retains is unique “[model security breach notification form](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billCompareClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB446&showamends=false)” included in the data breach statute. (*See* Cal. Civil Code Section 1798.82(d).) The “plain language” notification incudes the title, “Notice of Data Breach,” with the following headings:

* “What Happened?”
* “What Information Was Involved?”
* “What We Are Doing”
* “What You Can Do”; and
* “For More Information.”

Other statutory details about the data breach include “the types of personal information that were or are reasonably believed to have been the subject of a breach,” “a general description of the breach incident, if that information is possible to determine at the time the notice is provided,” and whether “identity theft prevention and mitigation services” will be provided, among other matters.

**Data Breach Risks and Costs**The costs of responding to a data breach remain high. According to the most recent IBM [Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025](https://www.ibm.com/downloads/documents/us-en/131cf87b20b31c91), at 11, “Average breach costs in the United States reached a record USD 10.22 million, a 9% increase over last year, driven in part by higher regulatory fines and detection and escalation costs.” While this does not apply to each data breach, it shows the costs of large data breaches and that costs continue to rise.

Where a data breach may impact residents in more than one state, many investigations are conducted by more than one regulator. A recent survey of more than 220 cases and settlements, 35 enforcement letters, and 20 public investigations during 2020–2024, found that, “Over 90% of the data breach enforcement actions were brought collaboratively as Multistate efforts.” *See* State Attorneys General & Privacy: Enforcement Trends, 2020–2024, at 3 (Oct. 2025).

Enforcement actions based on non-compliance with data breach notification standards have resulted in substantial penalties. For example, in August the New York Department of Financial Services [imposed a **$2 million** fine](https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/NYDFS-Penalty-Cybersecurity-Regs.html) for failure to notify within 72 hours of a cybersecurity event, among other non-compliance issues. Also in August, the Massachusetts Attorney General’s Office obtained a [**$795,000** fine](https://www.mass.gov/news/ag-campbell-reaches-795000-settlement-with-property-management-company-for-failing-to-protect-the-personal-information-of-thousands-of-massachusetts-residents) after a property management company “unlawfully delay[ed] required data breach notifications” and “fail[ed] to adequately protect the personal information.”

Enforcers also review the sufficiency and accuracy of the data breach notification. For example, last year, the California Attorney General obtained a [**$6.75 million** fine](https://oag.ca.gov/news/press-releases/attorney-general-bonta-secures-675-million-settlement-against-blackbaud-over) from a software company for misleading “the public of the full impact of the data breach.”

**Next Steps for Businesses**Based on the new requirements, companies can review and update their incident response plans to ensure compliance with the new timelines along with other federal and state notification deadlines. Contracts should be reviewed with third-party service providers to ensure timely cyber incident reporting. Legal guidance from experienced counsel can assist in reviewing the sufficiency and accuracy of any data breach notifications and assisting to mitigate risk in litigation and regulatory enforcement.

This is a legal alert from Pillsbury Law (by Mark L. Krotoski and Alexandria Marx, dated October 31, 2025) announcing that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill No. 446 into law on October 3, 2025, making significant changes to California's data breach notification statute, effective January 1, 2026. The law passed with no votes in opposition.

Key changes:
1. Businesses and government agencies must notify affected California residents "within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the data breach" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(a)(2)), joining five other states with 30-day deadlines (Colorado, Florida, Maine, New York, Washington). Previously, California required notification "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay."
2. Two exceptions permit delayed notification: (1) to accommodate legitimate needs of law enforcement, or (2) as necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore reasonable integrity of the data system.
3. If a breach affects more than 500 California residents, a sample copy of the consumer notification must be provided to the California Attorney General "within 15 days of notifying affected consumers" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(f)). Previously, no deadline existed for this notice.

Background context: California was the first state to enact a data breach notification statute in 2002. Since then, all 50 states and four U.S. jurisdictions (DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, Virgin Islands) have enacted their own requirements. Thirty other states have a similar "most expedient time possible" standard.

The statute retains California's unique "model security breach notification form" with headings including "What Happened?", "What Information Was Involved?", "What We Are Doing", "What You Can Do", and "For More Information."

Cost/risk data: According to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, average breach costs in the U.S. reached a record $10.22 million, a 9% increase over the prior year. A survey of 220+ cases from 2020-2024 found over 90% of data breach enforcement actions were brought collaboratively as multistate efforts. Examples of enforcement penalties include a $2 million NYDFS fine for failure to notify within 72 hours of a cybersecurity event, a $795,000 Massachusetts AG fine for delayed notifications, and a $6.75 million California AG fine against a software company for misleading the public about a breach.

Senator Melissa Hurtado (SB 446 author) stated the law closes a loophole because affected individuals "may not be informed for months—or even a year or more later—delaying their ability to take preventive measures."

Next steps for businesses: update incident response plans for the new timelines, review contracts with third-party service providers for timely cyber incident reporting, and obtain legal guidance on notification sufficiency and accuracy.

## Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security Act (SHIELD Act)

### What is the significance of this law?

The SHIELD Act, signed into law on July 25, 2019, by Governor Andrew Cuomo, amends New York’s 2005 Information Security Breach and Notification Act. The SHIELD Act significantly strengthens New York’s data-security laws by:

* expanding the types of private information for which companies must provide consumer notice in the event of a breach
* requiring that companies develop, implement, and maintain reasonable safeguards to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of the private information

### What types of security breaches are covered by this law?

Under the 2005 law, a security breach is defined as an unauthorized acquisition of computerized data that compromises the security, confidentiality, or integrity of private information. The SHIELD Act expands the definition of a security breach to any "access" to computerized data that compromises the confidentiality, security, or integrity of private data.

### What does private information consist of?

Under the 2005 law, private information was any personal information concerning a natural person in combination with any one or more of the following data elements in combination any required security code:

* Social Security number
* driver’s license number
* account number

The SHIELD Act expands the law to include biometric information, username or email address, and password credentials.

### What safeguards are included in the SHIELD Act?

The SHIELD Act requires any person or business that maintains private information to adopt administrative, technical, and physical safeguards. The act lists some safeguards, but is not meant to be an exhaustive list.

### Reasonable administrative safeguards include:

* designating one or more employees to coordinate the security program
* identifying reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks
* assessing the sufficiency of safeguards in place to control the identified risks
* training and managing employees in the security program's practices and procedures
* selecting service providers capable of maintaining appropriate safeguards, and requiring those safeguards by contract
* adjusting the security program in light of business changes or new circumstances

### Reasonable technical safeguards include:

* assessing risks in network and software design
* assessing risks in information processing, transmission and storage
* detecting, preventing, and responding to attacks or system failures
* regularly testing and monitoring the effectiveness of key controls, systems, and procedures

### Reasonable physical safeguards include:

* assessing risks of information storage and disposal
* detecting, preventing, and responding to intrusions
* protecting against unauthorized access to or use of private information during or after the collection, transportation, and destruction or disposal of information
* disposing of private information within a reasonable amount of time after it is no longer needed for business purposes by erasing electronic media so that the information cannot be read or reconstructed

### What are the obligations of businesses when a breach occurs?

The law requires that the person or business notify the affected consumers after discovering a breach in the security of its computer data system that affects private information. The disclosure must be made in the most expedient time possible, consistent with legitimate needs of law enforcement agencies. While the law requires notice to the Office of the New York State Attorney General (OAG), the New York Department of State, and the New York State Police of the timing, content, and distribution of the notices and approximate number of affected persons, submission of a breach form through the OAG's data-breach-reporting portal is sufficient, as the information is automatically sent to all three credit reporting entities listed below.

#### EQUIFAX

 Atlanta GA 30348

 [www.equifax.com](https://www.equifax.com)

 [www.transunion.com](https://www.transunion.com)

If you are a consumer affected by a breach, [file a complaint](https://formsnym.ag.ny.gov/OAGOnlineSubmissionForm/faces/OAGBITHome). Do not submit a breach notification.

### Are there any exceptions to the notification requirements?

The law also provides for substitute notice to consumers if the business demonstrates to the Office of the New York State Attorney General that:

* the cost of providing regular notice would exceed $250,000
* the affected class of persons exceeds 500,000
* the entity or business does not have sufficient contact information

Where substitute notice is used, it must consist of all of the following, as applicable:

* email notice
* conspicuous posting on the entity’s web site
* notification to statewide media

In addition, the law does not require consumer notification if:

* the exposure of private information was an inadvertent disclosure by persons authorized to access private information
* the person or business reasonably determines such exposure will not likely result in misuse of such information or financial harm to the affected persons, or in emotional harm in the case of unknown disclosure of online credentials

Such a determination must be documented in writing and maintained for at least five years. If the incident affects over 500 residents of New York, the person or business must provide the written determination to the Attorney General within 10 days after the determination.

### What are the penalties for violations of the SHIELD Act?

Under the SHIELD Act, the Attorney General may seek injunctive relief, restitution, and penalties against any business entity for violating the law. For failure to provide timely notification, the court may impose a civil penalty of up to $20 per instance of failed notification, not to exceed $250,000. For failure to maintain reasonable safeguards, the court may impose a civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Zscaler (Zpedia) explains the SEC's new cybersecurity disclosure rules announced on July 26, 2023, which apply to public companies. The rules mandate timely disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents and annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance.

**Key Requirements:**
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Material cybersecurity incidents must be reported within four business days of a materiality determination. A new, broader definition of "cybersecurity incident" now includes "a series of related unauthorized occurrences."
- **Temporary Delay:** Companies may delay disclosure up to 120 days (with US Attorney General approval and SEC consent) if disclosure poses national security or public safety risks.
- **Updated Incident Disclosures:** Incomplete Form 8-K data must be acknowledged and later amended within four business days of obtaining missing information.
- **Form 10-K (Regulation S-K Item 106):** Annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and board oversight is required. Companies must describe management's role and responsibilities but are NOT required to disclose board members' cybersecurity expertise.
- **Foreign Private Issuers:** Must file comparable disclosures on Forms 6-K and 20-F.
- **Structured Data:** Disclosures must be tagged in Inline XBRL format, though compliance was delayed by one year.

**Effective Dates and Compliance Timelines:**
- Rules became effective September 5, 2023.
- Larger public companies must comply with Form 8-K Item 1.05 by December 15, 2023.
- Smaller reporting companies have until June 24, 2024, for Item 1.05 compliance.
- Item 106 applies to annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.

**Compliance Preparation Steps:** Review rules with security/filing teams, establish materiality determination processes, draft cyber risk assessment descriptions, engage board of directors in cyber risk oversight, and identify board members with cybersecurity expertise.

**Materiality Definition:** An incident is material if it significantly impacts operations, finances, or reputation, based on quantitative factors (costs) and qualitative factors (reputational damage, litigation exposure).

The page also promotes Zscaler Risk360™ as a tool for cyber risk quantification, financial exposure detail, and board-ready reporting to help companies comply with the new rules.
</summary>

**Source:** Deloitte Heads Up, Volume 30, Issue 13

### Background
On July 26, 2023, the SEC issued a final rule requiring registrants to provide enhanced and standardized disclosures regarding cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incidents. **1. Material Cybersecurity Incidents (Form 8-K, Item 1.05)**
- Registrants must file a Form 8-K within four business days of determining a cybersecurity incident is material.
- A cybersecurity incident is defined as "an unauthorized occurrence, or a series of related unauthorized occurrences, on or conducted through a registrant's information systems that jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of a registrant's information systems or any information residing therein."
- Required disclosures include: material aspects of the nature, scope, timing of the incident, and the material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant (including financial condition and results of operations).
- Amended Form 8-K must be filed within four business days if information becomes available later or previously disclosed information is inaccurate.

**2. Materiality Assessment**
- Materiality determinations must be made "without unreasonable delay."
- Materiality is consistent with U.S. Supreme Court standards (TSC Industries, Basic, Matrixx).
- Factors include: probability of adverse outcome, potential significance of loss, nature and extent of harm to individuals, customers, vendor relationships, reputation, and competitiveness.
- Erik Gerding (SEC Division of Corporation Finance director) clarified that materiality may not be determined on the same date the incident occurred.

**3. Temporary Delay for National Security**
- The U.S. Attorney General may determine that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety.
- Initial delay: up to 30 days; secondary delay: additional 30 days; final extraordinary circumstances: up to 60 days; further delays via SEC exemptive order.
- The FBI provided guidance on requesting delays, noting early outreach is critical.

**4. Risk Management, Strategy, and Governance (Form 10-K, Item 1C)**
- Registrants must disclose processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats.
- Disclosures required on: integration into overall risk management, use of third-party assessors, and oversight of third-party service provider risks.
- **Board oversight:** Description of board's oversight of cybersecurity risks, identification of responsible committees, and processes for informing the board.
- **Management responsibilities:** Which positions/committees are responsible, their relevant expertise, processes for monitoring incidents, and reporting to the board.

### Transition Provisions
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Effective December 18, 2023 (all registrants except smaller reporting companies); June 15, 2024 (smaller reporting companies).
- **Regulation S-K Item 106 (Form 10-K):** Effective for annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.
- Inline XBRL tagging required one year after initial compliance dates.

### Changes from Proposed Rule
- Narrowed scope of cyber incident disclosures with added national security delay.
- Amended Form 8-K used instead of Forms 10-Q/10-K for updates.
- Aggregation of immaterial incidents removed (but series of related unauthorized occurrences may still require Form 8-K).
- Removed proposed requirement to disclose cybersecurity expertise of the board.
- Added transition provisions.

### All filers affected
Including domestic registrants, foreign private issuers (FPIs), smaller reporting companies, and emerging growth companies.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 18, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York dismissed most of the SEC's landmark cyber enforcement litigation against SolarWinds Corp. and its Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) Timothy Brown. In a 107-page opinion in Securities and Exchange Commission v. SolarWinds Corp. & Timothy G. Brown (Judge Paul Engelmayer presiding), the court rejected the SEC's efforts to expand the Securities Exchange Act's "internal accounting controls" provision to encompass cybersecurity controls. The court also limited the SEC's use of the "disclosure controls and procedure" provision, finding that innocent errors are "an inadequate basis" on which to plead deficient disclosure controls. Only a subset of material misrepresentation claims related to the Security Statement published on the company's website survived, and the case proceeds toward discovery.

BACKGROUND: SolarWinds, a software company with the Orion Platform, posted a Security Statement on its website in late 2017. In January 2019, nation-state hackers exploited a vulnerability and inserted malicious code into Orion software builds - known as the SUNBURST attack. In 2020, SolarWinds was notified by the USTP and Palo Alto Networks of suspicious activity but couldn't determine the root cause. After Mandiant identified the malicious code, SolarWinds filed a Form 8-K on Dec. 14, 2020, detailing the attack. The SEC filed its complaint in 2023 and an amended complaint on Feb. 16, 2024, charging violations of antifraud provisions, disclosure controls, and internal controls.

KEY COURT RULINGS: 1) Internal Accounting Controls: The court found the SEC "clearly correct" to be challenged on the plain language of Section 13(b), holding that "cybersecurity controls are outside the scope of Section 13(b)(2)(B)" and dismissing the claim entirely. 2) Disclosure Controls: The court dismissed this claim, finding "[w]ithout more, the existence of two misclassified incidents is an inadequate basis on which to plead deficient disclosure controls," and that "second-guessing by hindsight" is disfavored. 3) Security Statement: The court found the SEC sufficiently alleged material misrepresentations concerning access controls and password protection policies on the company's public website. 4) Cyber Risk Disclosures: Dismissed, as fraud claims based on risk disclosures are actionable only where "the warned risk has already occurred." 5) Brown's public statements: Found to be "non-actionable corporate puffery." 6) Form 8-K disclosures: Dismissed as fraud by hindsight; the court found the Form 8-K "captured the big picture: the severity of the SUNBURST attack," noting the stock dropped 16% on filing day and 8% the next day.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The SEC failed to expand internal accounting controls to cover cybersecurity. The SEC must now allege systemic deficiencies (not innocent errors) for disclosure controls violations. Cyber risk disclosure fraud claims are limited to narrow circumstances where the warned risk has already occurred. Courts will consider practical time constraints (including the SEC Cybersecurity Rules' four-business-day disclosure requirement) when assessing Form 8-K filings. Companies should avoid warning about risks that have already occurred, and risk disclosures should convey severity without arming threat actors.

SUGGESTED ACTION ITEMS for issuers: 1) Develop well-designed disclosure controls and incident response plans. 2) Include risk disclosures that convey manner and severity without providing a road map to threat actors. 3) Have a practiced plan for responding to cyber incidents. 4) Engage experienced cybersecurity counsel. This Holland & Knight analysis was authored by Shardul Desai, Allison Kernisky, and Jessica B. Magee on July 24, 2024.
</summary>

- **"Fog of war"**: In the chaotic first hours after a breach, organizations must assess incident significance in hours, not weeks

3. **Rich forensics**: Detailed logs of every connection attempt, blocked lateral movement, and policy action strengthen CIRCIA reports

Key points of the Updated Advisory include:

- **Continued Opposition to Ransomware Payments**: OFAC maintains that the U.S. government "strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands" and recommends focusing on defensive and resilience measures. - **New Mitigating Factors**: The Updated Advisory identifies two significant mitigating factors in any OFAC enforcement response:
  1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps taken to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices, such as those in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide (co-developed with MS-ISAC), will be considered a "significant mitigating factor."
  2. **Notification and Cooperation with U.S. Government**: Promptly reporting ransomware attacks to law enforcement, CISA, Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection (OCCIP), or other relevant agencies, along with ongoing cooperation (including providing technical details, ransom payment demands, and payment instructions), constitutes a "significant mitigating factor." The article was authored by Covington & Burling LLP attorneys Ashden Fein, Peter Flanagan, Jim Garland, Mike Nonaka, and Moriah Daugherty. On July 15, 2024, the SEC Division of Corporation Finance, through Director Erik Gerding, issued additional guidance clarifying cybersecurity incident disclosure rules under the SEC's July 26, 2023 rules (effective December 18, 2023), which require public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents within four business days under Item 1.05 of Form 8-K.

Two key guidance statements were issued:

1. **May 21, 2024 Guidance** ("Disclosure of Cybersecurity Incidents Determined To Be Material and Other Cybersecurity Incidents"): Clarified that Item 1.05 is exclusively reserved for incidents deemed material. Non-material incidents, or those still under investigation, should be voluntarily disclosed under Item 8.01 (Other Events) of Form 8-K instead. The guidance warned that filing under Item 1.05 before a materiality determination risks confusing investors. If a company discloses an immaterial incident under Item 8.01 but later determines it is material, it must file an Item 1.05 Form 8-K within four business days of that subsequent determination.

2. **June 20, 2024 Guidance** ("Selective Disclosure of Information Regarding Cybersecurity Incidents"): Addressed Regulation FD concerns, clarifying that Item 1.05 does not prohibit private discussion of material incidents with vendors, customers, and other affected parties beyond what was disclosed in the Form 8-K. Such sharing is valuable for "remediation, mitigation, or risk avoidance efforts." Regulation FD exclusions may apply if the information is immaterial, if recipients are not covered persons, if recipients owe a duty of trust or confidence (e.g., attorneys, investment bankers, accountants), or if recipients enter into confidentiality agreements.

The guidance aims to preserve the value of Item 1.05 disclosures and prevent investor confusion between material and immaterial incidents. A "material" incident is defined as one where there is a "substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important in making an investment decision, or if it would have significantly altered the 'total mix' of information made available." The disclosure must describe the material aspects of the nature, scope, timing, and anticipated impact of the incident. Further SEC guidance is expected as the rules continue to evolve. The memorandum was authored by David Owen (Partner) and Ken Ritz (Associate) at Cahill law firm.

**Joint Computer-Security Incident Notification Rule** (issued by OCC, FRB, and FDIC; 86 Fed. Reg. 66,424, Nov. 23, 2021):

- **Computer-security incident** is defined as an occurrence that results in actual harm to an information system or the information contained within it.
- **Bank service provider** is defined as a bank service company or other person who performs "covered services" (services subject to the Bank Service Company Act, 12 U.S.C. 1861-1867).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page explains the proposed HIPAA Security Rule update (still NOT final as of mid-2026), which would represent the most significant change since the rule's original 2003 adoption. The NPRM was published in the Federal Register on January 6, 2025; the comment period closed March 7, 2025; and OCR has not issued a final rule. OMB's Unified Agenda (RIN 0945-AA22) now targets July 2027 for final action (pushed back from an earlier spring 2026 target), though these timelines are not legally binding.

Key proposed changes include: (1) mandatory annual Security Risk Assessments (the current rule has no specified frequency); (2) mandatory encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit, removing the "addressable" designation; (3) required multi-factor authentication for all systems accessing ePHI; (4) regular vulnerability scanning and penetration testing; (5) enhanced documentation requirements; and (6) comprehensive technology asset inventory and network mapping. The proposed rule would also require annual BAA verification (documenting the verification itself, not just keeping the BAA on file) and a 240-day implementation runway (60 days effective plus 180 days to compliance).

HHS estimated $9 billion in year-one costs and $34 billion across years one through five. In February 2025, CHIME joined seven other associations and 100+ hospital/provider organizations in a letter asking the Trump administration to withdraw the proposal, arguing small and rural providers cannot absorb these costs. HHS retained the July 2027 target despite pushback but signaled willingness to credit good-faith, phased compliance from critical access hospitals and safety-net providers.

The January 2026 OCR Cybersecurity Newsletter emphasized: system hardening as a documented expectation (patch management, default-credential elimination, configuration baselines), evolution from risk analysis to risk management (requiring timely documented remediation, not just an assessment document), and that risk analysis must surface unpatched-software and firmware vulnerabilities (45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)).

The page provides a preparation timeline: gap analysis, SRA, asset inventory, encryption assessment, and MFA planning through mid-2026; encryption deployment, MFA rollout, vulnerability scanning, documentation updates, and training through December 2026; then ongoing annual SRA cycles, continuous vulnerability management (critical patches within 72 hours, scans at least quarterly), and compliance monitoring. Common mistakes warned against: waiting for the final rule, treating compliance as purely a technology project, underestimating documentation requirements, ignoring business associate compliance, and trying to do everything at once. OCR continues to enforce the current Security Rule, under which risk analysis remains the most-frequently-cited deficiency.

- 635 SARs and 458 transactions related to ransomware were filed between January 1 and June 30, 2021, a 42% increase from 2020 (when 487 SARs covering $416 million were received).

--- SOURCE 29: Ransomware Attacks—Financial Crimes Compliance Requirements ---
URL: https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/client-alerts/20201008-ransomware-attacks-financial-crimes-compliance-requirements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a client alert from the law firm WilmerHale, authored by partners Jason C. Chipman and David M. Horn, analyzing two US government advisories issued on October 1, 2020, addressing the risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments: the OFAC Ransomware Advisory (regarding potential sanctions risks) and the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory (FIN-2020-A006, regarding ransomware and use of the financial system for ransom payments). These represented the first time OFAC and FinCEN issued guidance specifically addressing ransomware payments, which increased in demand during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The advisories identify two main areas of regulatory risk:
1. Violation of OFAC's sanctions regulations – OFAC may impose civil penalties based on strict liability (a person may be held civilly liable even without knowledge), particularly because ransomware attackers can obscure their identity and some are linked to sanctioned actors (e.g., North Korean government and Russian cybercriminals). Ransomware typically involves convertible virtual currency (CVC), which further obscures payouts. Where attackers are known targets of sanctions, OFAC reviews license applications "on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial."
2. Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing requirements for financial institutions – institutions may be required to file SARs whether they are victims of ransomware attacks or merely processing payments for victimized clients. The FinCEN advisory provides specific SAR filing instructions to reference the advisory.

The advisories also apply to cyber insurance, digital forensics, and incident response firms, which should maintain compliance programs and may face money transmission registration requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act and state money transmission laws. Both advisories encourage cooperation with law enforcement; OFAC considers a "self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement" as a significant mitigating factor in enforcement outcomes.

The FinCEN Advisory identifies five trends of ransomware attacks: (1) "big-game hunting" targeting larger enterprises for bigger payouts; (2) sharing of resources and partnerships among cybercriminals; (3) "double extortion schemes" involving data theft and threats to publish; (4) use of anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies (AECs) with discounted rates for AEC payments; and (5) "fileless" ransomware using malicious code in system memory. FinCEN also identified red-flag indicators for financial institutions, including transactions with digital forensics firms known to make ransom payments, rapid back-to-back cryptocurrency movements, accounts lacking obvious connection to customer business, "chain-hopping" techniques, and transactions with exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

While the advisories create no new legal requirements, they indicate that OFAC and FinCEN expect risk-based compliance programs and a high level of coordination with law enforcement. Failure to report attacks to law enforcement may increase exposure to OFAC monetary penalties. Companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture.
</summary>

URL: https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-issues-financial-trend-analysis-ransomware

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued a Financial Trend Analysis (FTA) on ransomware incidents reported in Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) data between 2022 and 2024, totaling more than $2.1 billion in ransomware payments. Unlike previous analyses that focused on filing dates, this report shifts focus to the actual incident dates of each ransomware attack, providing greater visibility into ransomware actor activities.

Key findings include:
- Ransomware incidents and payments reached an all-time high in 2023 with 1,512 incidents totaling $1.1 billion in payments (a 77% year-over-year increase from 2022); incidents decreased to 1,476 in 2024 following law enforcement disruptions of two high-profile ransomware groups, reflecting $734 million in aggregate payments.
- Median single ransomware transaction amounts: $124,097 (2022), $175,000 (2023), and $155,257 (2024). The most common payment range was below $250,000.
- During the three-year review period (January 2022–December 2024), FinCEN received 7,395 BSA reports related to 4,194 ransomware incidents totaling over $2.1 billion. By comparison, the previous nine-year period (2013–2021) saw 3,075 reports totaling approximately $2.4 billion.
- Most impacted industries: manufacturing (456 incidents, ~$284.6 million), financial services (432 incidents, ~$365.6 million), and healthcare (389 incidents, ~$305.4 million).
- The Onion Router (TOR) was the most common communication method used by threat actors (67% of reports specifying a method); others used email or private encrypted messaging.
- More than 200 ransomware variants were identified; the most reported variants were Akira, ALPHV/BlackCat, LockBit, Phobos, and Black Basta. The top 10 variants by payment amounts accounted for approximately $1.5 billion in payments.

The report is available online, and FinCEN provides additional ransomware resources at www.fincen.gov/resources/fincen-combats-ransomware. The FTA fulfills obligations under section 6206 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020.

This webpage from the Society of Chemical Manufacturers & Affiliates (SOCMA) provides information about the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program and SOCMA's advocacy efforts regarding it.

**About CFATS:** CFATS is the nation's first regulatory program focused specifically on security at high-risk chemical facilities. Managed by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), it identifies and regulates high-risk facilities to reduce the risk that dangerous chemicals could be weaponized by terrorists. Under CFATS, a chemical facility is any establishment or individual that possesses (or plans to possess) any of the more than 300 chemicals of interest (COI) listed in Appendix A at or above the screening threshold quantity (STQ) and concentration.

2. SOCMA and other associations sent a letter to Senate Leadership urging inclusion of the CFATS Program in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) Fiscal Year 2024.
3. In the wake of the CFATS lapse, DHS has pointed individuals to ChemLock's voluntary resources that remain available during the program lapse.

**Contact:** Robert Helminiak, Vice President of Legal & Government Relations, at government.relations@socma.org, is the contact for CFATS-related issues.

--- SOURCE 2: Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) Update — American Coatings Association ---
URL: https://www.paint.org/aca-advocacy/enhancing-chemical-security-and-cfats

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The American Coatings Association (ACA) webpage provides an update on the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program as of April 9, 2024. 

**Background:** CFATS was developed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in November 2007 to prevent chemicals of interest from being stolen, diverted, sabotaged, or deliberately released by terrorists. Under the program, facilities possessing threshold amounts of specific explosive, toxic, or other chemicals of interest must submit a "top-screen" to DHS. DHS can then require a Security Vulnerability Assessment (SVA), which determines the facility's tier (Tiers 1-2 highest risk, Tiers 3-4 lowest). Tier assignment triggers a Site Security Plan (SSP) or Alternative Security Plan (ASP) requirement. As of July 2023, approximately 3,200 chemical facilities were covered under CFATS. The program's statutory authorization lapsed on July 27, 2023, after Congress allowed it to expire.

**ACA Action:** Many ACA member facilities are subject to CFATS, with a clear majority classified as Tier 4 and a few as Tier 3. ACA has strongly supported CFATS reauthorization. In July 2023, ACA sent letters to Congressional leadership urging immediate reauthorization. The U.S. House passed H.R. 4470 on a 409-1 vote to extend authorization for two years, but the companion Senate bill (S. 2499) did not advance, and a motion to consider the House bill was blocked in the Senate on July 26, 2023.

**After Expiration:** The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) suspended all enforcement and compliance assistance activities and suspended requirements for facilities to maintain site security plans and report chemicals of interest. CISA encouraged facilities to maintain security measures voluntarily and promoted its ChemLock initiative (a toolkit of on-site assessments, exercise packages, training, and guidance). Without reauthorization, chemical sector security now relies mainly on voluntary public-private partnerships. ACA is actively working with Congress, DHS, and trade associations to swiftly reinstate the program.

**ACA Staff Contacts:** Rhett Cash (Counsel, Government Affairs) and Heidi K. McAuliffe (Vice President, Government Affairs).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"CFATS provides a uniform, national program for regulating chemical security. Continuity of this framework provides the certainty required for the considerable planning and investment decisions that are needed to protect both our facilities and the surrounding communities. Allowing CFATS to expire would open the door for agencies with no anti-terrorism expertise to fill the void, or a patchwork of state and local regulations that may vary widely in scope and effectiveness. This could result in inconsistent anti-terrorism standards across the country and could undermine national security."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 6: Water Utilities: Congress Temporarily Extends Cyber Laws, EPA Releases New Guidance ---
URL: https://www.nossaman.com/newsroom-insights-water-utilities-congress-temporarily-extends-cyber-laws-epa-releases-new-guidance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a law firm (Nossaman LLP) article discussing recent federal developments in water utility cybersecurity. On November 12, 2025, President Trump signed a bipartisan funding package that reopened the federal government after a six-week shutdown and temporarily reinstated two cybersecurity authorities that expired on September 30: the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 (CISA Act) and the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP), both extended through January 30, 2026. The reinstatement restores liability protections, reestablishes real-time cyber threat information sharing, and ensures continued access to federal cybersecurity funding for drinking water and wastewater utilities.

On October 23, 2025, the EPA released an updated suite of cybersecurity and emergency planning tools, including a revised Emergency Response Plan (ERP) guide, a Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan (CIRP) template, incident-specific checklists, and a cybersecurity procurement checklist. This is part of EPA's broader "Powering the Great American Comeback" strategy and builds on the agency's August 2025 announcement of over $9 million in grant funding for midsize and large water systems. The guidance emphasizes a two-pronged approach: updating risk and resilience assessments to include cybersecurity threats and incorporating findings into updated ERPs. Key recommended actions include reducing internet exposure, changing default passwords, performing regular cybersecurity assessments, developing manual operation procedures for automated systems, securing Human-Machine Interfaces, completing asset inventories, and conducting regular training and exercises.

Background context notes a 2024 GAO report (GAO-24-106744) finding nearly 170,000 U.S. water systems face cyber risks, and a 2024 EPA Inspector General report (25-N-0004) identifying critical or high-severity vulnerabilities in 97 drinking water systems serving 27 million people. Challenges include outdated software, unsupported operating systems, inadequate network segmentation, and limited monitoring capacity. Key timeline details: CIRCIA was signed into law in March 2022, representing CISA's most significant regulatory expansion to date. CISA published its Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) in April 2024, outlining sector-based and size-based criteria across 16 critical infrastructure sectors. After extensive public feedback, CISA missed its initial October 2025 statutory deadline and revised its target to May 2026. A lapse in Department of Homeland Security appropriations postponed stakeholder engagement, with virtual town hall sessions rescheduled to June 2026, where over 1,200 industry representatives participated.

The proposed size-based criteria will capture any organization exceeding Small Business Administration standards within the 16 critical infrastructure sectors. The alert emphasizes significant compliance challenges for multinational enterprises and healthcare systems already navigating GDPR, HIPAA, or SEC cybersecurity rules, noting increased regulatory overlap. Organizations must use the remaining months to audit third-party vendor risks, update data governance frameworks, and test cross-departmental communication channels between CISOs, legal counsel, and compliance leaders. CISA is currently streamlining requirements and preparing final regulations for release in fall 2026.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"CIRCIA turns incident reporting into as much a data visibility problem as a cybersecurity problem. A 72-hour deadline leaves little time to determine which systems were affected, what sensitive data they held, who owned it, and whether the incident meets the reporting threshold. Organizations that wait for an attack to answer those questions will spend critical hours searching for basic facts. Readiness starts before the incident—with current data inventories, ownership, retention policies and tested escalation paths. When an event occurs, digital forensics can then establish what happened, preserve defensible evidence and support accurate reporting. Data governance provides the map; incident response determines where the damage occurred." — Robert Bond, Product Marketing Manager, Digital Forensics, Exterro

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Privacy Rights Clearinghouse published the "Data Breach Notification Laws: A 50-State Survey (2026 Edition)" on January 28, 2026. This comprehensive survey analyzes and compares data breach notification laws across all 50 U.S. states plus the District of Columbia, reflecting statutes enacted as of January 1, 2026. The survey uses a standardized framework of 50 questions applied to 51 jurisdictions, examining notification timing, covered data types, notification recipients, enforcement mechanisms, and consumer remedies. A full PDF report (4.45 MB) and an interactive map are available for state-by-state analysis and comparison.

Key findings from the survey include:
- Notification Timing: 20 states (39%) specify numeric deadlines ranging from 30 to 60 days. Specifically, 30-day deadlines exist in California, Colorado, Florida, New York, and Washington; 45-day deadlines in Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Vermont, and Wisconsin; and 60-day deadlines in Connecticut, Delaware, Louisiana, South Dakota, and Texas. The remaining 31 states use qualitative language such as "without unreasonable delay."
- Personal Information Coverage: 22 states explicitly cover biometric data; 24 states cover medical/health data; only 9 states (18%) cover paper record breaches.
- Transparency Gap: 36 states (71%) require entities to report breaches to the Attorney General or another state agency, but only 21 states make that data publicly accessible through searchable online portals.
- Consumer Remedies: 24 states (47%) provide a private right of action for breach notification violations; 6 states (12%) require free credit monitoring for affected consumers.

--- SOURCE 22: Data Breach Notification Laws by State (2026) | Deadlines & AG Thresholds | CyberRiskPolicy.com ---
URL: http://cyberriskpolicy.com/data-breach-notification-laws.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from CyberRiskPolicy.com provides a comprehensive plain-language reference guide to U.S. state and federal data breach notification laws, reviewed by C. Constantin Poindexter (CPCU, JD, MA, AFSB), an insurance/surety underwriting specialist since 1994, with statutes current as of early 2026.

Key points covered:

1. **Universal coverage**: All 50 states plus DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands now have data breach notification laws. Alabama and South Dakota were the last to adopt them in 2018, completing the patchwork.

2. **Deadlines**: Roughly 20 states set a numeric deadline of 30 to 60 days to notify affected individuals; the rest require notice "without unreasonable delay." For multi-state breaches, the strictest applicable clock governs. States with 30-day deadlines include California, Colorado, Florida, Maine, New Jersey, and Washington. States with 45-day deadlines include Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, Maryland, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Vermont, and Wisconsin. States with 60-day deadlines include Connecticut, Delaware, Louisiana, South Dakota, and Texas.

3. **Three notification audiences**: (a) Affected individuals (required in every state), (b) state attorneys general (required in ~36 states once a resident-count threshold is crossed, commonly 250, 500, or 1,000), and (c) consumer reporting agencies (typically required at 1,000+ residents per FACTA).

4. **Attorney-general thresholds**: Texas triggers at 250+ residents (within 30 days, filed to a public breach portal); California at 500+ (within 15 days of individual notice per SB 446, 2026); Colorado at 500+ (with individual notice); Oklahoma at 500+ (within 60 days of individual notice per SB 626, 2026); Indiana at 500+ (without unreasonable delay). In states like Texas, AG filings become searchable public records.

5. **Definition of personal information**: Every state covers name plus at least one of: SSN, driver's license/state-ID number, or financial account/payment-card number. Growing states expand coverage to medical/health info, biometrics, online credentials, and government-issued identifiers. Some states apply a risk-of-harm analysis.

6. **Substitute notice**: Allowed when direct contact isn't feasible (contact info unavailable, cost exceeds statutory ceiling commonly $50,000–$100,000, or very large affected populations) — a website posting plus statewide media notice.

7. **Federal overlays**: HIPAA/HITECH (health sector, notify HHS, media notice for 500+ in a state), GLBA (financial institutions), SEC Reg S-P (broker-dealers/investment companies), SEC public-company rule (Form 8-K disclosure within 4 business days of materiality), and CIRCIA (critical infrastructure — report to CISA within 72 hours, ransom payments within 24 hours; final rule pending 2026).

8. **2026 changes**: California's SB 446 (effective Jan 1, 2026) replaced "without unreasonable delay" with a hard 30-calendar-day deadline and requires AG notice within 15 days for 500+ affected Californians. Oklahoma's SB 626 expanded covered data to biometrics and government IDs and added AG notification for 500+ residents. Both track a trend toward shorter clocks and broader data definitions.

9. **Cyber insurance role**: Breach-response coverage funds the breach coach (privacy counsel), notification and call-center costs, credit monitoring/identity protection, and regulatory defense. Coverage is as much about the expert response team engaged at hour zero as the dollars.

10. **Frequently asked questions**: Confirms all 50 states require breach notification; deadlines vary by state (30–60 days fixed or "without unreasonable delay"); AG notification triggers at 250, 500, or 1,000 residents depending on state.

The page includes a disclaimer that it is plain-language reference material, not legal advice, and recommends verifying current statutes with qualified counsel and authoritative trackers like the IAPP state chart. It also promotes CyberRiskPolicy.com's cyber insurance offerings, including a downloadable coverage application and contact at (800) 373-2804.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 23: California tightens data breach notification timelines, imposes 30-day notice requirement | Data Protection Report ---
URL: https://www.dataprotectionreport.com/2025/11/california-tightens-data-breach-notification-timelines-imposes-30-day-notice-requirement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
California has signed into law Senate Bill No. 446, amending Section 1798.82 of its Civil Code (its data breach notification law) to require covered companies to notify affected California residents within 30 calendar days of discovery of a data breach. The amendment takes effect January 1, 2026.

Key points of the amendment:
- Replaces California's previous flexible "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" standard with a specific 30-day deadline.
- California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002, and as a leading privacy regulator, this move may prompt more states to adopt firm notice timelines.
- Several states already impose specific notice timeframes: New York (30 days), Texas (30 days), Colorado (30 days), Florida (30 days), and Delaware (60 days). Some states require notice to the attorney general simultaneously with or prior to notice to individuals—more stringent than California's requirement to notify the attorney general within 15 days of notice to individuals.
- In practice, many businesses make regulatory notices close in time to individual notices to address differing state obligations.

The authors (Annmarie Giblin and Susana Medeiros) offer a critical "take" on the change: shorter notice timelines do not necessarily improve notification outcomes. Even weeks after discovery, breach victims may not know the scope of impact, affected data types, or geographic residence of individuals—even with considerable investigative resources. While many state laws (including California's as amended) exempt disclosure where necessary to determine breach scope, this view is not universal. For example, the Connecticut Attorney General has clarified that Connecticut's 60-day notice requirement "runs from the date that a company becomes aware of suspicious activity, not the date it determines the full impact to personal information."

Companies in highly regulated sectors (critical infrastructure, insurance, banking) often face even shorter notice periods—as short as 72 hours—and regulators have fined companies for untimely reporting. The article advises companies to assess and update their incident response procedures, particularly for larger and more complex incidents, to meet shorter disclosure expectations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002 and since then, Section 1798.82 has required businesses and state agencies to notify individuals 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.' SB 446 replaces this flexible, reasonableness standard with a specific 30‑day deadline."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 24: California Imposes New Data Breach Notification Requirements ---
URL: https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/california-data-breach-notification-requirements.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a legal alert from Pillsbury Law (by Mark L. Krotoski and Alexandria Marx, dated October 31, 2025) announcing that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill No. 446 into law on October 3, 2025, making significant changes to California's data breach notification statute, effective January 1, 2026. The law passed with no votes in opposition.

Key changes:
1. Businesses and government agencies must notify affected California residents "within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the data breach" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(a)(2)), joining five other states with 30-day deadlines (Colorado, Florida, Maine, New York, Washington). Previously, California required notification "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay."
2. Two exceptions permit delayed notification: (1) to accommodate legitimate needs of law enforcement, or (2) as necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore reasonable integrity of the data system.
3. If a breach affects more than 500 California residents, a sample copy of the consumer notification must be provided to the California Attorney General "within 15 days of notifying affected consumers" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(f)). Previously, no deadline existed for this notice.

Background context: California was the first state to enact a data breach notification statute in 2002. Since then, all 50 states and four U.S. jurisdictions (DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, Virgin Islands) have enacted their own requirements. Thirty other states have a similar "most expedient time possible" standard.

The statute retains California's unique "model security breach notification form" with headings including "What Happened?", "What Information Was Involved?", "What We Are Doing", "What You Can Do", and "For More Information."

Cost/risk data: According to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, average breach costs in the U.S. reached a record $10.22 million, a 9% increase over the prior year. A survey of 220+ cases from 2020-2024 found over 90% of data breach enforcement actions were brought collaboratively as multistate efforts. Examples of enforcement penalties include a $2 million NYDFS fine for failure to notify within 72 hours of a cybersecurity event, a $795,000 Massachusetts AG fine for delayed notifications, and a $6.75 million California AG fine against a software company for misleading the public about a breach.

Senator Melissa Hurtado (SB 446 author) stated the law closes a loophole because affected individuals "may not be informed for months—or even a year or more later—delaying their ability to take preventive measures."

Next steps for businesses: update incident response plans for the new timelines, review contracts with third-party service providers for timely cyber incident reporting, and obtain legal guidance on notification sufficiency and accuracy.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: SHIELD Act | New York Attorney General ---
URL: https://ag.ny.gov/resources/organizations/data-breach-reporting/shield-act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Office of the New York Attorney General (AG) and provides a detailed overview of the Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security Act (SHIELD Act), which was signed into law on July 25, 2019, by Governor Andrew Cuomo. The SHIELD Act amends New York's 2005 Information Security Breach and Notification Act and significantly strengthens New York's data-security laws.

KEY PROVISIONS:
- Expands the types of private information for which companies must provide consumer notice in the event of a breach.
- Requires companies to develop, implement, and maintain reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect private information.

EXPANDED DEFINITIONS:
- Security breach: Expanded from "unauthorized acquisition" of computerized data to any "access" to computerized data that compromises confidentiality, security, or integrity of private data.
- Private information: Originally included Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and account numbers (in combination with required security codes). The SHIELD Act expands this to include biometric information, username or email address, and password credentials.

REQUIRED SAFEGUARDS:
- Administrative: designating employees to coordinate the security program, identifying foreseeable risks, assessing safeguards, training employees, selecting capable service providers with contractual safeguards, and adjusting the program as circumstances change.
- Technical: assessing risks in network/software design, information processing/transmission/storage, detecting/preventing/responding to attacks or system failures, and regularly testing key controls and systems.
- Physical: assessing risks of information storage and disposal, detecting/preventing/responding to intrusions, protecting against unauthorized access, and properly disposing of private information.

BREACH NOTIFICATION OBLIGATIONS:
- Businesses must notify affected consumers in the most expedient time possible, consistent with legitimate law enforcement needs.
- Notice must be provided to the OAG, NY Department of State, and NY State Police. Submitting a breach form through the OAG's data-breach-reporting portal is sufficient as it automatically sends the information to all three credit reporting entities (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion — contact info provided for each).
- Consumers affected by a breach should file a complaint (not a breach notification).

EXCEPTIONS TO NOTIFICATION:
- Substitute notice allowed if: cost of regular notice exceeds $250,000, affected class exceeds 500,000, or the entity lacks sufficient contact information. Substitute notice may consist of email, conspicuous website posting, and/or statewide media notification.
- Consumer notification not required for inadvertent disclosure by authorized persons if the business reasonably determines exposure will not likely result in misuse, financial harm, or emotional harm (in case of unknown online credential disclosure). Such determinations must be documented in writing and maintained for at least five years. If the incident affects over 500 NY residents, the written determination must be provided to the AG within 10 days.

PENALTIES:
- For failure to provide timely notification: civil penalty of up to $20 per instance of failed notification, not to exceed $250,000.
- For failure to maintain reasonable safeguards: civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation.
- The Attorney General may seek injunctive relief, restitution, and penalties for violations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The SHIELD Act, signed into law on July 25, 2019, by Governor Andrew Cuomo, amends New York's 2005 Information Security Breach and Notification Act."
</key_excerpts>

Client Alerts | November 3, 2025

# Final NYDFS Cybersecurity Rules Take Effect: What Financial Services Companies Must Do Now

[Christian M. Auty](https://www.steptoe.com/en/lawyers/christian-m-auty.html)

As of November 1, 2025, two critical updates to the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) Cybersecurity Regulation (the Cybersecurity Regulation or "Part 500") took effect for Financial Services Companies.[1](#_ftn1)

Covered Entities must now finalize implementation of two critical security components: (1) mandatory Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for nearly all Covered Entities in nearly all cases; and (2) development of a comprehensive, documented Asset Inventory Program.

### Background of the Cybersecurity Regulation

The NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation establishes a robust, principles-based framework designed to manage cyber risk in the state's financial sector.

The Cybersecurity Regulation governs "Covered Entities," defined as persons operating under or required to operate under a license, registration, charter, certificate, permit, accreditation or similar authorization under New York's Banking Law, Insurance Law or Financial Services Law.[2](#_ftn2)The Regulation's core requirements include annual risk assessments,[3](#_ftn3) written cybersecurity policies and procedures,[4](#_ftn4) data governance and CISO reporting requirements,[5](#_ftn5)access privilege and management controls,[6](#_ftn6)MFA,[7](#_ftn7) asset inventory and management,[8](#_ftn8)incident response and business continuity requirements,[9](#_ftn9)and an annual certification of compliance.[10](#_ftn10)

In November 2023, NYDFS's Second Amendment to Part 500 became effective, introducing enhanced obligations with new deadlines and thresholds. Key changes, for example, the 24-hour notification and explanation requirement for cyber extortion payments,[11](#_ftn11) were driven by lessons learned through enforcement and evolving global threats. The final requirements of this amendment took effect on November 1, 2025, and focus on strengthening foundational cyber practices for nearly all Covered Entities.

### Supervisory Context Under New DFS Leadership

The implementation of these amendments comes amid a leadership change at NYDFS. Following the departure of Superintendent Adrienne Harris, Kaitlin Asrow has been appointed as Acting Superintendent.

Under Acting Superintendent Asrow, NYDFS recently issued [guidance](https://www.dfs.ny.gov/industry-guidance/industry-letters/il20251021-guidance-managing-risks-third-party) reiterating that Covered Entities remain ultimately accountable for managing the cybersecurity risks posed by third-party vendors and cannot delegate this compliance responsibility.  This continuity in focus—holding Covered Entities accountable for supply chain security—is directly relevant to both the MFA and Asset Inventory requirements discussed below, particularly as they relate to third-party applications and cloud-based assets. NYDFS’s statement that regulated entities "are still ultimately accountable for protecting consumers and managing risk" underscores the need for thorough, contractual compliance with vendors and other third-party providers.[12](#_ftn12)

The stakes are high. Earlier this year, NYDFS entered into a consent order for alleged violations of Part 500, [resulting in a $2 million civil penalty](https://www.steptoe.com/en/news-publications/three-key-takeaways-from-the-ny-dfs-healthplex-settlement.html).[13](#_ftn13)

### Key Takeaways

Effective November 1, 2025, two major new requirements are mandatory for most Covered Entities:[14](#_ftn14)

**1. Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)**

The prior version of the Cybersecurity Regulation only mandated MFA for access to internal networks from outside the network; the amended rule significantly broadens this requirement. Covered Entities are now required to implement MFA for all individuals remotely accessing information systems from which data is accessed or to which data is provided, including remote access to third-party applications..

The net result is that MFA is required for virtually all remote access. Covered entities must ensure that their MFA program extends beyond just internal VPNs and includes:

* Cloud Applications: For example, access to services like Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, or other Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) providers; and
* Third-Party Vendors: Any third-party system or application used by the Covered Entity’s personnel (or third-party personnel) that provides access to the Covered Entity’s information or systems.

Many Covered Entities will already have these controls in place. Still, professionals in both compliance and security should work together to ensure that the scope of the Part 500 mandate aligns with their organization’s security posture.

The MFA requirement also reinforces that the Covered Entity is responsible for ensuring the security of its data, even when that data is being accessed via a third-party application. As noted above, the NYDFS has emphasized that Covered Entities cannot delegate responsibility for compliance to Third-Party Service Providers (TSPs).[16](#_ftn16) While a Covered Entity can rely on a TSP’s native MFA software (*e.g.,* in a SaaS platform), the Covered Entity retains the ultimate responsibility to ensure that the TSP’s MFA implementation meets the requirements of the Cybersecurity Regulation.

**2. Comprehensive Asset Inventory Program**

Covered Entities also must formalize their asset inventory into a documented and regularly maintained program,[17](#_ftn17)through written policies and procedures that provide for the creation and maintenance of a complete, accurate, and documented inventory of all information systems.[18](#_ftn18)

These policies must describe how assets are tracked—including ownership, classification or sensitivity, location, the date the application will no longer be supported, and recovery time objectives—as well as the frequency at which the inventory will be updated and validated. The Cybersecurity Regulation also calls for secure disposal of non-public information that is no longer necessary for business operations.[19](#_ftn19)

Simply having a list of assets is no longer sufficient. The compliance mandate shifted from a static list to a dynamic, documented program that formalizes the procedural steps for program creation and maintenance, details the responsible owner(s) for each asset’s information, the triggers for updates (*e.g.*, procurement or decommissioning), and the mechanism for validating the inventory’s accuracy. This includes hardware, software, cloud services, and network infrastructure, all tied to the sensitivity of the Non-Public Information (NPI) processed or stored.

### Our Take and Next Steps for Covered Entities

Steptoe recommends Covered Entities take or consider the following actions in light of the new requirements:

* **Scope and Implement MFA Broadly:**
  + Identify **every application and system** that stores, transmits, or processes NPI, regardless of whether it is hosted internally or by a third-party vendor (*e.g.*, Salesforce, document management systems).
  + Ensure MFA is mandatory for all access methods to these systems, prioritizing phishing-resistant MFA methods where feasible.[20](#_ftn20) For example, consider hardware security keys or FIDO2-compliant push notification authentication.
  + Review current third-party contracts to ensure the language requires third parties to support the Covered Entity’s MFA implementation.
* **Formalize the Asset Inventory Program:**
  + Design and update **written policies and procedures** for your Asset Inventory Program.
  + Confirm that the inventory tracking mechanism captures all required data points, including asset owner, data classification, network location, and maintenance/patch status.
  + Establish a periodic risk-based schedule (*e.g.*, quarterly, semi-annually) for validating the inventory and assign clear ownership roles for maintenance.
* **Validate Risk Assessment Alignment:**
  + Ensure your comprehensive Risk Assessment addresses all newly identified assets and access points.
* **Prepare for 2026 Certification:**
  + Compliance with these requirements must be included in the Annual Certification of Compliance due on **April 15, 2026**.

As the final NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation requirements are now in effect, Covered Entities should act swiftly to validate their compliance posture. **Steptoe’s cross-disciplinary team of cybersecurity, financial services, and regulatory attorneys is available to assist with implementation, risk assessments, and certification readiness.**Please contact us to discuss how we can support your organization’s compliance strategy under Part 500.
