In 2022, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced numerous settlements with cryptocurrency exchanges. These settlements serve as “fair warnings” to all cryptocurrency service providers who are “U.S. persons” or who offer services to U.S. persons. The term “U.S. persons” is defined in 31 C.F.R. §560.314 as “any United States citizen, permanent resident alien, entity organized under the laws of the United States or any jurisdiction within the United States (including foreign branches), or any person in the United States.”

This article focuses on these “fair warnings” as they have accumulated from prior settlements and from OFAC’s published guidance on compliance requirements that have been public for some time.

This article uses two late 2022 OFAC settlement announcements—with West-Coast-based Bittrex, Inc. and Payward, Inc. d/b/a Kraken—to make clear that OFAC was adhering to a previously announced requirement on providers of financial services. Specifically, OFAC requires more than verification of identity at onboarding and periodic checking of customers against OFAC’s Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. Additionally, providers should employ lifetime-of-the-transaction and in-process geolocation checking in their interdiction screening. Geolocation screening in lifetime-of-the-relationship and in-process transactions raised the stakes for providers to block or reject transactions that would violate the sanctions regimes OFAC enforces.

The last part of this article walks through other fair warnings provided by settlements agreed to since March 2015 or other public guidance. Before discussing the two late 2022 settlements or the fair warnings, it may help to have the foundation of the March 2015 settlement OFAC made with PayPal, Inc.

## 1. OFAC’s Early Foray into In-Process Transactions in Newer Electronic Payments and Services: PayPal, Inc. (March 2015)

OFAC claimed new territory when it announced its settlement with PayPal, Inc. on March 25, 2015. 1

1[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref1) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/126/20150325_paypal_settlement.pdf](about:blank).

 OFAC maintained that PayPal “did not screen in-process transactions in order to block or reject prohibited transactions.” The settlement highlighted, among other things, two types of deficiencies in PayPal’s sanctions compliance program. In the first, PayPal’s automatic interdiction filter failed to identify at least one customer as a potential SDN when OFAC made the SDN designation because its automatic interdiction filter was not “working properly.” PayPal’s agents “dismissed” on at least five occasions one customer’s SDN match and proceeded with transactions. On one other occasion, the filter “flagged” this customer’s account, but a PayPal agent again dismissed the match despite receiving additional information that showed a date of birth and place of birth identical to the SDN. These failures resulted in 136 transactions with a single individual on the SDN list that violated the “Weapons of Mass Destruction Proliferators Sanctions Regulations.” 2

2[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref2) 31 C.F.R. §544.

 The March 2015 settlement also addressed violations by PayPal of other U.S. sanctions regulations, and PayPal agreed to pay civil penalties totaling $7,658,300. 3

3[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref3) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/126/20150325_paypal_settlement.pdf](about:blank).

## 2. The Late 2022 Settlements

### 2.1. Bittrex, Inc.

Bittrex, Inc. is a private company based in Bellevue, Washington. Bittrex provides both virtual-currency-exchange and hosted-wallet services. OFAC’s settlement announcement explained that from March 2014 to December 31, 2017, Bittrex operated more than 1,700 accounts, processed 116,421 virtual-currency-related transactions, and transacted $263,451,600.13 in violation of law and OFAC regulations.

Bittrex apparently showed “some understanding” of OFAC regulations by August 2015, months after OFAC settled with PayPal. However, until October 2017, Bittrex had no internal controls to screen customers or transactions for connections to sanctioned jurisdictions. OFAC described other failings in Bittrex’s compliance efforts, including:

*   not screening IP address or physical address information that customers were in sanctioned jurisdictions;
*   not paying attention to customers providing Iranian passports or identifying themselves as being in Iran at account opening;
*   not scrutinizing customers or transactions for nexus to sanctioned jurisdictions; and
*   failing to have _any sanctions compliance program_ from March 2014 to February 2016 _. Ouch!_

OFAC cited the absence of any sanctions compliance program for two years as one of three aggravating factors in determining the civil monetary penalty of more than $24 million. Among the penalty-mitigating factors was the “swiftness” with which Bittrex responded to OFAC’s Apparent Violations notice.

### 2.2. Kraken

On November 28, 2022, OFAC announced a settlement 4

4[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref4) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/126/20221128_kraken.pdf](about:blank).

 with Kraken for violations of the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulation. 5

5[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref5) 31 C.F.R. § 560.204.

 Kraken’s parent, Payward, Inc., is based in San Francisco.

Based on IP address data, Kraken continued to deal with customers who had opened accounts outside of sanctioned jurisdictions and subsequently transacted business with Kraken from Iran, a sanctioned jurisdiction. The violations occurred between October 14, 2015, and June 29, 2019. Kraken’s violations began _six months after_ the PayPal settlement was announced.

OFAC cited Kraken’s failure to employ geolocational in-process and after-onboarding screening as an “aggravating factor” in its penalty calculations. OFAC had concluded that Kraken had “reason to know based on available IP addresses that transactions appear to be” emanating from Iran. _Ouch._

The settlement confirms that it is not sufficient to screen customers at onboarding or account opening or to perform daily checks to identify new entries on OFAC’s SDN list. Because customers may transact from sanctioned jurisdictions after establishment of accounts, daily monitoring needs to track IP addresses that are the source of transaction requests and instructions to identify transactions coming from jurisdictions that are on the sanctioned lists.

In the settlement, Kraken also agreed to implement more analytical tools such as “multiple blockchain analytics tools” (MBAT). These tools are geolocation controls including Internet Protocol (IP) address-blocking systems. MBAT may be a term or service not familiar to everyone. Prominent providers of MBAT include brand-name commercial providers such as Chainalysis and CipherTrace. MBAT tools assist with the basic identification and nationality verification requirements OFAC has implemented. Kraken has agreed to do more, including screening for OFAC’s “50 Percent Rule,” which requires detailed reports on beneficial ownership of assets and blocking of clients’ access to accounts and assets.

## 3. Fair Warnings Specifically Related to Crypto Entities’ Compliance Programs

OFAC’s settlements with Bittrex and Kraken are examples of enforcement actions presaged by prior enforcement actions and other OFAC guidance. These actions might still be cited as “regulation by enforcement” to the extent that prior enforcement actions frame the standards being enforced against each company. For example, OFAC made its focus on newer financial products and services clear beginning with its enforcement action against PayPal, Inc. in March 2015. These issues and statements of regulatory approach are described in section A of this article.

Since PayPal’s March 2015 settlement, managers updating and maintaining suitable interdiction-filtering procedures and programs had further fair warnings of OFAC’s approach and should have implemented screening of clients who may move to sanctioned jurisdictions, or who may be sanctioned by OFAC after accounts are opened. Kraken’s transactions mentioned in the settlement announcement all came later than OFAC’s action against PayPal, Inc.

The Bittrex and Kraken settlements provide at least five specific “fair warnings” about sufficient sanctions controls programs’ components, including warnings about (1) geolocation/IP address tools, (2) efficacy of controls, (3) being involved with facilitation of violations, (4) use of blockchain analytical tools, and (5) the totality for components of a proper sanctions compliance program. Let’s look at each.

1.   _Fair warning about geolocation tools._ Kraken agreed to deploy tools such as the automated interdiction-compliance filters that commercial banks, securities firms, and insurance companies use to manage the day-to-day issues of account maintenance over the course of the provider’s relationship with its customers _._ For Kraken, this meant adding geolocation in-process transaction screening.
2.   _Fair warning about efficacy of controls._ In addition to settlement announcements, OFAC has issued its 2021 “Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry” (2021 Guidance). 6 6[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref6) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/recent-actions/20211015](about:blank).  OFAC mentions two actions, both involving money laundering and one of which involved “facilitating” Russian ransomware actors. OFAC urged the virtual currency industry to “implement effective sanctions compliance controls to mitigate the risk of sanctioned persons and other actors exploiting virtual currencies to undermine U.S. foreign policy interests and national security.”
3.   _Fair warning about facilitation of violations._ The OFAC 2021 Guidance also reminded actors that “for some sanctions programs, U.S. persons, wherever located, … are prohibited from facilitating actions on behalf of non-U.S. persons if the activity would be prohibited by sanctions regulations if directly performed by a U.S. person or within the United States.”

 Virtual currency compliance programs, OFAC advised, should include “sanctions list and geographic screening,” among other measures. Details on “internal controls” in the 2021 Guidance include providers making more active use of users’ IP addresses. Additional details suggest controls via IP addresses that prevent persons in comprehensively sanctioned jurisdictions, such as Iran or Syria, from accessing providers’ platforms. OFAC expects that entities will “ensure [they are] utilizing all available information for sanctions compliance purposes.”
4.   _Fair warning on blockchain analytic tools and ongoing screening._ The 2021 guidance document also suggests that virtual currency companies “consider conducting a historic lookback of transactional activity after OFAC lists a virtual currency address on the SDN list to identify connections to listed addresses.” Providers are encouraged to use blockchain analytic tools to identify and manage sanctions risks. OFAC also mentioned “ongoing sanctions screening and risk-based re-screening” to account for updated customer information, changes in OFAC’s SDN lists, or changes in regulatory requirements.

 In 2018, OFAC included known virtual currency addresses as identifying information for persons on its SDN list and allowed searches of those addresses using the “ID #” field in it Sanctions List FAQs 562, 7 7[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref7) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/faqs/562](about:blank). 563, 8 8[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref8) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/faqs/563](about:blank).  and 594. 9 9[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref9) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/faqs/594](about:blank).  OFAC provided more detail in its FAQs, some of which it updated in association with its 2022 press release announcing its settlement with Kraken.
5.   _Fair warning about components of a functional sanctions compliance program._ OFAC also published on May 2, 2019, “A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments.” 10 10[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref10) Available at [https://home.treasury.gov/system/files/126/framework_ofac_cc.pdf](about:blank).  The Framework covers foreign entities that conduct business in or with the United States or U.S. persons or that use goods or services exported from the United States. The Framework identifies five aspects of a sanctions compliance program: management commitment, risk assessment, training, internal controls, and testing/auditing. Additionally, OFAC has published and codified “Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines.” 11 11[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref11) 31 C.F.R. Part 501, App. A. 

Admittedly, some of the guidance that OFAC issued came after the violations covered by Kraken’s November 2022 settlement. Adding the Kraken settlement and OFAC’s FAQs updated at the time of the Kraken settlement to the universe of OFAC’s guidance provides important benchmarks for providers in the virtual currency industry.

## 4. A Generally Applicable Fair Warning on Voluntary Self-Disclosure of Possible Violations

OFAC seldom reveals how it becomes alerted to possible sanctions violations. It often is alerted by the entity itself through a procedure known as “voluntary self-disclosure.” 12

12[](https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements#_ftnref12) OFAC FAQ 13 (December 4, 2020), available at [https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/faqs/13](https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financial-sanctions/faqs/13).

 Companies that self-disclose violations can negotiate much lower civil penalties. Self-disclosure requires robust and risk-based internal screening and policies to deter and detect violations of sanctions regimes. The voluntary self-disclosure must reach OFAC before OFAC learns of a violation from another source, such as a bank or freight forwarder.

In the cases of Bittrex and Kraken, OFAC did not mention self-disclosures, which signals that another entity or government had alerted OFAC or its sister agency, the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) of possible violations.

Accordingly, one more generic “fair warning” should be on the fair warnings list: _If you identify violations, get started on your self-disclosure promptly._ Or, to be more blunt: _fess up when you mess up!_

## 5. Conclusion

As the tools available to those intending to circumvent sanctions laws and their enablers improve, OFAC has expanded the range of tools it expects entities subject to OFAC’s strict liability regimes to employ. This requires U.S. person subject to OFAC’s risk-based compliance expectations to reassess their compliance tools and procedures. Although the Federal Aviation Administration may use a thirty-year-old software to run a notice to pilots before take-off, providers of financial products and services subject to OFAC’s jurisdiction should not fail to update their systems that can detect and prevent transactions with sanctioned individuals and entities or sanctioned nation-states. Finally, providers should make voluntary self-examination and self-disclosure protocols key parts of their OFAC compliance programs.

This article, published in the ABA's Business Law Today (March 2023) by Sarah Jane Hughes of Indiana University Maurer School of Law, analyzes OFAC's late 2022 settlements with cryptocurrency exchanges Bittrex and Kraken as "fair warnings" to all cryptocurrency service providers subject to U.S. sanctions laws. The article argues that OFAC requires more than one-time onboarding identity verification and periodic SDN list screening—providers must implement "lifetime-of-the-relationship" and "in-process geolocational" checks.

Key cases examined:
- **PayPal (March 2015):** OFAC's first major foray into in-process transaction screening for newer electronic payments. PayPal's automatic interdiction filter failed to identify an SDN match, resulting in 136 transactions violating the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proliferators Sanctions Regulations (31 C.F.R. §544). PayPal paid $7,658,300 in civil penalties.
- **Bittrex (2022):** The Bellevue, Washington-based exchange operated 1,700+ accounts, processed 116,421 virtual-currency transactions, and transacted $263,451,600.13 in violation of sanctions law from March 2014 to December 31, 2017. Bittrex had no sanctions compliance program at all from March 2014 to February 2016, failed to screen IP addresses or physical addresses, and did not scrutinize customers providing Iranian passports. The absence of any compliance program for two years was an aggravating factor in a civil penalty exceeding $24 million.
- **Kraken (November 28, 2022):** Payward, Inc. d/b/a Kraken (San Francisco) violated the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulation (31 C.F.R. §560.204) between October 14, 2015 and June 29, 2019. Based on IP address data, Kraken continued dealing with customers who opened accounts outside sanctioned jurisdictions then transacted from Iran. OFAC cited Kraken's failure to employ geolocational in-process and after-onboarding screening as an aggravating factor. Kraken agreed to implement "multiple blockchain analytics tools" (MBAT) such as Chainalysis and CipherTrace, and to screen for OFAC's "50 Percent Rule" regarding beneficial ownership.

Five specific "fair warnings" from these settlements: (1) geolocation/IP address tools for in-process transaction screening; (2) efficacy of controls per OFAC's 2021 "Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry"; (3) prohibitions on facilitating violations by non-U.S. persons; (4) use of blockchain analytic tools and ongoing/risk-based re-screening (including historic lookbacks after OFAC lists a virtual currency address on the SDN list); and (5) components of a functional compliance program per OFAC's May 2, 2019 "A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments" (management commitment, risk assessment, training, internal controls, and testing/auditing).

The article also emphasizes the importance of "voluntary self-disclosure"—companies that self-disclose violations before OFAC learns from other sources can negotiate much lower civil penalties. Neither Bittrex nor Kraken self-disclosed, suggesting another entity or FinCEN alerted OFAC. The author's blunt takeaway: "fess up when you mess up."
args.key_excerpts: "OFAC requires more than verification of identity at onboarding and periodic checking of customers against OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. Additionally, providers should employ lifetime-of-the-transaction and in-process geolocation checking in their interdiction screening."

Research practical lessons and best practices for enterprises developing ransomware payment disclosure procedures in the U.S. as of mid-2026, synthesizing guidance from official sources and reputable expert commentary. Cover these areas with actionable specificity:

1. Under SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 (final rule effective December 18, 2023), how a company should determine materiality of a ransomware incident and the four-business-day timeline; the interplay between the materiality investigation period (which must still be reasonably prompt), the requirement to disclose ransomware payment details such as whether a ransom was paid, the amount, and whether a known sanctioned entity was involved; the two-part immaterial incident aggregation analysis the SEC staff described; and how legal, IT, and finance teams should operationalize a materiality determination workflow within 4 business days while the investigation is often still ongoing.

2. Coordination of the 8-K four-business-day deadline with other notification regimes: OFAC expectations, CISA's CIRCIA 72-hour and 24-hour ransom payment reporting (if final rule in effect by August 2026), bank regulator 36-hour notifications, NYDFS 72-hour notifications, HIPAA 60-day/HHS notification windows, TSA 12-hour pipeline reporting, state breach notification laws (30-45 days), and insurance/cyber insurer notification clauses — including practical tips for sequencing notifications, preserving privilege, and avoiding premature public disclosure that could complicate law enforcement or investor communications.

3. The pay vs. not-pay decision: OFAC compliance obligations before any payment (screening the recipient against the SDN list and sanctions programs, checking IP addresses and wallets against OFAC sanctions lists, considering whether the actor is a sanctioned entity or in a sanctioned jurisdiction, preventing payments to Specially Designated Nationals, using blockchain analytics, documenting due diligence, and evaluating license options); DOJ's "voluntary self-disclosure" and charging guidance (April 2022 DOJ memo — companies that report ransomware payments to law enforcement within 48 hours, in compliance with OFAC, and cooperate may be eligible for a presumption in favor of a declination or non-prosecution); CISA/FBI guidance discouraging payment and reporting all ransom payments to CISA or IC3; the "combating the financing of ransomware" money laundering reporting requirements (FinCEN's September 2021 advisory and May 2025 activities under Treasury's AML rules — report suspicious activity of ransomware-related payments); and state-level ransom payment prohibitions such as NYDFS 23 NYCRCR Part 500 rule (as of 2023, regulated financial entities may not pay ransoms absent explicit written approval from the NYDFS superintendent).

4. Internal governance and coordination: Roles of the CEO, board (including the Item 106 board cyber expertise disclosure), CISO, general counsel, CFO/treasury (who executes any wire), and communications teams; the importance of a pre-scripted ransomware response playbook; board notification obligations; coordination to ensure statements to investors, media, and regulators are consistent and not misleading (given SEC's SolarWinds enforcement theory about statements of material risk controls being misleading); pitfalls such as boilerplate risk-factor disclosures that are materially misleading post-incident; and the need for accurate statements about scope (e.g., Blackbaud's failure to disclose that sensitive bank and Social Security data had been accessed).

5. Common pitfalls that led to prior enforcement actions, with practical checklists: delayed disclosure pending internal investigation without justification; issuing an 8-K prematurely with incomplete scope that later required correction; disclosure that overstates or understates the incident; failure to aggregate immaterial incidents; failure to screen the ransom payee pre-payment; inconsistent statements to different stakeholders; and updating risk factors and cybersecurity disclosures in periodic reports (10-K/10-Q) to reflect actual incidents and governance.

Provide named sources where possible (e.g., the SEC's 2022-2025 enforcement orders, DOJ guidance, CISA StopRansomware advice, law firm client alerts with substantive analysis), with direct links to primary guidance documents where feasible, and organize the output as an actionable synthesis appropriate for an enterprise risk analyst drafting incident disclosure procedures. Also note open questions and evolving areas as of August 2026 (e.g., CIRCIA final rule timing, possible federal ransom payment prohibition legislation, SEC litigation outcomes still pending).

--- SOURCE 1: SEC Cybersecurity Rules: A Snapshot ---
URL: https://arch.bdo.com/sec-cybersecurity-rules-a-snapshot

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This BDO publication provides a snapshot of the SEC's cybersecurity rules, which require registrants to disclose material cybersecurity incidents in Form 8-K within four business days of determining materiality, and to make annual disclosures about cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance under Regulation S-K Item 106 and Form 20-F Item 16K.

**Key Requirements:**
- **Annual Disclosures (S-K Item 106):** Registrants must describe processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material cybersecurity risks, board oversight, and management's role. At the 2024 AICPA & CIMA Conference, SEC staff noted that mere statements that a process exists are insufficient; disclosure must clearly describe the process and individual expertise within management groups.
- **Incident Disclosures (Form 8-K Item 1.05):** Material cybersecurity incidents must be disclosed within four business days. Materiality follows the standard "reasonable investor" test, considering both quantitative and qualitative factors. Foreign private issuers file on Form 6-K.
- **Definitions:** A "cybersecurity incident" includes unauthorized occurrences on or through a registrant's information systems; "information systems" includes resources "used by" the registrant (including third-party systems).

**BDO Insights:**
- Incidents can include "a series of related unauthorized occurrences" (e.g., continuous small attacks by the same actor that are collectively material).
- Registrants must have processes and controls to evaluate incidents for disclosure.

**SEC Staff Guidance on Voluntary Disclosure (May 2024):**
- Material incidents must be disclosed under Item 1.05.
- Immaterial incidents or those with incomplete materiality assessments should be disclosed under Item 8.01, not Item 1.05, to avoid confusing investors.

**Ransomware Guidance (C&DIs):**
- Paying a ransom does not eliminate the obligation to assess materiality or disclose if material.
- Insurance reimbursement does not automatically make an incident immaterial.
- Small dollar ransom payments do not automatically make an incident immaterial; qualitative factors (e.g., reputational harm) must be considered.
- Multiple individually immaterial incidents that are related and collectively material require disclosure.

**Delay of Disclosure:**
- Disclosure may be delayed only if the U.S. Attorney General notifies the SEC in writing that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety. Initial delay up to 30 days, extendable up to 90 days total.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"If a registrant has a process for identifying, assessing, and managing significant cybersecurity risks, the disclosure should clearly describe this process to inform investors. Merely stating that a process exists is not enough.", "The SEC staff believes the distinction between disclosing a material cybersecurity incident under Item 1.05 and voluntarily disclosing under another item, such as Item 8.01, allows investors to make better investing and voting decisions related to material cybersecurity incidents.", "The registrant may not conclude the incident is immaterial based solely on the fact that all or a substantial portion of the ransomware payment was reimbursed under its insurance policy.", "The definition of a cybersecurity incident includes 'a series of related unauthorized occurrences' to reflect that cyberattacks can compound over time, rather than occurring at a point in time.", "The SEC staff reminded registrants that determining the materiality of a cybersecurity incident involves an assessment of both quantitative and qualitative factors and must be made without unreasonable delay."
</key_excerpts>

**Key Rule Mechanics:**
- Item 1.05 (mandatory): Clock starts on materiality determination, not incident discovery. Halliburton determined materiality in 2 days; UnitedHealth in 1 day; AT&T took 84 calendar days.

- Diversified mid- and large-caps averaged -0.1% (essentially flat).
- Micro-caps and nano-caps showed high variance due to thin trading volume.

1. Market is pricing these disclosures with significant dispersion based on whether trust is part of the product.
2. Materiality clock is faster than discovery clock; pre-documenting the materiality framework is critical.
3. Vendor incidents drive Item 8.01 filings; third-party notification protocols need four-business-day awareness.

--- SOURCE 5: Exchange Act Form 8-K ---
URL: https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/compliance-disclosure-interpretations/exchange-act-form-8-k

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) official interpretive guidance document for Exchange Act Form 8-K (Last Update: June 24, 2024). It provides questions and answers (Q&As) on Form 8-K compliance, replacing earlier interpretations from 1997, 2003, and 2004.

Key guidance includes:

**General Guidance (Section 101):**
- A triggering event occurring within four business days before filing a periodic report may be disclosed in that report (Form 10-Q Item 5 or Form 10-K Item 9B), EXCEPT for Item 4.01 (Changes in Certifying Accountant) and Item 4.02 (Non-Reliance on Previously Issued Financial Statements), which must always be reported on Form 8-K.
- Triggering events apply to registrants AND subsidiaries.
- "Exchange" in General Instruction E refers only to domestic exchanges.

**Item 1.01 - Material Definitive Agreements:**
- An agreement that becomes material after execution does NOT require an Item 1.01 Form 8-K, but must be filed as an exhibit to the periodic report covering the period when it became material.
- Registrants may omit underwriter identities to preserve the Rule 135c safe harbor.
- Material agreements must be summarized in the body of the Form 8-K even if filed as an exhibit (incorporation by reference insufficient).
- As of March 2022, registrants can redact sensitive terms without confidential treatment requests; absent unusual circumstances, agreements should be filed as exhibits within the four business day timeframe.

**Item 1.02 - Termination of Material Agreements:**
- Receipt of advance written notice of termination (even during negotiation/resolution efforts) triggers an Item 1.02 filing.
- Sending a non-renewal notice triggers disclosure (not the eventual termination date); automatic renewal per agreement terms does not trigger Item 1.01.
- Expiration on stated termination date without renewal does not trigger Item 1.02.

**Item 1.05 - Material Cybersecurity Incidents (extensive coverage):**
- Registrant must file within four business days of determining incident is material; requesting Attorney General delay does not change obligation unless AG determines substantial risk to national security/public safety and notifies the Commission.
- If a delay period expires or is lifted, the filing is due within four business days of that event.
- Consulting with DOJ does not itself make an incident material; materiality determination considers all facts and circumstances using traditional materiality standards (substantial likelihood a reasonable shareholder would consider it important).
- Ransomware payment, insurance reimbursement, or cessation of the incident does NOT relieve the registrant of the materiality determination or disclosure obligation.
- Size of ransomware payment is not determinative of materiality (no quantifiable trigger adopted).
- A series of related immaterial incidents may collectively be material and require disclosure (definition includes "a series of related unauthorized occurrences").

**Item 2.02 - Results of Operations:**
- Audio files, slides, or transcripts of webcasts can satisfy the conditional exemption for oral/telephonic/webcast earnings presentations, provided they contain all previously undisclosed material financial information.
- Required information must be posted on the company's website at the time of the oral presentation.
- Filing earnings release as an exhibit to Form 10-Q before a conference call does not preclude reliance on the Item 2.02(b) exemption.
- Failure to timely furnish an Item 2.02 Form 8-K does NOT affect Form S-3 eligibility (since it is "furnished," not "filed"), though it would violate Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act.
- Preliminary earnings releases must comply with all Item 2.02 requirements.

**Item 2.03 - Direct Financial Obligations:**
- Registrants must maintain disclosure controls to capture off-balance sheet obligations; Instruction 2 provides an extra four business day "grace" period.
- Refinancing/refunding obligations require a facts-and-circumstances materiality determination (may be immaterial if on similar terms).

**Item 2.04 - Triggering Events:**
- If agreement requires declaration/notice of default before acceleration, Item 2.04 is not triggered until such declaration/notice; automatic acceleration without notice does trigger disclosure if material.

**Item 2.05 - Exit/Disposal Costs:**
- Not limited to SFAS 146 costs; also includes FASB Statements 87, 88, 106, and 112.
- For employee terminations, Form 8-K need not be filed until affected employees have been informed.

**Item 2.06 - Material Impairments:**
- No Item 2.06 filing required if impairment conclusion coincides with financial statement preparation/review/audit and is disclosed in a timely-filed periodic report.
- Deferred tax asset re-measurement due to tax rate/law changes (e.g., Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) is not an impairment under ASC Topic 740; SAB 118 "measurement period" approach may apply.

**Item 3.02 - Unregistered Sales:**
- Stock option grants not constituting a "sale" or "offer to sell" under Section 2(a)(3) need not be reported.
- Sales of shares not currently outstanding still count toward volume thresholds.

**Item 4.01 - Changes in Certifying Accountant:**
- Must disclose if accountant's PCAOB registration was revoked.
- A new principal accountant that is a separate legal entity and separately PCAOB-registered (even if affiliated with former accountant) triggers a filing.
- Business combinations between accounting firms require case-by-case analysis.

**Item 4.02 - Non-Reliance on Financial Statements:**
- No second Form 8-K needed if auditor independently reaches same conclusion, unless it relates to a different error/matter.
- Does NOT apply to pro forma financial information.
- Errors in Interactive Data Files alone do not trigger Item 4.02(a); amendments are required to correct them.

**Item 5.02 - Director Departures:**
- Reporting obligation triggered by notice of decision to resign (written or oral), whether conditional or not; must specify effective date.
- Status as "named executive officer" is based on the most recent required Summary Compensation Table disclosure, not current compensation levels.
</summary>

Gerding acknowledged the difficulty of materiality determinations and encouraged companies to consider factors such as impact on financials, reputation, customer relationships, and potential regulatory actions — noting that a significant incident could be material even before its financial impact is assessed.

**SEC Settlement with ICE (May 22, 2024):** The SEC settled charges with The Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) for failing to timely notify the SEC of a cyber intrusion under Regulation Systems Compliance and Integrity (SCI). Regulation SCI (promulgated in 2015) applies to key market participants like national securities exchanges and requires them to "immediately" notify the SEC of SCI events when they have a "reasonable basis to conclude" one occurred, with written notification within 24 hours, unless the event is immediately determined to be de minimis. On April 15, 2021, ICE was notified of a "zero-day" VPN vulnerability; the next day ICE identified malicious code on a VPN device, triggering the immediate reporting obligation. ICE failed to report immediately, instead concluding after four days of analysis that no unauthorized access had occurred and declaring it de minimis. The SEC found this violated Regulation SCI, since ICE could not reasonably estimate the event was de minimis right away.

**Context and Key Takeaways:** The ICE settlement follows other SEC enforcement actions — a complaint against SolarWinds (October 2023) and a settlement with Blackbaud (March 2023) regarding cybersecurity disclosures. The article notes differing requirements: Regulation SCI-covered entities must report "immediately," while other public companies have four business days. Gerding stated the cybersecurity rules aim to ensure "consistent and comparable disclosures" rather than prescribe particular cybersecurity defenses. Key practical guidance: public companies may prefer voluntary disclosure under Item 8.01 until materiality is determined, while Regulation SCI entities must notify the SEC as soon as they have a reasonable basis to believe an SCI event occurred unless they immediately determine it to be de minimis.
</summary>

"public companies are only required to disclose a cybersecurity incident under Item 1.05 of Form 8-K if the incident is 'determined by the registrant to be material'" - Erik Gerding, SEC Division of Corporate Finance. "When it comes to cybersecurity, especially events at critical market intermediaries, every second counts and four days can be an eternity." - Gurbir S. Grewal, SEC Director of Enforcement. "If the SEC receives multiple reports across a number of these types of entities, then it can take swift steps to protect markets and investors." - SEC, explaining the strict reporting requirement reasoning.

The case represents the SEC's first-ever litigated action against a public company concerning its cybersecurity disclosures and the first-ever charges against an individual (a CISO) in connection with public company cybersecurity disclosures.

The SEC's amended complaint alleges two theories: (1) SolarWinds and Brown made material misrepresentations in cybersecurity disclosures, and (2) the company maintained deficient disclosure and internal controls. The case stems from the SUNBURST attack, where nation-state hackers inserted malicious code into SolarWinds' Orion software updates, affecting over 18,000 customers worldwide.

- Public statements by Brown about cybersecurity practices that the SEC alleges were false/misleading

The defendants' motion to dismiss aggressively challenges the SEC's claims. The Court's decision is pending and will likely have significant implications for the future of SEC cybersecurity enforcement.

The company paid the ransom, and on July 16, 2020, disclosed the incident, stating the attacker did not access bank account information or social security numbers. However, by late July 2020, Blackbaud's cybersecurity team learned the attacker had in fact accessed bank account information and SSNs in unencrypted form. Blackbaud agreed to pay a $3 million civil penalty and cease and desist from future violations.

**SEC's Increased Focus on Cybersecurity:** The SEC has nearly doubled its Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit and proposed a comprehensive rule requiring public companies to report material cyber incidents in a Form 8-K within four days of concluding materiality, along with enhanced disclosure requirements for cybersecurity risk management, governance, and incident reporting.

**Key Takeaways for Issuers:**
1. Ensure disclosure controls are designed to promptly escalate material information about cyber breaches as investigations evolve.
2. Be cautious in describing the extent of sensitive data compromised while investigations remain ongoing.
3. Regularly assess recurring/boilerplate cybersecurity risk disclosures to confirm they remain materially accurate after incidents.
4. Monitor the SEC's anticipated cybersecurity rule changes and reassess compliance once effective.
</summary>

SolarWinds Corporation has reached an agreement in principle with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to settle a landmark cybersecurity enforcement action alleging securities fraud tied to the 2020 "Sunburst" cyberattack. The proposed settlement, which still requires formal SEC approval, prompted a federal judge in New York to pause all proceedings while final terms are reviewed. The case, SEC v. SolarWinds Corp. (Case No. 1:23-cv-09518), is pending in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, with the parties required to provide a status update by September 12th.

This was a first-of-its-kind enforcement action: it was the first SEC case alleging a public company committed fraud by misrepresenting cybersecurity practices before a breach, and the first time the SEC named a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) as an individual defendant. SolarWinds filed for summary judgment, but the parties reached a tentative settlement as oral arguments were being prepared.

Key takeaways for public companies include: the SEC is signaling willingness to bring enforcement actions when public cybersecurity statements don't match internal realities; naming the CISO as a defendant could indicate a trend toward personal liability in cybersecurity reporting; companies must ensure post-breach statements are accurate and based on verified facts; and internal communications, technical documentation, and policy implementation records may become critical in litigation. Specific settlement terms have not yet been disclosed. The article was authored by Sean V. Patel, Christopher J. Seusing, and Timothy D. Shea of the law firm WSHB.

--- SOURCE 1: OFAC Issues Updated Guidance on Ransomware Payments ---
URL: https://www.insideprivacy.com/cybersecurity-2/ofac-issues-updated-guidance-on-ransomware-payments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," which supersedes an earlier advisory from October 1, 2020. The Updated Advisory is directed at not only organizations victimized by ransomware attacks but also financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and forensic and incident-response firms that assist victims.

Key points of the Updated Advisory include:

- **Continued Opposition to Ransomware Payments**: OFAC maintains that the U.S. government "strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands" and recommends focusing on defensive and resilience measures. Payments may violate U.S. sanctions prohibitions, and penalties may be imposed on a strict liability basis, meaning companies could face enforcement even if they didn't know a payment would violate sanctions.

- **New Mitigating Factors**: The Updated Advisory identifies two significant mitigating factors in any OFAC enforcement response:
  1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps taken to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices, such as those in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide (co-developed with MS-ISAC), will be considered a "significant mitigating factor."
  2. **Notification and Cooperation with U.S. Government**: Promptly reporting ransomware attacks to law enforcement, CISA, Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection (OCCIP), or other relevant agencies, along with ongoing cooperation (including providing technical details, ransom payment demands, and payment instructions), constitutes a "significant mitigating factor." Timely self-disclosure to these agencies may be considered a voluntary self-disclosure for mitigation purposes.

- **First-Ever Sanctions Designation of a Cryptocurrency Exchange**: Also on September 21, 2021, OFAC designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (also known as "Successful Exchange"), a Russian cryptocurrency exchange, for property-blocking sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13694 (as amended by EO 13757). OFAC alleged SUEX OTC facilitated numerous ransomware payments for malicious cyber actors. U.S. persons are now prohibited from engaging in virtually all transactions with SUEX OTC. The exchange was identified on the SDN List by name, address, and digital currency addresses in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether. OFAC had previously designated other parties by digital currency address in 2018 (two Iranian individuals in the SamSam ransomware scheme).

- **Anticipated Further Guidance**: Press reporting indicates further related guidance may be forthcoming, likely from FinCEN, including action on the proposed application of the travel rule to cryptocurrency transactions and additional anti-money laundering efforts. This aligns with FinCEN's October 1, 2020 advisory (issued in parallel with the 2020 OFAC Advisory) on "red flags" for suspicious ransomware transactions, which noted that consultants facilitating ransomware payments could be considered "money transmitters" under the Bank Secrecy Act.

The article was authored by Covington & Burling LLP attorneys Ashden Fein, Peter Flanagan, Jim Garland, Mike Nonaka, and Moriah Daugherty. The article notes that it remains unclear how OFAC will assess compliance with the new mitigating factors, including which agencies and standards will be used for evaluation, but emphasizes the importance of preparation—developing a strong cybersecurity posture before an attack and timely reporting to and cooperation with government agencies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The U.S. government strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands and recommends focusing on strengthening defensive and resilience measures to prevent and protect against ransomware attacks."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: The Guide to Sanctions - Seventh Edition - Practical issues in cyber-related sanctions as OFAC designations highlight renewed focus on digital currency - Global Investigations Review ---
URL: https://globalinvestigationsreview.com/guide/the-guide-sanctions/seventh-edition/article/practical-issues-in-cyber-related-sanctions-ofac-designations-highlight-renewed-focus-digital-currency

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published 14 July 2026 in GIR's The Guide to Sanctions (Seventh Edition), examines practical issues in US cyber-related sanctions, particularly focusing on recent OFAC designations highlighting renewed attention on digital currency. Authored by Timothy O'Toole, Collmann Griffin, Melissa Burgess, and Arooshe Giroti of Miller & Chevalier, the article provides a comprehensive overview of the US cyber-related sanctions regime.

KEY LEGAL FRAMEWORK:
- The primary authority is Executive Order (EO) 13694 (Cyber1, issued 1 April 2015), amended and strengthened by EO 13757 (Cyber2, 2016), EO 14144 (Cyber3, 2025), and EO 14306 (Cyber4, 2025). Congress codified EOs 13694 and 13757 into statute under the Countering America's Adversaries Through Sanctions Act (CAATSA, signed 2 August 2017).
- OFAC administers these through the Cyber-Related Sanctions Regulations (31 CFR Part 578). Other authorities used include EO 13722 (North Korea), EO 13848 (election interference), and EO 14024 (Russian harmful foreign activities, 15 April 2021, amended by EO 14114 in December 2023 to authorize secondary sanctions on foreign financial institutions).
- The sanctions target cyber-enabled activities including: harm to critical infrastructure computer networks, disruption of service availability, misappropriation of funds/trade secrets/personal identifiers, and election interference.

GUIDANCE AND ADVISORIES:
- 2020 Ransomware Advisory (1 October 2020) and 2021 Ransomware Advisory (21 September 2021) warn that ransomware payments to blocked persons carry strict liability penalties; cooperation with law enforcement is a mitigating factor.
- Virtual Currency Guidance (15 October 2021) clarifies that sanctions obligations apply equally to virtual and fiat currencies.
- FinCEN issued its own Ransomware Advisory (1 October 2021) with red flag indicators.

ENFORCEMENT AND DESIGNATIONS:
- OFAC has designated numerous parties including individual hackers, money launderers, troll farms (Internet Research Agency), cybercriminal organizations (Kimsuky, Genesis Market, Evil Corp, Hydra Market, Garantex), spyware providers (Intellexa Consortium), virtual currency mixers (Blender.io, Sinbad), and state-linked actors from Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea.
- Notable designations include Iran's Ministry of Intelligence and Security (September 2022), Zservers (Russia-based bulletproof hosting, February 2025), and Southeast Asia-based cyber scam networks.
- OFAC civil penalty settlements have targeted virtual currency platforms for sanctions violations: CoinList Markets LLC ($1,252,280 in transactions), Binance Holdings ($706 million, 1,667,153 violations), Poloniex LLC ($15.3 million, 65,942 violations), Uphold HQ Inc ($180,575.80), and Bittrex Inc (over $263 million, 116,421 violations). A recurring theme was failure to use IP address, KYC, and geolocation data for screening.

NOTABLE LEGAL DEVELOPMENT:
- In Van Loon v Treasury (2024), a US Court of Appeals overturned OFAC's designations of Tornado Cash (a decentralized virtual currency mixer), holding that immutable "smart contracts" (self-executing software code) fall outside the definition of "property" or "services" OFAC can block under IEEPA. However, on 6 August 2025, a jury convicted Tornado Cash developer Roman Storm of conspiring to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business (deadlocked on money laundering and sanctions counts, with retrial anticipated). Co-developer Roman Semenov remains under sealed indictment.

COMPLIANCE RISKS:
- Ransom payments to sanctioned parties or jurisdictions risk penalties without a specific OFAC licence.
- Digital currency sector faces heightened scrutiny; businesses must implement risk-based screening, IP blocking, geofencing, and blockchain tracking.
- Cybertheft of export-controlled information may constitute unauthorized export and could expose victim entities to liability for failing to prevent compromise.
- OFAC expects companies to use all reasonably accessible information (IP addresses, KYC data, onboarding data, geolocation) in screening—merely relying on user location attestations is insufficient.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OFAC administers a variety of sanctions targeting malicious cyber-related activities, such as cyber espionage, cyber intrusions on critical infrastructure and computer networks, and disinformation campaigns conducted from abroad."

--- SOURCE 5: OFAC's Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual ... ---
URL: https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/913571/download?inline=

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is the official "Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry" issued by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). The guidance assists the virtual currency industry (technology companies, exchangers, administrators, miners, wallet providers, and users) in understanding and complying with OFAC sanctions requirements, which apply equally to transactions involving virtual currencies and traditional fiat currencies.

KEY CONTENT:
- OFAC administers over 35 sanctions programs that can be comprehensive (broad trade sanctions on countries like Cuba, Iran, North Korea, Syria, and Crimea) or targeted (government/regime sanctions, list-based sanctions, sectoral sanctions).
- The SDN (Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons) List contains over 9,000 names of designated individuals and entities. Under the "50 Percent Rule," entities owned 50% or more by blocked persons are also considered blocked.
- Enforcement examples: In March 2020, OFAC sanctioned two Chinese nationals involved in a North Korean money-laundering scheme (~$100 million in stolen virtual currency). In September 2021, OFAC designated a Russian virtual currency exchange facilitating transactions for ransomware actors (over 40% of transactions associated with illicit actors).
- Who must comply: All U.S. persons (citizens, lawful permanent residents, entities within the U.S., and entities organized under U.S. law, including foreign branches). Key point: OFAC enforces strict liability—civil penalties can be imposed even without knowledge of the violation.
- Blocked virtual currency must be reported to OFAC within 10 business days and annually thereafter; it need not be converted to fiat currency.

REQUIREMENTS:
- Reporting: Initial blocked property reports (10 business days), annual blocked property reports (by September 30), rejected transaction reports (10 business days), and on-demand reports via administrative subpoena.
- Recordkeeping: Five years of full and accurate records for each transaction and for blocked property (five years after unblocking).
- Licensing: General licenses (self-executing) and specific licenses (case-by-case applications).

CONSEQUENCES: Civil and criminal penalties can be substantial. Voluntary self-disclosure may reduce proposed civil penalties by 50%.

FIVE ESSENTIAL COMPONENTS OF A SANCTIONS COMPLIANCE PROGRAM (per A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments):
1. Management Commitment - senior management must endorse policies, provide resources, appoint a dedicated sanctions compliance officer.
2. Risk Assessment - routine, ongoing review of company's touchpoints to foreign jurisdictions/persons, tailored to products, services, customers, and geographic locations.
3. Internal Controls - screening, investigation, transaction monitoring; best practices include geolocation tools/IP address blocking, KYC procedures (collecting names, dates of birth, addresses, IP addresses, government IDs for individuals; entity names, ownership, location info for businesses), transaction monitoring and investigation software, and remedial measures.
4. Testing and Auditing - comprehensive, independent, and objective testing of program effectiveness, including sanctions list screening, keyword screening, IP blocking, and investigation/reporting procedures.
5. Training - sanctions-specific training for all appropriate employees at least annually, updating for new technologies.

Risk indicators/red flags to monitor: inaccurate/incomplete KYC information, access attempts from IP addresses/VPNs connected to sanctioned jurisdictions, refusal to provide updated information, and attempts to transact with virtual currency addresses associated with blocked persons.

OFAC began including virtual currency addresses in the SDN List in 2018, searchable via the "ID #" field in the Sanctions List Search tool. Companies should conduct historical lookbacks and use blockchain analytics tools.

OFAC contact resources include the Compliance Hotline (1-800-540-6322), and websites for the OFAC Reporting System, Licensing Portal, and Sanctions List Search tool.
</summary>

"OFAC sanctions compliance obligations apply equally to transactions involving virtual currencies and those involving traditional fiat currencies. Members of the virtual currency industry are responsible for ensuring that they do not engage, directly or indirectly, in transactions prohibited by OFAC sanctions, such as dealings with blocked persons or property, or engaging in prohibited trade- or investment-related transactions."

--- SOURCE 6: DOJ’s New Corporate Enforcement & Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy: Implications for Government Contractors | BuildSmart ---
URL: https://www.buildsmartbradley.com/2026/03/dojs-new-corporate-enforcement-voluntary-self-disclosure-policy-implications-for-government-contractors

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Bradley's BuildSmart blog (authored by Aron Beezley and Nathaniel Greeson) examines the intersection of two regulatory frameworks affecting government contractors: the U.S. Department of Justice's revised Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP) and the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) mandatory disclosure rule.

**Key Points:**

1. **DOJ's Revised CEP**: The DOJ recently expanded and clarified its CEP, creating a structured framework with predictable benefits. Under the revised policy, companies that (1) voluntarily self-disclose misconduct, (2) fully cooperate with investigators, (3) timely remediate, and (4) have no aggravating circumstances will purportedly receive a declination of prosecution. This represents a shift from prior versions that only offered a presumption of declination. Even with aggravating circumstances, self-disclosing companies may receive nonprosecution agreements, reduced penalties, or no corporate monitor. The key message: early disclosure is the most valuable form of cooperation.

2. **FAR Mandatory Disclosure Rule (FAR 52.203-13)**: Federal contractors must timely disclose credible evidence that a principal, employee, agent, or subcontractor committed violations of federal criminal law involving fraud, conflict of interest, bribery, gratuities, or the civil False Claims Act in connection with federal contracts, in writing to agency OIGs and contracting officers. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This client alert from WilmerHale (authored by partners Jason C. Chipman and David M. Horn) analyzes two U.S. advisories issued on October 1, 2020, addressing ransomware payment risks: the OFAC "Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments" (OFAC Ransomware Advisory) and the FinCEN "Advisory on Ransomware and the Use of the Financial System to Facilitate Ransom Payments" (FIN-2020-A006, FinCEN Ransomware Advisory). These represent the first OFAC and FinCEN guidance specifically addressing ransomware payments, which increased during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The advisories identify two main regulatory risk areas:

1. **OFAC Sanctions Risk**: OFAC may impose civil penalties for sanctions violations based on strict liability—a person subject to U.S. jurisdiction can be held liable even without knowing a transaction was prohibited. This risk is heightened because attackers can obscure their identities and some ransomware hackers are linked to sanctioned actors (North Korean government, Russian cybercriminals). Many ransomware schemes use convertible virtual currency (CVC), further obscuring payment destinations. Where attackers are known targets of OFAC sanctions, license applications are reviewed "on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial."

2. **Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) Requirements**: Financial institutions may be required to file SARs whether they are ransomware victims themselves or merely process payments for victimized clients. FinCEN provided specific SAR filing instructions requiring reference to the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory.

Key compliance expectations: Cyber insurance, digital forensics, and incident response firms facilitating ransom payments may be deemed money transmitters, requiring FinCEN registration as money service businesses and triggering Bank Secrecy Act obligations and state money transmission licensing. OFAC will consider a "self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement" as a significant mitigating factor in enforcement outcomes. Voluntary SAR filings and information sharing under USA PATRIOT Act Section 314(b) are also contemplated.

**Five FinCEN-identified ransomware trends**: (1) "big-game hunting" of larger enterprises for bigger payouts; (2) resource sharing among cybercriminals (ransomware exploit kits and partnerships); (3) "double extortion schemes" (theft of data plus encrypted systems, with threats to publish/sell data); (4) use of anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies (AECs), sometimes with discounted rates for AEC payments; and (5) "fileless" ransomware using malicious code in system memory.

**Red-flag indicators** for financial institutions (especially cryptocurrency exchanges): transactions with digital forensics firms known to make ransom payments; rapid back-to-back cryptocurrency movements; accounts/trades lacking connection to customer's business; "chain-hopping" (converting between cryptocurrencies to obfuscate fund sources/destinations); and transactions with exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

While not creating new legal requirements, the advisories signal that OFAC and FinCEN expect risk-based compliance programs and high coordination with law enforcement. Failure to report and cooperate with law enforcement may increase exposure to OFAC monetary penalties. The alert concludes that companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture given the dilemma between regulatory consequences of paying ransoms and business consequences of not paying.
</summary>

- §500.7 Access Controls (annual access reviews by May 1, 2025)

- §500.9 Risk Assessment (at least annually)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 18, 2021, the U.S. federal banking agencies (FDIC, FRB, and OCC) issued long-awaited computer security incident rules ("the Rules") imposing new regulatory notice obligations for banks and certain service providers regarding significant computer security incidents. Covered entities must comply by May 1, 2022.

Key requirements:
- Banking organizations must notify their primary federal regulator as soon as possible but no later than 36 hours after determining a "notification incident" occurred (via email, phone, or similar method).
- A "notification incident" is a computer security incident that has materially disrupted/degraded, or is reasonably likely to disrupt/degrade: (1) a banking organization's ability to carry out banking operations or deliver products/services to a material portion of its customer base; (2) a product or service whose failure would result in material loss of revenue, profit, or franchise value; or (3) operations whose failure would threaten U.S. financial stability.
- A "computer security incident" is defined as an occurrence that results in "actual harm" to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of an information system or the information it processes.

Coverage:
- FDIC: insured state nonmember banks, insured state-licensed branches of foreign banks, state savings associations.
- FRB: U.S. bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, state member banks, U.S. operations of foreign banking organizations, Edge and agreement corporations.
- OCC: national banks, federal savings associations, federal branches and agencies of foreign banks.
- Rules also apply to "bank service providers" (under the Bank Service Company Act), who must notify affected bank customers as soon as possible after experiencing a computer security incident causing four or more hours of material service disruption. Notification must go to a bank-designated point of contact, or if none designated, to the CEO and CIO (or two comparable individuals). Scheduled maintenance/testing/updates previously communicated are exempt.
- The Rules do NOT apply to systemically important financial market utilities designated by the Financial Stability Oversight Council.

Key takeaways:
- The Rules are NOT breach notification rules—they focus on the impact of computer security events regardless of cause (including non-malicious events like fires, floods, failed upgrades, or earthquakes), emphasizing severe business disruption.
- The 36-hour notice requirement is faster than typical state breach laws, NYDFS (72 hours), and GDPR (72 hours).
- The Rules uniquely impose obligations directly on service providers, rather than flowing down through contracts.
- Events may overlap with GLBA incident response guidance and state data breach laws (e.g., a ransomware attack that also exfiltrates customer data).
- Banks and service providers should update incident response plans, designate points of contact in advance, and implement notification processes to avoid operational challenges during critical events.

If no point of contact was previously designated, notification must go to the CEO and CIO (or two individuals of comparable responsibility).
- The final rule takes effect April 1, 2022, with full compliance extended to May 1, 2022. The FDIC will provide logistics for notification in early 2022.

The FIL applies to all FDIC-supervised institutions. Suggested routing includes Chief Information Officer, Chief Information Security Officer, Chief Operating Officer, Chief Risk Officer, and Chief Technology Officer. The full text of the Final Rule is available as an attachment (PDF).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: A Summary of the Final Amendments to the NYDFS Cyber ... ---
URL: https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/2023/11/14/a-summary-of-the-final-amendments-to-the-nydfs-cyber-rules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) adopted the second amendment to its Cybersecurity Regulation (Part 500), known as the "Second Amendment" or "Final Amendment." This followed the June 2023 Proposal and incorporated revisions in response to public comments. The Department also released a 38-page Assessment of Public Comments (APC) explaining acceptances/rejections of comments.

The Final Amendment imposes new obligations in six categories, with phased compliance dates beginning December 1, 2023, through November 1, 2025. NYDFS published implementation timelines for small businesses, Class A businesses, and covered entities.

Key changes include:

1. **New Obligations for Class A Companies**: The amendment creates a "Class A" category for covered entities with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue in each of the last two years from New York operations (and affiliates), and either (i) over 2,000 employees or (ii) $1 billion in gross annual revenue for each of the past two fiscal years. Affiliates count only if they share information systems, cybersecurity resources, or part of a cybersecurity program. Class A companies face additional cybersecurity obligations.

2. **New Governance Requirements**: Enhanced requirements for CISOs, management, and boards beyond the original Part 500 (which already required board cybersecurity reporting and written policies approved by a senior officer).

3. **New Technical Requirements**: All covered entities face new technical obligations. Notably, MFA definitions were changed to remove the reference to "text message on a mobile phone" — while still acceptable, text-message MFA is considered weaker. The device used for authentication (e.g., office workstation, mobile phone, or laptop with biometrics or authenticator apps) may serve as an authentication factor. Physical security tokens (like PIV cards and security keys) offer phishing resistance, though NYDFS noted it would be too costly to require phishing-resistant MFA for all covered entities at this time.

4. **Incident Response and Business Continuity (BCDR)**: New requirements for incident response and BCDR plans.

5. **Expanded Breach Notification Obligations**: The original rule required notification to NYDFS within 72 hours of determining a cybersecurity event occurred that (1) had a reasonable likelihood of materially harming normal operations, or (2) required notification to another regulatory body. The Final Amendment expands these obligations.

6. **Enforcement**: New enforcement-related provisions.

Notably, throughout the process, NYDFS was determined to set standards for larger companies rather than deferring entirely to risk-based decision-making, though it demonstrated understanding of the complex nature of cybersecurity governance.

The article was written by Debevoise & Plimpton attorneys (Luke Dembosky, Avi Gesser, Erez Liebermann, and others) and references a November 28, 2023 webcast on the amendments.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services ('NYDFS' or the 'Department') announced the adoption of the second amendment to its Cybersecurity Regulation (the 'Second Amendment' or 'Final Amendment') that reflects NYDFS's revisions as a result of comments it received on the proposed amendment released in June 2023.", "Throughout the amendment process, the Department was resolute in promulgating a set of standards for larger companies rather than deferring to those companies to make all risk-based decision-making.", "The Final Amendment creates a category of 'Class A' companies that are covered entities with at least $20,000,000 in gross annual revenue in each of the last two years from all business operations of the entity and the business operations in New York State of its affiliates, and either (i) over 2,000 employees or (ii) $1 billion in gross annual revenue for each of the past two fiscal years.", "'Text message MFA, while still acceptable, is widely considered to be a weaker form of MFA, and the Department encourages the adoption of more secure forms of MFA, in particular phishing-resistant forms of MFA.'", "The definition of MFA has also been changed to remove the reference to 'text message on a mobile phone.'"
</key_excerpts>

The Second Amendment, adopted in November 2023, imposed a multi-year rollout of new requirements—the first set went into effect in November 2023, with the final requirements now taking effect on November 1, 2025.

The November 1 requirements focus on two key sections:
- Section 500.12: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) — the requirements expand MFA obligations for all covered entities.

The regulation grants a limited exemption to the MFA requirement for certain covered entities with employees, revenue, or assets falling under defined thresholds (the "small business exception"). Entities falling within this exception are only required to use MFA for: 1) remote access to information systems; 2) remote access to third-party applications; and 3) all privileged accounts other than service accounts.

These final requirements, along with those that took effect on May 1, 2025, will be subject to the annual certification requirement on April 15, 2026, which applies for calendar year 2025.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) released the finalized "Second Amendment" to 23 NYCRR Part 500, marking the most significant modifications to the cybersecurity regulations since their original enactment in 2017. The changes aim to address the increasing sophistication of threat actors, the prevalence and ease of executing cyberattacks, and the availability of additional controls to manage cyber risk at reasonable cost. The revisions culminated an approximately yearlong process beginning in July 2022 with a pre-proposed draft, revised on November 9, 2022 and June 28, 2023, before finalization on November 1, 2023.

The new rules carry significant implications: (1) new obligations may require substantial enhancement and investment in cybersecurity programs; (2) the rules portend increased NYDFS investigative and enforcement activity regarding cybersecurity; and (3) these stricter requirements may be adopted by other regulators, potentially impacting non-NYDFS entities (e.g., the FTC recently updated the GLBA Safeguards Rule).

Covered entities should prioritize: identifying key compliance dates; reviewing incident response plans for new incident reporting requirements (effective December 1, 2023); assessing whether they constitute a "Class A" company (which has additional requirements); and considering the impact on the 2023 certification process (occurring in April 2024, as of December 31, 2023).

Key compliance deadlines include December 1, 2023 for section 500.17(a) (notice of cybersecurity events reported to other authorities and ransomware), and April 15, 2024 for section 500.17(b) (Certification of Material Compliance or Acknowledgment of Noncompliance for 2023). The rules take effect via staggered transition periods: 180 days for most sections; one year for sections 500.4(b), 500.5, 500.9, 500.12, and 500.14(b); 18 months for sections 500.6, 500.8, 500.13, 500.14(a), and 500.15; and two years for section 500.11. The Department hosted training webinars (starting November 15, 2023) with recordings to be posted publicly.

Notable definitions include: Covered Entity ("any person operating under a license, registration, charter, certificate, permit, accreditation or similar authorization under the Banking Law, the Insurance Law or the Financial Services Law"); independent audit; and "senior governing body." Even under limited exceptions, MFA remains required for remote access to information systems, remote access to third-party applications (including cloud-based) from which nonpublic information is accessible, and all privileged accounts (except service accounts prohibiting interactive login). The authors are Kirk Nahra (Partner, Co-Chair of AI and Cybersecurity/Privacy Practices), Amy Gopinathan (Senior Associate), and Ali Jessani (Counsel).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: What Is 23 NYCRR Part 500? NYDFS Cybersecurity ... ---
URL: https://www.saltycloud.com/blog/what-is-23-nycrr-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive guide by the SaltyCloud Research Team (updated Aug 2, 2025) explaining 23 NYCRR Part 500, the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) cybersecurity regulation. The regulation applies to all NYDFS-regulated entities (banks, insurers, mortgage companies, money transmitters, credit unions, etc.), requiring them to implement cybersecurity programs, conduct risk assessments, and report incidents.

**History/Timeline:** Introduced March 2017 with a stepped phase-in (180 days to 2 years); fully enforced by March 1, 2019. First amendment (April 2020) moved certification deadline to April 15. Second Amendment (2023–2025) added Class A Company obligations, 72-hour breach notification, 24-hour ransomware payment reporting, and required CISO and senior executive signoffs, with deadlines continuing through November 1, 2025.

**Class A Companies:** Organizations with ≥$20M gross annual revenue in each of last two fiscal years AND (more than 2,000 employees OR more than $1B gross annual revenue). They face enhanced requirements including annual independent cybersecurity audits (§500.2(c)), enhanced privileged access controls (§500.7), and endpoint detection & response (§500.14).

**Key Requirements (by section):**
- §500.2 Cybersecurity Program: risk-based program protecting confidentiality, integrity, availability; documents must be available to superintendent
- §500.3 Cybersecurity Policy: written, approved annually by senior officer, covering 14+ domains (access control, data governance, incident response, vendor management, etc.)
- §500.4 Governance: designated CISO accountable for compliance; annual board reporting
- §500.5 Vulnerability Management: annual internal/external pen testing, automated scanning by May 1, 2025
- §500.6 Audit Trails: 5-year retention
- §500.7 Access Controls: need-to-know basis, annual access reviews by May 1, 2025
- §500.8 Application Security
- §500.9 Risk Assessment: annual, documented; foundation for all controls
- §500.11 Third-Party/Vendor Security Policy
- §500.12 MFA for all system access, remote logins, privileged accounts by November 1, 2025
- §500.13 Asset Inventory by November 1, 2025
- §500.14 Monitoring & Awareness: annual cybersecurity training; Class A requires EDR and centralized logging
- §500.16 Incident Response Plan: tested yearly, with BCDR
- §500.17 Reporting: 72-hour incident notice, 24-hour ransomware payment notice (30-day explanation), annual certification by April 15 signed by CISO + senior executive, 5-year records retention

**Exemptions (§500.19):** Entities with fewer than 20 employees, under $7.5M annual revenue (past 3 years), or under $15M total assets may qualify. Must file Notice of Exemption within 30 days.

**Enforcement:** Under Financial Services Law §408, penalties include civil monetary fines, license revocation, and cease-and-desist orders. Recent penalties: Block Inc. ($40M), PayPal ($2M), Gemini Trust Co. ($37M + $1.1B restitution).

**Frameworks for compliance:** NIST CSF, CIS Controls v8.1 (with mapping), CRI Profile, ISO/IEC 27001/27002, and Secure Controls Framework. Third-party vendors are not directly regulated but covered entities remain accountable for vendor cybersecurity under §500.11.

The page also promotes Isora GRC as compliance software for managing NYDFS 23 NYCRR 500 compliance, offering automated workflows, dashboards, and audit trails.
</summary>
