--- SOURCE 6: U.S. Department of Justice Announces New Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy for all U.S. Attorney’s Offices ---
URL: https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/230223-new-voluntary-self-disclosure-policy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On February 22, 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) announced a new corporate Voluntary Self-Disclosure (VSD) policy applicable to all 94 U.S. Attorney's Offices across the United States and its territories. Announced by Damian Williams (U.S. Attorney for SDNY and Chair of the Attorney General's Advisory Committee) and Breon Peace (U.S. Attorney for EDNY and Chair of the White Collar Fraud Subcommittee), the policy aims to incentivize companies to voluntarily self-disclose misconduct, fully cooperate with investigations, and timely remediate misconduct by offering standardized, transparent benefits including avoidance of a guilty plea, substantially reduced fines, and no independent compliance monitor.

The policy fulfills a September 15, 2022 directive from Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco (the "Monaco Memo"), which instructed all DOJ components to implement VSD policies modeled on existing programs like the Antitrust Division's Leniency Program and the Criminal Division's Corporate Enforcement Policy (CEP).

Key components of the U.S. Attorney's Office VSD policy include: (1) A disclosure is voluntary only if made to the U.S. Attorney's Office with no preexisting obligation to disclose, made before an "imminent threat of disclosure or government investigation," within a reasonably prompt time after becoming aware of misconduct, and including all relevant facts known to the company; (2) U.S. Attorney's Offices will not seek a guilty plea and may resolve through declination, non-prosecution agreement, or deferred prosecution agreement when no aggravating factor is present and the company has self-disclosed, fully cooperated, and remediated; (3) Companies may receive at least a 50% fine reduction off the low end of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines fine range absent aggravating factors, or a 50-75% reduction when aggravating circumstances are present.

The policy differs from the Criminal Division's CEP in several respects: the CEP provides a rebuttable presumption of declination while the USAO VSD policy only provides a presumption of no guilty plea; the CEP considers additional aggravating factors (egregiousness, profit, recidivism) while the USAO policy considers involvement of executive management, deep pervasiveness, and threats to national security/public health/environment; the CEP provides fine reductions for companies that cooperate and remediate without self-disclosing, while the USAO VSD policy requires self-disclosure for any benefits. Both policies use very similar standards for avoiding an independent compliance monitor.

For joint prosecutions between U.S. Attorney's Offices and other DOJ components (e.g., FCPA cases with the Criminal Division's Fraud Section), the specialized section's VSD policy will likely apply, though the USAO may apply provisions of alternate policies with approval. The policy creates a substantial new incentive for companies to self-disclose rather than rely solely on cooperation and remediation.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco announced new DOJ guidance and policies for corporate criminal enforcement... The Monaco Memo instructed all DOJ components to implement a policy to provide credit to companies that voluntarily self-disclose potential misconduct, "Through resolution under more favorable terms than if the government had learned of the misconduct through other means.", "Standardize how voluntary self-disclosures are defined and credited by U.S. Attorney's Offices nationwide," "incentivize companies to maintain effective compliance programs . . . and cooperate fully with the government in corporate criminal investigations," and provide "transparency and predictability to companies and the defense bar concerning the concrete benefits" for voluntarily self-disclosing misconduct.
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: DOJ Announces Key Revisions to Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy | Fenwick ---
URL: https://www.fenwick.com/insights/publications/doj-announces-key-revisions-to-corporate-enforcement-and-voluntary-self-disclosure-policy

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On May 12, 2025, the head of the DOJ's Criminal Division, Matthew Galeotti, announced a new white collar enforcement plan in a memorandum titled "Focus, Fairness, and Efficiency in the Fight Against White-Collar Crime." The plan includes key revisions to the Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP) providing greater incentives for corporations to investigate and voluntarily self-disclose employee misconduct and cooperate with DOJ investigations.

Key changes to the revised CEP include:
- **Guaranteed declinations**: Unlike the prior CEP which offered only a "presumption" of declination, companies that meet core requirements "will" receive a declination—an agreement by DOJ not to seek criminal resolution. Galeotti stated, "Companies that meet our core requirements . . . will not be required to enter into a criminal resolution. This is a clear path to declination."
- **Discretion despite aggravating circumstances**: Prosecutors retain discretion to recommend a CEP declination based on weighing the severity of aggravating circumstances against the company's cooperation and remediation. CEP declinations require companies to pay all disgorgement/forfeiture and restitution/victim compensation payments.
- **"Near Miss" voluntary disclosure**: If a company fully cooperated and remediated but is ineligible for a declination because (1) a good-faith self-disclosure doesn't meet the definition of voluntary self-disclosure, or (2) aggravating factors warrant criminal resolution, the Criminal Division "shall" provide certain benefits. This category provides increased incentives for self-disclosure even when mandatory declination isn't available.
- **Non-self-reporting consequences**: Companies that don't self-report in good faith cannot access the above benefits, though prosecutors retain discretion to recommend any resolution form, with a three-year term, monitor, and up to 50% fine reduction.
- **Whistleblower overlap**: Retains the key exception that if a whistleblower makes both an internal report and a DOJ submission, the company still qualifies for a presumption of declination if it self-reports within 120 days of the internal report and meets other requirements.

The revised CEP aligns with the recently launched Corporate Whistleblower Awards Pilot Program and includes a flow chart mapping the path to declination. Corporations, especially in-house counsel and compliance officers, should review their compliance programs and internal reporting channels to ensure eligibility for guaranteed declinations. The article is from Fenwick & West LLP and was published by lawyers including David Feder, Ben Kingsley, Jon Lenzner, Christopher Steskal, Noah Solowiejczyk, and Hamdi Soysal.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On February 22, 2023, the U.S. Department of Justice announced the Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (VSD Policy) for all 94 U.S. Attorneys' Offices (USAOs). The policy, effective immediately, standardizes how USAOs define and credit voluntary self-disclosure of corporate criminal conduct, following Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco's September 2022 memorandum directing DOJ components to review or create self-disclosure policies. The policy was developed by the White Collar Fraud Subcommittee under U.S. Attorney Breon Peace and approved by the Office of the DAG.

KEY CRITERIA FOR VOLUNTARY SELF-DISCLOSURE: (1) The disclosure must be voluntary (not pursuant to a preexisting obligation, regulation, contract, or prior DOJ resolution, nor previously reported by a third party/whistleblower); (2) timing must be prior to an imminent threat of disclosure or government investigation, prior to public disclosure, and within a reasonably prompt time after the company becomes aware of the misconduct; (3) the disclosure must include all relevant facts known at the time, with expectations for timely preservation, collection, and production of documents and factual updates.

BENEFITS: Absent aggravating factors, a USAO will not seek a guilty plea against a company that voluntarily self-discloses, fully cooperates, and timely remediates. Instead, the USAO may decline prosecution or enter into an NPA or DPA. The USAO will not impose a criminal penalty greater than 50% below the U.S.S.G. fine range. Aggravating factors include misconduct that poses a grave threat to national security, public health, or the environment; is deeply pervasive; or involved current executive management. If aggravating factors warrant a guilty plea, the USAO will recommend a 50% to 75% reduction off the low end of the U.S.S.G. fine range and will not require a monitor if an effective compliance program is in place.

COMPARISON TO THE CRIMINAL DIVISION'S CEP: While standards for voluntary self-disclosure are generally consistent, the VSD Policy is less favorable than the Criminal Division's Corporate Enforcement Policy (CEP) in significant respects. Under the CEP, voluntary self-disclosure plus full cooperation and remediation creates a presumption of declination (absent aggravating factors), while the VSD Policy does not provide any presumption of declination and instead contemplates NPAs or DPAs as alternatives. The CEP also provides up to a 50% reduction for cooperation and remediation without self-disclosure, while the VSD Policy specifies no such benefit. Notably, a USAO may choose to apply another component's self-disclosure policy (such as the CEP) in place of the VSD Policy, which may create greater incentive to disclose to the Criminal Division where both have jurisdiction.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 10: DOJ Implements Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy for US Attorneys’ Offices | Insights | Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP ---
URL: https://www.skadden.com/insights/publications/2023/03/doj-implements-voluntary-self-disclosure

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On February 22, 2023, the Department of Justice (DOJ) adopted a new policy establishing a national standard for voluntary self-disclosure credit in corporate criminal enforcement actions brought by U.S. Attorneys' Offices (USAO). The policy was developed at the direction of Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco and is substantively aligned with the DOJ Criminal Division's updated Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy. It is authored by Skadden attorneys including Maria Cruz Melendez, Jack P. DiCanio, Andrew M. Good, Ryan D. Junck, Bradley A. Klein, Steve Kwok, David Meister, and Bora P. Rawcliffe.

Policy Objectives: The USAO's goal is to standardize how voluntary self-disclosures are defined and credited, and to incentivize companies to promptly and voluntarily self-disclose misconduct. The policy notes that even absent timely self-disclosure, prosecutors will continue to consider pre-indictment conduct (e.g., cooperation) in charging decisions. It also encourages companies to conduct internal investigations, fully cooperate, and remediate misconduct as part of compliance programs.

Voluntary Self-Disclosure Requirements: Both policies define voluntary self-disclosure as circumstances where a company makes a timely disclosure, discloses relevant facts and evidence, and agrees to cooperate and remediate. Key differences: The Criminal Division policy requires disclosure "at the earliest possible time" even without completing an internal investigation, whereas the USAO policy lacks this language (though timeliness will likely be assessed similarly in practice). The burden is on the company to demonstrate timeliness. The USAO policy also does not specifically mention disclosing facts about individuals, but this is required per the Monaco Memo to receive cooperation credit.

Benefits: Where a company fully meets USO policy requirements, the USAO may decline prosecution or seek a deferred/nonprosecution agreement rather than imposing a criminal penalty. In any event, no criminal penalty will be greater than 50% below the low end of the USSG fine range. Absent aggravating factors, USAOs will not seek a guilty plea. Aggravating factors include misconduct that is harmful to market integrity, national security, or public health, among others. Unlike the Criminal Division policy (which recommends up to a 50% fine reduction for cooperation/remediation without self-disclosure, and provides a declination presumption with specific declination guidance even with aggravating circumstances), the USAO policy does not describe monetary benefits for companies that fail to self-disclose but cooperate, nor does it detail declination circumstances.

--- SOURCE 18: What are the HIPAA Breach Notification Requirements? ---
URL: https://www.hipaajournal.com/hipaa-breach-notification-requirements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from The HIPAA Journal (authored by Steve Alder, posted January 12, 2026) provides a comprehensive guide to HIPAA Breach Notification Requirements, which require covered entities to notify HHS's Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and individuals whose unsecured Protected Health Information (PHI) has been exposed within specified timeframes.

**Key Requirements:**
The HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.400-414) requires covered entities and business associates to report breaches of unsecured electronic and physical PHI. A breach is defined as the acquisition, access, use, or disclosure of unsecured PHI not permitted by HIPAA Rules. An impermissible use or disclosure is presumed to be a breach unless a risk assessment demonstrates a low probability of compromise based on four factors: (1) nature/extent of PHI involved, (2) the unauthorized person involved, (3) whether PHI was actually acquired or viewed, and (4) extent of mitigation.

**Four Notification Requirements:**
1. **Notify Individuals:** Letters must be sent within 60 days of breach discovery (unless state law requires shorter or law enforcement requests delay), by first-class mail or email (if prior authorization given). Letters must be in plain language, explain what happened, what information was exposed, mitigation steps, and prevention measures, plus provide a toll-free number and contact details.
2. **Notify HHS:** More than 500 individuals affected - within 60 days of discovery; fewer than 500 - within 60 days of the end of the calendar year in which the breach was discovered.
3. **Notify Media:** If the breach impacts more than 500 individuals, notification must be issued to prominent media outlets in the states/jurisdictions where victims reside (45 CFR §164.406) within 60 days.
4. **Substitute Notice on Website:** If up-to-date contact information is not held for 10+ individuals, a substitute breach notice must be posted prominently on the home page for 90 consecutive days.

**Business Associates:** Business Associate Agreements must stipulate that all security incidents be reported to covered entities whether they result in a breach or not (45 CFR §164.314(a)(2)(i)). Breaches must be reported to covered entities within 60 days of discovery without unnecessary delay. Covered entities are usually responsible for notifying individuals.

**Penalties:** Violations can result in financial penalties. In 2017, Presence Health became the first covered entity to settle with OCR solely for a Breach Notification Rule violation - it exceeded the 60-day timeframe and paid $475,000. In January 2021, an amendment to HITECH gave OCR enforcement discretion for good-faith compliance attempts in the 12 months preceding a breach.

**Additional Key Facts:**
- The Rule came into force September 23, 2009 (via HITECH Act, 2009).
- Most states have breach notification laws, some stricter than HIPAA; 44 states have medical privacy laws that can preempt HIPAA.
- The Rule applies to covered entities, business associates, and some vendors of Personal Health Records (regulated by the FTC rather than HHS).
- Secured PHI (encrypted) does not require breach notification unless the encryption key was compromised or it involves a ransomware attack.
- Exceptions include breaches of secured/encrypted data, unintentional good-faith acquisitions within scope of authority, inadvertent disclosures to other authorized workforce members, and good-faith belief that information could not have been retained.
- After notification to HHS, the report is reviewed; the agency may conduct a compliance investigation, offer technical assistance, impose corrective action plans, or issue civil monetary penalties; knowing/wrongful disclosures may be referred to the Department of Justice.

The article also includes an extensive FAQ section covering topics such as the difference between breaches and violations, secured vs. unsecured PHI, staff training requirements, breach reporting timelines, and regulator responsibilities (HHS OCR, FTC, and State Attorneys General). The HIPAA Journal is described as the leading provider of HIPAA training, news, and independent compliance advice.

Key content includes:

DEFINITION OF BREACH: A breach is an impermissible use or disclosure under the Privacy Rule that compromises the security or privacy of PHI. An impermissible use or disclosure is presumed to be a breach unless the entity demonstrates a low probability that the PHI was compromised based on a risk assessment. There are three exceptions to the definition of "breach": (1) unintentional acquisition/access/use by a workforce member in good faith within the scope of authority; (2) inadvertent disclosure to another authorized person; and (3) when there is a good faith belief that the unauthorized person could not retain the information.

UNSECURED PHI: Notifications are only required if the breach involved unsecured PHI—information not rendered unusable, unreadable, or indecipherable through technologies specified by the Secretary. The Secretary's guidance (first issued April 2009, reissued after public comment) specifies encryption and destruction as the methods for securing PHI. Entities that secure information per this guidance are relieved from notification obligations.

BREACH NOTIFICATION REQUIREMENTS:
• Individual Notice: Covered entities must notify affected individuals in writing (first-class mail or email if agreed). If contact info is insufficient for 10+ individuals, substitute notice must be posted on the website home page for at least 90 days or provided through major media, with a toll-free phone number active for at least 90 days. For fewer than 10 individuals, alternative written notice, telephone, or other means may be used.
• Media Notice: Breaches affecting more than 500 residents of a State/jurisdiction require notice to prominent media outlets (typically via press release).
• Notice to Secretary: Covered entities submit breach reports via the HHS website. Breaches affecting 500+ individuals require notification within 60 days; breaches affecting fewer than 500 individuals may be reported annually, due no later than 60 days after the end of the calendar year.

All individual and media notifications must be provided without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after breach discovery, and must include a description of the breach, types of information involved, steps individuals should take, investigation/mitigation efforts, and contact information.

BUSINESS ASSOCIATES: If a breach occurs at or by a business associate, it must notify the covered entity without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days from discovery, providing identification of affected individuals and other required information.

ADMINISTRATIVE REQUIREMENTS: Covered entities bear the burden of proof that notifications were made or that no breach occurred. --- SOURCE 1: Final NYDFS Cybersecurity Rules Take Effect: What Financial Services Companies Must Do Now | Steptoe ---
URL: https://www.steptoe.com/en/news-publications/final-nydfs-cybersecurity-rules-take-effect-what-financial-services-companies-must-do-now.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 1, 2025, two critical updates to the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) Cybersecurity Regulation ("Part 500") took effect for Covered Entities, requiring finalization of (1) mandatory Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) for nearly all Covered Entities in nearly all cases, and (2) development of a comprehensive, documented Asset Inventory Program.

**Background:** The NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation provides a principles-based framework managing cyber risk in New York's financial sector, governing "Covered Entities" (those operating under licenses or authorizations under New York's Banking, Insurance, or Financial Services Law). Core requirements include annual risk assessments, written cybersecurity policies, data governance/CISO reporting, access controls, MFA, asset inventory/management, incident response, and annual compliance certification. The November 2023 Second Amendment introduced enhanced obligations, including a 24-hour notification requirement for cyber extortion payments. The final requirements of this amendment took effect November 1, 2025.

**Supervisory Context:** The amendments take effect amid NYDFS leadership change — following Superintendent Adrienne Harris's departure, Kaitlin Asrow was appointed Acting Superintendent. NYDFS recently issued guidance (October 21, 2025) confirming Covered Entities remain ultimately accountable for third-party vendor cybersecurity risks and cannot delegate this responsibility. NYDFS has shown enforcement seriousness, entering a consent order against Healthplex earlier in 2025 resulting in a $2 million civil penalty for Part 500 violations.

**Key Requirement 1 — Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA):** The amended rule significantly broadens the prior requirement (which only mandated MFA for external network access). Now MFA is required for all individuals remotely accessing information systems where data is accessed or provided, including remote access to third-party applications. This covers cloud applications (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, SaaS providers) and third-party vendor systems. Covered Entities retain ultimate responsibility to ensure third-party MFA implementations meet Part 500 requirements, even when relying on a TSP's native MFA software.

**Key Requirement 2 — Comprehensive Asset Inventory Program:** Covered Entities must formalize their asset inventory into a documented, regularly maintained program through written policies and procedures covering all information systems. Policies must describe asset tracking (ownership, classification/sensitivity, location, end-of-support dates, recovery time objectives) and update/validation frequency. The regulation also requires secure disposal of non-public information no longer needed. The mandate shifts from a static asset list to a dynamic, documented program covering hardware, software, cloud services, and network infrastructure tied to Non-Public Information (NPI) sensitivity.

**Exemptions:** Under § 500.19(a), small businesses with fewer than 20 employees/independent contractors, less than $7.5 million in gross annual revenue from NY operations, or less than $15 million in year-end total assets are exempt from certain Part 500 requirements and subject to a narrower MFA requirement.

**Recommended Next Steps (per Steptoe):**
- Scope and implement MFA broadly across every application/system storing, transmitting, or processing NPI (including third-party systems); prioritize phishing-resistant MFA (hardware security keys, FIDO2); review third-party contracts for MFA support.
- Formalize Asset Inventory Program with written policies/procedures; capture all required data points (owner, classification, location, patch status); establish periodic risk-based validation schedule.
- Validate Risk Assessment alignment with newly identified assets and access points.
- Prepare for 2026 Annual Certification of Compliance due April 15, 2026.

Steptoe's cross-disciplinary team of cybersecurity, financial services, and regulatory attorneys is available to assist with implementation, risk assessments, and certification readiness.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"As of November 1, 2025, two critical updates to the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) Cybersecurity Regulation (the Cybersecurity Regulation or 'Part 500') took effect for Financial Services Companies."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: Cybersecurity Regulation 23 NYCRR Part 500 - DFS.NY.gov ---
URL: https://www.dfs.ny.gov/cybersecurity/23-NYCRR-Part-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is an unofficial version of the Second Amendment to 23 NYCRR Part 500, the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) Cybersecurity Requirements for Financial Services Companies, promulgated by Superintendent Adrienne A. Harris. The regulation establishes cybersecurity minimum standards for DFS-regulated entities (financial services companies) to protect customer information and information technology systems from growing cyber threats posed by nation-states, terrorist organizations, and independent criminal actors.

Key provisions include:
- **Definitions (500.1)**: Defines key terms including "Class A company" (covered entities with ≥$20M gross annual revenue in each of last two fiscal years AND either over 2,000 employees averaged over two years OR over $1B in gross annual revenue), "covered entity," "cybersecurity incident," "multi-factor authentication," "nonpublic information," "penetration testing," and "third-party service provider."
- **Cybersecurity Program (500.2)**: Each covered entity must maintain a program based on its risk assessment performing six core functions: identify/assess risks, protect systems via defenses, detect events, respond to mitigate effects, recover from events, and fulfill regulatory reporting obligations. Class A companies must conduct independent audits.
- **Cybersecurity Policy (500.3)**: Written policies approved at least annually must address 15 areas including information security, data governance, access controls, business continuity, security awareness, vendor management, incident response, and vulnerability management.
- **Governance (500.4)**: Each covered entity must designate a CISO who reports annually in writing to the senior governing body; the senior governing body must exercise oversight of cybersecurity risk management.
- **Vulnerability Management (500.5)**: Requires annual penetration testing from inside and outside boundaries, automated vulnerability scans, and prompt remediation with prioritization based on risk.
- **Audit Trail (500.6)**: Systems to reconstruct material financial transactions (records kept 5+ years) and audit trails to detect/respond to cyber events (records kept 3+ years).
- **Access Privileges (500.7)**: Limit user access and privileged accounts to job-necessary functions, annually review access, disable remote control protocols, promptly terminate access after departures. Class A companies must monitor privileged access and block commonly used passwords.
- **Risk Assessment (500.9)**: Periodic risk assessments reviewed at least annually and upon material changes to business/technology.
- **Third-Party Service Providers (500.11)**: Written policies for identifying, assessing, and overseeing third-party providers with access to nonpublic information.
- **Multi-Factor Authentication (500.12)**: Required for anyone accessing information systems (or for remote access, third-party apps, and privileged accounts if limited exemption applies).
- **Asset Management (500.13)**: Complete, accurate asset inventory with secure disposal policies for unneeded nonpublic information.
- **Monitoring and Training (500.14)**: Monitor authorized user activity, protect against malicious code, and provide annual cybersecurity awareness training including social engineering. Class A companies must implement endpoint detection/response and centralized logging/alerting.
- **Encryption (500.15)**: Written policy requiring industry-standard encryption for nonpublic information in transit and at rest.
- **Incident Response and BCDR (500.16)**: Written incident response and business continuity/disaster recovery plans covering goals, roles, communications, recovery from backups, root cause analysis; requires annual testing and protected backups.
- **Notices to Superintendent (500.17)**: Must notify superintendent within 72 hours of determining a cybersecurity incident occurred; file annual compliance certification or acknowledgment by April 15 (signed by highest-ranking executive and CISO); provide notice of extortion payments within 24 hours and a written description within 30 days of the payment.
- **Exemptions (500.19)**: Limited exemption for entities with fewer than 20 employees, less than $7.5M gross annual revenue (last 3 fiscal years), or less than $15M in year-end total assets. Notices of Exemption must be filed within 30 days. Entities ceasing to qualify have 180 days to comply.
- **Enforcement (500.20)**: A single prohibited act or failure to act constitutes a violation; a material failure to comply for any 24-hour period constitutes a violation. Superintendent considers 16 factors in assessing penalties, including cooperation, good faith, intent, harm to consumers, history of violations, and alignment with frameworks like NIST.
- **Effective Dates (500.21-500.22)**: Original Part effective March 1, 2017; Second Amendment effective November 1, 2023. Transitional periods range from 30 days to two years for different new requirements (e.g., 30 days for Section 500.17 notices, one year for sections 500.4, 500.15, 500.16, 500.19(a), 18 months for 500.5(a)(2), 500.7, 500.14(a)(2), 500.14(b), and two years for 500.12 and 500.13(a)).
- **Electronic Filing Exemptions (500.24)**: Filers may request exemptions from electronic filing requirements by written request at least 30 days prior.
</summary>

"This regulation is designed to promote the protection of customer information as well as the information technology systems of regulated entities. This regulation requires each company to assess its specific risk profile and design a program that addresses its risks in a robust fashion."

URL: https://www.saltycloud.com/blog/what-is-23-nycrr-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a comprehensive guide by the SaltyCloud Research Team (updated Aug 2, 2025) explaining 23 NYCRR Part 500, the New York State Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) cybersecurity regulation. The regulation applies to all NYDFS-regulated entities (banks, insurers, mortgage companies, money transmitters, credit unions, etc.), requiring them to implement cybersecurity programs, conduct risk assessments, and report incidents.

**History/Timeline:** Introduced March 2017 with a stepped phase-in (180 days to 2 years); fully enforced by March 1, 2019. First amendment (April 2020) moved certification deadline to April 15. Second Amendment (2023–2025) added Class A Company obligations, 72-hour breach notification, 24-hour ransomware payment reporting, and required CISO and senior executive signoffs, with deadlines continuing through November 1, 2025.

**Class A Companies:** Organizations with ≥$20M gross annual revenue in each of last two fiscal years AND (more than 2,000 employees OR more than $1B gross annual revenue). They face enhanced requirements including annual independent cybersecurity audits (§500.2(c)), enhanced privileged access controls (§500.7), and endpoint detection & response (§500.14).

**Key Requirements (by section):**
- §500.2 Cybersecurity Program: risk-based program protecting confidentiality, integrity, availability; documents must be available to superintendent
- §500.3 Cybersecurity Policy: written, approved annually by senior officer, covering 14+ domains (access control, data governance, incident response, vendor management, etc.)
- §500.4 Governance: designated CISO accountable for compliance; annual board reporting
- §500.5 Vulnerability Management: annual internal/external pen testing, automated scanning by May 1, 2025
- §500.6 Audit Trails: 5-year retention
- §500.7 Access Controls: need-to-know basis, annual access reviews by May 1, 2025
- §500.8 Application Security
- §500.9 Risk Assessment: annual, documented; foundation for all controls
- §500.11 Third-Party/Vendor Security Policy
- §500.12 MFA for all system access, remote logins, privileged accounts by November 1, 2025
- §500.13 Asset Inventory by November 1, 2025
- §500.14 Monitoring & Awareness: annual cybersecurity training; Class A requires EDR and centralized logging
- §500.16 Incident Response Plan: tested yearly, with BCDR
- §500.17 Reporting: 72-hour incident notice, 24-hour ransomware payment notice (30-day explanation), annual certification by April 15 signed by CISO + senior executive, 5-year records retention

**Exemptions (§500.19):** Entities with fewer than 20 employees, under $7.5M annual revenue (past 3 years), or under $15M total assets may qualify. Must file Notice of Exemption within 30 days.

**Enforcement:** Under Financial Services Law §408, penalties include civil monetary fines, license revocation, and cease-and-desist orders. Recent penalties: Block Inc. ($40M), PayPal ($2M), Gemini Trust Co. ($37M + $1.1B restitution).

**Frameworks for compliance:** NIST CSF, CIS Controls v8.1 (with mapping), CRI Profile, ISO/IEC 27001/27002, and Secure Controls Framework. Third-party vendors are not directly regulated but covered entities remain accountable for vendor cybersecurity under §500.11.

The page also promotes Isora GRC as compliance software for managing NYDFS 23 NYCRR 500 compliance, offering automated workflows, dashboards, and audit trails.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) released the finalized "Second Amendment" to 23 NYCRR Part 500, marking the most significant modifications to the cybersecurity regulations since their original enactment in 2017. The changes aim to address the increasing sophistication of threat actors, the prevalence and ease of executing cyberattacks, and the availability of additional controls to manage cyber risk at reasonable cost. The revisions culminated an approximately yearlong process beginning in July 2022 with a pre-proposed draft, revised on November 9, 2022 and June 28, 2023, before finalization on November 1, 2023.

The new rules carry significant implications: (1) new obligations may require substantial enhancement and investment in cybersecurity programs; (2) the rules portend increased NYDFS investigative and enforcement activity regarding cybersecurity; and (3) these stricter requirements may be adopted by other regulators, potentially impacting non-NYDFS entities (e.g., the FTC recently updated the GLBA Safeguards Rule).

Covered entities should prioritize: identifying key compliance dates; reviewing incident response plans for new incident reporting requirements (effective December 1, 2023); assessing whether they constitute a "Class A" company (which has additional requirements); and considering the impact on the 2023 certification process (occurring in April 2024, as of December 31, 2023).

Key compliance deadlines include December 1, 2023 for section 500.17(a) (notice of cybersecurity events reported to other authorities and ransomware), and April 15, 2024 for section 500.17(b) (Certification of Material Compliance or Acknowledgment of Noncompliance for 2023). The rules take effect via staggered transition periods: 180 days for most sections; one year for sections 500.4(b), 500.5, 500.9, 500.12, and 500.14(b); 18 months for sections 500.6, 500.8, 500.13, 500.14(a), and 500.15; and two years for section 500.11. The Department hosted training webinars (starting November 15, 2023) with recordings to be posted publicly.

Notable definitions include: Covered Entity ("any person operating under a license, registration, charter, certificate, permit, accreditation or similar authorization under the Banking Law, the Insurance Law or the Financial Services Law"); independent audit; and "senior governing body." Even under limited exceptions, MFA remains required for remote access to information systems, remote access to third-party applications (including cloud-based) from which nonpublic information is accessible, and all privileged accounts (except service accounts prohibiting interactive login). The authors are Kirk Nahra (Partner, Co-Chair of AI and Cybersecurity/Privacy Practices), Amy Gopinathan (Senior Associate), and Ali Jessani (Counsel).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: A Summary of the Final Amendments to the NYDFS Cyber ... ---
URL: https://www.debevoisedatablog.com/2023/11/14/a-summary-of-the-final-amendments-to-the-nydfs-cyber-rules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) adopted the second amendment to its Cybersecurity Regulation (Part 500), known as the "Second Amendment" or "Final Amendment." This followed the June 2023 Proposal and incorporated revisions in response to public comments. The Department also released a 38-page Assessment of Public Comments (APC) explaining acceptances/rejections of comments.

The Final Amendment imposes new obligations in six categories, with phased compliance dates beginning December 1, 2023, through November 1, 2025. NYDFS published implementation timelines for small businesses, Class A businesses, and covered entities.

Key changes include:

1. **New Obligations for Class A Companies**: The amendment creates a "Class A" category for covered entities with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue in each of the last two years from New York operations (and affiliates), and either (i) over 2,000 employees or (ii) $1 billion in gross annual revenue for each of the past two fiscal years. Affiliates count only if they share information systems, cybersecurity resources, or part of a cybersecurity program. Class A companies face additional cybersecurity obligations.

2. **New Governance Requirements**: Enhanced requirements for CISOs, management, and boards beyond the original Part 500 (which already required board cybersecurity reporting and written policies approved by a senior officer).

3. **New Technical Requirements**: All covered entities face new technical obligations. Notably, MFA definitions were changed to remove the reference to "text message on a mobile phone" — while still acceptable, text-message MFA is considered weaker. The device used for authentication (e.g., office workstation, mobile phone, or laptop with biometrics or authenticator apps) may serve as an authentication factor. Physical security tokens (like PIV cards and security keys) offer phishing resistance, though NYDFS noted it would be too costly to require phishing-resistant MFA for all covered entities at this time.

4. **Incident Response and Business Continuity (BCDR)**: New requirements for incident response and BCDR plans.

5. **Expanded Breach Notification Obligations**: The original rule required notification to NYDFS within 72 hours of determining a cybersecurity event occurred that (1) had a reasonable likelihood of materially harming normal operations, or (2) required notification to another regulatory body. The Final Amendment expands these obligations.

6. **Enforcement**: New enforcement-related provisions.

Notably, throughout the process, NYDFS was determined to set standards for larger companies rather than deferring entirely to risk-based decision-making, though it demonstrated understanding of the complex nature of cybersecurity governance.

The article was written by Debevoise & Plimpton attorneys (Luke Dembosky, Avi Gesser, Erez Liebermann, and others) and references a November 28, 2023 webcast on the amendments.
</summary>

"On November 1, 2023, the New York Department of Financial Services ('NYDFS' or the 'Department') announced the adoption of the second amendment to its Cybersecurity Regulation (the 'Second Amendment' or 'Final Amendment') that reflects NYDFS's revisions as a result of comments it received on the proposed amendment released in June 2023.", "Throughout the amendment process, the Department was resolute in promulgating a set of standards for larger companies rather than deferring to those companies to make all risk-based decision-making.", "The Final Amendment creates a category of 'Class A' companies that are covered entities with at least $20,000,000 in gross annual revenue in each of the last two years from all business operations of the entity and the business operations in New York State of its affiliates, and either (i) over 2,000 employees or (ii) $1 billion in gross annual revenue for each of the past two fiscal years.", "'Text message MFA, while still acceptable, is widely considered to be a weaker form of MFA, and the Department encourages the adoption of more secure forms of MFA, in particular phishing-resistant forms of MFA.'", "The definition of MFA has also been changed to remove the reference to 'text message on a mobile phone.'"

<summary>
On March 30, 2026, the US Department of Justice (DOJ) National Security Division (NSD) issued updated guidance clarifying how companies should report voluntary self-disclosures (VSDs) of potential criminal violations of US national security laws (including export controls and sanctions) under DOJ's new department-wide Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP), released March 10, 2026. The CEP explicitly supersedes all previous DOJ component policies, including NSD's prior Enforcement Policy for Business Organizations (last revised March 2024). While the NSD's announcement introduces no new substantive cooperation or remediation standards, it provides procedural clarity.

Key points:
- Companies seeking VSD credit should submit disclosures under the CEP framework rather than NSD's prior standalone policy; NSD remains the primary evaluator for national security matters, but all components now apply the same department-wide framework.
- All VSDs concerning potential criminal violations of US national security laws should be sent to NSD.VSD@usdoj.gov.
- Covered laws include the Arms Export Control Act (AECA, 22 U.S.C. § 2778), Export Control Reform Act (ECRA, 50 U.S.C. § 4801 et seq.), and International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA, 50 U.S.C. § 1701 et seq.).
- Under the CEP, disclosures must go to the appropriate DOJ component (NSD in this context), and all resolutions must be approved by the Assistant Attorney General (AAG); a good faith disclosure to one component later brought to another appropriate component still qualifies for declination.
- The CEP applies only to potential criminal violations and does not affect parallel civil VSD regimes run by OFAC and BIS, which have distinct standards; a civil disclosure made solely to OFAC or BIS will NOT qualify for criminal VSD credit under the CEP.
- Key change: The CEP now provides qualifying companies (prompt disclosure, full cooperation, timely remediation) with a declination of prosecution—a shift from the superseded NSD policy, which presumed a non-prosecution agreement and no fine (rather than a declination).

--- SOURCE 8: DOJ's Corporate Enforcement Policy Is Tested and Shows Self-Disclosure Works ---
URL: https://www.foxrothschild.com/publications/dojs-corporate-enforcement-policy-is-tested-and-shows-self-disclosure-works

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On June 18, 2026, Fox Rothschild LLP published a legal alert by Saverio S. Romeo analyzing the first declination issued by the U.S. Department of Justice's National Security Division (NSD) under the new Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP). On June 17, 2026, DOJ declined to prosecute German engineering company Robert Bosch GmbH for export control violations involving shipments to Huawei Technologies Co. Bosch exported approximately $72.4 million in Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) sensor products and software to Huawei and its affiliates between September 2020 and September 2024 through two non-U.S. subsidiaries (Bosch Sensortec GmbH and ETAS GmbH). The products fell under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) via the Huawei Foreign Direct Product Rule (FDPR), which extends U.S. jurisdiction to certain foreign-made items produced with covered U.S. technology.

Despite the declination, Bosch faced significant monetary consequences: BIS imposed a civil penalty of $36,184,680 (roughly half the value of unlicensed shipments), and Bosch agreed to disgorge $11,430,098 in pre-tax profits, with DOJ crediting $7,829,069 paid to BIS, resulting in an actual disgorgement payment of approximately $3.6 million. Bosch's remediation included organizational changes, discipline of responsible personnel, adding 66 employees to its trade compliance organization, and updating internal policies.

DOJ's new department-wide CEP, released March 10, 2026, establishes a single uniform framework for voluntary self-disclosure across nearly all DOJ criminal components (excluding the Antitrust Division). Under the CEP, DOJ will decline prosecution when four conditions are met: (1) voluntary self-disclosure, (2) full cooperation, (3) timely and appropriate remediation, and (4) no aggravating circumstances. This shifts the presumptive outcome from a non-prosecution agreement to a full declination. Even without full declination, companies may receive an NPA of fewer than three years, no independent compliance monitor, and a fine reduction of 50-75% below the Sentencing Guidelines range.

Key takeaways: self-disclosure now offers concrete benefits (not just aspirational); monetary penalties persist but criminal exposure is eliminated; U.S. export control reach continues to expand (this case involved German products shipped to a Chinese buyer); compliance infrastructure must be fit for purpose (DOJ faulted Bosch for inadequately trained compliance personnel and ignoring third-party warnings); timeliness matters (CEP requires disclosure "within a reasonably prompt time" after becoming aware of misconduct); and individual exposure remains—the declination does not protect individuals. Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg characterized the declination as reflecting "the clear benefits for companies that promptly disclose potential violations and fully assist in our investigations."
</summary>

## SEC Issues New Requirements for Cybersecurity Disclosures

**Source:** Deloitte Heads Up, Volume 30, Issue 13  
**Date:** July 30, 2023 (Updated December 19, 2023)

### Background
On July 26, 2023, the SEC issued a final rule requiring registrants to provide enhanced and standardized disclosures regarding cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incidents. The rule addresses investor concerns over timely and consistent cybersecurity information amid rising digital threats.

### Key Requirements

**1. Material Cybersecurity Incidents (Form 8-K, Item 1.05)**
- Registrants must file a Form 8-K within four business days of determining a cybersecurity incident is material.
- A cybersecurity incident is defined as "an unauthorized occurrence, or a series of related unauthorized occurrences, on or conducted through a registrant's information systems that jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of a registrant's information systems or any information residing therein."
- Required disclosures include: material aspects of the nature, scope, timing of the incident, and the material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant (including financial condition and results of operations).
- Amended Form 8-K must be filed within four business days if information becomes available later or previously disclosed information is inaccurate.

**2. Materiality Assessment**
- Materiality determinations must be made "without unreasonable delay."
- Materiality is consistent with U.S. Supreme Court standards (TSC Industries, Basic, Matrixx).
- Factors include: probability of adverse outcome, potential significance of loss, nature and extent of harm to individuals, customers, vendor relationships, reputation, and competitiveness.
- Erik Gerding (SEC Division of Corporation Finance director) clarified that materiality may not be determined on the same date the incident occurred.

**3. Temporary Delay for National Security**
- The U.S. Attorney General may determine that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety.
- Initial delay: up to 30 days; secondary delay: additional 30 days; final extraordinary circumstances: up to 60 days; further delays via SEC exemptive order.
- The FBI provided guidance on requesting delays, noting early outreach is critical.

**4. Risk Management, Strategy, and Governance (Form 10-K, Item 1C)**
- Registrants must disclose processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats.
- Disclosures required on: integration into overall risk management, use of third-party assessors, and oversight of third-party service provider risks.
- **Board oversight:** Description of board's oversight of cybersecurity risks, identification of responsible committees, and processes for informing the board.
- **Management responsibilities:** Which positions/committees are responsible, their relevant expertise, processes for monitoring incidents, and reporting to the board.

### Transition Provisions
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Effective December 18, 2023 (all registrants except smaller reporting companies); June 15, 2024 (smaller reporting companies).
- **Regulation S-K Item 106 (Form 10-K):** Effective for annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.
- Inline XBRL tagging required one year after initial compliance dates.

### Changes from Proposed Rule
- Narrowed scope of cyber incident disclosures with added national security delay.
- Amended Form 8-K used instead of Forms 10-Q/10-K for updates.
- Aggregation of immaterial incidents removed (but series of related unauthorized occurrences may still require Form 8-K).
- Removed proposed requirement to disclose cybersecurity expertise of the board.
- Added transition provisions.

### All filers affected
Including domestic registrants, foreign private issuers (FPIs), smaller reporting companies, and emerging growth companies.
</summary>

This is a WilmerHale legal client alert analyzing joint guidance issued on October 9, 2025, by the US Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) and the prudential regulators, which clarifies regulatory expectations for Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs). The guidance comes in the form of a Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) document aimed at reducing unnecessary filings and helping financial institutions concentrate resources on high-value law enforcement activities.

The FAQ clarifies three key areas:
1. **Structuring**: Financial institutions are NOT required to file structuring SARs absent information that a transaction (or series of transactions) is designed to evade reporting requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA). "Structuring" refers to a customer breaking a large transaction into smaller ones to avoid triggering a Currency Transaction Report (CTR) filing requirement (which applies to US currency transactions aggregating over $10,000 in one day). Previously, institutions often filed structuring SARs on legitimate small businesses and restaurants making multiple cash deposits that aggregated to $10,000 in a day, leading to potential loss of banking access.
2. **Continuing Activity Reviews**: Financial institutions are NOT required to manually review a customer or account after filing a SAR to determine whether suspicious activity has continued. Institutions may instead rely on risk-based internal policies, procedures, and controls to monitor and report suspicious activity. This preserves exemptive relief allowing filings as appropriate, rather than every 30 days.
3. **No-SAR Documentation**: Financial institutions are NOT required to document a decision not to file a SAR. If an institution chooses to document such decisions, FinCEN advises that documentation "may vary based on the specifics of the activity being reviewed" and in most cases "a short, concise statement" will suffice.

The guidance follows statements by Administration officials about modernizing AML/CFT regulation. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated the Administration was making "commonsense yet consequential reforms that will ease regulatory burdens without undermining law enforcement efforts." FinCEN Director Andrea M. Gacki testified that there is "an urgent need to modernize the AML/CFT regime in the United States so that it is effective, risk-based and focused on the greatest threats." Undersecretary John K. Hurley described the Administration's "North Star" for AML reform as allocating "limited resources...to the most pressing threats."

The alert anticipates further AML reforms, including a new AML Program Rule that will "re-center supervision" on the effectiveness of a bank's AML/CFT program rather than a "zero-tolerance focus on process and documentation," and potential support for innovation including AI, blockchain analysis, digital identity, and application programming interfaces. The authors recommend financial institutions update their compliance programs in line with the new guidance.

This webpage contains the FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) Frequently Asked Questions regarding the FinCEN Suspicious Activity Report (SAR). The FAQs were issued to assist financial institutions in using the FinCEN SAR, with four additional FAQs issued on October 9, 2025.

Key topics covered across 23 FAQs include:

1. **Critical vs. Non-critical Items**: Financial institutions should complete all items for which they have relevant information. Critical items require either the information or checking "Unknown." Non-critical fields may be left blank when information is not readily available, and no new data collection obligations are created.

2. **Filing Software Limitations**: If software doesn't permit including known information in non-asterisk fields, institutions should complete discrete filings until the software is updated. Amended filings should be completed once updated.

3. **BSA E-Filing Access**: General users need permission from supervisory users to access new FinCEN reports. Supervisory users must reassign roles through "Manage Users" in the BSA E-Filing System.

4. **Filing Instructions**: Available in Attachment C of the "FinCEN SAR Electronic Filing Requirements" document, accessible via the BSA E-Filing System homepage or FinCEN's Forms page.

5. **Filing Names**: Institutions can choose any name (e.g., "Bank SAR 4-4-2013"), but should NOT include names of subjects to avoid inappropriate disclosure.

6. **Corrected/Amended SARs**: Filers should check "Correct/amend prior report" and enter the previous DCN/BSA ID. If the prior ID is unknown, enter 14 zeros (per October 31, 2011 notice). New BSA IDs begin with "31."

7. **Recordkeeping**: The BSA E-Filing System is NOT a record keeping program. Filers must save copies themselves (printed or electronic) and generally retain filings for five years per 31 CFR regulations cited.

8. **Filing Steps (Discrete SAR)**: Complete report, click "Validate," "Sign with PIN," "Save," then "Submit." After submission, a Confirmation Page appears; within 48 hours, the status changes to "Acknowledged" and an official BSA ID is sent to the Secure Mailbox.

9. **Numbering on the SAR**: Field numbers appear out of order because Parts IV and III are completed first to enable "auto population" of certain data elements based on institution type.

10. **NAICS Codes**: Not mandatory; institutions may provide text responses in the "Occupation" field. Batch filers must use only approved 3-4 digit NAICS codes; discrete filers use the drop-down list.

11. **Continuing Suspicious Activity**: Institutions may file SARs for continuing activity with a 120-calendar-day deadline after the previously related SAR. The date range should cover the entire 90-day period following the initial SAR.

12. **Computer Intrusion vs. Account Takeover**: "Computer intrusion" is replaced by "unauthorized electronic intrusion," defined as gaining access to a computer system to affect funds, critical information, or critical systems. It excludes DDoS attacks and attempts on non-critical systems. "Account takeover" differs as the customer is the primary target. Filers should check box 35q for unauthorized electronic intrusion.

13. **Role in Transaction (Items 56/68)**: Non-critical fields indicating "Selling location," "Paying Location," or "Both." Only completed when applicable to the reported activity.

14. **RSSD Numbers**: Depository institutions use RSSD numbers - the filing institution's RSSD in Item 84 and the location where activity occurred in Item 51 (branch-level in Item 66). Credit unions use the overall financial institution RSSD.

15. **Part IV Completion**: Includes examples for bank holding companies filing enterprise-wide, single depository institutions with multiple branches, and joint filings between depository institutions and MSBs. Agents (independent institutions with contractual relationships) require separate Part IIIs.

16. **Contact Office (Item 96)**: Enter the name of the office to contact (e.g., "Compliance Office," "Security Office," "BSA Office"). Item 97 should be that office's phone number.

17. **Item 29 (Amount Involved)**: Aggregate all amounts regardless of transaction type. Never enter "0" or small placeholder amounts. Use boxes 29a ("Amount unknown") or 29b ("No amount involved") as applicable. For continuing activity SARs, only include amounts from the current time period.

This is the FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) official webpage listing its Alerts, Advisories, Notices, Bulletins, and Fact Sheets issued to financial institutions. FinCEN, through its Financial Institution Advisory Program, issues public and non-public advisories concerning money laundering and terrorist financing threats. These advisories typically contain illicit activity typologies, red flags for monitoring, and compliance guidance to help financial institutions enhance their Anti-Money Laundering (AML) monitoring systems and suspicious activity reporting.

The page is organized into four main categories:

1. **Alerts** (most recent listed first): Includes FIN-2026-Alert004 (07/24/2026) on fraud schemes targeting federal student aid; FIN-2026-Alert003 (06/30/2026) on fuel smuggling and tax evasion on the Southern border tied to Mexico-based cartels; FIN-2026-Alert002 (05/11/2026) on Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps front companies and digital asset infrastructure sanctions evasion; FIN-2026-Alert001 (01/09/2026) on fraud rings exploiting federal child nutrition programs in Minnesota; FIN-2025-Alert003 (11/28/2025) on cross-border funds transfers involving illegal aliens; FIN-2025-Alert002 (05/01/2025) on oil smuggling on the U.S. Southwest border; FIN-2025-Alert001 (03/31/2025) on bulk cash smuggling by Mexico-based transnational criminal organizations; FIN-2024-Alert005 (12/18/2024) on fraud schemes abusing FinCEN's name; FIN-2024-Alert004 (11/13/2024) on deepfake media fraud schemes; FIN-2024-Alert003 (10/23/2024) on countering Hizballah financing; two rescinded alerts (as of 01/29/2025) on Israeli extremist violence in the West Bank; plus earlier alerts on COVID-19 Employee Retention Credit fraud, Hamas terrorist financing, "pig butchering" virtual currency scams, Russian export control evasion, mail theft-related check fraud, Russian elite real estate investments, human smuggling, convertible virtual currency Twitter scams, and more.

2. **Recent Advisories**: Includes FIN-2026-A002 (06/05/2026) on non-work authorized populations and financial system risks; FIN-2026-A001 (03/30/2026) on health care fraud targeting Medicare/Medicaid; FIN-2025-A003 (08/28/2025) on Chinese money laundering networks used by Mexico-based transnational criminal organizations; and FIN-2025-A002 (06/06/2025) on Iranian illicit oil smuggling, shadow banking, and weapons procurement.

3. **FinCEN Notices**: Includes FIN-2026-NTC1 (05/11/2026) on human trafficking threats during the 2026 FIFA World Cup; FIN-2025-NTC2 (09/8/2025) on financially motivated sextortion; FIN-2025-NTC1 (08/4/2025) on convertible virtual currency kiosks for scams; FIN-2025-CTA1 (02/18/2025) extending the Beneficial Ownership Information reporting deadline by 30 days and announcing intent to revise the rule; joint notices with OFAC and FBI on timeshare fraud; counterfeit U.S. passport cards; export control evasion reporting; payroll tax evasion and workers' comp fraud in construction; environmental crimes; online child sexual exploitation; antiquities and art trade; and multiple COVID-19 related notices (2020-2021).

4. **Bulletins and Fact Sheets**: Includes the GENIUS CIP NPRM Fact Sheet (06/18/2026) on customer identification program requirements; Treasury AML/CFT and SCP NPRM Fact Sheet (04/08/2026) implementing GENIUS Act obligations; FinCEN AML/CFT Program NPRM Fact Sheet (04/07/2026) proposing fundamental reform of financial institution AML/CFT programs; Whistleblower Bulletin (02/13/2026) on fraud-related AML and sanctions violations; FinCEN Year in Review reports (FY24, FY23, FY22); Investment Adviser Final Rule Fact Sheet and Residential Real Estate Final Rule Fact Sheet (both 08/28/2024); Financial Trend Analyses on Russian export controls, Russian oligarchs, ransomware, and wildlife trafficking; Rapid Response Program fact sheets; 314(a) and 314(b) fact sheets; MSB quick reference guides; SAR Bulletins (1999-2002); and historical fact sheets dating back to 1997-2007 covering the Bank Secrecy Act, USA PATRIOT Act Section 312, BSA Direct E-Filing, and commonly used acronyms.

Many documents are available in both English and Spanish. Some alerts have been rescinded (the two West Bank-related alerts were rescinded as of January 29, 2025). The page also provides contact information, subscription options for FinCEN news updates, and links to related government resources (Treasury.gov, IRS.gov, Regulations.gov, USA.gov, Vote.gov).

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the official U.S. Department of the Treasury homepage, providing a comprehensive portal to the department's general information, offices, bureaus, budget and financial reporting, history, careers, and policy areas (tax, economic, terrorism and illicit finance, financing the government, financial markets, consumer policy, international, small business, and tribal affairs). It also links to key data resources including interest rates, Treasury yield curves, national debt, quarterly refunding, and the Troubled Assets Relief Program, as well as services related to bonds and securities, grants, payments, currency and coins, auctions, taxes, and forms.

The featured news story announces that FinCEN (Financial Crimes Enforcement Network) issued an Advisory urging financial institutions to detect and report illicit activity related to the unlawful employment of illegal aliens. Key details include:
- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated: "President Trump has done more than anyone in history to secure our nation's borders. Part of that effort includes securing our financial system. This Administration will not allow illegal aliens to abuse financial institutions to steal billions of dollars from hardworking American taxpayers."
- The Advisory was issued jointly with the FDIC, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, National Credit Union Administration, and in coordination with the IRS.
- It supports Executive Order 14406, "Restoring Integrity to America's Financial System."
- The Advisory highlights identity theft and payroll fraud schemes in agriculture, construction, domestic service, hospitality, and other industries, often involving shell companies and unregistered money services businesses.
- It encourages banks to consider Individual Taxpayer Identification Numbers (ITINs) as a risk factor in customer due diligence.
- The Advisory includes 18 red flag indicators for detecting suspicious activity. Financial institutions should use key term "FINANCIALINTEGRITY-2026-A002" in SAR field 2.
- One case study describes a payroll scheme that cost the U.S. more than $38 million.
- Tips about employers exploiting unauthorized workers can be reported to ICE's Tip Form or by calling (866) 347-2423.
- FinCEN maintains an Advisory Program and a Whistleblower Program (www.fincen.gov/whistleblower-program) for reporting Bank Secrecy Act violations.
</summary>

## Timeline of Cyber Incidents Involving Financial Institutions

This timeline chronicles ~200 cyber incidents targeting financial institutions since 2007, and can be filtered by country, region, year, attribution, incident type, and actor type. Cybersecurity risks to the financial system have grown in recent years, in part because the cyber threat landscape is worsening; in particular, state-sponsored cyberattacks targeting financial institutions are becoming more frequent, sophisticated, and destructive. In 2017, the G20 warned that cyberattacks could “[undermine the security and confidence and endanger financial stability](https://carnegieendowment.org/files/g20-communique.pdf).”

To keep track of the evolution of the threat landscape, Carnegie’s Technology and International Affairs Program updates this timeline with data from provided by the Cyber Threat Intelligence unit of BAE Systems. The timeline has not been designed to cover every single incident but rather to provide insight into key trends and how the threat landscape is evolving over time.

This webpage is from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace's FinCyber Project, presenting an interactive timeline chronicling approximately 200 cyber incidents targeting financial institutions since 2007. The timeline is maintained by Carnegie's Technology and International Affairs Program with data provided by BAE Systems' Cyber Threat Intelligence unit. It can be filtered by country, region, year, attribution, incident type, and actor type.

The timeline is organized chronologically, with detailed entries for each incident. Key incidents from 2022 include:
- Beanstalk Farms cryptocurrency theft ($180M lost, April 17, 2022, United States)
- Fakecalls banking trojan targeting South Korean banks (April 11, 2022)
- CashMama data breach in India (April 6, 2022)
- Lazarus 'Trojanised' DeFi app spearphishing (April 1, 2022, North Korean state-sponsored, high confidence)
- Ronin cryptocurrency theft ($615M, second largest crypto heist to date, attributed to Lazarus Group, March 23, 2022)
- TransUnion SA data breach affecting ~3 million customers (South Africa, March 17, 2022)
- Moscow Stock Exchange and Sberbank DDoS attacks attributed to Ukrainian IT Army (February 28, 2022)
- Aon ransomware attack (February 25, 2022)
- Ukrainian government and banking sector DDoS attacks attributed to Moscow (February 15, 2022)
- IRA Financial Trust crypto theft ($36M, February 8, 2022)
- Medusa Android banking trojan expansion (February 2022)
- Wormhole crypto theft ($322M, February 2, 2022)
- Qubit Finance crypto theft ($80M, January 27, 2022)
- TeaBot and FluBot banking trojan resurgence (January 26, 2022)
- Multichain crypto theft ($1.4M, January 17, 2022)
- Crypto.com 2FA bypass hack ($35M, affecting 483 accounts, January 17, 2022)

# Information Technology: OCC Points of Contact for Banks’ Computer-Security Incident Notifications

Share This Page:

### To

Chief Executive Officers of All National Banks, Federal Savings Associations, and Federal Branches and Agencies; Department and Division Heads; All Examining Personnel; and Other Interested Parties

## Summary

Effective May 1, 2022, banks[1](#ftn1) must use the designated points of contact listed in this bulletin to satisfy the incident notification requirements established in the interagency final rule for banks and their bank service providers dated November 23, 2021. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation published the final rule to help promote early awareness of emerging threats to banks, their bank service providers, and the broader financial system and to help the agencies react to these threats before they become systemic.[2](#ftn2)

Banks and their bank service providers must comply with the final rule starting May 1, 2022. Under the final rule, a notification incident generally includes a significant computer-security incident that disrupts or degrades, or is reasonably likely to disrupt or degrade, the viability of the bank’s operations; results in customers being unable to access their deposit and other accounts; or impacts the stability of the financial sector. Incidents may include a major computer-system failure; a cyber-related interruption, such as a distributed denial of service or ransomware attack; or another type of significant operational interruption.

### Note for Community Banks

This bulletin applies to community banks.

## Highlights

## OCC Points of Contact for Banks

Starting on May 1, 2022, banks may satisfy the notification requirement of the final rule by contacting their supervisory office or by using one of the following to communicate a notification incident:

If a bank is unsure whether it is experiencing a notification incident for purposes of the final rule, the bank should contact its supervisory office.[3](#ftn3)

## Further Information

Share This Page:

### To

Chief Executive Officers of All National Banks, Federal Savings Associations, and Federal Branches and Agencies; Department and Division Heads; All Examining Personnel; and Other Interested Parties

## Summary

On November 23, 2021, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation published a final rule to establish computer-security incident notification requirements for banking organizations and their bank service providers.

### Note for Community Banks

This final rule applies to community banks.[1](#ft1)

## Highlights

## Background

Computer-security incidents can result from destructive malware or malicious software (cyberattacks), as well as nonmalicious failure of hardware and software, personnel errors, and other causes. Cyberattacks targeting the financial services industry have increased in frequency and severity in recent years. These cyberattacks can adversely affect a bank’s networks, data, and systems and, ultimately, its ability to resume normal operations.

In addition, banks have become increasingly reliant on bank service providers to provide essential services. Such third parties may also experience computer-security incidents that could disrupt or degrade the provision of services to their bank customers or have other significant impact on a customer bank.

This rule will help ensure that the OCC knows about and can respond in a timely manner to material and adverse computer-security incidents affecting banks.

## Further Information

Please contact Patrick Kelly, Director, Critical Infrastructure Policy, (202) 649-5519; or Carl Kaminski, Assistant Director, or Priscilla Benner, Senior Attorney, Chief Counsel’s Office, (202) 649-5490.

Benjamin W. McDonough
