--- SOURCE 6: Securities Litigation 2025 Year-End Update - Gibson Dunn ---
URL: https://www.gibsondunn.com/securities-litigation-2025-year-end-update

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Gibson Dunn client alert provides a comprehensive overview of major developments in federal and state securities litigation during 2025, covering filing/settlement trends, Supreme Court matters, Delaware corporate law developments, industry-specific issues, and class certification rulings.

**I. FILING AND SETTLEMENT TRENDS:** 207 federal cases were filed in 2025, a decrease from 2024 and well below the 2017-2019 peak. Health and Technology Services sector filings rose again in 2025 (surpassing 2021-2022 levels), while Electronic Technology filings dropped slightly; together these sectors comprised over 50% of filings. Finance sector filings declined from 11% to 9%. Rule 10b-5 filings made up the vast majority of federal filings. Most filings occurred in the Second and Ninth Circuits, with Second Circuit filings consistent with 2024 but Ninth Circuit filings down significantly. AI-related filings continued to increase, while SPAC and Cybersecurity/Customer Privacy Breach filings decreased since 2021. The average settlement value was $40 million (slight drop from last year), and the median settlement value increased notably from $14 million in 2024 to $17 million in 2025—the highest figure in at least a decade.

**II. SUPREME COURT MATTERS:** (1) The Court heard oral argument in FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund on whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act of 1940 provides a private right of action and rescission remedy; a decision is expected between March and June 2026. (2) The Court granted certiorari in SEC v. Sripetch to address whether the SEC must show pecuniary harm as a precondition to disgorgement awards, resolving a circuit split between the Ninth/Fifth Circuits (no showing required) and the Second Circuit (showing required). (3) Barton v. SEC awaits a certiorari decision on whether the Fifth Circuit's broad grant of a receivership over defendant's assets constitutes unduly punitive pre-trial punishment. (4) In Handal v. Innovative Indus. Props., the Third Circuit held that "neither 'corporate trauma' nor 'ordinary negligence' amounts to securities fraud" and the antifraud provisions do not function as "a general charter of shareholder protection."

**III. DELAWARE DEVELOPMENTS:** (1) On February 27, 2026, the Delaware Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of Senate Bill 21's challenged provisions in Rutledge v. Clearway Energy Group, holding they neither divested the Court of Chancery of equity jurisdiction nor retroactively extinguished vested rights. (2) In Brola v. Lundgren, the Court of Chancery dismissed a derivative complaint, holding that "fiduciary liability is not a catch-all for every wrong committed in the workplace simply because the perpetrator happens to hold a title" and that workplace misconduct generally falls outside Delaware corporate law. (3) In Witmer v. Armistice Capital, the court dismissed derivative claims against a 41.4% stockholder, finding it was not a controlling stockholder (despite large stake, it did not "control the board, dictate its decision making, or compel the challenged outcomes") and that "[a]n investor does not become a fiduciary simply because it has a board designee." (4) In December 2025, the Delaware Supreme Court reinstated Elon Musk's 2018 equity compensation package and slashed the plaintiff attorneys' $345 million fee award in In re Tesla, Inc. Derivative Litig.

**IV. INDUSTRY DEVELOPMENTS:** (1) Digital assets: In re EthereumMax certified four state-specific classes but refused a nationwide class due to territorial limitations in California/Florida securities statutes; Underwood v. Coinbase resolved discovery disputes over whether Coinbase is a "statutory seller" based on title transfer. (2) Howey test applications diverged: Real v. Yuga Labs dismissed securities claims (public blockchain, independent exchanges, non-proprietary NFTs undermined commonality), while Holland v. CryptoZoo held tokens were plausibly securities (economic reality prevails over disclaimers). The SEC filed SEC v. Morocoin Tech Corp., alleging a crypto "confidence scam" that misappropriated at least $14 million from U.S. investors using AI-generated "signals" and deepfake videos. (3) Regulatory: SEC-CFTC joint statement (Sept. 2, 2025) clarified that designated contract markets and exchanges may facilitate spot crypto asset trading; SEC Crypto Task Force held "Crypto on the Road" meetings and a Financial Surveillance and Privacy roundtable (Dec. 15, 2025); SEC established a new AI task force led by Valerie Szczepanik. (4) ESG/DEI: Lyall v. Elsevier dismissed greenwashing claims for failure to plead loss causation; Target consolidated shareholder actions over its 2023 Pride campaign were transferred to Minnesota; Spence v. American Airlines found ERISA fiduciary breaches for ESG investing focus but awarded no monetary damages (though over $4.5M in attorney's fees); SEB Inv. Mgmt. AB v. Wells Fargo (fake interviews for diversity compliance) settled in November 2025 after class certification.

**V. CLASS CERTIFICATION:** (1) The Ninth Circuit's first decision applying Goldman—Jaeger v. Zillow Group—affirmed class certification, rejecting defendants' mismatch challenge to price impact. Lower courts continue scrutinizing mismatch arguments; Gambrill v. CS Disco recommended denying certification because corrective disclosures did not sufficiently "match" challenged statements. (2) The Fifth Circuit granted interlocutory review in Bozorgi v. Cassava Sciences to address whether the Basic presumption applies in "meme stock" markets allegedly divorced from traditional informational efficiency—potentially the first circuit-level guidance on this issue.
</summary>

This webpage from Cohen Milstein Sellers & Toll PLLC describes the firm's role in the MOVEit Data Breach Litigation, a multidistrict litigation (MDL) case pending in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts (Case No. 1:23-md-03083), involving a massive data breach linked to Progress Software Corp.'s MOVEit Transfer file-sharing software.

--- SOURCE 8: SEC Charges R.R. Donnelley for Ransomware Attack ... ---
URL: https://www.hunton.com/privacy-and-cybersecurity-law-blog/sec-charges-r-r-donnelley-for-ransomware-attack-response

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On June 18, 2024, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced a settlement with R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. (RRD) for violating federal securities laws' internal controls and disclosure controls provisions in connection with its response to a 2021 ransomware attack. RRD was ordered to pay a $2.125 million civil penalty and cease further violations of Section 13(b)(2)(B) of the Securities Exchange Act and Exchange Act Rule 13a-15(a).

The attack began on November 29, 2021, when RRD's intrusion detection systems issued malware alerts. A third-party managed security services provider (SSP) escalated three alerts to RRD, but RRD failed to investigate or take infected instances off the network until December 23, 2021, when another company with shared network access alerted RRD's CISO. During this period, the threat actor installed encryption software, exfiltrated 70 GB of data (including personal and financial information belonging to 29 of RRD's 22,000 clients), and compromised a domain controller server.

The SEC found RRD failed to design effective cybersecurity incident controls, citing: insufficient oversight of the SSP's resource allocation; lack of clear prioritization and escalation workflows for alerts; inadequate audit procedures for the SSP; and RRD personnel having insufficient time to review escalated alerts due to other job responsibilities. Crucially, the SEC treated RRD's IT systems as an "asset" under the internal accounting controls provision—a move two dissenting commissioners argued was an overly expansive interpretation that conflates internal accounting controls with broader administrative controls. The SEC considered RRD's cooperation and remedial actions in accepting the settlement, including reporting the attack to the SEC before disclosing to investors, revising policies, adopting new technology, and increasing cybersecurity staffing.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
The SEC alleged that RRD 'did not take the infected instances off the network and failed to conduct its own investigation of the activity, or otherwise take steps to prevent further compromise before December 23, 2021', The dissenting commissioners argued the SEC's 'expansive interpretation of what constitutes an asset under Section 13(b)(2)(B)(iii)' ignored the distinction between internal accounting controls and broader administrative controls, The SEC noted that RRD's internal policies 'failed to sufficiently identify lines of responsibility and authority, set out clear criteria for alert and incident prioritization, and establish clear workflows for alert review and incident response and reporting'
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 9: SEC's $2.1M fine on RR Donnelly over hack response ... ---
URL: https://www.legaldive.com/news/sec-21m-fine-ransomware-victim-slammed-overreach/719808

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) settled charges against R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. for approximately $2.1 million, alleging the company violated Section 13(b)(2)(B) of the Securities Exchange Act by failing to "devise and maintain a system of cybersecurity-related internal accounting controls." The charges stemmed from the company's response to a 2021 ransomware attack that occurred between November 29 and December 23, 2021.

Key facts of the case:
- The threat actor used "deceptive hacking techniques" to install encryption software on R.R. Donnelley computers and exfiltrated 70 gigabytes of data, including data from 29 of the company's 22,000 clients, some containing personal identification and financial information.
- The company's investigation found no evidence that the threat actor accessed financial systems or corporate financial and accounting data.
- The SEC alleged R.R. Donnelley failed to design effective disclosure-related controls and procedures around cybersecurity incidents, and that its cybersecurity alert review and incident response policies "failed to adequately establish a prioritization scheme and to provide clear guidance to internal and external personnel on procedures for responding to incidents."
- Without admitting or denying the findings, R.R. Donnelley agreed to pay the $2.1 million civil penalty and cease and desist from violating Section 13(b)(2)(B) and Exchange Act Rule 13a-15a.

This enforcement action represents the SEC's latest assertion of jurisdiction under Section 13(b)(2)(B) to punish companies for alleged failures that don't impact financial reporting or accounting controls, and is the second time the agency has used the provision for a cybersecurity breach. The first such action was against SolarWinds, which is currently being litigated in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York.

Legal analysts have criticized the action as an overreach:
- Charu Chandrasekhar, partner at Debevoise & Plimpton, said the application to cybersecurity systems "is not consistent with the purpose of the provision and the context in which the provision has historically been applied by the SEC."
- Mark Schonfeld, litigation partner at Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, said the interpretation puts the SEC in the position of "basically judging or second-guessing the strength and adequacy of a company's cybersecurity controls" and questioned whether this was what Congress intended.
- Nicole Friedlander, partner at Sullivan & Cromwell, noted that under the SEC's reading, the agency could "punish any company that is the victim of a cybercrime."
- The SEC's two Republican commissioners, Hester Peirce and Mark Uyeda, issued a joint dissenting statement, saying the interpretation "gives the Commission a hook to regulate public companies' cybersecurity practices."

The SEC has been sharpening its cybersecurity enforcement focus, including new rules effective December 2023 requiring public companies to disclose "material" cybersecurity incidents within four days of determining a material breach. Jorge Tenreiro, acting chief of the SEC's Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit, noted that R.R. Donnelley cooperated "in a meaningful way," which was reflected in the settlement terms.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"As the dissenting SEC commissioners noted, it's arguably an aggressive expansion of the SEC's use of this provision. I don't think the application to cybersecurity systems is consistent with the purpose of the provision and the context in which the provision has historically been applied by the SEC." — Charu Chandrasekhar, Debevoise & Plimpton partner
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 10: The SEC’s Controls-Based Approach to Cybersecurity Enforcement Continues, with an Accounting Twist ---
URL: https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/240625-the-sec-s-controls-based-approach-to-cybersecurity

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This MoFo Client Alert discusses the SEC's June 18, 2024 settlement with R.R. Donnelley & Sons Co. (RRD) for a $2.125 million civil penalty based on alleged failures to design effective disclosure controls and procedures (Exchange Act Rule 13a-15(a)) and to maintain adequate internal accounting controls (Exchange Act Section 13(b)(2)(B)) related to cybersecurity. This marks the SEC's second application of Section 13(b)(2)(B) to cybersecurity controls after a cyber incident.

Key facts of the case: Between November and December 2021, RRD suffered a ransomware intrusion. RRD's third-party managed security services provider (MSSP) escalated some but not all alerts to RRD's internal security personnel beginning November 29, 2021. RRD failed to take infected systems off the network and did not investigate until December 23, 2021. At least 20 additional alerts regarding the same malware were not escalated. The threat actor exfiltrated 70 GB of client data (including personal identification and financial information), though no evidence showed access to RRD's financial systems or corporate financial/accounting data. RRD self-reported to the SEC on December 27, 2021.

Key takeaways: (1) This is the SEC's second application of Section 13(b)(2)(B) to cybersecurity controls; (2) The SEC's first cyber enforcement action with Section 13(b)(2)(B) charges is being litigated in SEC v. SolarWinds Corp. (SDNY, Judge Paul Engelmayer, motion to dismiss stage) — a SolarWinds victory could affect future SEC enforcement; (3) Public companies should review incident response and escalation policies to ensure clear personnel authority, unambiguous alert prioritization guidelines, and well-defined internal escalation/reporting processes, plus adequate resourcing.

SEC Commissioners Hester Peirce and Mark Uyeda dissented, arguing Section 13(b)(2)(B) was intended for accounting controls, not cybersecurity or IT systems. Commissioner Peirce asserted that "computer systems," while technically corporate property, are not the type of assets covered by Section 13(b)(2)(B) because they are not the subject of corporate transactions, and cautioned against agency overreach. This mirrors their November 2023 dissent in the SEC's settlement with Charter Communications regarding stock buybacks and Rule 10b5-1 trading plans. Authors: Haimavathi V. Marlier, Miriam H. Wugmeister, Nicole K. Serfoss, and Dan Baskerville.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The SEC's first cyber enforcement action including Section 13(b)(2)(B) charges is currently under consideration by Judge Paul Engelmayer in the Southern District of New York at the motion to dismiss stage. A victory by SolarWinds on its 13(b)(2)(B) defense could affect how the SEC approaches future Section 13(b)(2)(B) cybersecurity enforcement actions involving exfiltration of computer code and software or access to IT infrastructure."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 11: OFAC Announces Settlement with Virtual Currency Exchange Kraken | Global Investigations & Compliance Review ---
URL: https://www.globalinvestigations.blog/anti-money-laundering/ofac-announces-settlement-with-virtual-currency-exchange-kraken

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On November 28, 2022, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Payward, Inc. (known as "Kraken"), a U.S.-based virtual currency exchange, regarding 826 apparent violations of the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations. Kraken agreed to pay $362,158.70 to resolve its potential civil liability—a sum significantly lower than the statutory maximum of $272,228,964—because OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, and mitigating factors including significant remedial measures were applied. Kraken also agreed to invest $100,000 in additional sanctions compliance controls.

The violations stemmed from a gap in Kraken's compliance program: although the company screened users for sanctions compliance at account onboarding (including reviewing IP address information to prevent users in sanctioned jurisdictions from using the exchange), it did not implement IP address blocking on subsequent transactional activity. This allowed users to continue using their accounts while located in Iran. OFAC cited this as the sole aggravating factor, noting Kraken "failed to exercise due caution or care for its sanctions compliance obligations when, knowing it had customers worldwide, it applied its geolocation controls only at the time of onboarding and not with respect to subsequent transactional activity."

In response, Kraken implemented remedial measures including: adding geolocation blocking to prevent users in prohibited jurisdictions from accessing accounts on the website, implementing multiple blockchain analytics tools for sanctions monitoring, investing in additional compliance training for staff, hiring a dedicated head of sanctions plus new sanctions compliance staff, adding screening capabilities for OFAC's 50 Percent Rule, and contracting with a vendor for identification and nationality verification.

OFAC's enforcement release emphasized that this case highlights the importance of geolocation tools and IP address blocking controls throughout the lifetime of an account, not just at onboarding. The settlement is part of broader recent Treasury Department efforts relating to virtual currency, including other OFAC and FinCEN enforcement actions, OFAC's sanctioning of the virtual currency mixer Tornado Cash, and Treasury reports on digital assets. The article also stresses that sanctions compliance programs in the virtual currency industry should incorporate geolocation tools for each transaction and provide sanctions-specific training that accounts for new and emerging technologies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Kraken failed to exercise due caution or care for its sanctions compliance obligations when, knowing it had customers worldwide, it applied its geolocation controls only at the time of onboarding and not with respect to subsequent transactional activity."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) took two significant actions: (1) issued an updated advisory on sanctions risks for facilitating ransomware payments, and (2) designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (SUEX), a virtual currency exchange, to the Specially Denominated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List for facilitating financial transactions for ransomware actors. These actions highlight the U.S. government's intensified focus on virtual currencies as a means of facilitating ransomware payments and money laundering.

The updated advisory shifted language from "does not encourage" to "strongly discourages" payment of cyber ransoms. OFAC identified two "significant mitigating factors" in determining enforcement actions and penalty amounts for sanctions violations tied to ransomware payments (including self-reporting, which increases the likelihood of a non-public response such as a No Action Letter or Cautionary Letter).

SUEX, reported to be a Czech-registered and Russian-owned company, was the first virtual currency exchange designated under Executive Order 13694, with over 40% of its known transaction history associated with illicit actors. SUEX operates as a "nested" exchange, accepting customers via intermediaries and trading through larger exchanges. The designation blocks all U.S.-jurisdiction property of SUEX and entities 50%+ owned by it, and prohibits U.S. persons from transacting with it, while non-U.S. persons face secondary sanctions risk for material support.

The advisory recommends that companies, particularly in the virtual currency space, enhance due diligence procedures—paying attention to peer-to-peer exchangers, mixers, tumblers, and similar illicit-facilitating services—and warns U.S. persons with hosted wallets to consider risks of future asset restrictions if custodial entities are designated. Additional designations and enforcement actions are expected as more ransomware information becomes available.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
These actions demonstrate the U.S. government's increasing focus on virtual currencies as a key means of facilitating ransomware payments and related money laundering, as well as OFAC's commitment to combating ransomware attacks and other malicious cyber activities.

Under US sanctions programs, violations are based on strict liability, meaning US persons may be held liable even without knowing they transacted with a blocked person. --- SOURCE 15: Fair Warnings from OFAC's Settlements with ... ---
URL: https://www.americanbar.org/groups/business_law/resources/business-law-today/2023-march/fair-warnings-from-ofacs-settlements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the ABA's Business Law Today (March 2023) by Sarah Jane Hughes of Indiana University Maurer School of Law, analyzes OFAC's late 2022 settlements with cryptocurrency exchanges Bittrex and Kraken as "fair warnings" to all cryptocurrency service providers subject to U.S. sanctions laws. The article argues that OFAC requires more than one-time onboarding identity verification and periodic SDN list screening—providers must implement "lifetime-of-the-relationship" and "in-process geolocational" checks.

Key cases examined:
- **PayPal (March 2015):** OFAC's first major foray into in-process transaction screening for newer electronic payments. PayPal's automatic interdiction filter failed to identify an SDN match, resulting in 136 transactions violating the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proliferators Sanctions Regulations (31 C.F.R. §544). PayPal paid $7,658,300 in civil penalties.
- **Bittrex (2022):** The Bellevue, Washington-based exchange operated 1,700+ accounts, processed 116,421 virtual-currency transactions, and transacted $263,451,600.13 in violation of sanctions law from March 2014 to December 31, 2017. Bittrex had no sanctions compliance program at all from March 2014 to February 2016, failed to screen IP addresses or physical addresses, and did not scrutinize customers providing Iranian passports. The absence of any compliance program for two years was an aggravating factor in a civil penalty exceeding $24 million.
- **Kraken (November 28, 2022):** Payward, Inc. d/b/a Kraken (San Francisco) violated the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulation (31 C.F.R. §560.204) between October 14, 2015 and June 29, 2019. Based on IP address data, Kraken continued dealing with customers who opened accounts outside sanctioned jurisdictions then transacted from Iran. OFAC cited Kraken's failure to employ geolocational in-process and after-onboarding screening as an aggravating factor. Kraken agreed to implement "multiple blockchain analytics tools" (MBAT) such as Chainalysis and CipherTrace, and to screen for OFAC's "50 Percent Rule" regarding beneficial ownership.

Five specific "fair warnings" from these settlements: (1) geolocation/IP address tools for in-process transaction screening; (2) efficacy of controls per OFAC's 2021 "Sanctions Compliance Guidance for the Virtual Currency Industry"; (3) prohibitions on facilitating violations by non-U.S. persons; (4) use of blockchain analytic tools and ongoing/risk-based re-screening (including historic lookbacks after OFAC lists a virtual currency address on the SDN list); and (5) components of a functional compliance program per OFAC's May 2, 2019 "A Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments" (management commitment, risk assessment, training, internal controls, and testing/auditing).

The article also emphasizes the importance of "voluntary self-disclosure"—companies that self-disclose violations before OFAC learns from other sources can negotiate much lower civil penalties. Neither Bittrex nor Kraken self-disclosed, suggesting another entity or FinCEN alerted OFAC. The author's blunt takeaway: "fess up when you mess up."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OFAC requires more than verification of identity at onboarding and periodic checking of customers against OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list. Additionally, providers should employ lifetime-of-the-transaction and in-process geolocation checking in their interdiction screening."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from The HIPAA Journal provides comprehensive healthcare data breach statistics updated through August 4, 2026, covering the period from October 21, 2009 to June 30, 2026. Key findings include:

**Overall Trends:** There has been a clear upward trend in data breaches since 2009, peaking in 2025 with 772 large breaches (affecting 500+ individuals). Between 2018-2021, data breaches doubled as cybercriminals adopted ransomware. From January 1 to April 30, 2026, 252 large breaches were reported (9.5% fewer than the same period in 2025), though OCR has been slow to publish data due to a 43-day government shutdown in late 2025.

**Mega Breaches:** The largest healthcare data breach of all time occurred in 2024 at Change Healthcare, affecting 192.7 million individuals. The third-largest (62.2 million at Conduent Business Services) was reported in 2025. Between 2009-2025, over 1 billion Americans' records were exposed across 7,418 large breaches.

**Causes of Breaches:** Hacking/IT incidents now account for over 80% of large breaches. Loss/theft incidents have declined significantly due to encryption and cloud storage. Unauthorized access/disclosure incidents increased in 2025, partly due to website tracking tools.

**OCR Enforcement:** OCR has a growing backlog of investigations (936 pending). Enforcement actions increased in 2024-2025. The largest HIPAA penalty was $16 million paid by Anthem in 2018. OCR's budget has remained flat since 2009 despite doubled workload.

**Notable 2025-2026 Breaches:** Conduent Business Services (62.2M), Aflac (13.9M), Episource (6.7M), and DentaQuest (15M in 2026) are among the largest recent breaches. The report emphasizes the importance of supply chain security and vendor due diligence.

--- SOURCE 1: NYDFS Fines First Unum and Paul Revere Insurance Companies $1.8 ... ---
URL: https://www.paulweiss.com/insights/client-memos/nydfs-fines-first-unum-and-paul-revere-insurance-companies-18-million-for-violations-arising-out-of-data-breaches

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Paul, Weiss client memorandum (May 20, 2021) reports on the New York Department of Financial Services' (NYDFS) enforcement action against First Unum and Paul Revere Life Insurance Companies, which resulted in a $1.8 million penalty for violations of NYDFS's Cybersecurity Regulation (Part 500 / 23 NYCRR 500).

KEY FACTS OF THE CASE:
- On May 13, 2021, NYDFS announced a consent order with First Unum and Paul Revere, imposing a $1.8 million penalty for violations of Part 500, including false certifications of compliance under 23 NYCRR 500.17.
- Following investigation of two reported phishing incidents, NYDFS found the companies violated Part 500 by failing to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) or reasonably equivalent access controls, which also led to false compliance certifications for 2018.
- The breaches exposed sensitive non-public-personal data of thousands of consumers nationally, including hundreds in New York.
- The companies were also required to improve cybersecurity programs, commission a third-party audit of MFA controls, and provide a comprehensive written Cybersecurity Risk Assessment within 120 days.

TIMELINE OF EVENTS:
- September 20, 2018: First Unum discovered a data breach from a phishing email; unauthorized access occurred June 1-October 20, 2018. Neither company had fully implemented MFA at that time.
- October 10, 2019: First Unum discovered a second breach where 15 email accounts were compromised (October 1-10, 2019). MFA had been implemented but a misconfiguration allowed bypass.
- First Unum and Paul Revere did not fully implement MFA until August 29, 2019.

VIOLATIONS CITED:
- Violation of 23 NYCRR 500.12(b) for failing to fully implement MFA (both companies) and for MFA misconfiguration allowing IP address bypass (First Unum).
- Violation of 23 NYCRR 500.17(b) for falsely certifying Part 500 compliance in 2018.

CONTEXT — PRIOR PART 500 ENFORCEMENT ACTIONS:
- First action (July 2020): Against First American Title Insurance Company (still ongoing).
- Second action (March 2021): Residential Mortgage Services, Inc. (RMS) paid $1.5 million for failing to investigate/notify NYDFS of a phishing breach and not conducting a comprehensive risk assessment.
- Third action (April 2021): National Securities Corporation (NSC) paid $3 million for failing to implement MFA, failing to timely notify NYDFS of two data breaches, and falsely certifying compliance for 2018 (NYDFS's first enforcement action for false certification).
- This case was the fourth enforcement action under Part 500.

IMPLICATIONS NOTED BY AUTHORS:
- NYDFS will now cite false certification of compliance as an additional violation in Part 500 enforcement actions.
- Failure to timely notify NYDFS of successful cybersecurity events may result in fines.
- NYDFS guidance indicates most unsuccessful attacks need not be reported, but Covered Entities must judge whether unsuccessful attacks are "sufficiently serious to raise a concern" (considering whether handling required extraordinary resources or measures).

The memorandum was authored by Richard C. Tarlowe and Cole A. Rabinowitz of Paul, Weiss's Cybersecurity & Data Protection practice.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"On May 13, 2021, the New York Department of Financial Services ('NYDFS') announced a consent order with First Unum Life Insurance Company of America ('First Unum') and Paul Revere Life Insurance Company ('Paul Revere') (collectively the 'Companies'), which imposed a $1.8 million penalty for violations of NYDFS's Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR 500) ('Part 500'), including false certifications of compliance under 23 NYCRR 500.17." "Following an investigation of two reported phishing incidents, the NYDFS found that the Companies violated Part 500 by failing to implement either multi-factor authentication ('MFA') or reasonably equivalent or more secure access controls, and that, for that reason, they also falsely certified compliance with Part 500 in 2018." "The violations 'caused the exposure of a substantial amount of sensitive, non-public-personal data' belonging to the Companies' customers, 'including thousands of consumers nationally and hundred in New York.'"

--- SOURCE 3: NYDFS Releases Consent Order in First Enforcement Action ... ---
URL: https://www.alstonprivacy.com/nydfs-releases-consent-order-in-first-enforcement-action-brought-under-the-cybersecurity-regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Alston & Bird Privacy, Cyber & Data Strategy Blog reports on the first enforcement action brought by the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) under its Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500). After a three-year investigation, NYDFS entered into a Consent Order with a large title insurer (referred to as "the Company") for violations of the Regulation, specifically its failure to protect non-public information (NPI).

The enforcement action was originally brought in July 2020, and the SEC conducted a separate investigation and enforcement that concluded in 2021. Although the initial statement of charges alleged numerous violations, the consent order reduced these to two violations related to the Company's failure to maintain reasonable access privileges and insufficient policies and practices around access controls.

**Alleged Regulation Violations:**
1. The Company failed to implement access controls sufficient to prevent unauthorized access to NPI through one of its applications, in violation of § 500.7. The application contained documents accessible via a link alone without login or authentication, and replacing the document ID in the URL with another sequential number could grant access to unrelated documents. These issues were identified in a December 2018 vulnerability assessment but remained unaddressed until a journalist discovered and published the vulnerability in May 2019.
2. The Company failed to adequately maintain and implement an effective cybersecurity policy related to access controls, in violation of §§ 500.3(b), (d), and (m). While the Company had many policies in place, it did not ensure complete implementation, including a risk assessment that incorrectly classified an application as not containing NPI when it actually housed documents with NPI.

**Settlement Provisions:**
The Company agreed to a $1 million penalty, which reflected its cooperation during the investigation. The Company also submitted a Remediation Overview and Compliance Summary to NYDFS for approval, detailing its efforts to address the violations and enhance its cybersecurity program.

The article notes this is consistent with NYDFS's recent amendments to the Regulation, which emphasize operationalizing cybersecurity policies through procedures developed, documented, and implemented in accordance with written policies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NYDFS found that the Company failed to implement access controls sufficient to prevent unauthorized users to gain access to NPI through one of the Company's applications in violation of § 500.7."

--- SOURCE 4: The NYDFS Part 500 Ransomware Update: What Every Covered Entity Needs to Know ---
URL: https://compassmsp.com/resources/articles/the-nydfs-part-500-ransomware-update-is-here-what-every-covered-entity-needs-to-know

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from CompassMSP (authored by Richard Mendoza, Director of vCISO services) explains the fully effective NYDFS Part 500 Second Amendment and its implications for covered entities. As of November 1, 2025, the multi-year phase-in of the Second Amendment is complete, and all requirements are now in full effect with an annual certification deadline of April 15, 2026 (covering calendar year 2025).

**Background & Scope:** NYDFS Part 500 was first enacted March 1, 2017, as the first-in-the-nation cybersecurity regulation for financial services. It applies to any entity operating under a license, registration, charter, or authorization from NYDFS — including banks, credit unions, insurance companies, agents/brokers, mortgage lenders, money transmitters, virtual currency businesses, and investment advisers. The regulation applies based on NYDFS authorization, not firm size; a five-person investment adviser is as covered as a 500-person bank. The small business exemption only reduces certain MFA obligations and does not eliminate core requirements like written programs, risk assessments, CISO designation, incident response planning, vendor oversight, or annual certification.

**Key Second Amendment Changes (adopted Nov 2023, fully effective Nov 1, 2025):**
1. **MFA:** Required for all remote access to any information system including cloud applications (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, SaaS). SMS and push-based authentication are flagged as weak; NYDFS recommends phishing-resistant methods (FIDO2, WebAuthn, hardware security keys).
2. **Written Asset Inventory:** Documented program accounting for hardware, software, data flows, and access points — must be current and defensible under examination. Genesis Global Trading was cited for this in Jan 2024.
3. **Ransomware Notification — 24 hours:** Ransomware payments must be reported to NYDFS within 24 hours; broader cybersecurity incidents within 72 hours.
4. **Third-Party Risk Management:** Covered entities responsible for ensuring vendors accessing nonpublic information maintain appropriate cybersecurity controls.
5. **Personal Executive Liability:** Annual certification requires dual signatures from CEO and CISO, both personally liable, with verifiable data retained for five years. False or optimistic certifications are independently actionable.

**Enforcement Record:** Since 2021, NYDFS has entered consent orders with 27 entities totaling over $144 million in fines. Notable cases include: (1) Healthplex, Inc. (Aug 2025) — $2 million penalty for a small licensed insurance agent/adjuster that suffered a phishing breach, missing MFA, no data retention policy, and a breach notification arriving 4 months late instead of within 72 hours; (2) Gemini Trust Company (Feb 2024) — $37 million penalty for failing to conduct due diligence on third party Genesis Global Capital, which defaulted on ~$1 billion in loans. Penalties start at $2,500/day per instance, scaling to $75,000/day for willful violations under New York Banking Law, with individual fines exceeding $30 million.

**April 15, 2026 Certification:** Covered entities must answer with documented evidence (not estimates) whether MFA is implemented across all systems, asset inventory is current, vendor agreements are updated, incident response includes notification workflows, and both CEO and CISO can attest to accuracy.

The article concludes with CompassMSP's marketing of its financial services compliance practice (vCISO services, gap assessments) and a subscription offer for its quarterly regulatory newsletter "The Fine Print." An extensive FAQ section covers scope, MFA requirements, notification deadlines, penalties, certification timing, applicability to insurance agencies, and differences between MSPs and MSSPs for compliance support.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The regulation applies based on your NYDFS authorization, not the size of your balance sheet or employee count. A five-person registered investment adviser is as covered as a 500-person regional bank and subject to the same rigorous controls."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation: Dates, Facts and Requirements

This Centraleyes blog post (published October 1, 2025; updated October 5, 2025, by Rebecca Kappel) provides a comprehensive guide to New York's DFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), with a focus on the final compliance phase taking effect November 1, 2025.

**Final Phase Requirements (November 1, 2025):**
1. **Enhanced Multifactor Authentication (MFA):** All covered entities must implement MFA comprehensively for remote access, privileged accounts, and access to any information system. Standard and Class A entities must apply MFA to every user accessing any system.

--- SOURCE 11: Cyber Case Study: UVM Health Network Ransomware Attack ---
URL: https://insurica.com/blog/uvm-health-network-ransomware-attack

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from INSURICA (an insurance/risk management firm) presents a detailed cyber case study of the University of Vermont (UVM) Health Network ransomware attack that occurred in October 2020. UVM Health Network is a six-hospital healthcare organization serving over 1 million patients across Vermont and upstate New York.

**The Incident:** In early October 2020, a UVM Health Network employee took their work laptop on vacation and checked personal emails, opening what appeared to be a legitimate email from their local homeowners association—which had actually been hacked. This phishing email launched malware on the laptop. When the employee reconnected to the network, cybercriminals used the malware to target the entire organization. On October 28, 2020, the attack was launched, spreading malware across the organization's systems. The IT department detected the issue, shut down computer and phone systems, and found a text file from the attackers demanding contact. UVM Health Network refused to pay, contacted the FBI, and Vermont Gov. Phil Scott deployed the National Guard to assist. No sensitive data (patient records or employee info) was stolen or exposed, and the organization recovered most data from backup copies.

**The Impact:** The attack cost an estimated $63 million, including rebuilding 1,300 damaged servers, restoring 600 disabled applications, scanning and cleaning 5,000 malware-ridden computers, and lost revenue of nearly $1.5 million per day. The organization's cyber insurance coverage was only $30 million—far below actual costs. The attack caused reputational damage, delayed patient care (delayed test results, appointment cancellations, rescheduled elective procedures), and pushed back the rollout of an updated electronic health record system (phases 2 and 3 delayed to November 2021 and April 2022, respectively).

**Key Lessons Learned:**
1. Employee education is critical—up to 90% of cyberattacks stem from human error; phishing detection training is essential.
2. Effective security software is necessary—including network-monitoring systems, antivirus programs, firewalls, endpoint-detection products, patch-management tools, and routine penetration testing.
3. Cyber incident response plans make a difference—UVM's lengthy recovery highlighted the need for timely response protocols, including potential attack scenarios, methods for maintaining operations, and designated responsibilities.
4. Ransomware attacks carry unique ramifications—not paying can extend recovery time, but contacting law enforcement (FBI) and working with insurance partners is vital.
5. Proper insurance coverage is crucial—no organization is immune, and policy limits should be carefully selected with professional guidance.
</summary>

During their speeches, they issued and updated the U.S. Department of Justice’s criminal policies on the federal prosecution of corporate crime.[1] These new policy changes are a testament to the ongoing efforts of the Department of Justice (DOJ) to strengthen its corporate criminal enforcement model, which was outlined in two memoranda issued on October 28, 2021, and September 15, 2022, respectively [the 2021 Monaco Memo and the 2022 Monaco Memo hereinafter].[2] The recent policy updates highlight the Department’s strong emphasis on promoting self-regulation and self-disclosure in corporate prosecution as well as its commitment of resources to corporate criminal enforcement. Title: DOJ Highlights Self-Disclosure And Cooperation By Corporate Entities - Corporate Crime - United States
On Jan. 17, 2023, the head of the Criminal Division of the Department of Justice, Assistant Attorney General Kenneth Polite, announced1 revisions to the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act ("FCPA") Corporate Enforcement Policy2 ("CEP") designed to further encourage self-reporting and cooperation by corporate entities. The Criminal Division created a voluntary self-disclosure program for FCPA cases in 2016, which became DOJ policy for all of their corporate prosecutions in 2018. The revised policy that Polite announced last week applies to *all* corporate criminal matters the Criminal Division of DOJ handles,3 and seeks to directly incentivize voluntary self-disclosure for all corporate entities in all federal criminal prosecutions. This comes four months after Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco released a memorandum4 ("Monaco Memo"), directing each DOJ Division involved in prosecuting corporate crime to adopt policies to be "sufficiently transparent such that the benefits of voluntary self-disclosure are clear and predictable." Like Monaco, Polite emphasized the strong focus on prosecuting corporate crime and the key role voluntary self-disclosure plays in that effort. The prior CEP created a presumption that DOJ would decline to prosecute corporate entities that voluntarily self-disclosed, fully cooperated, and appropriately remediated the problem. Unlike the former version of the Criminal Division's CEP, the revised policy creates a clear path to declination even where aggravating circumstances are present. Previously, the Monaco Memo stated that the DOJ ordinarily "will not seek a guilty plea where a corporation has voluntarily self-disclosed, fully cooperated, and timely and appropriately remediated the criminal conduct." The revised CEP reaffirms this principle. Under the prior CEP, when a corporation self-disclosed the unlawful conduct but aggravating circumstances dictated a criminal resolution and not a declination of charges, the Criminal Division "offer[ed] 50% off of the low end of the applicable Sentencing Guidelines penalty range." This advisory from Alston & Bird's Consumer Protection/FTC Team analyzes the FTC's settlement with Drizly LLC, an alcoholic beverage delivery platform (a subsidiary of Uber Technologies since April 2021), and its CEO James Cory Rellas, announced on October 24, 2022.

**The Complaint:** The FTC alleged that Drizly's security failures—including reusing the same password and failing to terminate or monitor a former executive's access to GitHub repositories—led to a threat actor stealing personal information of 2.5 million consumers. The executive had used a seven-character alphanumeric password that he also used on other personal accounts, which a malicious actor obtained through credential reuse from an unrelated breach. - No civil penalty or monetary relief (reflecting the post-AMG world where the FTC lost Section 13(b) leverage for monetary damages)

**Takeaways:** The FTC is continuing privacy-related enforcement actions despite limited monetary relief authority. It will hold individuals personally liable in some cases. Commissioner Rebecca Kelly Slaughter agreed, while Republican Commissioner Christine Wilson dissented, arguing Rellas lacked the requisite knowledge and participation for individual liability under the FTC Act. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Sarah Cabral, a senior scholar for business ethics at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics at Santa Clara University, examines whether CEOs should be personally held accountable for their companies' data security breaches, using the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) 2022 proposed order against Drizly and its CEO James (Cory) Rellas as the case study.

**Background/Context:**
- Drizly is a Boston-based alcohol delivery company founded in 2012 by Nick Rellas, Justin Robinson, and Nick's cousin Cory Rellas after Nick texted Justin "Why can't you get alcohol delivered?"
- Uber acquired Drizly for $1.1 billion in 2021.
- In 2018, a Drizly employee posted company login information to GitHub, which hackers used to mine cryptocurrency.
- In 2020, hackers again accessed company login information via GitHub by hacking a Drizly employee account and stole customers' personal information.
- The proposed FTC order is a response to the company's failure to address security problems first identified in 2018, affecting data of 25 million consumers.

**The Controversy:**
- All four FTC commissioners voted to issue the order to Drizly, but Commissioner Christine Wilson dissented on including Cory Rellas personally. Rellas would be required to implement an information security program if he moves to another company collecting information on 25,000+ consumers.
- Wilson noted the FTC was not alleging Rellas had direct knowledge of the practices leading to the investigation, but rather that he should have prioritized hiring a senior executive to oversee data security. Wilson argued the FTC should not "substitute its own judgment about corporate priorities and governance decisions for those of companies."

**Ethical Analysis:**
- From a utilitarian/consequentialist lens, Rellas' inclusion could be justified because other CEOs will pay attention and tighten security protocols, benefiting many consumers; the penalty also seems relatively minor.
- From a rights/means-end perspective, one could object that Rellas is being used merely as a means to send a message to other CEOs, violating his personal autonomy to make free and rational decisions for his company.
- Rellas is not the first CEO individually named by the FTC—James Vargo (ClixSense) and Zhijun Liu (i-Dressup) have also faced penalties.

**Recommendation:**
- Cabral suggests Congress should allow the FTC to fine companies so heavily that they choose to prioritize data security in the first place. She argues Drizly ignored warning signs and should face financial penalties, not just corrective security measures.

The article was published October 31, 2022, during Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and relates to the Markkula Center's "Introduction to Cybersecurity Ethics" resource and related case studies.

--- SOURCE 24: Drizly (2020) - Public Cloud Security Breaches ---
URL: https://www.breaches.cloud/incidents/drizly

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage documents the Drizly (2020) public cloud security breach, part of the breaches.cloud database that documents cloud security mistakes. In July 2020, Drizly, an on-demand alcohol delivery service, suffered a data breach exposing personal information of over 2 million users.

The breach originated from an executive's GitHub account compromised via a credential-stuffing attack. In April 2018, Drizly granted an executive GitHub access for a one-day hackathon but never revoked permissions afterward. In July 2020, an attacker used credentials from an unrelated breach (the password was only seven characters with no special characters, and MFA was not enabled) to access the executive's GitHub account. The attacker cloned a repository containing AWS credentials, manipulated AWS security group settings to access an RDS database, and exfiltrated 2.5 million consumer records.

Timeline of key events: April 2018 (executive granted GitHub access), July 2020 (breach), July 28, 2020 (public disclosure), October 24, 2022 (FTC investigation), January 10, 2023 (FTC finalized complaint), January 15, 2024 (Uber announced shutting down Drizly, acquired in Feb 2021 for $1.1 billion), March 2024 (division shutdown).

The FTC investigation was notable because it required CEO James Cory Rellas to implement information security programs at any future company he works for. Drizly was also sued in a class action, with a settlement valued between $3.35 million and $7 million.

Key cloud security lessons learned: (1) Failure to scan GitHub for secrets (AWS and RDS credentials were found in source code), (2) Failure to ensure all GitHub Organization users had Multi-Factor Authentication, and (3) Failure to review GitHub access to ensure users were active and limited only to necessary repositories.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Rules: Key Details & Compliance Tips ---
URL: https://www.zscaler.com/zpedia/new-sec-cybersecurity-disclosure-rules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Zscaler (Zpedia) explains the SEC's new cybersecurity disclosure rules announced on July 26, 2023, which apply to public companies. The rules mandate timely disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents and annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance.

**Key Requirements:**
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Material cybersecurity incidents must be reported within four business days of a materiality determination. A new, broader definition of "cybersecurity incident" now includes "a series of related unauthorized occurrences."
- **Temporary Delay:** Companies may delay disclosure up to 120 days (with US Attorney General approval and SEC consent) if disclosure poses national security or public safety risks.
- **Updated Incident Disclosures:** Incomplete Form 8-K data must be acknowledged and later amended within four business days of obtaining missing information.
- **Form 10-K (Regulation S-K Item 106):** Annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and board oversight is required. Companies must describe management's role and responsibilities but are NOT required to disclose board members' cybersecurity expertise.
- **Foreign Private Issuers:** Must file comparable disclosures on Forms 6-K and 20-F.
- **Structured Data:** Disclosures must be tagged in Inline XBRL format, though compliance was delayed by one year.

**Effective Dates and Compliance Timelines:**
- Rules became effective September 5, 2023.
- Larger public companies must comply with Form 8-K Item 1.05 by December 15, 2023.
- Smaller reporting companies have until June 24, 2024, for Item 1.05 compliance.
- Item 106 applies to annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.

**Compliance Preparation Steps:** Review rules with security/filing teams, establish materiality determination processes, draft cyber risk assessment descriptions, engage board of directors in cyber risk oversight, and identify board members with cybersecurity expertise.

**Materiality Definition:** An incident is material if it significantly impacts operations, finances, or reputation, based on quantitative factors (costs) and qualitative factors (reputational damage, litigation exposure).

The page also promotes Zscaler Risk360™ as a tool for cyber risk quantification, financial exposure detail, and board-ready reporting to help companies comply with the new rules.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## SEC Issues New Requirements for Cybersecurity Disclosures

**Source:** Deloitte Heads Up, Volume 30, Issue 13  
**Date:** July 30, 2023 (Updated December 19, 2023)

### Background
On July 26, 2023, the SEC issued a final rule requiring registrants to provide enhanced and standardized disclosures regarding cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incidents. The rule addresses investor concerns over timely and consistent cybersecurity information amid rising digital threats.

### Key Requirements

**1. Material Cybersecurity Incidents (Form 8-K, Item 1.05)**
- Registrants must file a Form 8-K within four business days of determining a cybersecurity incident is material.
- A cybersecurity incident is defined as "an unauthorized occurrence, or a series of related unauthorized occurrences, on or conducted through a registrant's information systems that jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of a registrant's information systems or any information residing therein."
- Required disclosures include: material aspects of the nature, scope, timing of the incident, and the material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant (including financial condition and results of operations).
- Amended Form 8-K must be filed within four business days if information becomes available later or previously disclosed information is inaccurate.

**2. Materiality Assessment**
- Materiality determinations must be made "without unreasonable delay."
- Materiality is consistent with U.S. Supreme Court standards (TSC Industries, Basic, Matrixx).
- Factors include: probability of adverse outcome, potential significance of loss, nature and extent of harm to individuals, customers, vendor relationships, reputation, and competitiveness.
- Erik Gerding (SEC Division of Corporation Finance director) clarified that materiality may not be determined on the same date the incident occurred.

**3. Temporary Delay for National Security**
- The U.S. Attorney General may determine that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety.
- Initial delay: up to 30 days; secondary delay: additional 30 days; final extraordinary circumstances: up to 60 days; further delays via SEC exemptive order.
- The FBI provided guidance on requesting delays, noting early outreach is critical.

**4. Risk Management, Strategy, and Governance (Form 10-K, Item 1C)**
- Registrants must disclose processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats.
- Disclosures required on: integration into overall risk management, use of third-party assessors, and oversight of third-party service provider risks.
- **Board oversight:** Description of board's oversight of cybersecurity risks, identification of responsible committees, and processes for informing the board.
- **Management responsibilities:** Which positions/committees are responsible, their relevant expertise, processes for monitoring incidents, and reporting to the board.

### Transition Provisions
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Effective December 18, 2023 (all registrants except smaller reporting companies); June 15, 2024 (smaller reporting companies).
- **Regulation S-K Item 106 (Form 10-K):** Effective for annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.
- Inline XBRL tagging required one year after initial compliance dates.

### Changes from Proposed Rule
- Narrowed scope of cyber incident disclosures with added national security delay.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 18, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York dismissed most of the SEC's landmark cyber enforcement litigation against SolarWinds Corp. and its Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) Timothy Brown. In a 107-page opinion in Securities and Exchange Commission v. SolarWinds Corp. & Timothy G. Brown (Judge Paul Engelmayer presiding), the court rejected the SEC's efforts to expand the Securities Exchange Act's "internal accounting controls" provision to encompass cybersecurity controls. The court also limited the SEC's use of the "disclosure controls and procedure" provision, finding that innocent errors are "an inadequate basis" on which to plead deficient disclosure controls. Only a subset of material misrepresentation claims related to the Security Statement published on the company's website survived, and the case proceeds toward discovery.

BACKGROUND: SolarWinds, a software company with the Orion Platform, posted a Security Statement on its website in late 2017. In January 2019, nation-state hackers exploited a vulnerability and inserted malicious code into Orion software builds - known as the SUNBURST attack. In 2020, SolarWinds was notified by the USTP and Palo Alto Networks of suspicious activity but couldn't determine the root cause. After Mandiant identified the malicious code, SolarWinds filed a Form 8-K on Dec. 14, 2020, detailing the attack. The SEC filed its complaint in 2023 and an amended complaint on Feb. 16, 2024, charging violations of antifraud provisions, disclosure controls, and internal controls.

KEY COURT RULINGS: 1) Internal Accounting Controls: The court found the SEC "clearly correct" to be challenged on the plain language of Section 13(b), holding that "cybersecurity controls are outside the scope of Section 13(b)(2)(B)" and dismissing the claim entirely. 2) Disclosure Controls: The court dismissed this claim, finding "[w]ithout more, the existence of two misclassified incidents is an inadequate basis on which to plead deficient disclosure controls," and that "second-guessing by hindsight" is disfavored. 3) Security Statement: The court found the SEC sufficiently alleged material misrepresentations concerning access controls and password protection policies on the company's public website. 4) Cyber Risk Disclosures: Dismissed, as fraud claims based on risk disclosures are actionable only where "the warned risk has already occurred." 5) Brown's public statements: Found to be "non-actionable corporate puffery." 6) Form 8-K disclosures: Dismissed as fraud by hindsight; the court found the Form 8-K "captured the big picture: the severity of the SUNBURST attack," noting the stock dropped 16% on filing day and 8% the next day.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The SEC failed to expand internal accounting controls to cover cybersecurity. The SEC must now allege systemic deficiencies (not innocent errors) for disclosure controls violations. Cyber risk disclosure fraud claims are limited to narrow circumstances where the warned risk has already occurred. Courts will consider practical time constraints (including the SEC Cybersecurity Rules' four-business-day disclosure requirement) when assessing Form 8-K filings. Companies should avoid warning about risks that have already occurred, and risk disclosures should convey severity without arming threat actors.

SUGGESTED ACTION ITEMS for issuers: 1) Develop well-designed disclosure controls and incident response plans. 2) Include risk disclosures that convey manner and severity without providing a road map to threat actors. 3) Have a practiced plan for responding to cyber incidents. 4) Engage experienced cybersecurity counsel. This Holland & Knight analysis was authored by Shardul Desai, Allison Kernisky, and Jessica B. Magee on July 24, 2024.
</summary>

Regulation FD exclusions may apply if the information is immaterial, if recipients are not covered persons, if recipients owe a duty of trust or confidence (e.g., attorneys, investment bankers, accountants), or if recipients enter into confidentiality agreements.

The guidance aims to preserve the value of Item 1.05 disclosures and prevent investor confusion between material and immaterial incidents. A "material" incident is defined as one where there is a "substantial likelihood that a reasonable shareholder would consider it important in making an investment decision, or if it would have significantly altered the 'total mix' of information made available." The disclosure must describe the material aspects of the nature, scope, timing, and anticipated impact of the incident. Further SEC guidance is expected as the rules continue to evolve. This Bloomberg Law article (published July 2023, authored by Dan Pepper and Esther Clovis of Norton Rose Fulbright US LLP) outlines the various cybersecurity incident notification requirements that apply to U.S. financial institutions. Key points:

**General Guidance**: Financial institutions experiencing cybersecurity incidents may face multiple regulations with different timing requirements. Each incident must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis to determine if it rises to the level of triggering a notification requirement.

**Joint Computer-Security Incident Notification Rule** (issued by OCC, FRB, and FDIC; 86 Fed. Reg. 66,424, Nov. 23, 2021):
- Banking organizations must notify federal regulators within **36 hours** of determining a "computer-security incident" occurred, if it qualifies as a "notification incident."

- A notification incident is one that has materially disrupted (or is reasonably likely to) the banking organization's ability to: (1) carry out banking operations or deliver products/services to a material portion of customers; (2) operate business lines that would result in material loss of revenue, profit, or franchise value; or (3) operate in ways that would pose a threat to U.S. financial stability.

**Safeguards Rule**: Institutions subject to their regulator's Safeguards Rule must notify their primary federal regulator "as soon as possible" when an unauthorized user accesses a customer's sensitive information (citing OCC, FRB, and FDIC regulations). - **NYDFS**: Must notify NYDFS within **72 hours** of a cybersecurity event (23 NYCRR § 500.17).

KEY PROVISIONS:
1. **Banking Organization Notification**: A banking organization must notify its primary Federal regulator of any "computer-security incident" that rises to the level of a "notification incident" as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after the banking organization determines that a notification incident has occurred.
2. **Bank Service Provider Notification**: A bank service provider must notify each affected banking organization customer (through at least one bank-designated point of contact) as soon as possible when the provider determines it has experienced a computer-security incident that has caused, or is reasonably likely to cause, a material service disruption or degradation for four or more hours.

KEY DATES: Effective date April 1, 2022; Compliance date May 1, 2022. The final rule applies to 12 CFR Parts 53 (OCC), 225 (Federal Reserve), and 304 (FDIC).

DEFINITIONS AND SCOPE:
- **Banking organizations** covered include: for OCC—national banks, Federal savings associations, and Federal branches/agencies of foreign banks; for the Board—U.S. bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, state member banks, U.S. operations of foreign banking organizations, and Edge/agreement corporations; for FDIC—insured state nonmember banks, insured state-licensed branches of foreign banks, and insured state savings associations.
- **Computer-security incident** is defined as an occurrence that results in actual harm to an information system or the information contained within it.
- **Bank service provider** is defined as a bank service company or other person who performs "covered services" (services subject to the Bank Service Company Act, 12 U.S.C. 1861-1867).
- **Designated financial market utilities (FMUs)** under Title VIII of the Dodd-Frank Act are excluded from the definitions of both "banking organization" and "bank service provider."

Timely notification allows agencies to have early awareness of emerging threats, assess threats, facilitate assistance through the Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection, provide guidance, and conduct horizontal analyses to prevent incidents from becoming systemic. The agencies noted that banking organizations increasingly rely on third-party service providers.

This article from Troutman Pepper Locke's Consumer Financial Services Law Monitor discusses the final rule issued on November 18, 2021 by federal banking agencies (Federal Reserve, FDIC, and OCC) establishing computer-security incident notification requirements for "banking organizations" and "bank service providers." The rule takes effect April 1, 2022, with compliance required by May 1, 2022.

Key requirements:
- Banking organizations must notify their regulator "as soon as possible" and no later than 36 hours after determining a "notification incident" has occurred. Notifications go to the agency's designated point of contact via email, telephone, or similar methods.

The 36-hour clock starts only when the organization "determines" a notification incident has occurred, which softens the harsh timing requirement.
- Bank service providers must notify at least one bank-designated point of contact at each affected banking organization customer as soon as possible when they determine they've experienced a computer-security incident materially disrupting or degrading covered services for four hours or more. The "computer-security incident" definition is broader than "notification incident." There is no specific deadline, but notice must be given "as soon as possible." If no point of contact is provided, notification goes to the CEO and CIO.
- Existing requirements under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, the Interagency Guidelines, and the Bank Secrecy Act (suspicious activity reports within 30 days) also apply, though the agencies noted these weren't designed to provide timely information about cyber incidents. Every state also has its own breach notification laws, which generally require notification if there is a risk of consumer harm, without specific timing requirements.

Compliance recommendations include: updating incident response plans with appropriate points of contact, conducting training exercises per the new timing requirements, incorporating applicable definitions into service provider contracts, and updating incident response playbooks. URL: https://medcurity.com/hipaa-security-rule-2026-update

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This page explains the proposed HIPAA Security Rule update (still NOT final as of mid-2026), which would represent the most significant change since the rule's original 2003 adoption. The NPRM was published in the Federal Register on January 6, 2025; the comment period closed March 7, 2025; and OCR has not issued a final rule. OMB's Unified Agenda (RIN 0945-AA22) now targets July 2027 for final action (pushed back from an earlier spring 2026 target), though these timelines are not legally binding.

Key proposed changes include: (1) mandatory annual Security Risk Assessments (the current rule has no specified frequency); (2) mandatory encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit, removing the "addressable" designation; (3) required multi-factor authentication for all systems accessing ePHI; (4) regular vulnerability scanning and penetration testing; (5) enhanced documentation requirements; and (6) comprehensive technology asset inventory and network mapping. The proposed rule would also require annual BAA verification (documenting the verification itself, not just keeping the BAA on file) and a 240-day implementation runway (60 days effective plus 180 days to compliance).

HHS estimated $9 billion in year-one costs and $34 billion across years one through five. In February 2025, CHIME joined seven other associations and 100+ hospital/provider organizations in a letter asking the Trump administration to withdraw the proposal, arguing small and rural providers cannot absorb these costs. HHS retained the July 2027 target despite pushback but signaled willingness to credit good-faith, phased compliance from critical access hospitals and safety-net providers.

The January 2026 OCR Cybersecurity Newsletter emphasized: system hardening as a documented expectation (patch management, default-credential elimination, configuration baselines), evolution from risk analysis to risk management (requiring timely documented remediation, not just an assessment document), and that risk analysis must surface unpatched-software and firmware vulnerabilities (45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)).

The page provides a preparation timeline: gap analysis, SRA, asset inventory, encryption assessment, and MFA planning through mid-2026; encryption deployment, MFA rollout, vulnerability scanning, documentation updates, and training through December 2026; then ongoing annual SRA cycles, continuous vulnerability management (critical patches within 72 hours, scans at least quarterly), and compliance monitoring. Common mistakes warned against: waiting for the final rule, treating compliance as purely a technology project, underestimating documentation requirements, ignoring business associate compliance, and trying to do everything at once. OCR continues to enforce the current Security Rule, under which risk analysis remains the most-frequently-cited deficiency.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a client alert from the law firm WilmerHale, authored by partners Jason C. Chipman and David M. Horn, analyzing two US government advisories issued on October 1, 2020, addressing the risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments: the OFAC Ransomware Advisory (regarding potential sanctions risks) and the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory (FIN-2020-A006, regarding ransomware and use of the financial system for ransom payments). These represented the first time OFAC and FinCEN issued guidance specifically addressing ransomware payments, which increased in demand during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The advisories identify two main areas of regulatory risk:
1. Violation of OFAC's sanctions regulations – OFAC may impose civil penalties based on strict liability (a person may be held civilly liable even without knowledge), particularly because ransomware attackers can obscure their identity and some are linked to sanctioned actors (e.g., North Korean government and Russian cybercriminals). Ransomware typically involves convertible virtual currency (CVC), which further obscures payouts. Where attackers are known targets of sanctions, OFAC reviews license applications "on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial."
2. Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing requirements for financial institutions – institutions may be required to file SARs whether they are victims of ransomware attacks or merely processing payments for victimized clients. The FinCEN advisory provides specific SAR filing instructions to reference the advisory.

The advisories also apply to cyber insurance, digital forensics, and incident response firms, which should maintain compliance programs and may face money transmission registration requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act and state money transmission laws. Both advisories encourage cooperation with law enforcement; OFAC considers a "self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement" as a significant mitigating factor in enforcement outcomes.

The FinCEN Advisory identifies five trends of ransomware attacks: (1) "big-game hunting" targeting larger enterprises for bigger payouts; (2) sharing of resources and partnerships among cybercriminals; (3) "double extortion schemes" involving data theft and threats to publish; (4) use of anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies (AECs) with discounted rates for AEC payments; and (5) "fileless" ransomware using malicious code in system memory. FinCEN also identified red-flag indicators for financial institutions, including transactions with digital forensics firms known to make ransom payments, rapid back-to-back cryptocurrency movements, accounts lacking obvious connection to customer business, "chain-hopping" techniques, and transactions with exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

While the advisories create no new legal requirements, they indicate that OFAC and FinCEN expect risk-based compliance programs and a high level of coordination with law enforcement. Failure to report attacks to law enforcement may increase exposure to OFAC monetary penalties. Companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 30: FinCEN Issues Financial Trend Analysis on Ransomware ---
URL: https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-issues-financial-trend-analysis-ransomware

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued a Financial Trend Analysis (FTA) on ransomware incidents reported in Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) data between 2022 and 2024, totaling more than $2.1 billion in ransomware payments. Unlike previous analyses that focused on filing dates, this report shifts focus to the actual incident dates of each ransomware attack, providing greater visibility into ransomware actor activities.

Key findings include:
- Ransomware incidents and payments reached an all-time high in 2023 with 1,512 incidents totaling $1.1 billion in payments (a 77% year-over-year increase from 2022); incidents decreased to 1,476 in 2024 following law enforcement disruptions of two high-profile ransomware groups, reflecting $734 million in aggregate payments.
- Median single ransomware transaction amounts: $124,097 (2022), $175,000 (2023), and $155,257 (2024). The most common payment range was below $250,000.
- During the three-year review period (January 2022–December 2024), FinCEN received 7,395 BSA reports related to 4,194 ransomware incidents totaling over $2.1 billion. By comparison, the previous nine-year period (2013–2021) saw 3,075 reports totaling approximately $2.4 billion.
- Most impacted industries: manufacturing (456 incidents, ~$284.6 million), financial services (432 incidents, ~$365.6 million), and healthcare (389 incidents, ~$305.4 million).
- The Onion Router (TOR) was the most common communication method used by threat actors (67% of reports specifying a method); others used email or private encrypted messaging.
- More than 200 ransomware variants were identified; the most reported variants were Akira, ALPHV/BlackCat, LockBit, Phobos, and Black Basta. The top 10 variants by payment amounts accounted for approximately $1.5 billion in payments.

The report is available online, and FinCEN provides additional ransomware resources at www.fincen.gov/resources/fincen-combats-ransomware. The FTA fulfills obligations under section 6206 of the Anti-Money Laundering Act of 2020.
</summary>

"Banks and other financial institutions play a key role in protecting our economy from ransomware and other cyber threats," said FinCEN Director Andrea Gacki. SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Society of Chemical Manufacturers & Affiliates (SOCMA) provides information about the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program and SOCMA's advocacy efforts regarding it.

**About CFATS:** CFATS is the nation's first regulatory program focused specifically on security at high-risk chemical facilities. Managed by the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), it identifies and regulates high-risk facilities to reduce the risk that dangerous chemicals could be weaponized by terrorists. Under CFATS, a chemical facility is any establishment or individual that possesses (or plans to possess) any of the more than 300 chemicals of interest (COI) listed in Appendix A at or above the screening threshold quantity (STQ) and concentration.

**Program Status:** The CFATS program expired in July 2023 due to inaction by the Senate. 2. SOCMA and other associations sent a letter to Senate Leadership urging inclusion of the CFATS Program in the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) Fiscal Year 2024.
3. In the wake of the CFATS lapse, DHS has pointed individuals to ChemLock's voluntary resources that remain available during the program lapse.

**Contact:** Robert Helminiak, Vice President of Legal & Government Relations, at government.relations@socma.org, is the contact for CFATS-related issues.

**Recent News Headlines:** SOCMA has published articles about its multi-industry letter advocating for CFATS reauthorization, the program's lapse as Congress failed to reauthorize by the July 27th expiration date, and calls for the Senate to reauthorize the program.
