--- SOURCE 2: Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) Update — American Coatings Association ---
URL: https://www.paint.org/aca-advocacy/enhancing-chemical-security-and-cfats

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The American Coatings Association (ACA) webpage provides an update on the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program as of April 9, 2024. 

**Background:** CFATS was developed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in November 2007 to prevent chemicals of interest from being stolen, diverted, sabotaged, or deliberately released by terrorists. Under the program, facilities possessing threshold amounts of specific explosive, toxic, or other chemicals of interest must submit a "top-screen" to DHS. DHS can then require a Security Vulnerability Assessment (SVA), which determines the facility's tier (Tiers 1-2 highest risk, Tiers 3-4 lowest). Tier assignment triggers a Site Security Plan (SSP) or Alternative Security Plan (ASP) requirement. As of July 2023, approximately 3,200 chemical facilities were covered under CFATS. The program's statutory authorization lapsed on July 27, 2023, after Congress allowed it to expire.

**ACA Action:** Many ACA member facilities are subject to CFATS, with a clear majority classified as Tier 4 and a few as Tier 3. ACA has strongly supported CFATS reauthorization. In July 2023, ACA sent letters to Congressional leadership urging immediate reauthorization. The U.S. House passed H.R. 4470 on a 409-1 vote to extend authorization for two years, but the companion Senate bill (S. 2499) did not advance, and a motion to consider the House bill was blocked in the Senate on July 26, 2023.

**After Expiration:** The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) suspended all enforcement and compliance assistance activities and suspended requirements for facilities to maintain site security plans and report chemicals of interest. CISA encouraged facilities to maintain security measures voluntarily and promoted its ChemLock initiative (a toolkit of on-site assessments, exercise packages, training, and guidance). Without reauthorization, chemical sector security now relies mainly on voluntary public-private partnerships. ACA is actively working with Congress, DHS, and trade associations to swiftly reinstate the program.

**ACA Staff Contacts:** Rhett Cash (Counsel, Government Affairs) and Heidi K. McAuliffe (Vice President, Government Affairs).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"CFATS provides a uniform, national program for regulating chemical security. Continuity of this framework provides the certainty required for the considerable planning and investment decisions that are needed to protect both our facilities and the surrounding communities. Allowing CFATS to expire would open the door for agencies with no anti-terrorism expertise to fill the void, or a patchwork of state and local regulations that may vary widely in scope and effectiveness. This could result in inconsistent anti-terrorism standards across the country and could undermine national security."
</key_excerpts>

<summary>
This is a law firm (Nossaman LLP) article discussing recent federal developments in water utility cybersecurity. On November 12, 2025, President Trump signed a bipartisan funding package that reopened the federal government after a six-week shutdown and temporarily reinstated two cybersecurity authorities that expired on September 30: the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 (CISA Act) and the State and Local Cybersecurity Grant Program (SLCGP), both extended through January 30, 2026. The reinstatement restores liability protections, reestablishes real-time cyber threat information sharing, and ensures continued access to federal cybersecurity funding for drinking water and wastewater utilities.

On October 23, 2025, the EPA released an updated suite of cybersecurity and emergency planning tools, including a revised Emergency Response Plan (ERP) guide, a Cybersecurity Incident Response Plan (CIRP) template, incident-specific checklists, and a cybersecurity procurement checklist. This is part of EPA's broader "Powering the Great American Comeback" strategy and builds on the agency's August 2025 announcement of over $9 million in grant funding for midsize and large water systems. The guidance emphasizes a two-pronged approach: updating risk and resilience assessments to include cybersecurity threats and incorporating findings into updated ERPs. Key recommended actions include reducing internet exposure, changing default passwords, performing regular cybersecurity assessments, developing manual operation procedures for automated systems, securing Human-Machine Interfaces, completing asset inventories, and conducting regular training and exercises.

Background context notes a 2024 GAO report (GAO-24-106744) finding nearly 170,000 U.S. water systems face cyber risks, and a 2024 EPA Inspector General report (25-N-0004) identifying critical or high-severity vulnerabilities in 97 drinking water systems serving 27 million people. Challenges include outdated software, unsupported operating systems, inadequate network segmentation, and limited monitoring capacity. EPA leads federal water sector cybersecurity efforts but lacks explicit statutory authority to mandate cybersecurity measures, relying instead on voluntary engagement, technical assistance, and coordination with CISA, state agencies, and sector partners. The article recommends utilities proactively examine emergency response plans, reassess vulnerabilities, and prepare for both cyber and physical threats, with seasoned advisors helping utilities secure funding, prepare grant applications, and navigate federal and state requirements.
</summary>

URL: http://cyberriskpolicy.com/data-breach-notification-laws.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from CyberRiskPolicy.com provides a comprehensive plain-language reference guide to U.S. state and federal data breach notification laws, reviewed by C. Constantin Poindexter (CPCU, JD, MA, AFSB), an insurance/surety underwriting specialist since 1994, with statutes current as of early 2026.

Key points covered:

1. **Universal coverage**: All 50 states plus DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands now have data breach notification laws. Alabama and South Dakota were the last to adopt them in 2018, completing the patchwork.

2. **Deadlines**: Roughly 20 states set a numeric deadline of 30 to 60 days to notify affected individuals; the rest require notice "without unreasonable delay." For multi-state breaches, the strictest applicable clock governs. States with 30-day deadlines include California, Colorado, Florida, Maine, New Jersey, and Washington. States with 45-day deadlines include Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, Maryland, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Vermont, and Wisconsin. States with 60-day deadlines include Connecticut, Delaware, Louisiana, South Dakota, and Texas.

3. **Three notification audiences**: (a) Affected individuals (required in every state), (b) state attorneys general (required in ~36 states once a resident-count threshold is crossed, commonly 250, 500, or 1,000), and (c) consumer reporting agencies (typically required at 1,000+ residents per FACTA).

4. **Attorney-general thresholds**: Texas triggers at 250+ residents (within 30 days, filed to a public breach portal); California at 500+ (within 15 days of individual notice per SB 446, 2026); Colorado at 500+ (with individual notice); Oklahoma at 500+ (within 60 days of individual notice per SB 626, 2026); Indiana at 500+ (without unreasonable delay). In states like Texas, AG filings become searchable public records.

5. **Definition of personal information**: Every state covers name plus at least one of: SSN, driver's license/state-ID number, or financial account/payment-card number. Growing states expand coverage to medical/health info, biometrics, online credentials, and government-issued identifiers. Some states apply a risk-of-harm analysis.

6. **Substitute notice**: Allowed when direct contact isn't feasible (contact info unavailable, cost exceeds statutory ceiling commonly $50,000–$100,000, or very large affected populations) — a website posting plus statewide media notice.

7. **Federal overlays**: HIPAA/HITECH (health sector, notify HHS, media notice for 500+ in a state), GLBA (financial institutions), SEC Reg S-P (broker-dealers/investment companies), SEC public-company rule (Form 8-K disclosure within 4 business days of materiality), and CIRCIA (critical infrastructure — report to CISA within 72 hours, ransom payments within 24 hours; final rule pending 2026).

8. **2026 changes**: California's SB 446 (effective Jan 1, 2026) replaced "without unreasonable delay" with a hard 30-calendar-day deadline and requires AG notice within 15 days for 500+ affected Californians. Oklahoma's SB 626 expanded covered data to biometrics and government IDs and added AG notification for 500+ residents. Both track a trend toward shorter clocks and broader data definitions.

9. **Cyber insurance role**: Breach-response coverage funds the breach coach (privacy counsel), notification and call-center costs, credit monitoring/identity protection, and regulatory defense. Coverage is as much about the expert response team engaged at hour zero as the dollars.

10. **Frequently asked questions**: Confirms all 50 states require breach notification; deadlines vary by state (30–60 days fixed or "without unreasonable delay"); AG notification triggers at 250, 500, or 1,000 residents depending on state.

The page includes a disclaimer that it is plain-language reference material, not legal advice, and recommends verifying current statutes with qualified counsel and authoritative trackers like the IAPP state chart. It also promotes CyberRiskPolicy.com's cyber insurance offerings, including a downloadable coverage application and contact at (800) 373-2804.

--- SOURCE 23: California tightens data breach notification timelines, imposes 30-day notice requirement | Data Protection Report ---
URL: https://www.dataprotectionreport.com/2025/11/california-tightens-data-breach-notification-timelines-imposes-30-day-notice-requirement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
California has signed into law Senate Bill No. 446, amending Section 1798.82 of its Civil Code (its data breach notification law) to require covered companies to notify affected California residents within 30 calendar days of discovery of a data breach. The amendment takes effect January 1, 2026.

Key points of the amendment:
- Replaces California's previous flexible "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" standard with a specific 30-day deadline.
- California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002, and as a leading privacy regulator, this move may prompt more states to adopt firm notice timelines.
- Several states already impose specific notice timeframes: New York (30 days), Texas (30 days), Colorado (30 days), Florida (30 days), and Delaware (60 days). Some states require notice to the attorney general simultaneously with or prior to notice to individuals—more stringent than California's requirement to notify the attorney general within 15 days of notice to individuals.
- In practice, many businesses make regulatory notices close in time to individual notices to address differing state obligations.

The authors (Annmarie Giblin and Susana Medeiros) offer a critical "take" on the change: shorter notice timelines do not necessarily improve notification outcomes. Even weeks after discovery, breach victims may not know the scope of impact, affected data types, or geographic residence of individuals—even with considerable investigative resources. While many state laws (including California's as amended) exempt disclosure where necessary to determine breach scope, this view is not universal. For example, the Connecticut Attorney General has clarified that Connecticut's 60-day notice requirement "runs from the date that a company becomes aware of suspicious activity, not the date it determines the full impact to personal information."

Companies in highly regulated sectors (critical infrastructure, insurance, banking) often face even shorter notice periods—as short as 72 hours—and regulators have fined companies for untimely reporting. The article advises companies to assess and update their incident response procedures, particularly for larger and more complex incidents, to meet shorter disclosure expectations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002 and since then, Section 1798.82 has required businesses and state agencies to notify individuals 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.' SB 446 replaces this flexible, reasonableness standard with a specific 30‑day deadline."

--- SOURCE 24: California Imposes New Data Breach Notification Requirements ---
URL: https://www.pillsburylaw.com/en/news-and-insights/california-data-breach-notification-requirements.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a legal alert from Pillsbury Law (by Mark L. Krotoski and Alexandria Marx, dated October 31, 2025) announcing that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill No. 446 into law on October 3, 2025, making significant changes to California's data breach notification statute, effective January 1, 2026. The law passed with no votes in opposition.

Key changes:
1. Businesses and government agencies must notify affected California residents "within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the data breach" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(a)(2)), joining five other states with 30-day deadlines (Colorado, Florida, Maine, New York, Washington). Previously, California required notification "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay."
2. Two exceptions permit delayed notification: (1) to accommodate legitimate needs of law enforcement, or (2) as necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore reasonable integrity of the data system.
3. If a breach affects more than 500 California residents, a sample copy of the consumer notification must be provided to the California Attorney General "within 15 days of notifying affected consumers" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(f)). Previously, no deadline existed for this notice.

Background context: California was the first state to enact a data breach notification statute in 2002. Since then, all 50 states and four U.S. jurisdictions (DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, Virgin Islands) have enacted their own requirements. Thirty other states have a similar "most expedient time possible" standard.

The statute retains California's unique "model security breach notification form" with headings including "What Happened?", "What Information Was Involved?", "What We Are Doing", "What You Can Do", and "For More Information."

Cost/risk data: According to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, average breach costs in the U.S. reached a record $10.22 million, a 9% increase over the prior year. A survey of 220+ cases from 2020-2024 found over 90% of data breach enforcement actions were brought collaboratively as multistate efforts. Examples of enforcement penalties include a $2 million NYDFS fine for failure to notify within 72 hours of a cybersecurity event, a $795,000 Massachusetts AG fine for delayed notifications, and a $6.75 million California AG fine against a software company for misleading the public about a breach.

Senator Melissa Hurtado (SB 446 author) stated the law closes a loophole because affected individuals "may not be informed for months—or even a year or more later—delaying their ability to take preventive measures."

Next steps for businesses: update incident response plans for the new timelines, review contracts with third-party service providers for timely cyber incident reporting, and obtain legal guidance on notification sufficiency and accuracy.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 25: SHIELD Act | New York Attorney General ---
URL: https://ag.ny.gov/resources/organizations/data-breach-reporting/shield-act

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is from the Office of the New York Attorney General (AG) and provides a detailed overview of the Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic Data Security Act (SHIELD Act), which was signed into law on July 25, 2019, by Governor Andrew Cuomo. The SHIELD Act amends New York's 2005 Information Security Breach and Notification Act and significantly strengthens New York's data-security laws.

KEY PROVISIONS:
- Expands the types of private information for which companies must provide consumer notice in the event of a breach.
- Requires companies to develop, implement, and maintain reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect private information.

EXPANDED DEFINITIONS:
- Security breach: Expanded from "unauthorized acquisition" of computerized data to any "access" to computerized data that compromises confidentiality, security, or integrity of private data.
- Private information: Originally included Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, and account numbers (in combination with required security codes). The SHIELD Act expands this to include biometric information, username or email address, and password credentials.

REQUIRED SAFEGUARDS:
- Administrative: designating employees to coordinate the security program, identifying foreseeable risks, assessing safeguards, training employees, selecting capable service providers with contractual safeguards, and adjusting the program as circumstances change.
- Technical: assessing risks in network/software design, information processing/transmission/storage, detecting/preventing/responding to attacks or system failures, and regularly testing key controls and systems.
- Physical: assessing risks of information storage and disposal, detecting/preventing/responding to intrusions, protecting against unauthorized access, and properly disposing of private information.

BREACH NOTIFICATION OBLIGATIONS:
- Businesses must notify affected consumers in the most expedient time possible, consistent with legitimate law enforcement needs.
- Notice must be provided to the OAG, NY Department of State, and NY State Police. Submitting a breach form through the OAG's data-breach-reporting portal is sufficient as it automatically sends the information to all three credit reporting entities (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion — contact info provided for each).
- Consumers affected by a breach should file a complaint (not a breach notification).

EXCEPTIONS TO NOTIFICATION:
- Substitute notice allowed if: cost of regular notice exceeds $250,000, affected class exceeds 500,000, or the entity lacks sufficient contact information. Substitute notice may consist of email, conspicuous website posting, and/or statewide media notification.
- Consumer notification not required for inadvertent disclosure by authorized persons if the business reasonably determines exposure will not likely result in misuse, financial harm, or emotional harm (in case of unknown online credential disclosure). Such determinations must be documented in writing and maintained for at least five years. If the incident affects over 500 NY residents, the written determination must be provided to the AG within 10 days.

PENALTIES:
- For failure to provide timely notification: civil penalty of up to $20 per instance of failed notification, not to exceed $250,000.
- For failure to maintain reasonable safeguards: civil penalty of up to $5,000 per violation.
- The Attorney General may seek injunctive relief, restitution, and penalties for violations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The SHIELD Act, signed into law on July 25, 2019, by Governor Andrew Cuomo, amends New York's 2005 Information Security Breach and Notification Act."
</key_excerpts>

The bulletin is directed to Chief Executive Officers of all National Banks, Federal Savings Associations, Federal Branches and Agencies, Department and Division Heads, all Examining Personnel, and other interested parties.

--- SOURCE 4: Cyber threat bulletin: The ransomware threat in 2021 - Canadian Centre for Cyber Security ---
URL: https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/cyber-threat-bulletin-ransomware-threat-2021

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Cyber Threat Bulletin from the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security (the Cyber Centre) provides an update on the ransomware threat in Canada and how it is expected to evolve. Published in late 2021 (based on information available as of 16 November 2021), the bulletin documents that ransomware has become the foremost cyber threat facing Canadians and Canadian organizations.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Global ransomware attacks increased by 151% in the first half of 2021 compared to the first half of 2020, with the highest ransoms and payouts ever recorded.
- The estimated average cost of a data breach in Canada is $6.35M CAD.
- The Cyber Centre has knowledge of 235 ransomware incidents against Canadian victims from 1 January to 16 November 2021, with more than half targeting critical infrastructure providers. Most ransomware events remain unreported, and victims are often attacked multiple times.
- Known ransom payments stabilized around $200,000 in 2021, but the global average total cost of recovery from a ransomware incident more than doubled from $970,722 CAD in 2020 to $2.3M CAD in 2021. The largest ransom payment ever was $48.4M CAD in 2021.

EVOLVING TRENDS:
- Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) business models have fueled the increased scale and impact of ransomware operations.
- The July 2021 Sodinokibi (REvil) attack on Kaseya VSA compromised 800-1,500 downstream organizations, demonstrating a shift toward software supply chain targeting.
- More than half of all Canadian ransomware victims from January to June 2021 were in critical infrastructure sectors (energy, health, manufacturing). Almost two thirds of Canadian victims were small- and medium-sized organizations.
- Ransomware groups have increasingly targeted hospitals and emergency services during the COVID-19 pandemic (e.g., Humber River Hospital in Ontario on 14 June 2021).
- The May 2021 Colonial Pipeline attack (attributed to Russia-based DarkSide) showed that even IT-only compromises can shut down OT operations.

RANSOMWARE ENABLERS:
- In the first six months of 2021, ransomware payments totaling $590M USD in cryptocurrency were made (vs. $416M USD for all of 2020).
- Cybercriminals are very likely to increasingly demand ransom in privacy coins like Monero to conceal their identity (e.g., a March 2021 Acer attack demanded $50M USD in Monero).
- Malicious use of Cobalt Strike (a legitimate commercial penetration testing tool) increased 161% from 2019 to 2020.

STATE-RANSOMWARE NEXUS:
- The Cyber Centre assesses that Russian intelligence services and law enforcement almost certainly maintain relationships with cybercriminals and allow them to operate with near impunity as long as attacks target outside Russia and the former Soviet Union.
- Examples cited include Iran's IRGC running a state-sponsored ransomware campaign (2020), and the US DOJ indictment of EvilCorp leader Maksim Yakubets.
- Following the June 2021 US-Russia summit, DarkSide and Sodinokibi shut down, but successors like BlackMatter returned by September 2021.

OUTLOOK FOR 2022:
- Ransomware will continue to pose a threat to Canada's national security and economic prosperity as it remains profitable for cybercriminals.
- Operators will likely become increasingly aggressive, including against critical infrastructure.
- Cybercriminals will almost certainly continue to rely on digital currencies; international efforts include sanctions on exchanges (e.g., US Treasury sanctions on Suex in September 2021) and disruption operations (e.g., the January 2021 takedown of the Emotet botnet by a worldwide coalition).
- The bulletin emphasizes that the vast majority of ransomware attacks can be prevented by implementing basic cyber security measures.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"We assess that ransom payments are likely reaching a market equilibrium, where cybercriminals are becoming better at tailoring their demands to what their victims are most likely to pay given the growth of recovery cost and the risk of reputational damage from public data leaks."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 7: Ransomware and Federal Law: Cybercrime and Cybersecurity | Congress.gov | Library of Congress ---
URL: https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R46932

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report (R46932), published October 5, 2021, by authors Peter G. Berris and Jonathan M. Gaffney, examining federal law responses to ransomware attacks under two primary approaches: criminal prosecution and cybersecurity regulation.

**Context and Scope:** Ransomware attacks—malware that denies users access to data to extort ransom—are prevalent. A notable example is the May 2021 Colonial Pipeline attack that shut down the company's network and impacted gasoline prices; the company reportedly paid over $4 million in Bitcoin. A subsequent attack on meat supplier JBS resulted in an ~$11 million Bitcoin ransom. In 2020 alone, the FBI received 2,474 ransomware complaints with adjusted losses exceeding $29.1 million, a figure likely under-inclusive due to underreporting. The report does not cover technological or policy considerations (covered in other CRS products).

**Federal Criminal Prosecution:** The Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA, 18 U.S.C. § 1030) is the preeminent federal anti-hacking law and can be used to prosecute ransomware attackers. Archetypal encryption-based attacks likely violate § 1030(a)(7)(C) (extortive threats involving computers), while "double extortion" schemes (data theft plus threats to disclose) implicate § 1030(a)(7)(B). Both are felonies punishable by fines and up to five years' imprisonment for first offenses (ten years for subsequent). Other relevant CFAA provisions include trespass into government computers (§ 1030(a)(3)) and intentional damage (§ 1030(a)(5)). The CFAA also contains asset forfeiture provisions (§ 1030(j)). The Economic Espionage Act (EEA) criminalizes trade secret theft and may apply to double extortion attacks, though DOJ's use of the EEA for ransomware specifically is unclear. The wire fraud statute (18 U.S.C. § 1343) has also been used.

**Criminal Enforcement of Ransomware Development:** The Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model, where developers sell or lease malware to others and share proceeds, may violate § 1030(a)(5). Inchoate offenses like conspiracy (18 U.S.C. § 371) and aiding and abetting (18 U.S.C. § 2) provide additional prosecution options. Proving criminal intent is easier for RaaS developers than for general-purpose tools like botnets, because RaaS developers clearly intend their tools to aid attacks.

**Criminal Enforcement from Abroad:** Ransomware attacks often originate overseas. While DOJ has used the CFAA, EEA, and wire fraud statutes for such charges, prosecution faces sovereignty, legal, practical, and diplomatic obstacles, including the absence of extradition treaties with some countries. DOJ can use civil asset forfeiture to recover ransom payments, as it did in June 2021 when seizing $2.3 million in Bitcoin paid to DarkSide in the Colonial Pipeline incident.

**Legality of Ransom Payments:** No federal statute expressly criminalizes making ransomware payments, but federal laws restricting transactions with certain parties can implicitly make payments a crime. The material support of terrorism statute (18 U.S.C. § 2339B) prohibits knowingly providing property to designated foreign terrorist organizations. A September 2021 Treasury Department advisory noted that OFAC regulations prohibit payments to Specially Designated Nationals (SDN List) or those covered by comprehensive embargoes, with possible civil or criminal penalties (if the payer knows the payment is unlawful). However, policy considerations, mitigating factors, and prosecutorial discretion may weigh against enforcement—for example, DOJ has never prosecuted hostage families for paying ransoms. Some have argued for banning ransom payments to remove profit motive, but the FBI opposes a ban out of concern it would enable blackmail of entities who violate it. At least four states are considering bills prohibiting state/local governments from making ransomware payments.
</summary>

- **HHS OCR Notification (Within 60 days):** Breaches affecting 500+ individuals must be reported within 60 days; smaller breaches reported annually no later than 60 days after calendar year end.
- **Media Notification (Concurrent, 500+):** Required for breaches affecting 500+ residents of a single state/jurisdiction.
- **State Laws:** Vary by state; stricter requirement applies. MA Chapter 93H requires notification within 30 days; NY SHIELD Act requires "expedient/reasonable time"; CT Public Act 21-59 requires 60 days with AG notification for 500+ residents; RI Identity Theft Protection Act requires 45 days with AG notification for 500+ residents.
- **OCR Investigation Response (Ongoing):** Documented policies, risk analysis, and evidence of safeguards significantly affect outcomes.

KEY STATISTICS: 60 days (individual & HHS deadline), 30 days (MA Chapter 93H), 500+ individuals triggers media notification, $1.9M average OCR settlement (2024).

MOST COMMON BREACH TRIGGERS: Phishing/BEC, ransomware, lost/stolen devices, impermissible disclosures, third-party vendor breaches, and insider misuse.

FAQ HIGHLIGHTS: Ransomware encrypting ePHI is presumed a breach unless forensic analysis demonstrates no exfiltration/access. A breach differs from a security incident—a failed phishing attempt is an incident but not a breach; successful phishing accessing PHI is a breach. Individual notifications must be sent by first-class mail (or email if agreed) and for large breaches include an HHS-approved toll-free number active at least 90 days.
</summary>

"HIPAA requires covered entities to notify affected individuals and HHS OCR no later than 60 calendar days from the date of discovery of the breach. The clock begins when any workforce member or agent of the covered entity knows or reasonably should have known about the breach — not when the investigation is complete."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a legal advisory article by Paul Hastings (authored by Hannah Edmonds, published January 11, 2024) summarizing the guidance issued by the FBI, DOJ, and SEC regarding requests for delayed reporting of material cybersecurity incidents under the newly effective SEC Form 8-K Item 1.05 Rules. The SEC adopted final rules on July 26, 2023, adding Item 1.05 to Form 8-K, which requires companies to report material cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining materiality. These rules became effective December 18, 2023.

The article covers three key guidance documents:

1. **FBI Guidance (released December 6, 2023):** The DOJ designated the FBI as responsible for taking delay requests. The FBI reviews the timing of the incident and materiality determination, type of incident, vulnerabilities leveraged, suspected attribution of cyber actors, and remediation status. If the FBI finds a credible threat to national security or public safety, it may refer the request to the DOJ for the Attorney General's final determination.

2. **DOJ Guidance (released December 12, 2023):** The DOJ emphasizes limited circumstances justify delays. Companies can request delays when: (a) the incident involves illicit cyber activity with no well-known mitigation and disclosure could lead to more incidents; (b) the incident primarily impacts systems with sensitive U.S. Government information; (c) the company is conducting remediation efforts for critical infrastructure and disclosure would undermine those efforts; or (d) an Agency is aware of the risk. The DOJ has sole discretionary authority to determine whether and how long a delay is warranted (up to 30 days per initial period). Government agencies may also initiate delay requests on behalf of companies.

3. **SEC Guidance (C&DIs updated December 14, 2023, Section 104B):** Key points include: a company may delay disclosure if the AG determines substantial risk exists and notifies the SEC in writing before the four-business-day deadline; the company must file within four business days after the delay period expires; if the AG determines the risk no longer exists during a delay, the company must file within four business days of notification; and merely consulting with the DOJ about a delay does not make an incident material.

Important note: Neither the request for delayed disclosure nor the government's consideration time tolls the four-business-day filing period. The article also references DOJ guidance on changes in circumstances, subsequent delay periods, and limits on the guidance's scope.
</summary>

**Background:** The SEC approved final rules on July 26, 2023, requiring public companies to report material cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining materiality. Further delays require an AG determination and an SEC exemptive order.

DOJ expects delays to be limited to four categories: (1) incidents involving techniques without well-known mitigations, (2) incidents impacting systems with sensitive U.S. Government information, (3) remediation efforts for critical infrastructure or systems, and (4) cases where a USG agency believes disclosure poses substantial risk. The AG must invoke the delay provision within four business days of the registrant's materiality determination, so early FBI notification is recommended—even before the materiality analysis is complete. DOJ guidelines will be reassessed after CIRCIA rulemaking (CISA must publish the NPRM by March 2024).

**Key Takeaway:** The exception is expected to be extremely limited, and early FBI notification is crucial. Companies should consider preparing delay requests in advance of finalizing materiality determinations, likely contemporaneously with making them.

--- SOURCE 18: Exchange Act Form 8-K ---
URL: https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/staff-guidance/compliance-disclosure-interpretations/exchange-act-form-8-k

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) official interpretive guidance document for Exchange Act Form 8-K (Last Update: June 24, 2024). It provides questions and answers (Q&As) on Form 8-K compliance, replacing earlier interpretations from 1997, 2003, and 2004.

Key guidance includes:

**General Guidance (Section 101):**
- A triggering event occurring within four business days before filing a periodic report may be disclosed in that report (Form 10-Q Item 5 or Form 10-K Item 9B), EXCEPT for Item 4.01 (Changes in Certifying Accountant) and Item 4.02 (Non-Reliance on Previously Issued Financial Statements), which must always be reported on Form 8-K.
- Triggering events apply to registrants AND subsidiaries.
- "Exchange" in General Instruction E refers only to domestic exchanges.

**Item 1.01 - Material Definitive Agreements:**
- An agreement that becomes material after execution does NOT require an Item 1.01 Form 8-K, but must be filed as an exhibit to the periodic report covering the period when it became material.
- Registrants may omit underwriter identities to preserve the Rule 135c safe harbor.
- Material agreements must be summarized in the body of the Form 8-K even if filed as an exhibit (incorporation by reference insufficient).
- As of March 2022, registrants can redact sensitive terms without confidential treatment requests; absent unusual circumstances, agreements should be filed as exhibits within the four business day timeframe.

**Item 1.02 - Termination of Material Agreements:**
- Receipt of advance written notice of termination (even during negotiation/resolution efforts) triggers an Item 1.02 filing.
- Sending a non-renewal notice triggers disclosure (not the eventual termination date); automatic renewal per agreement terms does not trigger Item 1.01.
- Expiration on stated termination date without renewal does not trigger Item 1.02.

**Item 1.05 - Material Cybersecurity Incidents (extensive coverage):**
- Registrant must file within four business days of determining incident is material; requesting Attorney General delay does not change obligation unless AG determines substantial risk to national security/public safety and notifies the Commission.
- If a delay period expires or is lifted, the filing is due within four business days of that event.
- Consulting with DOJ does not itself make an incident material; materiality determination considers all facts and circumstances using traditional materiality standards (substantial likelihood a reasonable shareholder would consider it important).
- Ransomware payment, insurance reimbursement, or cessation of the incident does NOT relieve the registrant of the materiality determination or disclosure obligation.
- Size of ransomware payment is not determinative of materiality (no quantifiable trigger adopted).
- A series of related immaterial incidents may collectively be material and require disclosure (definition includes "a series of related unauthorized occurrences").

**Item 2.02 - Results of Operations:**
- Audio files, slides, or transcripts of webcasts can satisfy the conditional exemption for oral/telephonic/webcast earnings presentations, provided they contain all previously undisclosed material financial information.
- Required information must be posted on the company's website at the time of the oral presentation.
- Filing earnings release as an exhibit to Form 10-Q before a conference call does not preclude reliance on the Item 2.02(b) exemption.
- Failure to timely furnish an Item 2.02 Form 8-K does NOT affect Form S-3 eligibility (since it is "furnished," not "filed"), though it would violate Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act.
- Preliminary earnings releases must comply with all Item 2.02 requirements.

**Item 2.03 - Direct Financial Obligations:**
- Registrants must maintain disclosure controls to capture off-balance sheet obligations; Instruction 2 provides an extra four business day "grace" period.
- Refinancing/refunding obligations require a facts-and-circumstances materiality determination (may be immaterial if on similar terms).

**Item 2.04 - Triggering Events:**
- If agreement requires declaration/notice of default before acceleration, Item 2.04 is not triggered until such declaration/notice; automatic acceleration without notice does trigger disclosure if material.

**Item 2.05 - Exit/Disposal Costs:**
- Not limited to SFAS 146 costs; also includes FASB Statements 87, 88, 106, and 112.
- For employee terminations, Form 8-K need not be filed until affected employees have been informed.

**Item 2.06 - Material Impairments:**
- No Item 2.06 filing required if impairment conclusion coincides with financial statement preparation/review/audit and is disclosed in a timely-filed periodic report.
- Deferred tax asset re-measurement due to tax rate/law changes (e.g., Tax Cuts and Jobs Act) is not an impairment under ASC Topic 740; SAB 118 "measurement period" approach may apply.

**Item 3.02 - Unregistered Sales:**
- Stock option grants not constituting a "sale" or "offer to sell" under Section 2(a)(3) need not be reported.
- Sales of shares not currently outstanding still count toward volume thresholds.

**Item 4.01 - Changes in Certifying Accountant:**
- Must disclose if accountant's PCAOB registration was revoked.
- A new principal accountant that is a separate legal entity and separately PCAOB-registered (even if affiliated with former accountant) triggers a filing.
- Business combinations between accounting firms require case-by-case analysis.

**Item 4.02 - Non-Reliance on Financial Statements:**
- No second Form 8-K needed if auditor independently reaches same conclusion, unless it relates to a different error/matter.
- Does NOT apply to pro forma financial information.
- Errors in Interactive Data Files alone do not trigger Item 4.02(a); amendments are required to correct them.

**Item 5.02 - Director Departures:**
- Reporting obligation triggered by notice of decision to resign (written or oral), whether conditional or not; must specify effective date.
- Status as "named executive officer" is based on the most recent required Summary Compensation Table disclosure, not current compensation levels.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"These interpretations replace the Form 8-K interpretations in the July 1997 Manual of Publicly Available Telephone Interpretations, the June 13, 2003 Frequently Asked Questions Regarding the Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures and the November 22, 2004 Form 8-K Frequently Asked Questions."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Skadden publication (Cybersecurity and Data Privacy Update) explains guidance released in December 2023 by the FBI, DOJ, and SEC regarding how companies may request delayed reporting of material cybersecurity incidents on SEC Form 8-K under the national security/public safety exception.

BACKGROUND: The SEC adopted final cybersecurity disclosure rules in 2023. Form 8-K Item 1.05 requires disclosure within four business days after a company determines a cybersecurity incident is material. Materiality determinations must be made "without unreasonable delay" after discovery. The rules allow delayed disclosure (i) up to 30 days if the U.S. Attorney General determines public disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety, (ii) an additional up to 30 days if the risk continues, and (iii) a final additional period of up to 60 days in extraordinary circumstances due to national security risks.

FBI GUIDANCE (Dec 6, 2023): Companies must make delay requests to the FBI "concurrently" with their materiality decision and provide the date/time (including time zone) of the materiality determination. Requests are submitted via dedicated email (cyber_sec_disclosure_delay_referrals@fbi.gov) and must include incident details (type, intrusion vectors, affected data/infrastructure, operational impacts), information about cyber actors if known, and status of mitigation/remediation efforts.

DOJ GUIDANCE (Dec 12, 2023): Determinations hinge on whether public disclosure of the incident threatens public safety or national security—not whether the incident itself poses such a risk. The DOJ expects to find substantial risk only in limited circumstances, including: incidents involving techniques without well-known mitigations; incidents primarily impacting systems with sensitive U.S. government information; ongoing remediation of critical infrastructure where required disclosure would undermine efforts; or a U.S. government agency believing disclosure poses substantial risk. Companies should provide information to the FBI as soon as possible, even before completing their materiality analysis, if they believe delayed disclosure may apply.

SEC CDIs (Dec 14, 2023): The SEC staff published four Compliance and Disclosure Interpretations: (1) a company awaiting the Attorney General's decision must still file Form 8-K within four business days of its materiality determination; (2) a company must file within four business days of the delay period's expiration even if an additional delay request is pending; (3) if the Attorney General grants a delay but later determines disclosure no longer poses substantial risk, the company has four business days from notification to file; (4) consulting the DOJ about delayed disclosure does not necessarily mean the incident is material.

TAKEAWAYS: Companies should engage law enforcement and U.S. government agencies early in assessing cybersecurity incidents where disclosure may pose national security/public safety risks. The SEC does not view such consultation as necessarily resulting in a materiality determination. The DOJ expects the delayed disclosure availability to be limited.
</summary>

[Miller & Chevalier](https://www.millerchevalier.com/)

# Publications

# DOJ Criminal Division Issues Updated Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy

International Alert

On January 17, 2023, following [remarks](https://www.justice.gov/opa/speech/assistant-attorney-general-kenneth-polite-jr-delivers-remarks-georgetown-university-law) by Assistant Attorney General (AAG) Kenneth A. Polite, Jr., at Georgetown University Law Center, the Department of Justice's (DOJ) Criminal Division issued its revised [Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy](https://www.justice.gov/opa/speech/file/1562851/download) (the Policy or CEP). The revised Policy follows Deputy Attorney General (DAG) Lisa Monaco's memorandum sharing "[initial revisions](https://www.millerchevalier.com/publication/doj-issues-revised-guidance-key-corporate-enforcement-requirements)" to the DOJ's corporate criminal policies in October 2021 and her memorandum detailing "[further revisions](https://www.millerchevalier.com/publication/new-doj-guidance-corporate-enforcement-focuses-timely-disclosures-prosecutions)" on September 15, 2022 (the Monaco Memorandum). Publication of the revised Policy was prompted in part by a request from the DAG for all DOJ components to issue formal policies that "clarify the benefits of promptly coming forward to self-report" and "make the case in the boardroom that voluntary self-disclosure is a good business decision."

The revisions to the CEP implement and further elaborate on policy changes announced in the Monaco Memorandum and likely reflect further consideration of public and private feedback on those policies after September 2022. To the likely disappointment of some compliance personnel, the revised Policy does not contain promised guidance on important issues such as how the DOJ will assess compensation clawbacks and specific DOJ expectations related to corporate policies on the management of use of personal devices and third-party messaging platforms. This alert highlights key changes and areas of interest for compliance personnel.

### A Single Policy Across the Criminal Division

The revised Policy supersedes what was previously known as the FCPA Corporate Enforcement Policy (the FCPA CEP) and will apply on a prospective basis "to all FCPA cases nationwide and all other corporate criminal matters handled by the Criminal Division." The policy formalizes the DOJ's practice of applying the FCPA CEP on a division-wide basis, which AAG Polite noted had been happening "[s]ince at least 2018."

### The DOJ's Three Fundamental Standards for Companies Remain the Same, But the Revised Policy Enhances Potential Benefits in Certain Circumstances

The primary revisions center on incentives that prosecutors may offer to companies with less-than-pristine criminal and compliance records or certain aggravating circumstances. Consistent with longstanding DOJ practice, the actions that companies need to take to be eligible for these incentives remain tied to three broad categories: (1) voluntary self-disclosure "at the earliest possible time"; (2) full cooperation with the DOJ's investigation; and (3) "timely and appropriate remediation" of the issues raised by the potential misconduct.

#### Presumption of Declination

Like the former FCPA CEP, the revised Policy establishes "a presumption that [a] company will receive a declination" if the company "has voluntarily self-disclosed misconduct to the Criminal Division, fully cooperated, and timely and appropriately remediated" under the Policy's standards, "absent aggravating circumstances involving the seriousness of the offense or the nature of the offender." In addition, a company must "pay all disgorgement, forfeiture, and/or restitution resulting from the misconduct at issue."

Also in line with the prior policy, the revised Policy defines "aggravating circumstances" as including "involvement by executive management of the company in the misconduct; a significant profit to the company from the misconduct; egregiousness or pervasiveness of the misconduct within the company; or criminal recidivism." Some DOJ public statements since the issuance of the Monaco Memorandum have suggested that recidivism may not be an aggravating factor, but the revised Policy makes clear that, as before, past violations can be considered as aggravating circumstances. As will be discussed below, the revised Policy gives DOJ prosecutors more discretion when dealing with recidivist companies.

#### Some Relief for Corporate Recidivists and Other Cases with "Aggravating Circumstances"

The revised Policy contains a new section on how companies in cases that present "aggravating circumstances" will be treated. Much of the focus of AAG Polite's speech on this aspect focused on recidivism as such a factor, though neither the revised Policy nor the speech added further context beyond the Monaco Memorandum as to how the DOJ will analyze which company is considered a recidivist. However, the revised Policy makes clear that similar considerations will inform other aggravating factors.

While in such cases the presumption of a declination would not apply (as was the case under the prior FCPA CEP), under the revised Policy prosecutors can still offer a declination (with disgorgement) if the following factors are present (emphasis added):

* Self-disclosure "was made *immediately* upon the company becoming aware of the allegation of misconduct"
* "*At the time of the misconduct* and disclosure, the company had an effective compliance program and system of internal accounting controls, which enabled the identification of the misconduct and led to the company's voluntary self-disclosure"
* "The company provided *extraordinary cooperation* with the Department's investigation and undertook *extraordinary remediation* that exceeds" the normal standards under the revised Policy

#### Enhanced Benefits for Companies Subject to Criminal Resolutions

The revised Policy offers added incentives to companies that self-disclose, fully cooperate, and effectively remediate, including corporate recidivists and companies facing other aggravating circumstances, in circumstances where the DOJ determines that a company is ineligible for a declination.

First, the Policy states that the DOJ "will accord, or recommend to a sentencing court, at least 50% and *up to a 75% reduction off of the low end* of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G.) fine range, except in the case of a criminal recidivist" (emphasis added). This marks an increase in the potential penalty calculation benefit, which the prior FCPA CEP set at a maximum of 50 percent reduction. Recidivists can still obtain "a reduction of at least 50% and up to 75%" but such a reduction "will generally not be from the low end of the U.S.S.G. fine range, and prosecutors will have discretion to determine the starting point for the reduction based on the particular facts and circumstances of the case."

Second, in such cases the DOJ "will generally not require a corporate guilty plea…absent the presence of particularly egregious or multiple aggravating circumstances…." Both the revised Policy and AAG Polite's related speech noted that this will also be the case for recidivist companies. The eligibility of recidivists for such a benefit softens earlier statements by DAG Monaco criticizing past patterns of successive deferred prosecution agreements (DPAs)/non-prosecution agreements (NPAs) for recidivist companies but is meant to emphasize the importance that the DOJ places on voluntary self-disclosure, especially.

Third, "generally" no Monitor will be required "if a company has, at the time of resolution, demonstrated that it has implemented and tested an effective compliance program and remediated the root cause of the misconduct." This aspect of the Policy aligns with both the prior FCPA CEP and the Monaco Memorandum and continues the DOJ's focus on companies ensuring that their compliance program is sufficiently tested before making a final determination on a monitorship.

#### Enhanced Incentives Even Where Self-Disclosure is Not Credited

The revised Policy updates the incentives offered by the DOJ in cases in which the company does not self-disclose, "but later fully cooperated and timely and appropriately remediated in accordance with the standards set forth" in the Policy. In such cases, "the company will receive, or the Criminal Division will recommend to a sentencing court, up to a 50% reduction off of the low end of the U.S.S.G. fine range." If recidivism is present, the company is still eligible to receive up to a 50 percent reduction, but the starting point to apply the reduction will "generally not be from the low end… of the fine range." As AAG Polite pointed out, this reduction is "twice the maximum amount of a reduction available under the prior version of the [FCPA] CEP."

Under the revised Policy, DOJ prosecutors "will have discretion to determine the specific percentage reduction and starting point in the range based on the particular facts and circumstances of the case." AAG Polite noted in his speech that "[a] reduction of 50% *will not be the new norm*; it will be reserved for companies that truly distinguish themselves and demonstrate extraordinary cooperation and remediation" (emphasis added). We comment on what may be meant by such "extraordinary" cooperation below. Generally, AAG Polite asserted that "having a greater range of cooperation and remediation credit available…and using the full spectrum of the Guidelines from which to apply those reductions — will allow our prosecutors to draw greater distinctions among the quality of companies' cooperation and remediation."

### Additional DOJ Definitions, Commentary, and Open Questions

The revised Policy contains some additional or updated commentary from the DOJ on several aspects of its core requirements but does not provide additional insight into some key open questions originating from the September 2022 Monaco Memorandum.

#### Timing and Effectiveness of Self-Disclosures

The revised Policy is the latest in a long line of DOJ pronouncements citing voluntary self-disclosure as a critical element for companies looking for favorable treatment in investigations. The Policy, while retaining the generally broad discretion available to prosecutors to address case-specific facts and circumstances, discusses significant and concrete benefits available to companies that disclose issues. The DOJ also continues to push companies toward disclosure at a very early stage.

In new language, the revised Policy states that the DOJ "encourages self-disclosure of potential wrongdoing *at the earliest possible time, even when a company has not yet completed an internal investigation, if it chooses to conduct one*" (emphasis added). Existing prior language requiring disclosure "within a reasonably prompt time after becoming aware of the misconduct, with the burden being on the company to demonstrate timeliness" remains. The pressure on companies facing "aggravating circumstances" is potentially even greater since, as noted, to gain benefits such companies must disclose "*immediately* upon the company becoming aware of the allegation of misconduct." New language notes, as well, that the DOJ will make a "careful assessment of the circumstances of the disclosure, including the extent to which the disclosure permitted the [DOJ] to preserve and obtain evidence as part of its investigation." Finally, the revised language makes clear that, to be credited, a disclosure "must be to the Criminal Division," implying that disclosures to other agencies will not be credited. The Policy does allow disclosure credit for a "good faith disclosure to another office or component of the" DOJ that is referred to the Criminal Division.

In his speech, AAG Polite stated that a company's "clearest path to avoiding a guilty plea or an indictment is voluntary self-disclosure" which is "also the clearest path to the greatest incentives that [the DOJ] offer[s], such as a declination with disgorgement of profits." He also noted that "a functioning compliance program with effective detection mechanisms best positions companies to not only identify misconduct…but to make the important decision of whether to disclose it." The speech asserts that the DOJ "fully understand[s] the significance of a company's decision to voluntarily self-disclose and fully cooperate, and the consequences that such a decision brings," but also admonishes that "a corporation that falls short of our [significant] expectations does so at its own risk."

As we have noted previously, given that FCPA investigations increasingly involve authorities in other countries, companies also will be forced to consider the costs and benefits of ever-earlier disclosure to non-U.S. enforcement agencies, such as the investigation costs of potential earlier involvement of local counsel or potential fallout if the company's disclosures to the various agencies are not aligned.

#### "Full"/"Extraordinary" Cooperation and Updated Foreign Data Privacy Law Requirements

The revised Policy's standards for credit for full cooperation mostly carry over the key considerations from the former FCPA CEP, though some revised language emphasizes DAG Monaco's consistent focus on prioritizing the sharing of evidence related to culpability of all involved individuals. The Policy states that a company must disclose "all relevant, non-privileged facts known to it, including all relevant facts and evidence about all individuals involved in or responsible for the misconduct at issue, including individuals inside and outside of the company regardless of their position, status, or seniority." Language requiring, for example, "attribution of facts to specific sources where such attribution does not violate the attorney-client privilege" and "rolling disclosures of information" as internal investigations proceed remains in place.

New commentary makes clear that "[a] cooperating company must earn credit for cooperation. In other words, *a company starts at zero cooperation credit and then earns credit for specific cooperative actions* (as opposed to starting with the maximum available credit and receiving reduced credit for deficiencies in cooperation)" (emphasis added). An additional new and lengthy paragraph discusses how prosecutors should weigh aspects of cooperation in line with the broad discretion indicated in the various sections on enhanced benefits discussed above.

The revised Policy continues to bolster the DOJ's insistence that, to receive credit for cooperation, companies must be "proactive," "voluntary," and "genuine" cooperators. The Policy notes that "the most substantial reductions [should be] reserved for only the most extraordinary levels of cooperation and remediation." In his speech, AAG Polite shared guidance that DOJ prosecutors will consider four concepts when assessing whether cooperation could be considered "extraordinary": "immediacy, consistency, degree, and impact." For example, prosecutors can consider whether a corporate defendant cooperated immediately from the start of an investigation; "consistently told the truth"; provided evidence that might be otherwise unobtainable – "like quickly obtaining and imaging electronic devices or [providing] recorded conversations"; and whether the assistance provided by the corporate defendant led to "results [such as] testifying at trial or providing information that leads to additional convictions."

Consistent with the Monaco Memorandum's statements of concern about the effect of foreign data privacy and similar laws on access to evidence, the Policy contains revised language as to companies' obligations in this area to receive cooperation credit. Companies continue to "bear the burden of establishing the existence of such a prohibition or restriction" on accessing or providing information and now must "identify[] reasonable and legal alternatives to help the Criminal Division preserve and obtain the necessary facts, documents, and evidence for its investigations and prosecutions." This language replaces the former FCPA CEP's requirement that companies "should work diligently to identify all available legal bases to provide such documents" – and could be read to allow for greater flexibility for companies to work out potential practical solutions or alternatives, though that will depend on future DOJ positions in each case.

#### Effective Remediation and No Additional Guidance on Executive Compensation or Management of "Personal Devices" and "Third Party Applications"

The language in the revised Policy largely duplicates the prior iteration's standards for companies to obtain credit for effective remediation, though there are several modifications to the eight criteria set out for an effective compliance program. For example, the Policy changes "culture of compliance" to a "commitment to instilling corporate values that promote compliance." The fourth element specifically adds consideration of "the access the compliance function has to senior leadership and governance bodies," recognizing this important aspect for ensuring effective program support. And new language calls for "testing" rather than "auditing" of compliance program effectiveness, a change likely intended to encourage the use of more varied tools to assess program performance.

Overall, a clear goal of the revised Policy is to encourage further the proactive development and maintenance of effective compliance programs, for companies at risk of being considered recidivists in particular. Recidivists or others facing aggravating circumstances can receive substantial benefits, but only if they have effective compliance programs in place "at the time of misconduct" that "enabled the identification of the misconduct and led to the company's voluntary self-disclosure." Given past public pronouncements by AAG Polite, the likely intention is to provide more concrete benefits that corporate compliance officers can cite to obtain appropriate resources for compliance programs and related controls.

The revised Policy does not include promised additional DOJ guidance on expectations related to compensation clawbacks and related remediation, which was a focus of the Monaco Memorandum. The language continues to state that discipline is expected for "those identified by the company as responsible for the misconduct, either through direct participation or failure in oversight, as well as those with supervisory authority over the area in which the criminal conduct occurred."

One potential challenge related to clawbacks is the revised Policy's continued requirement that, to obtain remediation credit, a "company must have effectively remediated at the time of the resolution." Given that clawbacks can result in sometimes protracted litigation, it is unclear how the DOJ will weigh the efforts of companies that engage in attempts to retrieve compensation related to potential wrongdoing but are unable to finalize the process before the time of a disposition with the DOJ.

The revised Policy does not include new DOJ expectations for corporate practices regarding use of personal devices and third-party messaging platforms; per the Monaco Memorandum, additional information on this topic is expected for the next reiteration of the DOJ's guidance on the Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs. The Policy includes the same language from the prior FCPA CEP that requires companies to "implement[] appropriate guidance and controls on the use of personal communications and messaging applications, including ephemeral messaging platforms, that may undermine the company's ability to appropriately retain business records or communications or otherwise comply with the company's document retention policies or legal obligations." One possibility that could play out under the revised Policy is that, to qualify for extraordinary cooperation that may lead to a declination, the DOJ may expect all types of companies to implement the stringent document retention requirements that are presently required of financial institutions, including ephemeral messaging and personal device prohibitions, testing and discipline for violators.

#### Merger & Acquisition Due Diligence and Remediation

Finally, the revised Policy's section on "M&A Due Diligence and Remediation" – which is largely the same as the prior FCPA CEP's section, including as to requirements for a presumption of declination – adds a new sentence at the end regarding "aggravating circumstances." The sentence notes that "[i]n appropriate cases, an acquiring company that voluntarily self-discloses misconduct as set forth in this paragraph may be eligible for a declination, even if aggravating circumstances existed as to the acquired entity."

\*\*\*\*

The revised Policy represents the latest DOJ attempt to encourage early self-disclosure, full cooperation, and substantial remediation efforts by companies facing FCPA and other criminal issues and sets out some concrete examples of benefits that will inure in such circumstances. AAG Polite in his speech discussed several recent cases (including non-FCPA matters) as examples of how the DOJ will apply the Policy in practice. We will address the FCPA matters in our upcoming FCPA Review. However, companies likely will continue to want to see further examples of coherent application of such benefits in future cases, especially as regards the always complicated decision regarding self-disclosure.

On January 17, 2023, following remarks by Assistant Attorney General (AAG) Kenneth A. Polite, Jr. at Georgetown University Law Center, the Department of Justice's Criminal Division issued its revised Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP). The revised Policy supersedes the former FCPA Corporate Enforcement Policy and applies prospectively to all FCPA cases nationwide and all other corporate criminal matters handled by the Criminal Division. It builds on DAG Lisa Monaco's October 2021 and September 15, 2022 memoranda.

Key elements of the revised Policy include:
- The three fundamental standards remain unchanged: voluntary self-disclosure "at the earliest possible time," full cooperation, and "timely and appropriate remediation." A presumption of declination applies when a company meets these standards absent aggravating circumstances, and must pay all disgorgement, forfeiture, and/or restitution.
- Aggravating circumstances include executive management involvement, significant profit from misconduct, egregiousness/pervasiveness of misconduct, or criminal recidivism.
- For cases with aggravating circumstances, prosecutors can still offer a declination (with disgorgement) if self-disclosure was made "immediately," the company had an effective compliance program "at the time of the misconduct" that enabled identification and disclosure, and the company provided "extraordinary cooperation" and "extraordinary remediation."
- Enhanced benefits for companies subject to criminal resolutions: DOJ will accord at least 50% and up to 75% reduction off the low end of the U.S.S.G. fine range (increased from a prior 50% maximum); recidivists can obtain reductions but generally not from the low end. DOJ "will generally not require a corporate guilty plea" absent particularly egregious or multiple aggravating circumstances, and "generally" no Monitor will be required if a company has demonstrated an effective, tested compliance program.
- Even without self-disclosure, companies that fully cooperate and remediate can receive up to a 50% reduction off the low end of the fine range (twice the prior maximum). AAG Polite noted a 50% reduction "will not be the new norm" and will be reserved for extraordinary cooperation.
- The DOJ encourages self-disclosure "at the earliest possible time, even when a company has not yet completed an internal investigation." Companies with aggravating circumstances must disclose "immediately" upon becoming aware of allegations. Disclosures must be made to the Criminal Division to receive credit.
- For "extraordinary" cooperation, prosecutors will consider four concepts: "immediacy, consistency, degree, and impact." Companies "start at zero cooperation credit and then earn credit for specific cooperative actions."
- Updated foreign data privacy law requirements: companies must now "identify reasonable and legal alternatives" to help the DOJ preserve and obtain necessary evidence.
- Remediation criteria were modified, including changing "culture of compliance" to a "commitment to instilling corporate values that promote compliance," adding consideration of compliance function access to senior leadership, and calling for "testing" rather than "auditing" of compliance programs.
- The Policy does NOT include promised guidance on compensation clawbacks or specific DOJ expectations on personal devices and third-party messaging platforms (expected in a future update of the Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs guidance).
- The M&A Due Diligence and Remediation section adds that an acquiring company that voluntarily self-discloses misconduct may be eligible for a declination even if aggravating circumstances existed as to the acquired entity.

<webpage_content>
# The DOJ’s New Corporate Enforcement Policy: A Familiar but Now Nationally Unified Framework for Voluntary Self-Disclosure

[Commercial Litigation Update](https://www.ebglaw.com/commercial-litigation-update/)

On March 10, 2026, the Department of Justice (“DOJ”) announced its “first ever” department-wide [Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy](https://www.justice.gov/dag/media/1430731/dl?inline) (“CEP”) for all criminal cases.

The new CEP – which is modeled very closely upon the prior DOJ Criminal Division policy– creates a nationalized policy for how DOJ awards companies cooperation credit for self-disclosure. It incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with DOJ investigations, and timely and appropriately remedy discovered wrongdoing in exchange for credit – mainly through either a declination of prosecution or a non-prosecution agreement.

Included in the new CEP is a flowchart of potential outcomes should a company choose to self-report.  Under this policy, well-intentioned companies will be rewarded for self-disclosing wrongdoing, cooperating with DOJ investigations, and remediating criminal misconduct.

## Outcomes Under the New CEP

### Self-Reports That Meet All Voluntary Self-Disclosure Requirements

Part I of the new CEP provides that the DOJ will decline to prosecute a company for criminal conduct where four factors are met:

Aggravating circumstances that could cause a self-report to fail to meet the requirements under Part I of the new CEP include, but are not limited to: the nature and seriousness of the offense, the egregiousness or pervasiveness of the misconduct within the company, and the severity of harm caused by the misconduct.  However, even where such aggravating circumstances may exist, prosecutors retain the discretion to recommend a CEP declination based on a holistic weighing of the severity of the aggravating circumstances against compliance with the first three factors of the voluntary self-disclosure requirements.

### Self-Reports to DOJ in Good Faith

In certain circumstances, a company may fully cooperate with a DOJ investigation and timely and appropriately remediate the criminal conduct but nonetheless be ineligible for declination under Part I of the new CEP.  Ineligibility could arise from a self-report not qualifying as a voluntary self-disclosure as defined by the new policy,[[1]](#_ftn1) or the existence of aggravating factors warranting a criminal resolution.  These circumstances are considered a “near miss” and are addressed under Part II of the new CEP.  Self-reports made in good faith that are a near-miss will still receive certain benefits under the new CEP, including a Non-Prosecution Agreement (absent particularly egregious aggravating circumstances), a term length of fewer than three years, no requirement of an independent compliance monitor, and a reduction of at least 50% but not more than 75% off the low end of the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines fine range.

### No Self-Report or Declination Inappropriate

If a company is not eligible under Part I or Part II of the new CEP, prosecutors maintain discretion to determine the appropriate resolution. Resolutions could ultimately still include a reduction in fine, but according to the CEP, the company will not receive, and the DOJ will not recommend a reduction of more than 50% off the fine under the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines. The prosecutors’ discretion also extends to the form, term length, and compliance obligations of an appropriate resolution.

## Takeaways

### Change in Scope

The most meaningful aspect of the new CEP is not a change in substance, but a change in scope.  Until now, the Department’s approach to voluntary self-disclosure developed through fragmented policies issued by Main Justice’s Criminal Division,  and a handful of U.S. Attorneys’ Offices nationwide.  Although those policies often reflected similar principles, they were not uniform.  Companies confronting potential misconduct therefore had to navigate a patchwork of guidance when assessing whether—and how—to disclose conduct to the government.

The new CEP replaces that fragmented framework with a single Department-wide policy applicable to nearly all DOJ criminal components, except the Antitrust Division.  For the first time, companies now face a single set of expectations governing most corporate criminal matters across the Department.

### Increased Transparency

At the same time, the policy continues DOJ’s recent effort to make the benefits of voluntary self-disclosure more explicit and to incentivize corporate participation, while signifying DOJ’s shift towards not prosecuting corporations criminally.  Earlier versions of the Criminal Division’s CEP offered companies that satisfied the policy’s requirements only a “presumption” of declination.  In May 2025, DOJ’s Criminal Division revised that language to provide that prosecutors “will” decline prosecution when those conditions are met and no aggravating circumstances are present.  The new CEP retains that formulation and extends it across DOJ components, reinforcing the Department’s effort to make the incentives for disclosure both clearer and more predictable.

### Practical Implications for Companies and Counsel

The new CEP simplifies companies’ self-disclosure calculus and offers meaningful benefits to companies that comply with the policy.  As Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche emphasized in announcing the policy, “well-intentioned businesses know that, across the Department, they will be rewarded when they self-disclose wrongdoing, cooperate with our investigations, and remediate the misconduct.”[[2]](#_ftn2)  Blanche, however, paired that assurance with an equally direct warning: “make no mistake—we will not hesitate to seek appropriate resolutions against companies and individuals alike that perpetrate white collar offenses.”  Although it remains to be seen how the new CEP will be applied in practice, the message is unambiguous: the Department has clarified and formalized the path to favorable treatment, but companies that fail to meet those expectations should expect a more traditional enforcement response.

For companies, the practical implications of the new CEP remain closely tied to internal compliance and investigative processes.  Greater clarity about the benefits of voluntary self-disclosure reduces uncertainty about DOJ’s expectations, but it also heightens the importance of detecting and investigating potential misconduct quickly enough to support timely disclosure decisions, and the importance of remediation when such misconduct is detected.  In practice, that requires corporate compliance functions that are capable of surfacing concerns promptly, preserving key facts, and supporting early internal investigations.  Companies should therefore consider whether their existing compliance and investigative processes are equipped to meet those demands.

Epstein Becker & Green, P.C. is equipped to advise companies on this changing landscape regarding voluntary self-disclosure and to navigate these requirements. If you have any questions, please contact the authors of this article, or the EBG attorney who regularly assists you.

### Endnotes

[[1]](#_ftnref1) U.S. Dep’t of Just., Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy, Appendix B (2026).  “For the purposes of the CEP, the Department defines voluntary self-disclosure as follows: 1. [t]he company must make a good faith disclosure of the misconduct to the appropriate Department component; 2. [t]he misconduct is not previously known to the Department; 3. [t]he company had no preexisting obligation to disclose the misconduct to the Department; 4. [t]he voluntary disclosure occurs prior to an imminent threat of disclosure or government investigation; and 5. [t]he company discloses the conduct to the Department within a reasonably prompt time after becoming aware of the misconduct, with the burden being on the company to demonstrate timeliness.”  *Id.* (citation modified).

[[2]](#_ftnref2) Press Release, U.S. Dep’t of Just., 26-230, *Department of Justice Releases First-Ever Corporate Enforcement Policy for All Criminal Cases* (March 10, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/department-justice-releases-first-ever-corporate-enforcement-policy-all-criminal-cases [https://perma.cc/A6FH-TFNJ].
