--- SOURCE 22: NYDFS Escalates and Expands Cybersecurity Enforcement - Goodwin ---
URL: https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/blogs/2022/11/nydfs-escalates-and-expands-cybersecurity-enforcement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Goodwin's Data, Privacy + Cybersecurity Insights blog (dated November 18, 2022) analyzes the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) escalation and expansion of cybersecurity enforcement under Part 500 of the New York Cybersecurity Regulation.

KEY EVENT: On October 18, 2022, NYDFS announced its sixth consent order for alleged Part 500 violations, imposing a $4.5 million fine on EyeMed Vision Care, LLC — one of the heftiest monetary penalties yet. This came just over two weeks before NYDFS released its official Proposed Amendments to Part 500, which would impose even more stringent requirements on covered entities.

HISTORY OF ENFORCEMENT: NYDFS did not enforce Part 500 (promulgated March 2017) vigorously initially. Its first action came July 22, 2020, against First American Title Insurance Company (alleging failure to remedy a vulnerability exposing millions of customers' data; the company challenged findings, case pending). In 2021, NYDFS entered three consent orders with fines ranging $1.5–$3 million. In 2022, three additional consent orders were entered against Carnival Corporation, Robinhood Crypto LLC, and EyeMed. Most recent actions imposed $4.5–$5 million penalties. Robinhood was an outlier: developed from a supervisory examination rather than a security incident, imposing a $30 million penalty for violations of Virtual Currency Regulation (Part 200), Money Transmitter Regulation (Part 417), and Transaction Monitoring Regulation (Part 504), in addition to Part 500.

CRITICAL ENFORCEMENT AREAS UNDER CURRENT REGULATION:
• MFA (Section 500.12(b)): top priority; all consent orders address failure to comply. Carnival's entity Princess Cruise Lines had not completed MFA rollout to Office 365 — showing companies may be held strictly liable for MFA violations affecting even a limited number of entities.
• Employee training (500.14): Carnival penalized; repetition of phishing incidents "within a period of less than four years, demonstrates that the Carnival Companies' training was inadequate."
• Risk assessments (500.02(b)): cited in Robinhood and EyeMed consent orders.
• New attention areas: EyeMed failed to limit user access privileges (nine employees shared credentials for one email account) violating 500.03 and 500.13; Robinhood depended on parent company's cybersecurity regime rather than ensuring its own tailored policies.

KEY PROPOSED CHANGES:
• "Class A Companies" — new subset of covered entities defined as those with $20M+ gross annual revenue in each of last two fiscal years with 2,000+ employees, or making $1B+ gross revenue annually. These face more onerous requirements: annual independent audit of cybersecurity programs, external experts for risk assessments every three years, and privileged access activity monitoring.
• Notification changes: two new scenarios triggering 72-hour notification (unauthorized access to a privileged account; ransomware deployed within a material part of the information system). New 24-hour notification when a ransomware payment is made, with explanation of necessity and alternatives considered.
• Annual certification: new alternative allowing written acknowledgment of non-compliance, requiring description of noncompliance areas and remedial plans with timelines — theoretically preventing multiple charges for the same infraction.
• Controls expansion: MFA required for remote/VPN access, applications where nonpublic information is accessible, and privileged accounts (currently only required for external network access by individuals).
• Clarification that failure to comply for any 24-hour period constitutes a violation — consistent with current enforcement practice but not yet codified.

The public comment period (60 days from State Register publication) ended January 9, 2023. The article concludes that the frequency of consent orders, increasing penalty sizes, and plans to strengthen the Regulation indicate rigorous accountability will continue into 2023.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a formal Statement of Charges and Notice of Hearing issued by the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) against First American Title Insurance Company, dated July 21, 2020, with the hearing scheduled for October 26, 2020. The charges stem from a massive data security breach involving First American's EaglePro document-sharing application and its FAST document repository.

**Overview of the Breach:**
- From at least October 2014 through May 2019, First American exposed tens of millions of documents containing consumers' sensitive personal information—including bank account numbers and statements, mortgage and tax records, Social Security numbers, wire transaction receipts, and drivers' license images—through a known vulnerability on its public-facing website.
- The vulnerability was introduced during an application software update in May 2014 and went undetected for years. Due to the use of sequentially numbered ImageDocumentIDs in URLs with no expiration dates, anyone could manipulate a URL by one or more digits to access any of the 850+ million documents stored in FAST without any login or authentication.
- The vulnerability was discovered during a penetration test in December 2018, but First American failed to remediate it for six more months until cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs publicized the breach on May 24, 2019.

**Key Data Points:**
- FAST contained approximately 753 million documents in April 2018 (65 million tagged as containing NPI) and over 850 million documents by May 2019.
- A random sampling of 1,000 untagged documents showed 30% also contained NPI.
- More than 350,000 documents were accessed without authorization by automated "bots" or "scraper" programs during an 11-month period from June 2018 to May 2019.
- Brian Krebs revealed that 885 million documents dating back to 2003 were exposed, and he was easily able to view sensitive data including Social Security numbers, drivers' licenses, and tax and banking information.

**Failures Identified by DFS:**
1. The vulnerability was erroneously classified as "medium severity" based on the mistaken belief that EaglePro could not transmit NPI.
2. First American failed to follow its own cybersecurity policies—no security overview or risk assessment was performed for EaglePro.
3. The Cyber Defense Team reviewed only 10 of hundreds of millions of exposed documents, found no NPI in those 10, and failed to recognize the seriousness of the situation.
4. The director of the Cyber Defense Team accidentally re-classified the vulnerability from "medium" to "low" severity in January 2019, which incorrectly allowed 90 days for remediation.
5. Remediation was assigned to a new, unqualified employee who never received the penetration test report.
6. First American relied solely on a manual process where title agents added the "SEC" prefix to files containing NPI—a process acknowledged as "highly prone to error."
7. After the breach was publicized, information security personnel's recommendations to add authentication and technical controls were rejected by senior management.
8. First American failed to timely encrypt documents containing NPI as required by the Cybersecurity Regulation.

**Six Formal Charges (Violations of 23 NYCRR Part 500):**
- **Charge I (500.02):** Failure to maintain a cybersecurity program based on risk assessment; no risk assessments for FAST and EaglePro applications (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge II (500.03):** Failure to maintain and implement written cybersecurity policies, including inadequate data governance, classification, and access controls (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge III (500.07):** Failure to limit user access privileges to Information Systems providing access to NPI (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge IV (500.09):** Failure to conduct periodic, documented Risk Assessments sufficient to inform the cybersecurity program (violation period: March 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge V (500.14(b)):** Failure to provide adequate cybersecurity awareness training for employees and title agents (violation period: March 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge VI (500.15):** Failure to encrypt NPI at rest and in transit or implement approved compensating controls (violation period: September 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).

DFS is seeking civil monetary penalties under Financial Services Law Section 408, an order requiring remediation of the violations, and other just and appropriate relief. The charges were signed by Katherine A. Lemire (Executive Deputy Superintendent, Consumer Protection and Financial Enforcement) and Justin S. Herring (Executive Deputy Superintendent, Cybersecurity Division).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 24: NY DFS 23NYCRR Part 500 Compliance Guidance | SCF ---
URL: https://securecontrolsframework.com/grc-fundamentals/common-cybersecurity-regulations/ny-dfs-23nycrr-part-500-compliance-guidance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the Secure Controls Framework (SCF) provides a comprehensive GRC (Governance, Risk, and Compliance) perspective on the New York Department of Financial Services (NY DFS) Cybersecurity Regulation, formally codified as 23 NYCRR Part 500. The regulation is a US state-level law that redefined cybersecurity regulation in the financial sector, setting a precedent for other states and federal agencies.

**Overview & Origins:** NY DFS issued the final rule for 23 NYCRR Part 500 on March 1, 2017, as a "first-in-the-nation" cybersecurity regulation. It became effective immediately with phased compliance deadlines extending into 2019. The regulation was prompted by high-profile breaches such as the 2014 JPMorgan Chase breach affecting 76 million households. It applies to all DFS-regulated "covered entities," including state-chartered banks and credit unions, insurance companies, licensed lenders, mortgage servicers, virtual currency businesses, and health/life insurers operating in New York. Small businesses (under 10 employees or less than $5 million gross revenue) may qualify for limited exemptions. The regulation was amended in 2023 to expand ransomware defense, business continuity, and board-level oversight requirements.

**Key Compliance Requirements (§500 sections):**
- §500.02: Comprehensive cybersecurity program based on risk assessment (data governance, access control, asset inventory, physical/environmental controls, network/application security)
- §500.03: Written cybersecurity policy covering 18 required topics, board-approved
- §500.04: Designated qualified CISO reporting annually to the board
- §500.05: Annual penetration testing and periodic vulnerability assessments
- §500.06: Audit trails retaining logs for at least five years with tamper-proofing
- §500.07: Least privilege and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) access management
- §500.09: Documented, repeatable, living risk assessments
- §500.14: Cybersecurity awareness training and continuous monitoring
- §500.17: 72-hour breach notification and annual compliance certification by April 15 each year

**Non-Compliance Consequences:** DFS can impose civil monetary penalties (ranging from hundreds of thousands to tens of millions of dollars), require public disclosures, demand remediation under consent orders, place institutions under heightened scrutiny, and in extreme cases revoke/suspend licenses to operate in New York. Violations of the regulation may also be cited as evidence of negligence in civil class action lawsuits following data breaches.

**Notable Enforcement Actions:**
- EyeMed Vision Care – $4.5 million (2022): Phishing attack compromised data of 1.3+ million individuals; violations included failure to implement MFA, insufficient logging, and delayed breach notification.
- First American Title Insurance – $1.05 million (2021): Vulnerability exposed 880 million documents; inadequate vulnerability management and failure to follow internal risk policies.
- Robinhood Crypto – $30 million (2022): Largest crypto-related DFS fine; lacked adequate cybersecurity protections and BSA compliance.

**Documentation Value:** Current, auditable, and accurate cybersecurity documentation is critical for compliance success. DFS examiners routinely request cybersecurity policies, system architecture/data flow diagrams, incident response and BCDR plans, risk assessment reports, CISO board reports, training logs, access recertification records, and annual certification justifications. Boilerplate templates and outdated policies are easily identified and increase enforcement risk. No official certification exists for NY DFS 23 NYCRR 500, though the SCF Conformity Assessment Program can provide third-party conformity assessment leading to "SCF Certified – NY DFS 23 NYCRR 500."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"23 NYCRR Part 500 is a US state-level regulation that redefined cybersecurity regulation in the financial sector, setting a precedent for other states and federal agencies. For covered entities, it is more than a compliance obligation where it is a strategic risk management framework embedded in law."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Secureframe provides a comprehensive guide to the NYDFS NYCRR 500 Cybersecurity Regulation and a compliance checklist for 2024. The regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), first issued in March 2017, establishes cybersecurity requirements for all covered financial institutions in New York. Significant amendments were announced in November 2023 with an effective date of April 29, 2024.

**Who Must Comply:** NYDFS NYCRR 500 applies to all DFS-regulated entities including state-chartered banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, insurance companies, health insurers, money transmitters, and other financial services institutions. The regulation designates three company types:
- **Covered entities:** All DFS-regulated organizations
- **Class A companies:** Introduced in the 2023 amendments; entities with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue in each of the last two fiscal years AND either at least 2,000 employees (averaged over two years) or over $1 billion in gross annual revenue. These face additional obligations including independent audits and stronger monitoring.
- **Small businesses:** Qualify for limited exemption (Section 500.19) if combined affiliates have fewer than 20 employees, less than $7.5 million in annual gross revenue in each of the last three years, or less than $15 million in year-end total assets.

**Key Requirements:**
- Periodic risk assessments
- Cybersecurity program with policies including Information Security, Access Control, Business Continuity/Disaster Recovery, Incident Response (now requiring root cause analysis), Data Retention/Disposal, Third-Party Service Provider Security, Asset Inventory, and Vulnerability Management policies
- Appointment of qualified cybersecurity leadership (senior governing body and CISO)
- Technical controls: multi-factor authentication, encryption (compensating controls no longer allowed for encryption in transit over external networks), systems/network security, application security, physical/environmental controls, data privacy controls, and security awareness training
- Continuous monitoring with annual penetration testing (now required from both inside and outside systems) and bi-annual vulnerability assessments
- Audit trail systems with records kept minimum five years
- 72-hour notification to NYDFS of cybersecurity events reasonably likely to impact operations, plus new reporting of third-party incidents and extortion payments

**Certification:** Covered entities submit an annual Certificate of Compliance (typically April 15, pushed to April 29, 2024 this year). Class A companies must undergo annual independent compliance audits. Documentation must be kept for five years.

**Enforcement:** NYDFS monitors through self-certification, audits, and mandatory reporting. Historical penalties include Robinhood Crypto ($30 million), OneMain Financial Group ($4.25 million), Residential Mortgage Services ($1.5 million), SA Stone Wealth Management ($1.35 million), and First American Title Insurance Company ($1 million). The 2023 amendment reaffirmed that even a single act of non-compliance could constitute a violation.

The article also promotes Secureframe's compliance automation platform with features like AI-driven risk management, policy generation, continuous monitoring, vendor management, cross-mapping controls, regulatory change management, and security training.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: DOJ Announces New Changes to Corporate Criminal Enforcement Policies | White & Case LLP ---
URL: https://www.whitecase.com/insight-alert/doj-announces-new-changes-corporate-criminal-enforcement-policies

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is a White & Case client alert titled "DOJ Announces New Changes to Corporate Criminal Enforcement Policies." Published in September 2022, the alert analyzes the DOJ Memo ("Further Revisions to Corporate Criminal Enforcement Policies Following Discussions with Corporate Crime Advisory Group") issued by Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco on September 15, 2022.

KEY CONTENT:

**Background:** The DOJ Memo was published eleven months after DAG Monaco established a Corporate Crime Advisory Group to review the DOJ's approach to corporate crime, including what constitutes corporate cooperation. It represents one of the DOJ's most elaborate overhauls of corporate enforcement in recent years, giving greater credit to companies that self-report, cooperate, and remediate corporate wrongdoing.

**Scope:** The principles apply to all corporations with a US nexus, including Asian companies with US operations. They cover all types of corporate crime under US law, including FCPA bribery and corruption, money laundering, embezzlement, and healthcare fraud for pharmaceutical companies.

**Individual Accountability:** The DOJ Memo stressed that the DOJ's "first priority" in corporate crime is to "hold accountable the individuals who commit and profit from corporate crime." This affirms the DOJ's longstanding approach (dating back to the 2015 Sally Yates memo) and provides greater incentives for corporations to disclose individual misbehavior in a timely manner.

**Corporate Accountability Principles:** The DOJ Memo enumerates principles for determining corporate culpability, including: (1) history of misconduct, (2) voluntary self-disclosure by companies, (3) evaluation of cooperation by companies, and (4) evaluation of corporate compliance programs.

SUMMARY:

On March 10, 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) released its first-ever department-wide Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (CEP), applying to all corporate criminal matters handled by the Department except violations of 15 U.S.C. §§ 1–38, which remain governed by the Antitrust Division's separate leniency program. The new CEP supersedes all component-specific or U.S. Attorney's Office-specific corporate enforcement policies, including the SDNY voluntary self-disclosure policy (February 2026), the May 2025 Criminal Division CEP, the February 2023 USAOs Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy, and the July 2023 National Security Division policy. The policy aims to promote consistency, transparency, and predictability in corporate criminal enforcement while incentivizing voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation, and remediation.

The new CEP largely tracks the prior Criminal Division CEP but makes several key changes: (1) Penalty Mitigation: replaces the flat 75% reduction off the low end of the U.S.S.G. fine range with "a reduction of at least 50% but not more than 75%," introducing prosecutorial discretion. (2) Prior Criminal History: removes the five-year look-back limitation for the recidivism aggravating factor, expanding it to any prior similar conduct, while echoing the September 2022 Monaco memorandum; notably, the new policy imposes no gradation weighing older conduct less heavily. (3) Whistleblower Disclosure Timing: drops the "presumption" of declination language and requires self-reporting "as soon as reasonably practicable" rather than within 120 days. (4) Cooperation Standard: consolidates two separate disclosure obligations into a single duty to "timely, truthfully, and accurately disclose[] all facts and non-privileged evidence relevant to the conduct at issue." (5) De-confliction Notice: adds a new provision requiring companies to notify the Department in advance where de-confliction requests may conflict with other legal obligations. (6) Financial Condition: removes the burden-shifting framework for financial hardship claims, replacing it with a directive that the Department will consider the company's "size, sophistication, and financial condition" when assessing cooperation. (7) Resolution Agreement Transparency: adds a requirement that prosecutors outline in resolution agreements why a company received a particular amount of cooperation credit.

Implications: The CEP ensures that, except for antitrust cases, the benefits of voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation, and remediation are governed by a single uniform policy, providing predictability and consistency regardless of which DOJ office handles a matter. The tradeoff is that the prior patchwork of policies offered some flexibility and, in certain instances, more favorable terms. Because the new policy hews closely to the prior Criminal Division CEP, companies can look to precedent cases under prior policies for guidance.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Picus Security webpage provides a comprehensive profile of the LockBit ransomware gang, a prominent threat group known for technically advanced and high-impact ransomware variants. Formerly called the ABCD group, LockBit operates a Ransomware-as-a-Service (RaaS) model that recruits affiliates and accelerates development through public bug bounty-style programs. The group advertises itself as the fastest encrypting ransomware in the market and relies on double extortion (data theft combined with file encryption) to pressure victims into payment. High-profile incidents have included Accenture, the Ministry of Justice in France, and Bangkok Airways.

Key metadata: LockBit is associated with Russia, was first seen in September 2019, and uses aliases including ABCD, Bitwise Spider, and Water Selkie, with UNC2165 as an affiliate. Target sectors include Education, Energy, Financial Services, Government, Healthcare, Legal, Manufacturing, Retail, Technology, Telecommunications, and Transportation. Target countries include the United States, Italy, Australia, Brazil, France, India, Mexico, Morocco, Taiwan, UAE, and the UK.

Business models include RaaS, double extortion, cooperation with Initial Access Brokers (IABs), collaboration with other groups (e.g., Maze), use of company insiders, and criminal bug bounties. Extortion tactics involve file encryption and data leakage. Initial access methods include exploiting public-facing applications and phishing. Impact methods include data encryption and data exfiltration.

Exploited vulnerabilities by LockBit include: ProxyShell RCE (CVE-2021-34473, CVSS 9.8), ProxyShell Privilege Escalation (CVE-2021-34523, CVSS 9.8), ProxyShell Security Feature Bypass (CVE-2021-31207, CVSS 7.2), F5 BIG-IP iControl REST API RCE (CVE-2022-22986, CVSS 8.8), Fortinet FortiGate SSL VPN Path Traversal (CVE-2018-13379, CVSS 9.8), and SonicWall SSLVPN SQL Injection (CVE-2021-20028, CVSS 9.8).

LockBit affiliates use a broad playbook across MITRE ATT&CK tactics. Initial access often comes from phishing, exposed remote services, valid accounts purchased from IABs, or exploitation of known vulnerabilities. Operators perform discovery, lateral movement, and privilege escalation using living-off-the-land binaries and common admin tools. Many intrusions include credential theft, disabling security software, and removing backups or shadow copies to maximize impact. LockBit variants support Windows, Linux, and VMware ESXi, enabling encryption across mixed environments. The operation maintains a leak site for publishing stolen data and manages negotiations through structured playbooks.

Utilized tools and malware by MITRE ATT&CK tactic include: Execution (PowerShell, PowerShell Empire, PSExec, Windows Task Scheduler, Windows Command Shell), Persistence (Reg.exe), Privilege Execution (UACme), Defense Evasion (GMER, GPEdit.msc, Invoke-GPUpdate, mshta, Process Hacker, wewtutil), Credential Access (Comsvcs.dll Minidump, Hakops Keylogger, Mimikatz), Discovery (ADfind.exe, Advanced Port Scanner, PsGetSid), Lateral Movement (PSExec), Command and Control (AnyDesk, Metasploit Meterpreter), Exfiltration (Mega, StealBit infostealer), and Impact (LockBit ransomware, Vssadmin, BCDEdit).

Recommended defensive measures include enforcing multi-factor authentication, hardening remote access, patching exposed services, segmenting critical assets, monitoring for data exfiltration, and continuously validating security controls against real attacker techniques.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Zscaler (Zpedia) explains the SEC's new cybersecurity disclosure rules announced on July 26, 2023, which apply to public companies. The rules mandate timely disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents and annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance.

**Key Requirements:**
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Material cybersecurity incidents must be reported within four business days of a materiality determination. A new, broader definition of "cybersecurity incident" now includes "a series of related unauthorized occurrences."
- **Temporary Delay:** Companies may delay disclosure up to 120 days (with US Attorney General approval and SEC consent) if disclosure poses national security or public safety risks.
- **Updated Incident Disclosures:** Incomplete Form 8-K data must be acknowledged and later amended within four business days of obtaining missing information.
- **Form 10-K (Regulation S-K Item 106):** Annual reporting on cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and board oversight is required. Companies must describe management's role and responsibilities but are NOT required to disclose board members' cybersecurity expertise.
- **Foreign Private Issuers:** Must file comparable disclosures on Forms 6-K and 20-F.
- **Structured Data:** Disclosures must be tagged in Inline XBRL format, though compliance was delayed by one year.

**Effective Dates and Compliance Timelines:**
- Rules became effective September 5, 2023.
- Larger public companies must comply with Form 8-K Item 1.05 by December 15, 2023.
- Smaller reporting companies have until June 24, 2024, for Item 1.05 compliance.
- Item 106 applies to annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.

**Compliance Preparation Steps:** Review rules with security/filing teams, establish materiality determination processes, draft cyber risk assessment descriptions, engage board of directors in cyber risk oversight, and identify board members with cybersecurity expertise.

**Materiality Definition:** An incident is material if it significantly impacts operations, finances, or reputation, based on quantitative factors (costs) and qualitative factors (reputational damage, litigation exposure).

The page also promotes Zscaler Risk360™ as a tool for cyber risk quantification, financial exposure detail, and board-ready reporting to help companies comply with the new rules.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## SEC Issues New Requirements for Cybersecurity Disclosures

**Source:** Deloitte Heads Up, Volume 30, Issue 13  
**Date:** July 30, 2023 (Updated December 19, 2023)

### Background
On July 26, 2023, the SEC issued a final rule requiring registrants to provide enhanced and standardized disclosures regarding cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incidents. The rule addresses investor concerns over timely and consistent cybersecurity information amid rising digital threats.

### Key Requirements

**1. Material Cybersecurity Incidents (Form 8-K, Item 1.05)**
- Registrants must file a Form 8-K within four business days of determining a cybersecurity incident is material.
- A cybersecurity incident is defined as "an unauthorized occurrence, or a series of related unauthorized occurrences, on or conducted through a registrant's information systems that jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of a registrant's information systems or any information residing therein."
- Required disclosures include: material aspects of the nature, scope, timing of the incident, and the material impact or reasonably likely material impact on the registrant (including financial condition and results of operations).
- Amended Form 8-K must be filed within four business days if information becomes available later or previously disclosed information is inaccurate.

**2. Materiality Assessment**
- Materiality determinations must be made "without unreasonable delay."
- Materiality is consistent with U.S. Supreme Court standards (TSC Industries, Basic, Matrixx).
- Factors include: probability of adverse outcome, potential significance of loss, nature and extent of harm to individuals, customers, vendor relationships, reputation, and competitiveness.
- Erik Gerding (SEC Division of Corporation Finance director) clarified that materiality may not be determined on the same date the incident occurred.

**3. Temporary Delay for National Security**
- The U.S. Attorney General may determine that disclosure poses a substantial risk to national security or public safety.
- Initial delay: up to 30 days; secondary delay: additional 30 days; final extraordinary circumstances: up to 60 days; further delays via SEC exemptive order.
- The FBI provided guidance on requesting delays, noting early outreach is critical.

**4. Risk Management, Strategy, and Governance (Form 10-K, Item 1C)**
- Registrants must disclose processes for assessing, identifying, and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats.
- Disclosures required on: integration into overall risk management, use of third-party assessors, and oversight of third-party service provider risks.
- **Board oversight:** Description of board's oversight of cybersecurity risks, identification of responsible committees, and processes for informing the board.
- **Management responsibilities:** Which positions/committees are responsible, their relevant expertise, processes for monitoring incidents, and reporting to the board.

### Transition Provisions
- **Form 8-K (Item 1.05):** Effective December 18, 2023 (all registrants except smaller reporting companies); June 15, 2024 (smaller reporting companies).
- **Regulation S-K Item 106 (Form 10-K):** Effective for annual reports for fiscal years ending on or after December 15, 2023.
- Inline XBRL tagging required one year after initial compliance dates.

### Changes from Proposed Rule
- Narrowed scope of cyber incident disclosures with added national security delay.
- Amended Form 8-K used instead of Forms 10-Q/10-K for updates.
- Aggregation of immaterial incidents removed (but series of related unauthorized occurrences may still require Form 8-K).
- Removed proposed requirement to disclose cybersecurity expertise of the board.
- Added transition provisions.

### All filers affected
Including domestic registrants, foreign private issuers (FPIs), smaller reporting companies, and emerging growth companies.
</summary>

<summary>
This article from NetDiligence examines the impact of the SEC Cyber Disclosure Rule (Item 1.05 of Form 8-K) one year after it took effect in December 2023, drawing on insights from Breach Coach® experts Jillian Seifrit and Daniel Pepper of Fisher Phillips LLP.

Key facts about the rule:
- Requires publicly traded companies to disclose material cyber incidents within four business days of determining materiality
- Must include the nature, scope, and timing of the incident, with amendments required as more information becomes known
- Applies to incidents material to investors (e.g., ransomware attacks, data breaches with customer/financial data exposure)
- A "material" incident is one a reasonable investor would consider important in investment decisions

Enforcement consequences:
- SEC has already issued enforcement orders with fines up to $4 million
- Unisys Corp. was fined $4 million for describing cybersecurity risks as "hypothetical" despite knowing about two SolarWinds-related intrusions
- Mimecast Ltd. was fined $990,000 for failing to disclose the nature of exfiltrated code and quantity of encrypted credentials accessed

Common mistakes and challenges:
- Companies face pressure to make rapid materiality judgments under uncertainty with incomplete data
- Many submit vague, boilerplate statements; fail to assess materiality promptly; or misjudge incident scope
- Key is amending the 8-K to reflect newly learned information

Best practices emerging from Year One:
- Pre-drafting templates for Item 1.05 disclosures
- Preparing materiality playbooks in incident response plans
- Establishing cross-functional breach response teams
- Conducting regular materiality training sessions
- Legal teams must partner with CISOs and communications teams in designing disclosure protocols

Key impacts:
- The rule makes cybersecurity a boardroom issue requiring executive oversight
- Worker missteps (phishing, data mishandling, unauthorized downloads) can now be material under SEC definitions
- CISOs are now more prominent in risk management, briefing leadership on materiality and timelines
- Disclosures can be delayed for national security reasons with written DOJ/DHS support
- Disclosure can create tension with labor law and employee privacy rights
- Third-party/vendor breaches must be disclosed if they materially impact the registrant, especially relevant for HR/employment cloud systems
- Underreporting or delayed disclosure risks reputational damage, SEC enforcement, litigation, and shareholder backlash

--- SOURCE 6: Court in SolarWinds Case Blows Down SEC's Cyber Enforcement ... ---
URL: https://www.hklaw.com/en/insights/publications/2024/07/court-in-solarwinds-case-blows-down-secs-cyber-enforcement-authority

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On July 18, 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York dismissed most of the SEC's landmark cyber enforcement litigation against SolarWinds Corp. and its Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) Timothy Brown. In a 107-page opinion in Securities and Exchange Commission v. SolarWinds Corp. & Timothy G. Brown (Judge Paul Engelmayer presiding), the court rejected the SEC's efforts to expand the Securities Exchange Act's "internal accounting controls" provision to encompass cybersecurity controls. The court also limited the SEC's use of the "disclosure controls and procedure" provision, finding that innocent errors are "an inadequate basis" on which to plead deficient disclosure controls. Only a subset of material misrepresentation claims related to the Security Statement published on the company's website survived, and the case proceeds toward discovery.

BACKGROUND: SolarWinds, a software company with the Orion Platform, posted a Security Statement on its website in late 2017. In January 2019, nation-state hackers exploited a vulnerability and inserted malicious code into Orion software builds - known as the SUNBURST attack. In 2020, SolarWinds was notified by the USTP and Palo Alto Networks of suspicious activity but couldn't determine the root cause. After Mandiant identified the malicious code, SolarWinds filed a Form 8-K on Dec. 14, 2020, detailing the attack. The SEC filed its complaint in 2023 and an amended complaint on Feb. 16, 2024, charging violations of antifraud provisions, disclosure controls, and internal controls.

KEY COURT RULINGS: 1) Internal Accounting Controls: The court found the SEC "clearly correct" to be challenged on the plain language of Section 13(b), holding that "cybersecurity controls are outside the scope of Section 13(b)(2)(B)" and dismissing the claim entirely. 2) Disclosure Controls: The court dismissed this claim, finding "[w]ithout more, the existence of two misclassified incidents is an inadequate basis on which to plead deficient disclosure controls," and that "second-guessing by hindsight" is disfavored. 3) Security Statement: The court found the SEC sufficiently alleged material misrepresentations concerning access controls and password protection policies on the company's public website. 4) Cyber Risk Disclosures: Dismissed, as fraud claims based on risk disclosures are actionable only where "the warned risk has already occurred." 5) Brown's public statements: Found to be "non-actionable corporate puffery." 6) Form 8-K disclosures: Dismissed as fraud by hindsight; the court found the Form 8-K "captured the big picture: the severity of the SUNBURST attack," noting the stock dropped 16% on filing day and 8% the next day.

KEY TAKEAWAYS: The SEC failed to expand internal accounting controls to cover cybersecurity. The SEC must now allege systemic deficiencies (not innocent errors) for disclosure controls violations. Cyber risk disclosure fraud claims are limited to narrow circumstances where the warned risk has already occurred. Courts will consider practical time constraints (including the SEC Cybersecurity Rules' four-business-day disclosure requirement) when assessing Form 8-K filings. Companies should avoid warning about risks that have already occurred, and risk disclosures should convey severity without arming threat actors.

SUGGESTED ACTION ITEMS for issuers: 1) Develop well-designed disclosure controls and incident response plans. 2) Include risk disclosures that convey manner and severity without providing a road map to threat actors. 3) Have a practiced plan for responding to cyber incidents. 4) Engage experienced cybersecurity counsel. This Holland & Knight analysis was authored by Shardul Desai, Allison Kernisky, and Jessica B. Magee on July 24, 2024.
</summary>

SolarWinds Corporation has reached an agreement in principle with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to settle a landmark cybersecurity enforcement action alleging securities fraud tied to the 2020 "Sunburst" cyberattack. The proposed settlement, which still requires formal SEC approval, prompted a federal judge in New York to pause all proceedings while final terms are reviewed. The case, SEC v. SolarWinds Corp. (Case No. 1:23-cv-09518), is pending in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York, with the parties required to provide a status update by September 12th.

This was a first-of-its-kind enforcement action: it was the first SEC case alleging a public company committed fraud by misrepresenting cybersecurity practices before a breach, and the first time the SEC named a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) as an individual defendant. The suit stemmed from the 2020 "Sunburst" attack, linked to threat actors allegedly connected to the Russian government, which exploited vulnerabilities in SolarWinds' Orion software platform and affected high-profile clients including the U.S. Departments of Homeland Security, Treasury, and Commerce.

The SEC alleged SolarWinds failed to adequately disclose known cybersecurity vulnerabilities to investors and misrepresented the strength of its internal controls, including a website security statement falsely conveying robust access controls and password protections. While the court dismissed several SEC claims (holding some post-breach disclosures were not misleading since the company lacked full knowledge of the scope of the incident), one key claim survived regarding the allegedly misleading online security statement. SolarWinds filed for summary judgment, but the parties reached a tentative settlement as oral arguments were being prepared.

Key takeaways for public companies include: the SEC is signaling willingness to bring enforcement actions when public cybersecurity statements don't match internal realities; naming the CISO as a defendant could indicate a trend toward personal liability in cybersecurity reporting; companies must ensure post-breach statements are accurate and based on verified facts; and internal communications, technical documentation, and policy implementation records may become critical in litigation. Specific settlement terms have not yet been disclosed. The article was authored by Sean V. Patel, Christopher J. Seusing, and Timothy D. Shea of the law firm WSHB.

<summary>
This article analyzes the SEC's decision in November 2025 to dismiss its remaining claims against SolarWinds and its CISO Tim Brown with prejudice, ending a closely watched cybersecurity enforcement case that began in October 2023. The SEC had alleged SolarWinds defrauded investors by overstating cybersecurity practices and understating risks following the 2020 supply-chain attack on its Orion software platform, attributed to the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service, which affected thousands of customers.

Key procedural developments: In July 2024, Judge Paul A. After a failed July 2025 settlement, the parties filed a Joint Stipulation to Dismiss on November 20, 2025, with the SEC agreeing to dismissal without settlement conditions.

The dismissal signals a shift in SEC enforcement toward "back to basics" fraud theories focused on egregious misstatements causing investor harm, rather than nuanced disclosure deficiencies. However, the article emphasizes risk remains high on multiple fronts:

1. Regulatory and litigation risk remains high—other federal, state, and international regulators may fill any void, and private litigation (securities class actions, derivative suits, consumer protection actions) remains active following cyber incidents.
2. Securities disclosure requirements have expanded—the SEC's December 2023 "Cyber Rules" impose new Form 8-K reporting requirements for material incidents and expanded annual report disclosures.
3. Executives are not off the hook—while individual CISO enforcement risk may now be higher in securities contexts, senior leaders may still face liability for misrepresentations, negligence, or oversight failures.
4. Enforcement will vary by impact—sectors with greater potential for operational disruption harm (financial institutions, pervasive technology providers, critical infrastructure) may face more scrutiny.
5. Enforcement priorities could shift again with administrations.

The article was authored by Andrew Tannenbaum and Anna Rudawski, partners at A&O Shearman, and is based on a firm memorandum. On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," which supersedes an earlier advisory from October 1, 2020. The Updated Advisory is directed at not only organizations victimized by ransomware attacks but also financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and forensic and incident-response firms that assist victims.

Key points of the Updated Advisory include:

- **Continued Opposition to Ransomware Payments**: OFAC maintains that the U.S. government "strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands" and recommends focusing on defensive and resilience measures. Payments may violate U.S. sanctions prohibitions, and penalties may be imposed on a strict liability basis, meaning companies could face enforcement even if they didn't know a payment would violate sanctions.

- **New Mitigating Factors**: The Updated Advisory identifies two significant mitigating factors in any OFAC enforcement response:
  1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps taken to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices, such as those in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide (co-developed with MS-ISAC), will be considered a "significant mitigating factor."
  2. **Notification and Cooperation with U.S. Government**: Promptly reporting ransomware attacks to law enforcement, CISA, Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection (OCCIP), or other relevant agencies, along with ongoing cooperation (including providing technical details, ransom payment demands, and payment instructions), constitutes a "significant mitigating factor." Timely self-disclosure to these agencies may be considered a voluntary self-disclosure for mitigation purposes.

- **First-Ever Sanctions Designation of a Cryptocurrency Exchange**: Also on September 21, 2021, OFAC designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (also known as "Successful Exchange"), a Russian cryptocurrency exchange, for property-blocking sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13694 (as amended by EO 13757). OFAC alleged SUEX OTC facilitated numerous ransomware payments for malicious cyber actors. U.S. persons are now prohibited from engaging in virtually all transactions with SUEX OTC. - **Anticipated Further Guidance**: Press reporting indicates further related guidance may be forthcoming, likely from FinCEN, including action on the proposed application of the travel rule to cryptocurrency transactions and additional anti-money laundering efforts. This aligns with FinCEN's October 1, 2020 advisory (issued in parallel with the 2020 OFAC Advisory) on "red flags" for suspicious ransomware transactions, which noted that consultants facilitating ransomware payments could be considered "money transmitters" under the Bank Secrecy Act.

The article was authored by Covington & Burling LLP attorneys Ashden Fein, Peter Flanagan, Jim Garland, Mike Nonaka, and Moriah Daugherty. The article notes that it remains unclear how OFAC will assess compliance with the new mitigating factors, including which agencies and standards will be used for evaluation, but emphasizes the importance of preparation—developing a strong cybersecurity posture before an attack and timely reporting to and cooperation with government agencies.

On June 24, 2024, the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance issued five new Compliance and Disclosure Interpretations (C&DIs) regarding cybersecurity incident reporting under Item 1.05 of Form 8-K, specifically addressing ransomware payment scenarios. The guidance clarifies that:

1. Companies that make a ransomware payment before determining materiality must still assess the incident's materiality.
2. Companies that determine an incident is material and make a payment before filing Form 8-K are still required to report.
3. Cyber insurance coverage for a ransomware payment alone does not make an incident immaterial.
4. The amount demanded or paid in a ransomware payment should not be the sole factor in materiality assessment.
5. Companies experiencing a series of individually immaterial ransomware attacks should consider whether related incidents are collectively material.

Additionally, on May 21, 2024, SEC Corporation Finance Director Erik Gerding issued guidance emphasizing that only material cybersecurity incidents should be disclosed under Item 1.05 of Form 8-K. Companies are encouraged to use Item 8.01 for voluntary disclosures of immaterial incidents. Gerding also issued a statement on June 20, 2024, clarifying that Item 1.05 does not prohibit private discussions about cybersecurity incidents with commercial counterparties and that several ways exist to share information without implicating Regulation FD.

KEY PROVISIONS:
1. **Banking Organization Notification**: A banking organization must notify its primary Federal regulator of any "computer-security incident" that rises to the level of a "notification incident" as soon as possible and no later than 36 hours after the banking organization determines that a notification incident has occurred.
2. **Bank Service Provider Notification**: A bank service provider must notify each affected banking organization customer (through at least one bank-designated point of contact) as soon as possible when the provider determines it has experienced a computer-security incident that has caused, or is reasonably likely to cause, a material service disruption or degradation for four or more hours.

KEY DATES: Effective date April 1, 2022; Compliance date May 1, 2022. The final rule applies to 12 CFR Parts 53 (OCC), 225 (Federal Reserve), and 304 (FDIC).

DEFINITIONS AND SCOPE:
- **Banking organizations** covered include: for OCC—national banks, Federal savings associations, and Federal branches/agencies of foreign banks; for the Board—U.S. bank holding companies, savings and loan holding companies, state member banks, U.S. operations of foreign banking organizations, and Edge/agreement corporations; for FDIC—insured state nonmember banks, insured state-licensed branches of foreign banks, and insured state savings associations.
- **Computer-security incident** is defined as an occurrence that results in actual harm to an information system or the information contained within it.
- **Bank service provider** is defined as a bank service company or other person who performs "covered services" (services subject to the Bank Service Company Act, 12 U.S.C. 1861-1867).
- **Designated financial market utilities (FMUs)** under Title VIII of the Dodd-Frank Act are excluded from the definitions of both "banking organization" and "bank service provider."

RATIONALE: Cyberattacks targeting the financial services industry have increased in frequency and severity. Timely notification allows agencies to have early awareness of emerging threats, assess threats, facilitate assistance through the Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection, provide guidance, and conduct horizontal analyses to prevent incidents from becoming systemic. This page explains the proposed HIPAA Security Rule update (still NOT final as of mid-2026), which would represent the most significant change since the rule's original 2003 adoption. The NPRM was published in the Federal Register on January 6, 2025; the comment period closed March 7, 2025; and OCR has not issued a final rule. OMB's Unified Agenda (RIN 0945-AA22) now targets July 2027 for final action (pushed back from an earlier spring 2026 target), though these timelines are not legally binding.

Key proposed changes include: (1) mandatory annual Security Risk Assessments (the current rule has no specified frequency); (2) mandatory encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit, removing the "addressable" designation; (3) required multi-factor authentication for all systems accessing ePHI; (4) regular vulnerability scanning and penetration testing; (5) enhanced documentation requirements; and (6) comprehensive technology asset inventory and network mapping. The proposed rule would also require annual BAA verification (documenting the verification itself, not just keeping the BAA on file) and a 240-day implementation runway (60 days effective plus 180 days to compliance).

HHS estimated $9 billion in year-one costs and $34 billion across years one through five. In February 2025, CHIME joined seven other associations and 100+ hospital/provider organizations in a letter asking the Trump administration to withdraw the proposal, arguing small and rural providers cannot absorb these costs. HHS retained the July 2027 target despite pushback but signaled willingness to credit good-faith, phased compliance from critical access hospitals and safety-net providers.

The January 2026 OCR Cybersecurity Newsletter emphasized: system hardening as a documented expectation (patch management, default-credential elimination, configuration baselines), evolution from risk analysis to risk management (requiring timely documented remediation, not just an assessment document), and that risk analysis must surface unpatched-software and firmware vulnerabilities (45 CFR § 164.308(a)(1)(ii)(A)).

The page provides a preparation timeline: gap analysis, SRA, asset inventory, encryption assessment, and MFA planning through mid-2026; encryption deployment, MFA rollout, vulnerability scanning, documentation updates, and training through December 2026; then ongoing annual SRA cycles, continuous vulnerability management (critical patches within 72 hours, scans at least quarterly), and compliance monitoring. Common mistakes warned against: waiting for the final rule, treating compliance as purely a technology project, underestimating documentation requirements, ignoring business associate compliance, and trying to do everything at once. On December 27, 2024, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), through the Office for Civil Rights (OCR), announced a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) to amend the HIPAA Security Rule, published in the Federal Register on January 6, 2025. - Updating definitions and adding specific compliance time periods.
- Requiring written documentation of all policies and procedures.

- Developing and maintaining a technology asset inventory and network map (updated at least every 12 months).
- Strengthening written risk assessment requirements, including review of asset inventory, identification of threats and vulnerabilities, and risk level assessments.
- Establishing a written incident response plan tested and revised every 12 months, with procedures to restore lost systems and data within 72 hours.
- Requiring covered entities to obtain verification from Business Associates at least every 12 months showing they have employed required technical safeguards, and requiring Business Associates to notify covered entities within 24 hours upon activation of contingency plans.

The proposed effective date of the final rule would be 60 days after publication, with a compliance date 180 days after that. --- SOURCE 29: Ransomware Attacks—Financial Crimes Compliance Requirements ---
URL: https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/client-alerts/20201008-ransomware-attacks-financial-crimes-compliance-requirements

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a client alert from the law firm WilmerHale, authored by partners Jason C. Chipman and David M. Horn, analyzing two US government advisories issued on October 1, 2020, addressing the risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments: the OFAC Ransomware Advisory (regarding potential sanctions risks) and the FinCEN Ransomware Advisory (FIN-2020-A006, regarding ransomware and use of the financial system for ransom payments). These represented the first time OFAC and FinCEN issued guidance specifically addressing ransomware payments, which increased in demand during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The advisories identify two main areas of regulatory risk:
1. Violation of OFAC's sanctions regulations – OFAC may impose civil penalties based on strict liability (a person may be held civilly liable even without knowledge), particularly because ransomware attackers can obscure their identity and some are linked to sanctioned actors (e.g., North Korean government and Russian cybercriminals). Ransomware typically involves convertible virtual currency (CVC), which further obscures payouts. Where attackers are known targets of sanctions, OFAC reviews license applications "on a case-by-case basis with a presumption of denial."
2. Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) filing requirements for financial institutions – institutions may be required to file SARs whether they are victims of ransomware attacks or merely processing payments for victimized clients. The FinCEN advisory provides specific SAR filing instructions to reference the advisory.

The advisories also apply to cyber insurance, digital forensics, and incident response firms, which should maintain compliance programs and may face money transmission registration requirements under the Bank Secrecy Act and state money transmission laws. Both advisories encourage cooperation with law enforcement; OFAC considers a "self-initiated, timely, and complete report of a ransomware attack to law enforcement" as a significant mitigating factor in enforcement outcomes.

The FinCEN Advisory identifies five trends of ransomware attacks: (1) "big-game hunting" targeting larger enterprises for bigger payouts; (2) sharing of resources and partnerships among cybercriminals; (3) "double extortion schemes" involving data theft and threats to publish; (4) use of anonymity-enhanced cryptocurrencies (AECs) with discounted rates for AEC payments; and (5) "fileless" ransomware using malicious code in system memory. FinCEN also identified red-flag indicators for financial institutions, including transactions with digital forensics firms known to make ransom payments, rapid back-to-back cryptocurrency movements, accounts lacking obvious connection to customer business, "chain-hopping" techniques, and transactions with exchanges in high-risk jurisdictions.

While the advisories create no new legal requirements, they indicate that OFAC and FinCEN expect risk-based compliance programs and a high level of coordination with law enforcement. Failure to report attacks to law enforcement may increase exposure to OFAC monetary penalties. Companies should prepare for ransomware attacks as part of their cybersecurity defense posture.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) issued a Financial Trend Analysis (FTA) on ransomware incidents reported in Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) data between 2022 and 2024, totaling more than $2.1 billion in ransomware payments. Unlike previous analyses that focused on filing dates, this report shifts focus to the actual incident dates of each ransomware attack, providing greater visibility into ransomware actor activities.

Key findings include:
- Ransomware incidents and payments reached an all-time high in 2023 with 1,512 incidents totaling $1.1 billion in payments (a 77% year-over-year increase from 2022); incidents decreased to 1,476 in 2024 following law enforcement disruptions of two high-profile ransomware groups, reflecting $734 million in aggregate payments.

- More than 200 ransomware variants were identified; the most reported variants were Akira, ALPHV/BlackCat, LockBit, Phobos, and Black Basta. The top 10 variants by payment amounts accounted for approximately $1.5 billion in payments.

--- SOURCE 2: Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) Update — American Coatings Association ---
URL: https://www.paint.org/aca-advocacy/enhancing-chemical-security-and-cfats

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The American Coatings Association (ACA) webpage provides an update on the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program as of April 9, 2024. 

**Background:** CFATS was developed by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in November 2007 to prevent chemicals of interest from being stolen, diverted, sabotaged, or deliberately released by terrorists. Under the program, facilities possessing threshold amounts of specific explosive, toxic, or other chemicals of interest must submit a "top-screen" to DHS. DHS can then require a Security Vulnerability Assessment (SVA), which determines the facility's tier (Tiers 1-2 highest risk, Tiers 3-4 lowest). Tier assignment triggers a Site Security Plan (SSP) or Alternative Security Plan (ASP) requirement. As of July 2023, approximately 3,200 chemical facilities were covered under CFATS. The program's statutory authorization lapsed on July 27, 2023, after Congress allowed it to expire.

**ACA Action:** Many ACA member facilities are subject to CFATS, with a clear majority classified as Tier 4 and a few as Tier 3. ACA has strongly supported CFATS reauthorization. In July 2023, ACA sent letters to Congressional leadership urging immediate reauthorization. The U.S. House passed H.R. 4470 on a 409-1 vote to extend authorization for two years, but the companion Senate bill (S. 2499) did not advance, and a motion to consider the House bill was blocked in the Senate on July 26, 2023.

**After Expiration:** The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) suspended all enforcement and compliance assistance activities and suspended requirements for facilities to maintain site security plans and report chemicals of interest. CISA encouraged facilities to maintain security measures voluntarily and promoted its ChemLock initiative (a toolkit of on-site assessments, exercise packages, training, and guidance). Without reauthorization, chemical sector security now relies mainly on voluntary public-private partnerships. ACA is actively working with Congress, DHS, and trade associations to swiftly reinstate the program.

**ACA Staff Contacts:** Rhett Cash (Counsel, Government Affairs) and Heidi K. McAuliffe (Vice President, Government Affairs).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"CFATS provides a uniform, national program for regulating chemical security. Continuity of this framework provides the certainty required for the considerable planning and investment decisions that are needed to protect both our facilities and the surrounding communities. Allowing CFATS to expire would open the door for agencies with no anti-terrorism expertise to fill the void, or a patchwork of state and local regulations that may vary widely in scope and effectiveness. This could result in inconsistent anti-terrorism standards across the country and could undermine national security."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is an official CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency) webpage about the Chemical Facility Anti-Terrorism Standards (CFATS) program. The page contains archived content reflecting the program's status.

KEY STATUS ANNOUNCEMENT: As of July 28, 2023, Congress allowed the statutory authority for the CFATS program (6 CFR Part 27) to expire. CISA can no longer enforce compliance with CFATS regulations, require facilities to report chemicals of interest, perform inspections, provide compliance assistance, or require implementation of Site Security Plans or Alternative Security Programs. CISA encourages facilities to maintain security measures voluntarily through the ChemLock program, and if CFATS is reauthorized, CISA will follow up with facilities. Contact: CFATS@hq.dhs.gov.

IMPACTS OF THE LAPSE: The 3,200 facilities previously designated as high-risk, plus communities surrounding them (including 7,000 schools, colleges, and universities within one mile of these facilities) are affected. Specific impacts include: CISA cannot inspect high-risk sites (average 160 inspections per month going unscheduled); cannot conduct terrorist vetting on personnel (9,000 names per month going unvetted); cannot require cyber and physical security measures (facilities typically improved security posture by nearly 60% to comply); cannot identify new facilities with high-risk chemicals; more than one third of inspections turned up security gaps that can no longer be addressed; more than 90% of CFATS visits confirmed outreach with law enforcement and local fire departments. More than 89 million people in the United States live or work within two miles of a high-risk chemical facility.

PROGRAM OVERVIEW: CFATS was the nation's first regulatory program focused specifically on security at high-risk chemical facilities. Managed by CISA, it identifies and regulates high-risk facilities to reduce risk that dangerous chemicals are weaponized by terrorists. A chemical facility is any establishment or individual possessing or planning to possess any of the more than 300 chemicals of interest (COI) in Appendix A at or above the screening threshold quantity (STQ) and concentration. Facilities must report via an online survey (Top-Screen). The regulation applies to chemical manufacturing, storage/distribution, energy/utilities, agriculture/food, explosives, mining, electronics, plastics, colleges/universities, laboratories, paint/coatings, and healthcare/pharmaceuticals.

--- SOURCE 18: U.S. Congress Passes Cyber Incident and Ransom Payment Reporting Requirement ---
URL: https://www.mofo.com/resources/insights/220311-cyber-incident-ransom-payment-reporting

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This client alert from Morrison & Foerster (MoFo), dated March 11, 2022, reports on the Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act of 2022, enacted by the U.S. Congress on March 10, 2022, and included in the $1.5 trillion government funding bill. The Act requires critical infrastructure entities ("covered entities") to report cyber incidents to the Department of Homeland Security's Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) within 72 hours and to report ransom payments in response to ransomware attacks within 24 hours. The Act is headed to the President's desk for signature, though key provisions—including the precise scope of covered entities and types of reportable incidents—will be further defined through CISA regulations.

Key reporting requirements: Covered entities must report a "covered cyber incident" to CISA within 72 hours after reasonably believing the incident occurred, and ransom payments within 24 hours of payment. Updates are required if new information becomes available or if a ransom payment is subsequently made. Reporting entities must preserve data relevant to the incident or payment. A "covered entity" may include entities in the 16 critical infrastructure sectors defined by Presidential Policy Directive 21, considering consequences to national security, economic security, or public health and safety. A "covered cyber incident" includes substantial incidents causing substantial loss of confidentiality, integrity, or availability of information systems, disruption of business operations, or unauthorized access or disruption caused by compromise of a cloud service provider, managed service provider, or supply chain compromise.

The Act includes "carrot and stick" enforcement provisions: CISA may issue requests for information and subpoenas to non-compliant entities (information from subpoenas may be shared with DOJ and other agencies for enforcement or criminal prosecution, while proactively shared information has limited use). It also includes protections for reported information, including liability protection, privacy and civil liberties protections, FOIA exemption, and restrictions on reports being used as evidence in proceedings.

The Act centralizes CISA's role by establishing: (1) a Cyber Incident Review Center as a central clearinghouse for incident reporting, publishing quarterly public reports and providing monthly threat assessments to Congress; (2) a Ransomware Vulnerability Warning Pilot Program to identify systems vulnerable to common ransomware attacks and notify owners; and (3) a Joint Ransomware Task Force to coordinate campaigns against ransomware actors, including disrupting actors, maintaining a list of highest-threat entities, and creating after-action reports.

Report content requirements include descriptions of the incident, affected information systems, unauthorized access, date ranges, impact to operations, categories of information accessed, ransom payment details (date, demand, currency/commodity, instructions, amount), vulnerabilities exploited and TTPs used, actor identification information, and reporting entity contact information including taxpayer identification number.
</summary>

The Privacy Rights Clearinghouse published the "Data Breach Notification Laws: A 50-State Survey (2026 Edition)" on January 28, 2026. This comprehensive survey analyzes and compares data breach notification laws across all 50 U.S. states plus the District of Columbia, reflecting statutes enacted as of January 1, 2026. The survey uses a standardized framework of 50 questions applied to 51 jurisdictions, examining notification timing, covered data types, notification recipients, enforcement mechanisms, and consumer remedies. A full PDF report (4.45 MB) and an interactive map are available for state-by-state analysis and comparison.

- Notification Timing: 20 states (39%) specify numeric deadlines ranging from 30 to 60 days. - Consumer Remedies: 24 states (47%) provide a private right of action for breach notification violations; 6 states (12%) require free credit monitoring for affected consumers.

--- SOURCE 22: Data Breach Notification Laws by State (2026) | Deadlines & AG Thresholds | CyberRiskPolicy.com ---
URL: http://cyberriskpolicy.com/data-breach-notification-laws.html

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from CyberRiskPolicy.com provides a comprehensive plain-language reference guide to U.S. state and federal data breach notification laws, reviewed by C. Constantin Poindexter (CPCU, JD, MA, AFSB), an insurance/surety underwriting specialist since 1994, with statutes current as of early 2026.

Key points covered:

1. **Universal coverage**: All 50 states plus DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, and the U.S. Virgin Islands now have data breach notification laws. Alabama and South Dakota were the last to adopt them in 2018, completing the patchwork.

2. **Deadlines**: Roughly 20 states set a numeric deadline of 30 to 60 days to notify affected individuals; the rest require notice "without unreasonable delay." For multi-state breaches, the strictest applicable clock governs. States with 30-day deadlines include California, Colorado, Florida, Maine, New Jersey, and Washington. States with 45-day deadlines include Alabama, Arizona, Indiana, Maryland, New Mexico, Ohio, Oregon, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Vermont, and Wisconsin. States with 60-day deadlines include Connecticut, Delaware, Louisiana, South Dakota, and Texas.

3. **Three notification audiences**: (a) Affected individuals (required in every state), (b) state attorneys general (required in ~36 states once a resident-count threshold is crossed, commonly 250, 500, or 1,000), and (c) consumer reporting agencies (typically required at 1,000+ residents per FACTA).

4. **Attorney-general thresholds**: Texas triggers at 250+ residents (within 30 days, filed to a public breach portal); California at 500+ (within 15 days of individual notice per SB 446, 2026); Colorado at 500+ (with individual notice); Oklahoma at 500+ (within 60 days of individual notice per SB 626, 2026); Indiana at 500+ (without unreasonable delay). In states like Texas, AG filings become searchable public records.

5. **Definition of personal information**: Every state covers name plus at least one of: SSN, driver's license/state-ID number, or financial account/payment-card number. Growing states expand coverage to medical/health info, biometrics, online credentials, and government-issued identifiers. Some states apply a risk-of-harm analysis.

6. **Substitute notice**: Allowed when direct contact isn't feasible (contact info unavailable, cost exceeds statutory ceiling commonly $50,000–$100,000, or very large affected populations) — a website posting plus statewide media notice.

7. **Federal overlays**: HIPAA/HITECH (health sector, notify HHS, media notice for 500+ in a state), GLBA (financial institutions), SEC Reg S-P (broker-dealers/investment companies), SEC public-company rule (Form 8-K disclosure within 4 business days of materiality), and CIRCIA (critical infrastructure — report to CISA within 72 hours, ransom payments within 24 hours; final rule pending 2026).

8. **2026 changes**: California's SB 446 (effective Jan 1, 2026) replaced "without unreasonable delay" with a hard 30-calendar-day deadline and requires AG notice within 15 days for 500+ affected Californians. Oklahoma's SB 626 expanded covered data to biometrics and government IDs and added AG notification for 500+ residents. Both track a trend toward shorter clocks and broader data definitions.

9. **Cyber insurance role**: Breach-response coverage funds the breach coach (privacy counsel), notification and call-center costs, credit monitoring/identity protection, and regulatory defense. Coverage is as much about the expert response team engaged at hour zero as the dollars.

10. **Frequently asked questions**: Confirms all 50 states require breach notification; deadlines vary by state (30–60 days fixed or "without unreasonable delay"); AG notification triggers at 250, 500, or 1,000 residents depending on state.

The page includes a disclaimer that it is plain-language reference material, not legal advice, and recommends verifying current statutes with qualified counsel and authoritative trackers like the IAPP state chart. It also promotes CyberRiskPolicy.com's cyber insurance offerings, including a downloadable coverage application and contact at (800) 373-2804.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 23: California tightens data breach notification timelines, imposes 30-day notice requirement | Data Protection Report ---
URL: https://www.dataprotectionreport.com/2025/11/california-tightens-data-breach-notification-timelines-imposes-30-day-notice-requirement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
California has signed into law Senate Bill No. 446, amending Section 1798.82 of its Civil Code (its data breach notification law) to require covered companies to notify affected California residents within 30 calendar days of discovery of a data breach. The amendment takes effect January 1, 2026.

Key points of the amendment:
- Replaces California's previous flexible "most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay" standard with a specific 30-day deadline.
- California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002, and as a leading privacy regulator, this move may prompt more states to adopt firm notice timelines.
- Several states already impose specific notice timeframes: New York (30 days), Texas (30 days), Colorado (30 days), Florida (30 days), and Delaware (60 days). Some states require notice to the attorney general simultaneously with or prior to notice to individuals—more stringent than California's requirement to notify the attorney general within 15 days of notice to individuals.
- In practice, many businesses make regulatory notices close in time to individual notices to address differing state obligations.

The authors (Annmarie Giblin and Susana Medeiros) offer a critical "take" on the change: shorter notice timelines do not necessarily improve notification outcomes. Even weeks after discovery, breach victims may not know the scope of impact, affected data types, or geographic residence of individuals—even with considerable investigative resources. While many state laws (including California's as amended) exempt disclosure where necessary to determine breach scope, this view is not universal. For example, the Connecticut Attorney General has clarified that Connecticut's 60-day notice requirement "runs from the date that a company becomes aware of suspicious activity, not the date it determines the full impact to personal information."

Companies in highly regulated sectors (critical infrastructure, insurance, banking) often face even shorter notice periods—as short as 72 hours—and regulators have fined companies for untimely reporting. The article advises companies to assess and update their incident response procedures, particularly for larger and more complex incidents, to meet shorter disclosure expectations.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"California was the first state to enact a data breach notification law in 2002 and since then, Section 1798.82 has required businesses and state agencies to notify individuals 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.' SB 446 replaces this flexible, reasonableness standard with a specific 30‑day deadline."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a legal alert from Pillsbury Law (by Mark L. Krotoski and Alexandria Marx, dated October 31, 2025) announcing that California Governor Gavin Newsom signed Senate Bill No. 446 into law on October 3, 2025, making significant changes to California's data breach notification statute, effective January 1, 2026. The law passed with no votes in opposition.

Key changes:
1. Businesses and government agencies must notify affected California residents "within 30 calendar days of discovery or notification of the data breach" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(a)(2)), joining five other states with 30-day deadlines (Colorado, Florida, Maine, New York, Washington). Previously, California required notification "in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay."
2. Two exceptions permit delayed notification: (1) to accommodate legitimate needs of law enforcement, or (2) as necessary to determine the scope of the breach and restore reasonable integrity of the data system.
3. If a breach affects more than 500 California residents, a sample copy of the consumer notification must be provided to the California Attorney General "within 15 days of notifying affected consumers" (Cal. Civil Code § 1798.82(f)). Previously, no deadline existed for this notice.

Background context: California was the first state to enact a data breach notification statute in 2002. Since then, all 50 states and four U.S. jurisdictions (DC, Puerto Rico, Guam, Virgin Islands) have enacted their own requirements. Thirty other states have a similar "most expedient time possible" standard.

The statute retains California's unique "model security breach notification form" with headings including "What Happened?", "What Information Was Involved?", "What We Are Doing", "What You Can Do", and "For More Information."

Cost/risk data: According to the IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025, average breach costs in the U.S. reached a record $10.22 million, a 9% increase over the prior year. A survey of 220+ cases from 2020-2024 found over 90% of data breach enforcement actions were brought collaboratively as multistate efforts. Examples of enforcement penalties include a $2 million NYDFS fine for failure to notify within 72 hours of a cybersecurity event, a $795,000 Massachusetts AG fine for delayed notifications, and a $6.75 million California AG fine against a software company for misleading the public about a breach.

Senator Melissa Hurtado (SB 446 author) stated the law closes a loophole because affected individuals "may not be informed for months—or even a year or more later—delaying their ability to take preventive measures."

Next steps for businesses: update incident response plans for the new timelines, review contracts with third-party service providers for timely cyber incident reporting, and obtain legal guidance on notification sufficiency and accuracy.
