--- SOURCE 4: OFAC’s Updated Advisory on Ransomware Payments ---
URL: https://www.hunton.com/insights/legal/ofacs-updated-advisory-on-ransomware-payments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the US Treasury Department's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments" warning companies about ongoing sanctions risks for making or facilitating ransomware payments. OFAC also designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O., a Russia-based virtual currency exchange, as a blocked person for facilitating financial transactions for sanctioned ransomware threat actors.

The Updated Advisory signals the US government's continued focus on: discouraging ransomware victims from making ransom payments (particularly where there is a sanctions nexus); discouraging financial institutions, negotiators, and insurance companies from facilitating ransom payments; encouraging risk-based compliance programs; and encouraging victims to report cyberattacks to law enforcement promptly and cooperate with investigations.

Key background and facts include: ransomware attacks increased during the COVID-19 pandemic, with "a nearly 21 percent increase in reported ransomware cases and a 225 percent increase in associated losses from 2019 to 2020." Over 40% of SUEX's known transaction history was associated with illicit actors, and it processed transactions for at least eight different ransomware variants. The advisory notes that virtual currency exchanges "are critical to the profitability of ransomware attacks."

Under US sanctions programs, violations are based on strict liability, meaning US persons may be held liable even without knowing they transacted with a blocked person. OFAC reinforced that it will bring enforcement actions against third-party intermediaries (financial institutions, incident response consultants, and cyber insurance companies) that negotiate or facilitate payments to sanctioned actors, and signaled such parties should consider FinCEN reporting obligations.

OFAC's mitigating factors for enforcement responses include: the existence and adequacy of the victim's sanctions compliance program; whether the victim followed CISA's suggestions (offline backups, incident response plans, employee training); whether the victim promptly and voluntarily turned over information including attack details and ransom amounts; and whether the victim demonstrated "full and ongoing cooperation" with law enforcement. Victims taking these steps are more likely to receive non-public responses (No-Action or Cautionary Letters) rather than public penalties.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"there was a nearly 21 percent increase in reported ransomware cases and a 225 percent increase in associated losses from 2019 to 2020."
</key_excerpts>

The U.S. Department of the Treasury homepage serves as the central navigation portal for all Treasury operations, including bureaus (IRS, BEP, U.S. Mint, OCC, FinCEN, TTB, BFS, and various Inspectors General), offices (Domestic Finance, Economic Policy, Tax Policy, International Affairs, Terrorism and Financial Intelligence), and policy areas covering tax policy, economic policy, terrorism and illicit finance, financing the government, financial markets, and international affairs.

--- SOURCE 6: United States Sanctions Affiliates of Russia-Based LockBit Ransomware Group | U.S. Department of the Treasury ---
URL: https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/jy2114

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is the official U.S. Department of the Treasury website (treasury.gov). The page consists of two main components: the department's comprehensive navigation structure and a featured press release announcing new sanctions.

The website navigation provides access to the Treasury's organizational structure, including its General Information section, Offices (Domestic Finance, Economic Policy, General Counsel, International Affairs, Management, Public Affairs, Tax Policy, Terrorism and Financial Intelligence), and Bureaus. The Treasury's bureaus include: Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB), Bureau of Engraving & Printing (BEP), Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN), Bureau of the Fiscal Service (BFS), Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), U.S. Mint, Office of Inspector General (OIG), Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration (TIGTA), and Special Inspector General for Pandemic Recovery (SIGPR). Key details of the sanctions announcement:

• The U.S. designated two LockBit affiliates: Ivan Gennadievich Kondratiev (a Russian national from Novomoskovsk, Russia, known as "Bassterlord" and "Fisheye," leader of the National Hazard Society affiliate sub-group, with ties to REvil, RansomEXX, and Avaddon groups) and Artur Sungatov (a Russian national and LockBit affiliate).

• The page includes information on OFAC's sanctions removal process (FAQ 897) and advisories on ransomware payment sanctions risks and virtual currency compliance.

<key_excerpts>
"The United States will not tolerate attempts to extort and steal from our citizens and institutions... We will continue our whole-of-government approach to defend against malicious cyber activities, and will use all available tools to hold the actors that enable these threats accountable," said Deputy Secretary of the Treasury Wally Adeyemo. OFAC is designating each of these individuals pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 13694, as amended by E.O. 13757, for being responsible for or complicit in, or having engaged in, directly or indirectly, an activity described in subsection (a)(ii)(D) of section 1 of E.O. 13694, as amended. As a result of today's action, all property and interests in property of the designated persons described above that are in the United States or in the possession or control of U.S. persons are blocked and must be reported to OFAC. --- SOURCE 7: OFAC Sanctions and Ransomware Payments: US Legal Obligations ---
URL: https://ransomwareauthority.com/ofac-ransomware-sanctions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage (from RansomwareAuthority, part of the Authority Network America network) explains the US legal obligations surrounding OFAC sanctions and ransomware payments. It details how the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) imposes strict prohibitions on financial transactions with sanctioned individuals/entities, which directly apply to ransom payments when the recipient threat actor is designated under US sanctions law.

KEY DEFINITIONS & AUTHORITY: OFAC operates within the US Treasury Department, deriving authority from IEEPA (50 U.S.C. §§ 1701–1708) and the Trading with the Enemy Act. It maintains the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List. The relevant guidance is the "Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," first issued October 1, 2020, and updated September 21, 2021. Designated ransomware actors include Evil Corp (Dec 2019), Lazarus Group (Sept 2019 under EO 13722 and 13694), and Chatex (Nov 2021).

ENFORCEMENT MECHANICS: OFAC applies a strict liability standard — US persons (including US-incorporated companies and foreign branches of US entities) may be liable even without knowledge the counterparty was sanctioned, distinguishing it from criminal law's mens rea requirement. Designation follows a four-step pathway: identification, designation (under EO 13694, EO 13757, or EO 13722), publication in the Federal Register (constructively notifying all US persons), and blocking of property (31 C.F.R. § 501.603). Civil penalties reach $356,579 per violation or twice the transaction value; criminal penalties reach $1 million and 20 years imprisonment (50 U.S.C. § 1705(c)).

DRIVERS: The intensified intersection since 2019 stems from (1) state-sponsored actor designation (Lazarus Group attributed to North Korea, linked to WannaCry); (2) cryptocurrency traceability (e.g., the 2022 Tornado Cash designation showing mixing infrastructure can be designated); and (3) proliferation of cyber-specific executive orders enabling designation of purely criminal groups.

CLASSIFICATION BOUNDARIES: Distinguishes designated vs. non-designated actors, US vs. non-US persons, direct vs. facilitated payment (insurers, DFIR firms, and exchanges can incur independent liability), and full blocking vs. sanctions risk (including the OFAC 50 Percent Rule for indirect ownership).

TRADEOFFS: Documents conflict between compliance and operational survival — OFAC has no general necessity exception, and license applications operate on timelines incompatible with typical 72-hour-to-7-day payment deadlines. The FBI discourages payment while CISA focuses on pre-incident resilience. The Lloyd's Market Association Bulletin Y5258 (2021) flagged sanctions compliance as material for cyber insurers.

COMMON MISCONCEPTIONS: Cryptocurrency exchanges don't eliminate OFAC risk; only the direct payer isn't at risk (facilitators are too); good-faith victims still face liability (cooperation is only mitigating); unknown actors still carry strict liability risk.

PROCEDURAL CHECKLIST (non-advisory): Phase 1 — identify attacker attribution and cross-reference wallet addresses against the SDN list and FBI/CISA advisories; Phase 2 — engage legal counsel, confirm insurance screening, document steps; Phase 3 — assess OFAC licensing needs, submit license applications, notify IC3 and CISA; Phase 4 — self-disclose to OFAC, file SARs with FinCEN if covered, preserve records 5+ years per 31 C.F.R. § 501.601. The page includes extensive citations to OFAC advisories, regulations, and federal resources.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"OFAC imposes strict legal prohibitions on financial transactions with sanctioned individuals, entities, and jurisdictions — prohibitions that apply directly to ransomware payments when the recipient threat actor or group has been designated under US sanctions law."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 8: OFAC Issues Updated Guidance on Ransomware Payments | Inside Privacy ---
URL: https://www.insideprivacy.com/cybersecurity-2/ofac-issues-updated-guidance-on-ransomware-payments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," which updates and supersedes a previous advisory from October 1, 2020. The Updated Advisory is directed at organizations victimized by ransomware attacks, as well as financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and forensic and incident-response firms assisting those victims.

The advisory reiterates the U.S. government's strong opposition to ransomware payments, emphasizing that making or facilitating such payments may violate U.S. sanctions prohibitions. It notes that penalties may be imposed on a strict liability basis, meaning companies could face enforcement even if they had no knowledge the payment would violate sanctions. However, the Updated Advisory adds important new guidance on mitigating factors, including:

1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices—such as those highlighted in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide—will be considered a "significant mitigating factor" in any OFAC enforcement response. This establishes a ransomware-specific mitigating factor not previously set forth in OFAC's Economic Sanctions Enforcement Guidelines.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Benefits Insights blog post from Bricker law firm, authored by Jamie Scott, discussing a significant HIPAA enforcement action. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) announced a $2.4 million settlement with Memorial Hermann Health System (MHHS) for improperly disclosing the name of a single patient.

Background of the case: A Mexican immigrant presented a fake Texas driver's license at an MHHS clinic. Staff reported the incident, and the patient was detained and arrested. In response to protests claiming medical facilities should be a "safe zone" for immigrants, MHHS issued a press release to media outlets explaining its actions, which included the patient's name. MHHS assumed that since the patient's name was publicly available in police records and had been widely published in other media reports, it was acceptable to include the name in its press release—but this assumption was incorrect.

Key legal takeaways: While disclosure of PHI to law enforcement is generally permitted, there is no exception for disclosing a patient's name to the public, even for purposes of correcting the record or defending the covered entity from negative publicity. The case is similar to a 2013 settlement with Shasta Regional Medical Center, which had provided patient PHI to the media to refute Medicare fraud allegations and paid $275,000. The primary lesson is that HIPAA does not allow a covered entity to defend itself in the media using PHI, even if that PHI is already in the public domain and is being used against the covered entity.

Notably, this settlement is unusual because prior large HIPAA settlements typically involved disclosures of hundreds or thousands of patient records, whereas this case involved the disclosure of a single patient's name.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Goodwin's Data, Privacy + Cybersecurity Insights blog (dated November 18, 2022) analyzes the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) escalation and expansion of cybersecurity enforcement under Part 500 of the New York Cybersecurity Regulation.

KEY EVENT: On October 18, 2022, NYDFS announced its sixth consent order for alleged Part 500 violations, imposing a $4.5 million fine on EyeMed Vision Care, LLC — one of the heftiest monetary penalties yet. This came just over two weeks before NYDFS released its official Proposed Amendments to Part 500, which would impose even more stringent requirements on covered entities.

HISTORY OF ENFORCEMENT: NYDFS did not enforce Part 500 (promulgated March 2017) vigorously initially. Its first action came July 22, 2020, against First American Title Insurance Company (alleging failure to remedy a vulnerability exposing millions of customers' data; the company challenged findings, case pending). In 2021, NYDFS entered three consent orders with fines ranging $1.5–$3 million. In 2022, three additional consent orders were entered against Carnival Corporation, Robinhood Crypto LLC, and EyeMed. Most recent actions imposed $4.5–$5 million penalties. Robinhood was an outlier: developed from a supervisory examination rather than a security incident, imposing a $30 million penalty for violations of Virtual Currency Regulation (Part 200), Money Transmitter Regulation (Part 417), and Transaction Monitoring Regulation (Part 504), in addition to Part 500.

CRITICAL ENFORCEMENT AREAS UNDER CURRENT REGULATION:
• MFA (Section 500.12(b)): top priority; all consent orders address failure to comply. Carnival's entity Princess Cruise Lines had not completed MFA rollout to Office 365 — showing companies may be held strictly liable for MFA violations affecting even a limited number of entities.
• Employee training (500.14): Carnival penalized; repetition of phishing incidents "within a period of less than four years, demonstrates that the Carnival Companies' training was inadequate."
• Risk assessments (500.02(b)): cited in Robinhood and EyeMed consent orders.
• New attention areas: EyeMed failed to limit user access privileges (nine employees shared credentials for one email account) violating 500.03 and 500.13; Robinhood depended on parent company's cybersecurity regime rather than ensuring its own tailored policies.

KEY PROPOSED CHANGES:
• "Class A Companies" — new subset of covered entities defined as those with $20M+ gross annual revenue in each of last two fiscal years with 2,000+ employees, or making $1B+ gross revenue annually. These face more onerous requirements: annual independent audit of cybersecurity programs, external experts for risk assessments every three years, and privileged access activity monitoring.
• Notification changes: two new scenarios triggering 72-hour notification (unauthorized access to a privileged account; ransomware deployed within a material part of the information system). New 24-hour notification when a ransomware payment is made, with explanation of necessity and alternatives considered.
• Annual certification: new alternative allowing written acknowledgment of non-compliance, requiring description of noncompliance areas and remedial plans with timelines — theoretically preventing multiple charges for the same infraction.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This document is a formal Statement of Charges and Notice of Hearing issued by the New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) against First American Title Insurance Company, dated July 21, 2020, with the hearing scheduled for October 26, 2020. The charges stem from a massive data security breach involving First American's EaglePro document-sharing application and its FAST document repository.

**Overview of the Breach:**
- From at least October 2014 through May 2019, First American exposed tens of millions of documents containing consumers' sensitive personal information—including bank account numbers and statements, mortgage and tax records, Social Security numbers, wire transaction receipts, and drivers' license images—through a known vulnerability on its public-facing website.
- The vulnerability was introduced during an application software update in May 2014 and went undetected for years. Due to the use of sequentially numbered ImageDocumentIDs in URLs with no expiration dates, anyone could manipulate a URL by one or more digits to access any of the 850+ million documents stored in FAST without any login or authentication.
- The vulnerability was discovered during a penetration test in December 2018, but First American failed to remediate it for six more months until cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs publicized the breach on May 24, 2019.

**Key Data Points:**
- FAST contained approximately 753 million documents in April 2018 (65 million tagged as containing NPI) and over 850 million documents by May 2019.
- A random sampling of 1,000 untagged documents showed 30% also contained NPI.
- More than 350,000 documents were accessed without authorization by automated "bots" or "scraper" programs during an 11-month period from June 2018 to May 2019.
- Brian Krebs revealed that 885 million documents dating back to 2003 were exposed, and he was easily able to view sensitive data including Social Security numbers, drivers' licenses, and tax and banking information.

**Failures Identified by DFS:**
1. The vulnerability was erroneously classified as "medium severity" based on the mistaken belief that EaglePro could not transmit NPI.
2. First American failed to follow its own cybersecurity policies—no security overview or risk assessment was performed for EaglePro.
3. The Cyber Defense Team reviewed only 10 of hundreds of millions of exposed documents, found no NPI in those 10, and failed to recognize the seriousness of the situation.
4. The director of the Cyber Defense Team accidentally re-classified the vulnerability from "medium" to "low" severity in January 2019, which incorrectly allowed 90 days for remediation.
5. Remediation was assigned to a new, unqualified employee who never received the penetration test report.
6. First American relied solely on a manual process where title agents added the "SEC" prefix to files containing NPI—a process acknowledged as "highly prone to error."
7. After the breach was publicized, information security personnel's recommendations to add authentication and technical controls were rejected by senior management.
8. First American failed to timely encrypt documents containing NPI as required by the Cybersecurity Regulation.

**Six Formal Charges (Violations of 23 NYCRR Part 500):**
- **Charge I (500.02):** Failure to maintain a cybersecurity program based on risk assessment; no risk assessments for FAST and EaglePro applications (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge II (500.03):** Failure to maintain and implement written cybersecurity policies, including inadequate data governance, classification, and access controls (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge III (500.07):** Failure to limit user access privileges to Information Systems providing access to NPI (violation period: March 1, 2017 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge IV (500.09):** Failure to conduct periodic, documented Risk Assessments sufficient to inform the cybersecurity program (violation period: March 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge V (500.14(b)):** Failure to provide adequate cybersecurity awareness training for employees and title agents (violation period: March 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).
- **Charge VI (500.15):** Failure to encrypt NPI at rest and in transit or implement approved compensating controls (violation period: September 1, 2018 – May 24, 2019).

DFS is seeking civil monetary penalties under Financial Services Law Section 408, an order requiring remediation of the violations, and other just and appropriate relief. The charges were signed by Katherine A. Lemire (Executive Deputy Superintendent, Consumer Protection and Financial Enforcement) and Justin S. Herring (Executive Deputy Superintendent, Cybersecurity Division).
</summary>

URL: https://secureframe.com/blog/nydfs-nycrr-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Secureframe provides a comprehensive guide to the NYDFS NYCRR 500 Cybersecurity Regulation and a compliance checklist for 2024. The regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), first issued in March 2017, establishes cybersecurity requirements for all covered financial institutions in New York. Significant amendments were announced in November 2023 with an effective date of April 29, 2024.

**Who Must Comply:** NYDFS NYCRR 500 applies to all DFS-regulated entities including state-chartered banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, insurance companies, health insurers, money transmitters, and other financial services institutions. The regulation designates three company types:
- **Covered entities:** All DFS-regulated organizations
- **Class A companies:** Introduced in the 2023 amendments; entities with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue in each of the last two fiscal years AND either at least 2,000 employees (averaged over two years) or over $1 billion in gross annual revenue. These face additional obligations including independent audits and stronger monitoring.
- **Small businesses:** Qualify for limited exemption (Section 500.19) if combined affiliates have fewer than 20 employees, less than $7.5 million in annual gross revenue in each of the last three years, or less than $15 million in year-end total assets.

**Key Requirements:**
- Periodic risk assessments
- Cybersecurity program with policies including Information Security, Access Control, Business Continuity/Disaster Recovery, Incident Response (now requiring root cause analysis), Data Retention/Disposal, Third-Party Service Provider Security, Asset Inventory, and Vulnerability Management policies
- Appointment of qualified cybersecurity leadership (senior governing body and CISO)
- Technical controls: multi-factor authentication, encryption (compensating controls no longer allowed for encryption in transit over external networks), systems/network security, application security, physical/environmental controls, data privacy controls, and security awareness training
- Continuous monitoring with annual penetration testing (now required from both inside and outside systems) and bi-annual vulnerability assessments
- Audit trail systems with records kept minimum five years
- 72-hour notification to NYDFS of cybersecurity events reasonably likely to impact operations, plus new reporting of third-party incidents and extortion payments

**Certification:** Covered entities submit an annual Certificate of Compliance (typically April 15, pushed to April 29, 2024 this year). Class A companies must undergo annual independent compliance audits. Documentation must be kept for five years.

**Enforcement:** NYDFS monitors through self-certification, audits, and mandatory reporting. Historical penalties include Robinhood Crypto ($30 million), OneMain Financial Group ($4.25 million), Residential Mortgage Services ($1.5 million), SA Stone Wealth Management ($1.35 million), and First American Title Insurance Company ($1 million). The 2023 amendment reaffirmed that even a single act of non-compliance could constitute a violation.

The article also promotes Secureframe's compliance automation platform with features like AI-driven risk management, policy generation, continuous monitoring, vendor management, cross-mapping controls, regulatory change management, and security training.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The NYDFS NYCRR 500 regulation is a cornerstone for cybersecurity in the New York financial sector, establishing some of the highest standards for information security regulations in the US."

This document is an SEC administrative cease-and-desist Order (Release No. 92176, June 14, 2021, File No. 3-20367) against First American Financial Corporation, a Delaware corporation headquartered in Santa Ana, California, that provides title insurance and escrow services for real estate transactions.

**Background and Violation:** In May 2019, a cybersecurity journalist notified First American that its "EaglePro" application (used to transmit title and escrow document images) had a vulnerability exposing over 800 million document images dating back to 2003, including sensitive personal data such as social security numbers and financial information. First American issued a press statement on May 24, 2019, and furnished a Form 8-K on May 28, 2019.

**Key Findings:**
- The EaglePro vulnerability, which existed since 2014, allowed users to alter digits in URLs to access other document images without authorization; some documents were also cached on public search engines.
- First American's information security personnel identified the vulnerability in a January 11, 2019 manual penetration test report (the "January 2019 Report"), which found a "serious" or level "3" vulnerability allowing "[a]ccess to PDF's and OrderDetails without authentication."

- As of May 24, 2019, First American had no disclosure controls and procedures related to cybersecurity.

**Violation and Sanctions:**
- First American violated Exchange Act Rule 13a-15(a) (17 C.F.R. § 240.13a-15), which requires issuers to maintain disclosure controls and procedures.
- The Order requires First American to cease and desist from future violations of Rule 13a-15 and pay a civil money penalty of $487,616 to the SEC within 14 days. First American consented to the Order without admitting or denying the findings, except as to the Commission's jurisdiction.

Key facts of the case:

Legal analysts have criticized the action as an overreach:

--- SOURCE 16: Key Takeaways from Recent SEC Cybersecurity Enforcement Actions ---
URL: https://corpgov.law.harvard.edu/2024/10/29/key-takeaways-from-recent-sec-cybersecurity-enforcement-actions

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a Harvard Law School Forum on Corporate Governance post (dated October 29, 2024) analyzing the SEC's recent cybersecurity disclosure enforcement settlements against four companies affected by the SolarWinds Orion network monitoring software compromise. The article was written by Jennifer Lee, Shoba Pillay, and H. Kurt von Moltke of Jenner & Block LLP, based on a firm memorandum.

BACKGROUND: In 2023, the SEC brought fraud charges against SolarWinds and its CISO in connection with the Orion compromise. The SEC's latest actions targeted four companies that used the compromised software and then allegedly minimized the cybersecurity incident in their public disclosures.

THE FOUR SETTLEMENTS (in descending order of penalties):
1. UNISYS ($4,000,000 penalty) - Post-incident Form 10-K disclosures described cybersecurity risks as "hypothetical" despite knowing it had experienced two SolarWinds-related intrusions starting January 2020. The company compromised at least seven network credentials and 34 cloud-based accounts, with 23 gigabytes of data transferred. Unisys failed to maintain adequate disclosure controls and procedures.
2. AVAYA ($1,000,000 penalty) - Form 10-Q disclosure (February 2021) stated a threat actor accessed a limited number of company emails, omitting that the attacker had accessed at least 145 files containing confidential/proprietary information including third-party application passwords, internal security procedures, remote access instructions, and product configuration information.
3. CHECK POINT ($995,000 penalty) - Form 20-F disclosures (April 2022) described cyber risks in generic terms despite knowledge of the Orion compromise affecting two corporate accounts with attempted lateral movement. Disclosures were "virtually unchanged" and not tailored to the company's specific risks.
4. MIMECAST ($990,000 penalty) - Form 8-K disclosures (January and March 2021) failed to disclose the nature of exfiltrated code and quantity of encrypted credentials accessed. The threat actor exfiltrated an authentication certificate used by ~10% of customers, compromised five customers' cloud platforms, and accessed encrypted credentials for ~31,000 customers and server configuration data for ~17,000 customers.

All four companies settled to negligence-based charges under Sections 17(a)(2) and 17(a)(3) of the Securities Act of 1933 and Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act of 1934, with various associated rules (12b-20, 13a-1, 13a-11, 13a-13, 13a-15(a)).

DISSENT: Commissioners Hester M. Peirce and Mark T. Uyeda issued a dissenting statement criticizing the settlements, noting the companies were victims of a cyberattack ("one of the most widespread and sophisticated hacking campaigns ever conducted against the federal government and the private sector"). They accused the SEC of "playing Monday morning quarterback" and questioned the materiality of threat actor identity and specific percentages of data accessed. They also noted the SolarWinds motion-to-dismiss ruling rejected the SEC's position that risk factor disclosures must be updated after major incidents.

KEY TAKEAWAYS:
1. Cybersecurity remains an SEC enforcement priority despite mixed results in the SolarWinds litigation.
2. The SEC reinforces the importance of disclosure and escalation procedures after major incidents—companies cannot issue generic risk factor disclosures or minimize incidents once they know they are severe.
3. The SEC is aggressive in seeking negligence-based fraud charges and significant penalties despite cooperation and remediation, but the enforcement landscape is uncertain given the dissenting statement and potential changes in administration.

The article concludes that public companies face considerable challenges in making disclosure decisions in an aggressive enforcement environment and should be prepared with incident response and disclosure policies before a major incident occurs.
</summary>

The settlements charged violations under Sections 17(a)(2) and 17(a)(3) of the Securities Act of 1933 on a no-admit, no-deny basis, along with periodic reporting requirements under Section 13(a) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 and related rules.

Key details per company:
- **Unisys ($4 million penalty)**: Compromises spanned 16 months, accessing network credentials, cloud-based accounts, 27,000 emails, 130 shared files, and 7GB of data exfiltrated. Filed two annual reports framing risks as hypothetical despite knowledge of the compromise and an additional ransomware incident. Lacked effective escalation controls.
- **Avaya ($1 million penalty)**: A single Form 10-Q failed to disclose likely nation-state attribution, unmonitored presence of the threat actor, and access to shared files with confidential information.
- **Check Point ($995,000 penalty)**: Two Forms 20-F contained nearly identical disclosures as prior filings, omitting new material cyber risks resulting from the compromise.
- **Mimecast ($990,000 penalty)**: Forms 8-K failed to disclose the number of customers whose credentials were accessed and the nature and significance of exfiltrated source code.

Commissioners Hester M. Peirce and Mark T. Uyeda dissented, criticizing the Commission for "Monday morning quarterback" hindsight review of the disclosures and disputing the materiality of omitted information. They also noted that allegations regarding cybersecurity risk disclosures in the pending SEC enforcement action against SolarWinds were dismissed by the district court.

These are the first cybersecurity-related settlements of the SEC's new fiscal year, following prior actions against R.R. Donnelley (previous fiscal year) and SolarWinds (2023, significantly cut back by district court). The actions signal that disclosures under the SEC's new cyber incident disclosure rules (effective December 2023) will bear exacting scrutiny, particularly around breach detail levels and accuracy of accompanying risk disclosures. The alert warns issuers to carefully consider when and how to disclose material cybersecurity incidents and to implement and maintain related disclosure controls.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The common theme across the four proceedings is the Commission playing Monday morning quarterback. Rather than focusing on whether the companies' disclosure provided material information to investors, the Commission engages in a hindsight review to second-guess the disclosure and cites immaterial, undisclosed details to support its charges." – Dissent by Commissioners Peirce and Uyeda
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 18: The SEC Settles Enforcement Actions with Four Companies for Cyber Disclosure Failures | Willkie Compliance Concourse ---
URL: https://complianceconcourse.willkie.com/articles/the-sec-settles-enforcement-actions-with-four-companies-for-cyber-disclosure-failures

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On October 22, 2024, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) announced settled enforcement actions against four public companies (Unisys, Mimecast, Check Point, and Avaya) for making materially misleading cybersecurity disclosures related to the SolarWinds Orion software compromise. The SEC found that a likely nation-state threat actor accessed these companies' systems, and each company negligently minimized the extent of its cybersecurity compromise in public filings, describing cyber risks as generic or hypothetical despite knowing actual incidents had occurred.

Key details of each settlement:
- **Unisys**: Filed 10-K reports for FY2020-2021 describing intrusions in hypothetical terms despite knowing of actual unauthorized access and data exfiltration. Also failed to maintain effective disclosure controls (cybersecurity personnel did not report findings to disclosure decision-makers for a year). Penalty: $4,000,000.
- **Mimecast**: Filed multiple Forms 8-K in early 2021 disclosing some details of the compromise but negligently omitting material aspects, including the large number of impacted customers and the percentage of exfiltrated code. Penalty: $990,000.
- **Check Point**: Disclosures in its 2021 and 2022 Forms 20-F were found to be generic and not tailored to the company's specific cybersecurity risks post-incident, framing intrusions as not material despite a nation-state actor being present unmonitored in its network. Penalty: $995,000.
- **Avaya**: Negligently made materially misleading statements in its 10-Q filed February 9, 2021, omitting facts about the threat actor's access to at least 145 shared files containing confidential information, the likely nation-state attribution, and the long-term unmonitored presence of the actor. Also stated there was "no current evidence" of access to other internal systems despite contrary knowledge. Penalty: $1,000,000.

The SEC found violations of Section 17(a)(2) and 17(a)(3) of the Securities Act, Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act, and Rule 12b-20, among others. The actions are notable because they demonstrate the SEC's position that: (1) risk disclosures are misleading if generic and not tailored to a company's actual risks even when they acknowledge routine targeting; and (2) the SEC will scrutinize materiality determinations and the level of detail in incident disclosures.

Commissioners Hester M. Peirce and Mark T. Uyeda issued a dissenting opinion, arguing that the identity of threat actors and many omitted details would not be material to reasonable investors, that filings read as a whole should not be deemed misleading if they capture the big picture, and that aggressive enforcement may cause companies to over-disclose immaterial events. The final takeaway emphasizes that the SEC expects firms to tailor cyber disclosures to their own particular risks and incidents, and not to minimize material cybersecurity breaches.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In general, the SEC found these companies' cyber disclosures to be generic or hypothetical, and thus misleading in light of the facts in these cases."
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On Oct. 22, 2024, the SEC announced settled charges against four public companies — Unisys, Avaya Holdings, Check Point Software Technologies, and Mimecast — for allegedly making materially misleading statements in their public disclosures regarding cybersecurity intrusions and risks following the SolarWinds software hack. The SEC alleged the settling issuers each "negligently minimized its [SolarWinds] cybersecurity incident," leaving "investors in the dark about the true scope of the incidents." Charges were brought under Sections 17(a)(2) and 17(a)(3) of the Securities Act of 1933, Section 13(a) of the Exchange Act, and Exchange Act Rule 12b-20, among other provisions.

**Individual Settlements:**
- **Unisys**: Paid $4 million; its 2020 and 2021 Form 10-K annual reports were allegedly materially misleading because the company described cyber risks as hypothetical possibilities when it knew of actual SolarWinds-related intrusions (unauthorized cloud/mailbox access and exfiltration of gigabytes of data). Also charged with deficient disclosure controls under Rule 13a-15(a).
- **Avaya Holdings**: Paid $1 million; its 2021 Form 10-Q negligently omitted material information, including likely attribution to a nation-state threat actor, long-term unmonitored presence in systems, access to at least 145 shared files with confidential/proprietary information, and that the accessed mailbox belonged to Avaya's own cybersecurity personnel.
- **Check Point Software**: Paid $995,000; its 2020 and 2021 Forms 20-F failed to update cyber risk disclosures despite known prolonged intrusions, increased cyber risks, and inability to fully scope incident impact. Disclosures were found too generic and not tailored to actual risks.
- **Mimecast**: Paid $990,000; three Form 8-Ks filed in January and March 2021 negligently minimized the attack by omitting that a majority of source code for three important functions was exfiltrated and that thousands of customers were impacted.

**Dissenting Opinion:** Commissioners Hester M. Peirce and Mark T. Uyeda dissented, accusing the SEC of "playing Monday morning quarterback" and engaging in a "hindsight review," arguing the SEC ignored the "reasonable investor standard" for materiality and that the settlements could encourage companies to over-disclose immaterial incident details (such as threat actor identity) under Item 1.05(a) of Form 8-K.

**Implications:** These orders offer rare guidance on what the SEC considers inadequate or materially misleading cyber disclosures. Key takeaways include: (1) once a company discloses an issue, the SEC may scrutinize omitted information (importance of impacted systems, duration of unauthorized access, assessment limitations, affected customer counts); (2) the SEC continues to focus on disclosure controls and procedures ensuring information flows from cyber professionals to senior management; (3) companies must update existing risk disclosures after an incident rather than continuing to describe risks as hypothetical. The SEC noted the impact was material for each company because they provide services dependent on safeguarding company or customer data. Prior related enforcement actions include penalties against R.R. Donnelley ($2.125M), Blackbaud ($3M), Pearson ($1M), and First American Financial ($487,616), and the SEC v. SolarWinds Corp. case (S.D.N.Y. July 2024).
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The settling issuers each 'negligently minimized its [SolarWinds] cybersecurity incident,' which served to 'further victimize their shareholders or other members of the investing public' and left 'investors in the dark about the true scope of the incidents.'"

URL: https://www.fenwick.com/insights/publications/the-sec-is-cracking-down-on-misleading-cybersecurity-disclosure

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On October 22, 2024, the SEC charged four companies—Unisys Corp., Check Point Software Technologies, Mimecast Limited, and Avaya Holdings Corp.—with making materially misleading statements about cybersecurity risks and attacks. The charges stemmed from an investigation into public companies affected by the SolarWinds Orion software compromise and related activity. This followed the SEC's landmark lawsuit against SolarWinds, the first civil fraud claim against a public company victimized by a cyberattack, though a federal judge partially dismissed that case in July 2024.

Each company learned between 2020 and 2021 that a threat actor linked to the SolarWinds hack had accessed their systems without authorization but negligently minimized the incidents in their SEC filings. All four were charged with violating the Securities Act of 1933, the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and related rules.

Key details of each order:
- **Unisys**: Made materially misleading cybersecurity risk disclosures in 10-K filings for fiscal years 2020 and 2021, describing intrusions in hypothetical terms despite knowing its systems had been compromised over at least 16 months starting January 2020. Failed to maintain adequate disclosure controls, with personnel not reporting incidents to decision makers for up to a year. Penalty: $4 million.
- **Check Point**: Framed cybersecurity risks generically in 20-F filings (April 2021 and 2022), omitting material risks from breaches occurring July–October 2020. Penalty: $995,000.
- **Mimecast**: Filed three Form 8-Ks in January and March 2021 disclosing a compromise but omitted material aspects including the large number of impacted customers (a majority) and the percentage/significance of code exfiltrated. Notably, the 2023 Cybersecurity Rule's Form 8-K requirements did not apply at the time. Penalty: $990,000.
- **Avaya**: Made misleading statements regarding a cyber incident as early as January 2020, stating a threat actor accessed a "limited number" of emails while knowing the hacker also accessed at least 145 files in its cloud file sharing environment. A February 2021 Form 10-Q minimized the compromise. Penalty: $1 million.

**The Dissent**: SEC Commissioners Pierce and Uyeda strongly dissented, criticizing the Commission for "a hindsight review to second-guess the disclosure and cit[ing] immaterial, undisclosed details to support its charges." They warned the actions could cause companies to fill disclosures with immaterial details or disclose immaterial incidents, potentially diverting investor attention and causing mispricing.

**Takeaways for Companies**: The SEC is aggressively focused on cybersecurity disclosures. Companies should avoid rushing to disclose, take time to thoroughly analyze incident scope and impacts, and prepare accurate, transparent disclosures if an incident is material. Item 1.05 of Form 8-K allows four days from the determination of materiality (not discovery) to disclose. Companies should ensure sufficient disclosure controls, escalation procedures, and consult experienced counsel, including considering both quantitative and qualitative factors in materiality assessments.

"As today's enforcement actions reflect, while public companies may become targets of cyberattacks, it is incumbent upon them to not further victimize their shareholders or other members of the investing public by providing misleading disclosures about the cybersecurity incidents they have encountered," said Sanjay Wadhwa, Acting Director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement.

--- SOURCE 1: OFAC Updates Ransomware Advisory and Sanctions ... ---
URL: https://www.clearytradewatch.com/2021/09/ofac-updates-ransomware-advisory-and-sanctions-virtual-currency-exchange

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) took two significant actions: (1) issued an updated advisory on sanctions risks for facilitating ransomware payments, and (2) designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (SUEX), a virtual currency exchange, to the Specially Denominated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List for facilitating financial transactions for ransomware actors. These actions highlight the U.S. government's intensified focus on virtual currencies as a means of facilitating ransomware payments and money laundering.

The updated advisory shifted language from "does not encourage" to "strongly discourages" payment of cyber ransoms. OFAC identified two "significant mitigating factors" in determining enforcement actions and penalty amounts for sanctions violations tied to ransomware payments (including self-reporting, which increases the likelihood of a non-public response such as a No Action Letter or Cautionary Letter).

SUEX, reported to be a Czech-registered and Russian-owned company, was the first virtual currency exchange designated under Executive Order 13694, with over 40% of its known transaction history associated with illicit actors. SUEX operates as a "nested" exchange, accepting customers via intermediaries and trading through larger exchanges. The designation blocks all U.S.-jurisdiction property of SUEX and entities 50%+ owned by it, and prohibits U.S. persons from transacting with it, while non-U.S. persons face secondary sanctions risk for material support.

The advisory recommends that companies, particularly in the virtual currency space, enhance due diligence procedures—paying attention to peer-to-peer exchangers, mixers, tumblers, and similar illicit-facilitating services—and warns U.S. persons with hosted wallets to consider risks of future asset restrictions if custodial entities are designated. Additional designations and enforcement actions are expected as more ransomware information becomes available.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
These actions demonstrate the U.S. government's increasing focus on virtual currencies as a key means of facilitating ransomware payments and related money laundering, as well as OFAC's commitment to combating ransomware attacks and other malicious cyber activities.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:

"Ransomware groups and criminal organizations have targeted American businesses and public institutions of all sizes and across sectors, seeking to undermine the backbone of our economy," said Deputy Secretary of the Treasury Wally Adeyemo. This WilmerHale client alert discusses OFAC's first-ever sanctions against a Russian-operated virtual currency exchange involved in ransomware payments, announced on September 21, 2021. Key developments include:

**New Sanctions & Updated Advisory:**

URL: https://www.carpedatumlaw.com/2021/09/ofac-issues-a-new-advisory-memo-on-potential-sanctions-risk-for-facilitating-ransomware-payments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the US Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an updated advisory memo on potential sanctions risks associated with facilitating ransomware payments. The memo strongly discourages companies (including financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and digital forensics/incident response companies) from facilitating ransom payments to cyber actors, warning that such facilitation "encourages future ransomware payment demands" and may violate OFAC regulations. The advisory was issued amid increased Biden Administration regulatory activity and followed OFAC's designation and sanctioning of SUEX OTC, S.R.O for facilitating financial transactions for ransomware actors involving proceeds from at least eight ransomware variants.

Key points from the memo include: (1) While paying a ransom is not illegal per se, payments made to sanctioned parties (SDNs) or comprehensively embargoed jurisdictions may result in civil penalties under a strict liability standard; (2) OFAC encourages risk-based sanctions compliance programs, noting that the existence and adequacy of such programs is a mitigating factor in enforcement actions; (3) OFAC strongly encourages victims to report ransomware incidents to CISA, their local FBI field office, the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, local U.S. Secret Service offices, and Treasury's OCCIP, with such reporting considered a potentially significant mitigating factor; (4) The memo references the CISA September 2020 Ransomware Guide, which outlines preventive steps including maintaining offline encrypted backups, developing incident response plans, cybersecurity training, regularly updating antivirus/anti-malware software, and employing authentication protocols.

The article's conclusion emphasizes that while the substance of the memo is not entirely new, its tone signals a "we mean business" attitude. The most critical takeaway for companies is the recommendation to maintain offline, encrypted, regularly tested data backups, since many ransomware variants attempt to find and delete accessible backups, and having offline backups eliminates the need to pay ransom for data that is readily accessible. The article is by Seyfarth Shaw's Carpe Datum Law (DATA Law) practice, which specializes in eDiscovery, data privacy, and cybersecurity.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Companies that facilitate ransomware payments to cyber actors on behalf of victims, including financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and companies involved in digital forensics and incident response, not only encourage future ransomware payment demands but also may risk violating OFAC regulations. The U.S. government strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands and recommends focusing on strengthening defensive and resilience measures to prevent and protect against ransomware attacks.", "Facilitating a ransomware payment that is demanded as a result of malicious cyber activities may enable criminals and adversaries with a sanctions nexus to profit and advance their illicit aims...Moreover, there is no guarantee that companies will regain access to their data or be free from further attacks themselves.", "under OFAC's enforcement guidelines, the existence, nature and adequacy of a sanctions compliance program is a factor that OFAC may consider when determining an appropriate enforcement response to an apparent violation of the US Sanctions laws or regulations.", "OFAC strongly encourages all victims and those involved with addressing ransomware attacks to report the incident to CISA, their local FBI field office, the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center, or their local U.S. Secret Service office as soon as possible...in doing so victims can receive significant mitigation from OFAC when determining an appropriate enforcement response in the event a sanctions nexus is found in connection with a ransomware payment.", "It is critical to maintain offline, encrypted backups of data and to regularly test your backups...Maintaining offline, current backups is most critical because there is no need to pay a ransom for data that is readily accessible to your organization."

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an updated advisory on the sanctions risks associated with ransomware payments. The advisory warns that companies facilitating ransomware payments on behalf of victims—including financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and digital forensics/incident response companies—may risk violating OFAC regulations and encourages strengthening defensive measures instead. The advisory urges victims to report incidents to CISA, the FBI, the U.S. Secret Service, and Treasury's OCCIP, and to contact OFAC if there is any reason to suspect a sanctions nexus. --- SOURCE 7: OFAC Issues Updated Guidance on Ransomware Payments ---
URL: https://www.insideprivacy.com/cybersecurity-2/ofac-issues-updated-guidance-on-ransomware-payments

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On September 21, 2021, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued an "Updated Advisory on Potential Sanctions Risks for Facilitating Ransomware Payments," which supersedes an earlier advisory from October 1, 2020. The Updated Advisory is directed at not only organizations victimized by ransomware attacks but also financial institutions, cyber insurance firms, and forensic and incident-response firms that assist victims.

Key points of the Updated Advisory include:

- **Continued Opposition to Ransomware Payments**: OFAC maintains that the U.S. government "strongly discourages all private companies and citizens from paying ransom or extortion demands" and recommends focusing on defensive and resilience measures. Payments may violate U.S. sanctions prohibitions, and penalties may be imposed on a strict liability basis, meaning companies could face enforcement even if they didn't know a payment would violate sanctions.

- **New Mitigating Factors**: The Updated Advisory identifies two significant mitigating factors in any OFAC enforcement response:
  1. **Strong Cybersecurity Practices**: Meaningful steps taken to reduce extortion risk through adopting or improving cybersecurity practices, such as those in CISA's September 2020 Ransomware Guide (co-developed with MS-ISAC), will be considered a "significant mitigating factor."
  2. **Notification and Cooperation with U.S. Government**: Promptly reporting ransomware attacks to law enforcement, CISA, Treasury's Office of Cybersecurity and Critical Infrastructure Protection (OCCIP), or other relevant agencies, along with ongoing cooperation (including providing technical details, ransom payment demands, and payment instructions), constitutes a "significant mitigating factor." Timely self-disclosure to these agencies may be considered a voluntary self-disclosure for mitigation purposes.

- **First-Ever Sanctions Designation of a Cryptocurrency Exchange**: Also on September 21, 2021, OFAC designated SUEX OTC, S.R.O. (also known as "Successful Exchange"), a Russian cryptocurrency exchange, for property-blocking sanctions pursuant to Executive Order 13694 (as amended by EO 13757). OFAC alleged SUEX OTC facilitated numerous ransomware payments for malicious cyber actors. U.S. persons are now prohibited from engaging in virtually all transactions with SUEX OTC. The exchange was identified on the SDN List by name, address, and digital currency addresses in Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Tether. OFAC had previously designated other parties by digital currency address in 2018 (two Iranian individuals in the SamSam ransomware scheme).

- **Anticipated Further Guidance**: Press reporting indicates further related guidance may be forthcoming, likely from FinCEN, including action on the proposed application of the travel rule to cryptocurrency transactions and additional anti-money laundering efforts. This aligns with FinCEN's October 1, 2020 advisory (issued in parallel with the 2020 OFAC Advisory) on "red flags" for suspicious ransomware transactions, which noted that consultants facilitating ransomware payments could be considered "money transmitters" under the Bank Secrecy Act.

The article was authored by Covington & Burling LLP attorneys Ashden Fein, Peter Flanagan, Jim Garland, Mike Nonaka, and Moriah Daugherty. This phishing email launched malware on the laptop. When the employee reconnected to the network, cybercriminals used the malware to target the entire organization. On October 28, 2020, the attack was launched, spreading malware across the organization's systems. The IT department detected the issue, shut down computer and phone systems, and found a text file from the attackers demanding contact. UVM Health Network refused to pay, contacted the FBI, and Vermont Gov. Phil Scott deployed the National Guard to assist. No sensitive data (patient records or employee info) was stolen or exposed, and the organization recovered most data from backup copies.

**The Impact:** The attack cost an estimated $63 million, including rebuilding 1,300 damaged servers, restoring 600 disabled applications, scanning and cleaning 5,000 malware-ridden computers, and lost revenue of nearly $1.5 million per day. The organization's cyber insurance coverage was only $30 million—far below actual costs. The attack caused reputational damage, delayed patient care (delayed test results, appointment cancellations, rescheduled elective procedures), and pushed back the rollout of an updated electronic health record system (phases 2 and 3 delayed to November 2021 and April 2022, respectively).

**Key Lessons Learned:**
1. Employee education is critical—up to 90% of cyberattacks stem from human error; phishing detection training is essential.
2. Effective security software is necessary—including network-monitoring systems, antivirus programs, firewalls, endpoint-detection products, patch-management tools, and routine penetration testing.
3. Cyber incident response plans make a difference—UVM's lengthy recovery highlighted the need for timely response protocols, including potential attack scenarios, methods for maintaining operations, and designated responsibilities.
4. Ransomware attacks carry unique ramifications—not paying can extend recovery time, but contacting law enforcement (FBI) and working with insurance partners is vital.
5. Proper insurance coverage is crucial—no organization is immune, and policy limits should be carefully selected with professional guidance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"In October 2020, the University of Vermont (UVM) Health Network—a six-hospital health care organization that serves over 1 million patients throughout Vermont and upstate New York—discovered that its systems had been compromised by cybercriminals in a ransomware attack."

URL: https://westoahu.hawaii.edu/cyber/ics-cybersecurity/ics-weekly-summaries/ransomware-attack-on-the-university-of-vermont-health-network

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, written by Edgar Namoca on March 4, 2021, analyzes the ransomware attack on the University of Vermont (UVM) Health Network. The attack was noticed on October 28, 2020, when UVM medical center employees experienced problems with patient care applications; a ransom note was discovered after investigation, though it did not state an amount but requested contact with adversaries—which UVM declined. On November 24, 2020, the National Guard cybersecurity unit was deployed to accelerate recovery, and with their assistance plus other government agencies, UVM restored 80% of the medical center's applications and functions. No patient personal data was stolen due to strong data protection and storage practices.

TECHNICAL: The attack used Ryuk ransomware, which is preceded by the TrickBot malware delivered via fake Microsoft documents with embedded macros. TrickBot provides backdoor access, allowing adversaries to pivot through the network and identify critical infrastructure before deploying Ryuk. Ryuk removes shadow files and backups before encrypting all files using RSA and AES encryption methods.

IMPACT: The attack resulted in 5,000 hospital laptops/computers and 1,300 servers being encrypted. UVM was forced to wipe all affected devices and reinstall software. As of December 8, 2020, UVM Medical Center President stated they were losing $1.5 million per day in revenue and extra expenses, totaling more than $63 million in losses. 300 employees were furloughed during the outage.

IMPORTANCE: In 2020, the health and public health (HPH) sector was the biggest target for cybercrime. On October 28, 2020, CISA, the FBI, and HHS released an alert on adversary tools and techniques targeting healthcare, following breaches at UVM and Universal Health Services (UHS). Both attacks involved TrickBot or BazarLoader, malware created by the advanced persistent threat group (APT) UNC1878.

CONCLUSION: The author emphasizes that the HPH sector has become the number one target for adversaries, with the COVID-19 pandemic expanding the attack surface through remote work. The author argues for reassessing critical infrastructure vulnerabilities, restricting access to only critical operations, and developing better, updated cyber threat response plans going into 2021 to reduce response time and improve decision-making during attacks.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: NYDFS Releases Consent Order in First Enforcement Action ... ---
URL: https://www.alstonprivacy.com/nydfs-releases-consent-order-in-first-enforcement-action-brought-under-the-cybersecurity-regulations

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Alston & Bird Privacy, Cyber & Data Strategy Blog reports on the first enforcement action brought by the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) under its Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500). After a three-year investigation, NYDFS entered into a Consent Order with a large title insurer (referred to as "the Company") for violations of the Regulation, specifically its failure to protect non-public information (NPI).

The enforcement action was originally brought in July 2020, and the SEC conducted a separate investigation and enforcement that concluded in 2021. Although the initial statement of charges alleged numerous violations, the consent order reduced these to two violations related to the Company's failure to maintain reasonable access privileges and insufficient policies and practices around access controls.

**Alleged Regulation Violations:**
1. The Company failed to implement access controls sufficient to prevent unauthorized access to NPI through one of its applications, in violation of § 500.7. The application contained documents accessible via a link alone without login or authentication, and replacing the document ID in the URL with another sequential number could grant access to unrelated documents. These issues were identified in a December 2018 vulnerability assessment but remained unaddressed until a journalist discovered and published the vulnerability in May 2019.
2. The Company failed to adequately maintain and implement an effective cybersecurity policy related to access controls, in violation of §§ 500.3(b), (d), and (m). While the Company had many policies in place, it did not ensure complete implementation, including a risk assessment that incorrectly classified an application as not containing NPI when it actually housed documents with NPI.

**Settlement Provisions:**
The Company agreed to a $1 million penalty, which reflected its cooperation during the investigation. The Company also submitted a Remediation Overview and Compliance Summary to NYDFS for approval, detailing its efforts to address the violations and enhance its cybersecurity program.

The article notes this is consistent with NYDFS's recent amendments to the Regulation, which emphasize operationalizing cybersecurity policies through procedures developed, documented, and implemented in accordance with written policies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"NYDFS found that the Company failed to implement access controls sufficient to prevent unauthorized users to gain access to NPI through one of the Company's applications in violation of § 500.7."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 2: NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500) - Rapid7 ---
URL: https://www.rapid7.com/fundamentals/nydfs-cybersecurity-regulation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Rapid7 is a comprehensive compliance guide to the NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), which sets cybersecurity standards for financial services firms in New York. The regulation requires New York insurance companies, banks, and other regulated financial services institutions—including agencies and branches of non-US banks licensed in New York—to assess their cybersecurity risk profiles and implement comprehensive cybersecurity programs.

Key facts:
- The regulation went into effect on March 1, 2017, with initial implementation required within 180 days (by August 28, 2017). The first Certification of Compliance was due by February 15, 2018.
- Covered entities must establish an effective cybersecurity program, create written cybersecurity policies, designate a Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), hire qualified cybersecurity personnel (or use third-party providers), and establish an incident response plan.
- Regulatory minimum standards include: risk-based standards for IT systems (data protection, encryption, access controls, penetration testing), adequately funded programs overseen by a CISO, effective incident response plans with timely NYDFS notification of material events, and annual compliance certifications.
- Covered entities include licensed lenders, state-chartered banks, trust companies, service contract providers, private bankers, mortgage companies, insurance companies in New York, and non-US banks licensed in New York.
- Exemptions apply to organizations with fewer than 10 employees, less than $5 million in gross annual revenue for three years, or less than $10 million in year-end total assets, though even exempt organizations may need to evaluate third-party risk management practices.

Key compliance milestones:
- March 1, 2017: Effective date of the final regulation
- August 28, 2017 (180-day mark): Compliance required with Sections 500.02, 500.03, 500.04, 500.10, and 500.16
- February 15, 2018: First Certification of Compliance due under Section 500.17(b)
- March 1, 2018 (one-year mark): CISO cybersecurity report (500.04b), penetration testing and vulnerability management (500.05), and bi-annual risk assessments (500.09) required
- September 3, 2018 (1.5-year mark): Audit trail maintenance (500.06) and application security protocols (500.08) required

Changes in the final regulation from earlier proposals include: audit trail data retention reduced from five to three years, clarified third-party service provider notice requirements, clarification on when cybersecurity event notice must be provided to NYDFS, expanded exemptions considering affiliates' revenue and employees, and clarified exemption rules for insurance companies.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation requires New York insurance companies, banks, and other regulated financial services institutions—including agencies and branches of non-US banks licensed in the state of New York—to assess their cybersecurity risk profile."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 3: A Guide to the NYDFS NYCRR 500 Cybersecurity Regulation + ... ---
URL: https://secureframe.com/blog/nydfs-nycrr-500

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from Secureframe provides a comprehensive guide to the NYDFS NYCRR 500 Cybersecurity Regulation and a compliance checklist for 2024. The regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500), first issued in March 2017, establishes cybersecurity requirements for all covered financial institutions in New York. Significant amendments were announced in November 2023 with an effective date of April 29, 2024.

**Who Must Comply:** NYDFS NYCRR 500 applies to all DFS-regulated entities including state-chartered banks, credit unions, mortgage companies, insurance companies, health insurers, money transmitters, and other financial services institutions. The regulation designates three company types:
- **Covered entities:** All DFS-regulated organizations
- **Class A companies:** Introduced in the 2023 amendments; entities with at least $20 million in gross annual revenue in each of the last two fiscal years AND either at least 2,000 employees (averaged over two years) or over $1 billion in gross annual revenue. These face additional obligations including independent audits and stronger monitoring.
- **Small businesses:** Qualify for limited exemption (Section 500.19) if combined affiliates have fewer than 20 employees, less than $7.5 million in annual gross revenue in each of the last three years, or less than $15 million in year-end total assets.

**Key Requirements:**
- Periodic risk assessments
- Cybersecurity program with policies including Information Security, Access Control, Business Continuity/Disaster Recovery, Incident Response (now requiring root cause analysis), Data Retention/Disposal, Third-Party Service Provider Security, Asset Inventory, and Vulnerability Management policies
- Appointment of qualified cybersecurity leadership (senior governing body and CISO)
- Technical controls: multi-factor authentication, encryption (compensating controls no longer allowed for encryption in transit over external networks), systems/network security, application security, physical/environmental controls, data privacy controls, and security awareness training
- Continuous monitoring with annual penetration testing (now required from both inside and outside systems) and bi-annual vulnerability assessments
- Audit trail systems with records kept minimum five years
- 72-hour notification to NYDFS of cybersecurity events reasonably likely to impact operations, plus new reporting of third-party incidents and extortion payments

**Certification:** Covered entities submit an annual Certificate of Compliance (typically April 15, pushed to April 29, 2024 this year). Class A companies must undergo annual independent compliance audits. Documentation must be kept for five years.

**Enforcement:** NYDFS monitors through self-certification, audits, and mandatory reporting. Historical penalties include Robinhood Crypto ($30 million), OneMain Financial Group ($4.25 million), Residential Mortgage Services ($1.5 million), SA Stone Wealth Management ($1.35 million), and First American Title Insurance Company ($1 million). The 2023 amendment reaffirmed that even a single act of non-compliance could constitute a violation.

The article also promotes Secureframe's compliance automation platform with features like AI-driven risk management, policy generation, continuous monitoring, vendor management, cross-mapping controls, regulatory change management, and security training.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The NYDFS NYCRR 500 regulation is a cornerstone for cybersecurity in the New York financial sector, establishing some of the highest standards for information security regulations in the US."
</key_excerpts>

--- SOURCE 4: NYDFS’ First Cybersecurity Enforcement Action - What Happened and Important Lessons for Organizations | Mintz ---
URL: https://www.mintz.com/insights-center/viewpoints/2826/2020-08-12-nydfs-first-cybersecurity-enforcement-action-what

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from Mintz law firm discusses the New York State Department of Financial Services' (NYDFS) first enforcement action under its Cybersecurity Regulation (Part 500 of Title 23) against First American Title Insurance Company, a leading title insurance provider.

**The Vulnerability:** From at least October 2014 through May 2019, a known vulnerability in First American's public-facing website exposed hundreds of millions of documents containing consumers' sensitive personal information (NPI), including bank account numbers and statements, mortgage and tax records, Social Security numbers, wire transaction receipts, and driver's license images. Anyone could access these documents without login or authentication by simply changing one or more digits in a website link (URL). More than 850 million documents were accessible to anyone with a URL providing access to a single document.

**NYDFS Allegations:** The Statement of Charges (filed July 2020) cites multiple failures in First American's handling of the exposure, including:
- Failure to follow internal policies and conduct security reviews/risk assessments
- Misclassification of the vulnerability as "low" severity despite the magnitude of exposure
- Failure to conduct a reasonable investigation (reviewing only 10 of millions of exposed documents after discovering the vulnerability via penetration test in December 2018)
- Failure to follow internal cybersecurity team recommendations

The vulnerability was publicly exposed by cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs on May 24, 2019. First American's own analysis showed that during the 11-month period following June 2018, more than 350,000 documents were accessed without authorization by automated "bots" or "scraper" programs.

**Alleged Regulatory Violations:** The Statement of Charges alleges violations of six specific sections of the Cybersecurity Regulation: 23 NYCRR 500.02 (risk assessments), 500.03 (data governance/classification), 500.07 (access controls), 500.09 (risk assessment informing cybersecurity program), 500.14(b) (employee cybersecurity training), and 500.15 (encryption of sensitive data).

**Penalties:** NYDFS seeks civil monetary penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, with each instance of NPI exposure constituting a separate violation — potentially leading to astronomical fines. A hearing was scheduled for October 26, 2020.

**Key Takeaways for Organizations:**
1. NYDFS is serious about enforcement — each violation carries penalties up to $1,000, and no specific consumer harm is required to trigger action
2. Don't let cybersecurity issues fall into a black hole — ensure thorough risk assessments, classification structures, and remediation procedures
3. Train employees and hold them accountable (First American's CISO disavowed ownership of certain cybersecurity issues)
4. Security measures must exist in practice, not just on paper — policies are meaningless if not implemented and followed
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"in other words, more than 850 million documents were accessible to anyone with a URL address providing access to a single document." — NYDFS Statement of Charges
</key_excerpts>

The New York State Department of Financial Services (DFS) filed its first cybersecurity enforcement action, a statement of charges against First American Title Insurance Company, for violating DFS's Cybersecurity Regulation (Part 500 of Title 23 of the NYCRR). DFS alleges First American—one of the largest US title insurance providers, which wrote over 50,000 policies in New York in 2019—exposed hundreds of millions of documents containing consumers' Nonpublic Information (including bank account numbers, mortgage and tax records, Social Security Numbers, wire transaction receipts, and drivers' license images) over several years. A vulnerability in First American's systems caused the exposure, and the company allegedly failed to remedy it promptly after discovering it in December 2018. DFS alleges First American violated six provisions of the Cybersecurity Regulation, with each instance of exposed Nonpublic Information constituting a separate violation carrying penalties of up to $1,000 each (per Section 408 of the Financial Services Law). The hearing was scheduled to begin October 26, 2020, at DFS offices on One State Street, New York. The Cybersecurity Regulation became effective in March 2017 (fully in effect by March 2019), was drafted with substantial industry input, and has served as a model for other regulators including the FTC, various states, and the NAIC. --- SOURCE 6: NYDFS Announces Cybersecurity Settlement, Addresses Multi-Factor Authentication Rules | Alston & Bird Privacy, Cyber & Data Strategy Blog ---
URL: https://www.alstonprivacy.com/nydfs-announces-cybersecurity-settlement-addresses-multi-factor-authentication-rules

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On April 14, 2021, the New York Department of Financial Services (NYDFS) announced a settlement with National Securities Corporation, a licensed insurer, under the NYDFS Cybersecurity Regulation (23 NYCRR Part 500). The consent order requires payment of a $3M civil monetary penalty—the largest published assessment to date for alleged violations of the Cybersecurity Regulation—plus mandatory remediation. The settlement stems from alleged failures to properly implement multi-factor authentication, failure to notify NYDFS of two cybersecurity events reported to other regulators in 2018 and 2019, and falsely certifying compliance for the 2018 calendar year.

The two cyber events involved threat actors accessing the email account of National Securities' Chief Financial Officer and accessing an employee's "secure document management system" associated with tax software. Although National Securities notified numerous regulators, NYDFS alleges it failed to receive proper notification. The company also certified compliance with the Cybersecurity Regulation on January 23, 2019, which NYDFS maintains was false.

Key issues addressed include NYDFS's interpretation of multi-factor authentication requirements under § 500.12(b). National Securities was faulted for failing to fully implement MFA (or maintain equivalent CISO-approved controls) for third-party cloud-based applications that accessed its internal network or contained consumer Nonpublic Information (NPI). The consent order raises the question of whether MFA is expected for all third-party cloud applications containing NPI, or only those that also access the licensee's internal network.

The consent order requires substantial remediation within 120 days, including: (1) a comprehensive written cybersecurity incident response plan, (2) a comprehensive Cybersecurity Risk Assessment, (3) risk-based policies, procedures and controls to monitor authorized user activity and detect unauthorized access to NPI, and (4) updated cybersecurity training materials for all personnel. National Securities must also provide "full cooperation" with NYDFS, though NYDFS acknowledged the company's "commendable cooperation" and significant financial resources devoted to enhancing cybersecurity.

This settlement follows a $1.5M assessment announced the previous month, and is the second order targeting undisclosed prior security incidents, as well as the first announced order to specifically fault a licensee for a false annual certification. It demonstrates NYDFS's continued active enforcement and interest in assessing past and current compliance.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The consent order demonstrates continued active enforcement of the Cybersecurity Regulation by the NYDFS. The $3M penalty is the largest published assessment to date for alleged violations of the Cybersecurity Regulation."
